Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Padarūpasiddhi

The Perfection of Word-Forms

Ganthārambha

Commencement of the Text

[Ka]

[Ka]

Visuddhasaddhammasahassadīdhitiṃ[M 0.0001],

Subuddhasambodhiyugandharoditaṃ;

Tibuddhakhettekadivākaraṃ jinaṃ,

Sadhammasaṅghaṃ sirasā’bhivandiya.

Having venerated with my head the Conqueror—the thousand-rayed radiance of the pure Good Dhamma, risen on the Yugandhara of perfect self-enlightenment, the one sun in the three Buddha-fields—together with the Dhamma and the Sangha.

[Kha]

[Kha]

Kaccāyanañcācariyaṃ namitvā,

Nissāya kaccāyanavaṇṇanādiṃ;

Bālappabodhatthamujuṃ karissaṃ,

Byattaṃ sukaṇḍaṃ padarūpasiddhiṃ.

Having paid homage to the teacher Kaccāyana, and relying on the Kaccāyana commentary and other works, I will compose the clear and well-sectioned Padarūpasiddhi in a straightforward way for the awakening of beginners.

1. Sandhikaṇḍa

1. The Chapter on Euphony

Tattha jinasāsanādhigamassa akkharakosallamūlakattā taṃ sampādetabbanti dassetuṃ abhidheyyappayojanavākyamidamuccate.

Therein, since skill in letters is the root for the attainment of the Conqueror's Dispensation, in order to show that this skill should be accomplished, this statement concerning the subject matter and purpose is uttered.

1. Attho akkharasaññāto.

1. Meaning is known through letters.

Yo koci lokiyalokuttarādibhedo vacanattho, so sabbo akkhareheva saññāyate. Sithiladhanitādiakkharavipattiyañhi atthassa dunnayatā hoti, tasmā [M 0.0002] akkharakosallaṃ bahūpakāraṃ buddhavacanesu, ettha padānipi akkharasannipātarūpattā akkharesveva saṅgayhanti.

Whatever meaning is to be expressed, whether of the mundane, supramundane, or other kinds, is all made known through letters. For when there is a defect in the letters—such as being unaspirated or aspirated, and so on—the meaning becomes difficult to grasp. Therefore, skill in letters is of great help in regard to the Buddha's words. Here, words too, since they are formed by an assemblage of letters, are included right under letters.

Tasmā akkharakosallaṃ, sampādeyya hitatthiko;

Upaṭṭhahaṃ garuṃ sammā, uṭṭhānādīhi pañcahi.

Therefore, one who seeks his own welfare should accomplish skill in letters, properly attending on a teacher with the five duties beginning with rising.

Saññāvidhāna

The Chapter on Terminology

Tatthādo tāva saddalakkhaṇe vohāraviññāpanatthaṃ saññāvidhānamārabhīyate.

Therein, to begin with, for the purpose of making known the conventional usage in the grammar of words, the chapter on terminology is commenced.

2. Akkharāpādayo ekacattālīsaṃ.

2. The letters, the primary ones, are forty-one.

Akkharā api ādayo ekacattālīsaṃ, te ca kho jinavacanānurūpā akārādayo niggahītantā ekacattālīsamattā vaṇṇā paccekaṃ akkharā nāma honti. Taṃ yathā – ā i ī u ū e o, ka kha ga gha ṅa, ca cha ja jha ña, ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa, ta tha da dha na, pa pha ba bha ma, ya ra lava sa ha ḷa aṃ-iti akkharā.

The letters, too, the primary ones, are forty-one. And those sounds, forty-one in number, from 'a' to the niggahīta, which are in conformity with the speech of the Conqueror, are each called a 'letter.' They are as follows: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, e, o, ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, ca, cha, ja, jha, ña, ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, ta, tha, da, dha, na, pa, pha, ba, bha, ma, ya, ra, la, va, sa, ha, ḷa, aṃ—these are the letters.

Nakkharantīti akkharā, a ādi yesaṃ te ādayo. Akārādīnamanukkamo panesa ṭhānādikkamasannissito, tathā hi ṭhānakaraṇappayatanehi vaṇṇā jāyante, tattha cha ṭhānāni kaṇṭhatālumuddhadantaoṭṭhanāsikāvasena.

They are called 'letters' (akkharā) because they are imperishable (na kharantīti). They are 'primary' (ādayo) because 'a' is their beginning. This sequence of letters beginning with 'a' is based on the order of place of articulation, etc. For sounds are produced by place, organ, and effort. Therein are six places: throat, palate, cerebrum, teeth, lips, and nose.

Tattha – avaṇṇa kavagga hakārā kaṇṭhajā.

Therein, the 'a'-sound, the k-group, and the letter 'h' are guttural.

Ivaṇṇa cavagga yakārā tālujā. Ṭavagga rakāra ḷakārā muddhajā. Tavagga lakāra sakārā dantajā. Uvaṇṇa pavaggā oṭṭhajā. Ekāro kaṇṭhatālujo. Okāro kaṇṭhoṭṭhajo.

The 'i'-sound, the c-group (c, ch, j, jh, ñ), and 'y' are palatal. The ṭ-group (ṭ, ṭh, ḍ, ḍh, ṇa), 'r', and 'ḷ' are cerebral. The t-group (t, th, d, dh, na), 'l', and 's' are dental. The 'u'-sound and the p-group (p, ph, b, bh, ma) are labial. 'E' is guttural-palatal. 'O' is guttural-labial.

Vakāro [M 0.0003] dantoṭṭhajo.

The letter 'v' is dento-labial.

Niggahītaṃ nāsikaṭṭhānajaṃ.

The niggahīta is produced from the nose.

Ṅa ña ṇa na mā sakaṭṭhānajā, nāsikaṭṭhānajā cāti.

Ṅa, ña, ṇa, na, and ma are produced from their own respective places and also from the nose.

Hakāraṃ pañcameheva, antaṭṭhāhi ca saṃyutaṃ;

Orasanti vadantettha, kaṇṭhajaṃ tadasaṃyutaṃ.

Some say that the letter 'h' when conjoined with the fifth letters of the groups and with the semi-vowels is pectoral (orasa). But the unconjoined 'h' is guttural.

Karaṇaṃ jivhāmajjhaṃ tālujānaṃ, jivhopaggaṃ muddhajānaṃ, jivhāggaṃ dantajānaṃ, sesā sakaṭṭhānakaraṇā.

For palatals, the organ of articulation is the middle of the tongue; for cerebrals, the part of the tongue near the root; for dentals, the tip of the tongue. For the remaining sounds, their own place of articulation is the organ.

Payatanaṃ saṃvutādikaraṇaviseso. Saṃvutattamakārassa, vivaṭattaṃ sesasarānaṃ sakārahakārānañca, phuṭṭhaṃ vaggānaṃ, īsaṃphuṭṭhaṃ yaralavānanti.

Effort (payatana) is a specific kind of action, such as 'closed.' The letter 'a' is closed; the remaining vowels and the letters 's' and 'h' are open; the plosives (vagga) are characterized by contact; and 'y,' 'r,' 'l,' and 'v' are characterized by slight contact.

Evaṃ ṭhānakaraṇappayatanasutikālabhinnesu akkharesu sarā nissayā, itare nissitā. Tattha –

Thus, among the letters differentiated by place, organ, effort, sound, and duration, the vowels are the support and the others are the supported. Therein—

Nissayādo sarā vuttā, byañjanā nissitā tato;

Vaggekajā bahuttādo, tato ṭhānalahukkamā.

The vowels are stated first because they are the support; then the consonants, which are supported. Then come the grouped consonants because of their multiplicity, then the single ones; after that, the order is by lightness of place.

Vuttañca –

And it is said:

“Pañcannaṃ pana ṭhānānaṃ, paṭipāṭivasāpi ca;

Nissayādippabhedehi, vutto tesamanukkamo”ti.

And also by the sequence of the five places, and by distinctions such as being the support, their order is stated.

Ekenādhikā cattālīsaṃ ekacattālīsaṃ, etena gaṇanaparicchedena –

Forty plus one is forty-one. By this numerical determination—

Adhikakkharavantāni, ekatālīsato ito;

Na buddhavacanānīti, dīpetācariyāsabho.

That which has more letters than these forty-one is not the word of the Buddha—so declares the pre-eminent teacher.

Apiggahaṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttānaṃ apekkhākaraṇatthaṃ.

The inclusion of `api` is for the purpose of creating a connection with what has been stated before.

3. Tatthodantā [M 0.0004] sarā aṭṭha.

3. Therein, the eight vowels end with 'o'.

Tattha tesu akkharesu akārādīsu okārantā aṭṭha akkharā sarā nāma honti. Taṃ yathā – a ā i ī u ū e o-iti sarā.

Therein, among those letters, the eight letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'o' are called vowels. They are as follows: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, e, o—these are the vowels.

O anto yesaṃ te odantā, dakāro sandhijo, saranti gacchantīti sarā, byañjane sārentītipi sarā.

Those that have 'o' as their end are `odantā`; the letter 'd' is born of sandhi. They are called 'vowels' (`sarā`) because they move or go (`saranti`); or because they cause the consonants to sound (`sārenti`).

“Tatthā”ti vattate.

The word `tattha` is carried forward.

4. Lahumattā tayo rassā.

4. Three of light measure are short.

Tattha aṭṭhasu saresu lahumattā tayo sarā rassā nāma honti. Taṃ yathā – a i u-iti rassā.

Therein, among the eight vowels, three vowels of light measure are called short. They are as follows: a, i, u—these are the short vowels.

Lahukā mattā pamāṇaṃ yesaṃ te lahumattā, mattāsaddo cettha accharāsaṅghātaakkhinimīlanasaṅkhātaṃ kālaṃ vadati, tāya mattāya ekamattā rassā, dvimattā dīghā, aḍḍhamattā byañjanā. Lahuggahaṇañcettha chandasi diyaḍḍhamattassāpi gahaṇatthaṃ. Rassakālayogato rassā, rassakālavanto vā rassā.

Those whose measure is light are `lahumattā`. Here the word `mattā` (measure) denotes the time taken for a finger-snap or the blink of an eye. By that measure, a short vowel has one `mattā`, a long vowel has two `mattā`, and a consonant has half a `mattā`. The inclusion of `lahu` is for the purpose of also including, in prosody, that which has one and a half `mattā`. They are called `rassā` (short) because of their connection with a short time, or because they possess a short time.

Sararassaggahaṇāni ca vattante.

The terms `sara` (vowel) and `rassa` (short) are also carried forward.

5. Aññe dīghā.

5. The others are long.

Tattha aṭṭhasu saresu rassehi aññe dvimattā pañca sarā dīghā nāma honti. Taṃ yathā – ā ī ū e o-iti dīghā.

Therein, among the eight vowels, the five vowels other than the short ones, which have two morae, are called long. They are as follows: ā, ī, ū, e, o—these are the long vowels.

Aññaggahaṇaṃ diyaḍḍhamattikānampi saṅgahaṇatthaṃ. Dīghakāle niyuttā, tabbanto vā dīghā. Kvaci saṃyogapubbā ekārokārā rassā iva vuccante. Yathā – ettha, seyyo, oṭṭho, sotthi. Kvacīti kiṃ? Maṃ ce tvaṃ nikhaṇaṃ vane. Putto tyāhaṃ mahārāja.

The inclusion of `aññe` (other) is for the purpose of including also those with one and a half morae. They are called `dīghā` (long) because they are employed for a long time, or because they possess a long time. Sometimes, 'e' and 'o' preceded by a consonant cluster are pronounced as if short, for example: `ettha`, `seyyo`, `oṭṭho`, `sotthi`. Why 'sometimes'? To show it is not always the case, as in: `Maṃ ce tvaṃ nikhaṇaṃ vane` and `Putto tyāhaṃ mahārāja`.

6. Dumhi [M 0.0005] garu.

6. Before a pair, a short vowel is heavy.

Dvinnaṃ samūho du, tasmiṃ dumhi. Saṃyogabhūte akkhare pare yo pubbo rassakkharo, so garusañño hoti. Yathā – datvā, hitvā, bhutvā.

`Du` is a collection of two; hence `dumhi`. When a consonant cluster follows, the preceding short letter is designated 'heavy' (`garu`). For example: `datvā`, `hitvā`, `bhutvā`.

“Garū”ti vattate.

The word `garu` is carried forward.

7. Dīgho ca.

7. And a long vowel.

Dīgho ca saro garusañño hoti. Yathā – nāvā, nadī, vadhū, dve, tayo. Garukato añño “lahuko”ti veditabbo.

A long vowel is also designated 'heavy.' For example: `nāvā`, `nadī`, `vadhū`, `dve`, `tayo`. What is other than heavy should be known as 'light' (`lahuko`).

8. Sesā byañjanā.

8. The remaining are consonants.

Ṭhapetvā aṭṭha sare sesā aḍḍhamattā akkharā kakārādayo niggahītantā tettiṃsa byañjanā nāma honti. Vuttehi aññe sesā. Byañjīyati etehi atthoti byañjanā. Taṃ yathā – ka kha ga gha ṅa, ca cha ja jha ña, ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa, ta tha da dha na, pa pha ba bha ma, ya ra lava sa ha ḷa aṃ-iti byañjanā. Kakārādīsvakāro uccāraṇattho.

Setting aside the eight vowels, the remaining thirty-three letters of half a mora, from 'k' to the `niggahīta`, are called consonants. 'Remaining' means other than those already mentioned. They are called 'consonants' (`byañjanā`) because meaning is manifested by them. They are as follows: ka kha ga gha ṅa, ca cha ja jha ña, ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa, ta tha da dha na, pa pha ba bha ma, ya ra la va sa ha ḷa aṃ—these are the consonants. In 'k' and the other consonants, the 'a' is for the purpose of pronunciation.

“Byañjanā”ti vattate.

The word `byañjanā` is carried forward.

9. Vaggā pañcapañcaso mantā.

9. The groups are in fives and end in 'm'.

Tesaṃ kho byañjanānaṃ kakārādayo makārantā pañcavīsati byañjanā pañcapañcavibhāgena vaggā nāma honti. Taṃ yathā – ka kha ga gha ṅa, ca cha ja jha ña, ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa, ta tha da dha na, pa pha ba bha ma-iti vaggā.

Indeed, among those consonants, the twenty-five consonants from 'k' to 'm', by a division into five each, are called 'groups' (`vaggā`). They are as follows: ka kha ga gha ṅa, ca cha ja jha ña, ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa, ta tha da dha na, pa pha ba bha ma—these are the groups.

Te pana paṭhamakkharavasena kavaggacavaggādivohāraṃ gatā, vaggoti samūho, tattha pañcapañcavibhāgenāti vā pañca pañca etesamatthīti [M 0.0006] vā pañcapañcaso, mo anto yesaṃ te mantā.

They, however, have acquired designations such as 'k-group' and 'c-group' based on their first letter. `Vagga` means a group. `Pañcapañcaso` means 'by a division into five each' or 'they have five each.' `Mantā` are those that have 'm' as their end.

10. Aṃiti niggahītaṃ.

10. The sound `aṃ` is the `niggahīta`.

Akāro uccāraṇattho, itisaddo panānantaravuttanidassanattho, aṃiti yaṃ akārato paraṃ vuttaṃ bindu, taṃ niggahītaṃ nāma hoti. Rassassaraṃ nissāya gayhati, karaṇaṃ niggahetvā gayhatīti vā niggahītaṃ.

The 'a' is for the purpose of pronunciation; the word `iti`, however, serves to point out what has just been stated. The dot (`bindu`) that is pronounced after 'a' as `aṃ` is called `niggahīta`. It is produced depending on a short vowel; or it is called `niggahīta` because it is produced by restraining the organ of articulation.

Karaṇaṃ niggahetvāna, mukhenāvivaṭena yaṃ;

Vuccate niggahītanti, vuttaṃ bindu sarānugaṃ.

That which is uttered with the mouth not open, after having restrained the organ of articulation, is called `niggahīta`; it is said to be a dot that follows a vowel.

Idha avuttānaṃ parasamaññānampi payojane sati gahaṇatthaṃ paribhāsamāha.

Here, for the purpose of adopting other terminologies not stated, when there is a need, he states a general rule:

11. Parasamaññā payoge.

11. Other terminologies [are to be accepted] in usage.

Yā ca pana parasmiṃ sakkataganthe, paresaṃ vā veyyākaraṇānaṃ samaññā ghosāghosalopasavaṇṇasaṃyogaliṅgādikā, tā payoge sati etthāpi yujjante.

And whatever terminology is found in another Sanskrit text, or belongs to other grammarians—such as voiced, unvoiced, elision, homogeneous letter, consonant cluster, gender, and so on—that too is applicable here when there is occasion for its use.

Parasmiṃ, paresaṃ vā samaññā parasamaññā, veyyākaraṇe, veyyākaraṇamadhītānaṃ vā samaññātyattho. Payujjanaṃ payogo, viniyogo.

Parasamaññā means the terminology in another text or of other grammarians; that is, the terminology in another grammar or of those who have studied grammar. Prayoga means application or employment.

Tattha vaggānaṃ paṭhamadutiyā, sakāro ca aghosā. Vaggānaṃ tatiyacatutthapañcamā, ya ra lava ha ḷā cāti ekavīsati ghosā nāma.

Therein, the first and second letters of the groups and 's' are unvoiced. The third, fourth, and fifth letters of the groups, and y, r, l, v, h, and ḷ—these twenty-one are called voiced.

Ettha ca vaggānaṃ dutiyacatutthā dhanitātipi vuccanti, itare sithilāti. Vināso lopo. Rassassarā sakadīghehi aññamaññaṃ savaṇṇā nāma, ye sarūpātipi vuccanti. Sarānantaritāni [M 0.0007] byañjanāni saṃyogo. Dhātuppaccayavibhattivajjitamatthavaṃ liṅgaṃ. Vibhatyantaṃ padaṃ. Iccevamādi.

Here, the second and fourth letters of the groups are also called aspirated (dhanitā); the others, unaspirated (sithilā). Elision (lopa) is disappearance. Short vowels together with their own long counterparts are mutually called homogeneous (savaṇṇā); they are also called similar (sarūpā). Consonants not interrupted by a vowel are a consonant cluster (saṃyoga). A meaningful sound devoid of root, suffix, and inflection is a stem (liṅga). What ends in an inflection is a word (pada). And so on.

Iti saññāvidhānaṃ.

Thus the Chapter on Terminology.

Sarasandhividhāna

The Method of Vowel Combination

Atha sarasandhi vuccate.

Now vowel sandhi is explained.

Loka aggapuggalo, paññā indriyaṃ, tīṇi imāni, no hi etaṃ, bhikkhunī ovādo, mātu upaṭṭhānaṃ, sametu āyasmā, abhibhū āyatanaṃ, dhanā me atthi, sabbe eva, tayo assu dhammā, asanto ettha na dissanti itīdha sarādisaññāyaṃ sabbasandhikaraṇaṭṭhāne byañjanaviyojanatthaṃ paribhāsamāha.

The foremost person in the world, the faculty of wisdom, these three, this is not so, advice to a bhikkhunī, attendance on mother, may the venerable one agree, the sphere of mastery, I have wealth, all indeed, may there be three qualities, the unvirtuous are not seen here. Thus here, for the designation of what begins with a vowel, in the context of making all sandhis and for the purpose of separating the consonant, he states a technical rule.

12. Pubbamadhoṭhitamassaraṃ sarena viyojaye.

12. One should separate the preceding consonant from the vowel, making it vowelless and placing it below.

Sarenāti nissakke karaṇavacanaṃ, sahayoge vā, sandhitabbe sarasahitaṃ pubbabyañjanaṃ anatikkamanto adhoṭhitamassarañca katvā sarato viyojayeti sarato byañjanaṃ viyojetabbaṃ. Ettha ca assaraggahaṇasāmatthiyena “byañjana”nti laddhaṃ.

The word sarena (with a vowel) is in the instrumental case indicating separation, or association. When a sandhi is to be made, one should not pass over the preceding consonant that is joined with a vowel, but should separate it from the vowel, making it vowelless and placing it below. Thus, a consonant is to be separated from a vowel. And here, by the force of the term 'vowelless' (assara), the word 'consonant' is understood.

13. Sarā sare lopaṃ.

13. Vowels undergo elision when a vowel follows.

Sarā kho sabbepi sare pare ṭhite lopaṃ papponti. Lopoti adassanaṃ anuccāraṇaṃ. Ettha sarāti kāriyīniddeso. Bahuvacanaṃ panettha ekekasmiṃ sare pare bahūnaṃ lopañāpanatthaṃ. Sareti nimittaniddeso, nimittasattamī cāyaṃ, nimittopādānasāmatthiyato vaṇṇakālabyavadhāne sandhikāriyaṃ na hoti. Lopanti kāriyaniddeso, idaṃ pana suttaṃ [M 0.0008] upari paralopavidhānato pubbalopavidhānanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, evaṃ sabbattha sattamīniddese pubbasseva vidhi, na parassa vidhānanti veditabbaṃ.

Indeed, all vowels undergo elision when a following vowel is present. 'Elision' means non-appearance, non-utterance. Here, sarā (vowels) designates that which is operated upon. The plural is used to indicate the elision of many kinds of preceding vowels before each kind of following vowel. Sare (when a vowel follows) designates the condition, and this is the locative of condition. By the force of specifying the condition, the sandhi operation does not occur if there is an interval of a letter or time. Lopaṃ (elision) designates the operation itself. This rule, however, should be understood as prescribing the elision of the preceding vowel, in contrast to a rule for eliding the following vowel that comes later. Thus, it should be understood that in all cases where the condition is designated by the locative case, the rule applies to the preceding element, not to the following one.

“Assaraṃ, adhoṭhita”nti ca vattate, siliṭṭhakathane paribhāsamāha.

The terms 'vowelless' and 'placed below' are carried forward. To explain the joining of what is connected, he states a technical rule:

14. Naye paraṃ yutte.

14. One should join it to the following letter when proper.

Sararahitaṃ kho byañjanaṃ adhoṭhitaṃ parakkharaṃ naye yutte ṭhāneti paranayanaṃ kātabbaṃ. Ettha yuttaggahaṇaṃ niggahītanisedhanatthaṃ, tena “akkocchi maṃ avadhi ma”ntiādīsu paranayanasandeho na hoti.

Indeed, a consonant that is devoid of a vowel and placed below should be joined to the following letter when it is proper; that is, it should be joined to what follows. Here, the inclusion of the word yutte (when proper) serves to prohibit this for the niggahīta. Therefore, in cases like 'He abused me, he struck me' (akkocchi maṃ avadhi maṃ), there is no doubt about joining to what follows.

Lokaggapuggalo, paññindriyaṃ, tīṇimāni, nohetaṃ, bhikkhunovādo, mātupaṭṭhānaṃ, sametāyasmā, abhibhāyatanaṃ, dhanā matthi, sabbeva, tayassu dhammā, asantettha na dissanti.

The foremost person in the world, the faculty of wisdom, these three, this is not so, the bhikkhunī's advice, attendance on mother, may the venerable one agree, the sphere of mastery, I have wealth, all indeed, may there be three qualities, the unvirtuous are not seen here.

Yassa idāni, saññā iti, chāyā iva, kathā eva kā, iti api, assamaṇī asi, cakkhu indriyaṃ, akataññū asi, ākāse iva, te api, vande ahaṃ, so ahaṃ, cattāro ime, vasalo iti, moggallāno āsi bījako, pāto evātīdha pubbalope sampatte “sare”ti adhikāro, idha pana “atthavasā vibhattivipariṇāmo”ti katvā “saro, saramhā, lopa”nti ca vattamāne –

Whose now, perception is, like a shadow, what speech indeed, thus also, you are not a female ascetic, the eye faculty, you are ungrateful, like the sky, they also, I venerate, I am he, these four, an outcast thus, Moggallāna was Bījaka, in the morning indeed. Here, when the elision of the preceding vowel would apply, the governing rule is sare. Here, however, on the principle that 'by force of meaning there is a change of case ending,' and with the terms 'a vowel, from a vowel, elision' being current—

15. Vā paro asarūpā.

15. A following vowel is optionally elided after a dissimilar vowel.

Asamānarūpamhā saramhā paro saro lopaṃ pappoti vā. Samānaṃ rūpaṃ assāti sarūpo, na sarūpo asarūpo, asavaṇṇo[M 0.0009]. Yasmā pana mariyādāyaṃ, abhividhimhi ca vattamāno āupasaggo viya vāsaddo dvidhā vattate, katthaci vikappe, katthaci yathāvavatthitarūpapariggahe, idha pana pacchime, tato niccamaniccamasantañca vidhimettha vāsaddo dīpeti. “Naye paraṃ yutte”ti paraṃ netabbaṃ.

A following vowel is optionally elided after a vowel of dissimilar form. Sarūpa is that which has a similar form; asarūpa is that which is not sarūpa, i.e., of a different class (asavaṇṇa). However, since the word vā (optionally), like the prefix ā, is used in the sense of a limit and of inclusivity, it operates in two ways: sometimes to indicate an option, and sometimes to accept a systematically established form. Here it is used in the latter sense. Therefore the word vā here indicates a rule that is sometimes obligatory, sometimes optional, and sometimes does not apply at all. The rule 'One should join it to the following letter when proper' is to be applied.

Yassadāni yassa idāni, saññāti saññā iti, chāyāva chāyā iva, kathāva kā kathā eva kā, itīpi iti api, assamaṇīsi assamaṇī asi. Cakkhundriya miti niccaṃ. Akataññūsi akataññū asi, ākāseva ākāse iva, tepi te api, vandehaṃ vande ahaṃ, sohaṃ so ahaṃ, cattārome cattāro ime, vasaloti vasalo iti, moggallānosi bījako moggallāno āsi bījako, pātova pāto eva.

yassadāni from yassa idāni; saññāti from saññā iti; chāyāva from chāyā iva; kathāva kā from kathā eva kā; itīpi from iti api; assamaṇīsi from assamaṇī asi. The sandhi in cakkhundriyaṃ is obligatory. akataññūsi from akataññū asi; ākāseva from ākāse iva; tepi from te api; vandehaṃ from vande ahaṃ; sohaṃ from so ahaṃ; cattārome from cattāro ime; vasaloti from vasalo iti; moggallānosi bījako from moggallāno āsi bījako; pātova from pāto eva.

Idha na bhavati – pañcindriyāni, saddhindriyaṃ, sattuttamo, ekūnavīsati, yassete, sugatovādo, diṭṭhāsavo, diṭṭhogho, cakkhāyatanaṃ, taṃ kutettha labbhā iccādi.

Here it does not apply: the five faculties, the faculty of faith, the best of beings, nineteen, whose are these, the advice of the Sugata, the taint of views, the flood of views, the eye base, 'how can that be got here?', and so on.

Bhavati ca vavatthitavibhāsāya.

And this occurs because of the principle of systematically defined options.

Avaṇṇato sarodānī-tīvevādiṃ vinā paro;

Na luppataññato dīgho, āsevādivivajjito.

A following vowel after a or ā is not elided, except for words like idāni, iti, iva, and eva. A long vowel following other vowels is not elided, except for words like āse.

Bandhussa iva, upa ikkhati, upa ito, ava icca, jina īritaṃ, na upeti, canda udayo, yathā udake itīdha pubbāvaṇṇassarānaṃ [M 0.0010] lope kate “paro, asarūpe”ti ca vattate, tathā “ivaṇṇo yaṃ navā”ti ito ivaṇṇaggahaṇañca, “vamodudantāna”nti ito uggahaṇañca sīhagatiyā idhānuvattetabbaṃ.

Like a kinsman, he looks upon, he has come near, having gone down, spoken by the Jina, he does not approach, the rising of the moon, as in the water. Here, when the elision of the preceding a-vowels has been made, the terms 'following' and 'dissimilar' are carried forward. Similarly, from the rule 'An i-vowel optionally becomes y' (ivaṇṇo yaṃ navā), the term 'i-vowel' should be brought forward here; and from the rule vamodudantānaṃ, the term 'u-vowel' should be brought forward, by the 'lion's leap' principle.

16. Kvacāsavaṇṇaṃ lutte.

16. Sometimes, when the preceding vowel is elided, a non-homorganic vowel is substituted.

Ivaṇṇabhūto, ukārabhūto ca paro saro asarūpe pubbassare lutte kvaci asavaṇṇaṃ pappoti. Natthi savaṇṇā etesanti asavaṇṇā, ekārokārā, tattha ṭhānāsannavasena ivaṇṇukārānamekārokārā honti.

A following vowel that is an i-vowel or a u-vowel, when a dissimilar preceding vowel is elided, sometimes becomes a non-homorganic vowel. Those that do not have a corresponding simple vowel are asavaṇṇā, namely e and o. There, due to the proximity of the place of articulation, i-vowels and u-vowels become e and o respectively.

Bandhusseva, upekkhati, upeto, avecca, jineritaṃ, nopeti, candodayo, yathodake. Kvacīti kiṃ? Tatrime, yassindriyāni, mahiddhiko, sabbītiyo, tenupasaṅkami, lokuttaro. Lutteti kiṃ? Cha ime dhammā, yathā idaṃ, kusalassa upasampadā. Asarūpeti kiṃ? Cattārimāni, mātupaṭṭhānaṃ.

bandhusseva (from bandhussa iva); upekkhati (from upa ikkhati); upeto (from upa ito); avecca (from ava icca); jineritaṃ (from jina īritaṃ); nopeti (from na upeti); candodayo (from canda udayo); yathodake (from yathā udake). Why is kvaci (sometimes) used? For cases like: tatrime, yassindriyāni, mahiddhiko, sabbītiyo, tenupasaṅkami, lokuttaro. Why is lutte (when elided) used? For cases like: cha ime dhammā, yathā idaṃ, kusalassa upasampadā. Why is asarūpe (dissimilar) used? For cases like: cattārimāni, mātupaṭṭhānaṃ.

Ettha ca satipi heṭṭhā vāggahaṇe kvacikaraṇato avaṇṇe eva lutte idha vuttavidhi hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tato idha na bhavati – diṭṭhupādānaṃ, pañcahupāli, mudindriyaṃ, yo missaroti.

And here it should be understood that, even though the word vā was included previously, because of the present use of kvaci (sometimes), the rule stated here applies only when a preceding a-vowel is elided. Therefore, it does not apply here: diṭṭhupādānaṃ, pañcahupāli, mudindriyaṃ, yo missaroti.

Tatra ayaṃ, buddha anussati, sa atthikā, paññavā assa, tadā ahaṃ, yāni idha bhūtāni, gacchāmi iti, ati ito, kikī iva, bahu upakāraṃ, madhu udakaṃ, su upadhāritaṃ, yopi ayaṃ[M 0.0011], idāni ahaṃ, sace ayaṃ, appassuto ayaṃ, itara itarena, saddhā idha vittaṃ, kamma upanissayo, tathā upamaṃ, ratti uparato, vi upasamo iccatra pubbassarānaṃ lope kate –

Here this, recollection of the Buddha, with a purpose, may he be wise, then I, whatever spirits are here, I go thus, gone beyond, like a blue jay, of much help, honey water, well-considered, whoever this is, now I, if this, this one of little learning, the one with the other, faith is the wealth here, kamma as support, a simile thus, ceased at night, calming. Here, when the preceding vowels have been elided—

“Kvacī”ti adhikāro, “paro, lutte”ti ca vattate.

The word kvaci (sometimes) is the governing term, and the words paro (following) and lutte (when elided) are carried forward.

17. Dīghaṃ.

17. Long.

Saro kho paro pubbassare lutte kvaci dīghabhāvaṃ pappotīti ṭhānāsannavasena rassassarānaṃ savaṇṇadīgho.

Indeed, a following vowel sometimes becomes long when a preceding vowel is elided. Thus, due to proximity of the place of articulation, short vowels are replaced by their corresponding long vowels.

Tatrāyaṃ, buddhānussati, sātthikā, paññavāssa, tadāhaṃ, yānīdha bhūtāni, gacchāmīti, atīto, kikīva, bahūpakāraṃ, madhūdakaṃ, sūpadhāritaṃ, yopāyaṃ, idānāhaṃ, sacāyaṃ, appassutāyaṃ, itarītarena, saddhīdha vittaṃ, kammūpanissayo, tathūpamaṃ, rattūparato, vūpasamo.

Here this, recollection of the Buddha, meaningful, may he be wise, then I, whatever spirits are here, I go thus, passed beyond, like a blue jay, of much help, honey-water, well-considered, whoever this is, now I, if this, this one of little learning, the one with the other, faith is wealth here, kamma as support, thus comparable, ceased at night, complete peace.

Kvacīti kiṃ? Aciraṃ vata’yaṃ kāyo, kimpimāya, tīṇimāni, pañcasupādānakkhandhesu, tassattho, pañcaṅgiko, munindo, satindriyaṃ, lahuṭṭhānaṃ, gacchāmahaṃ, tatridaṃ, pañcahupāli, natthaññaṃ. Lutteti kiṃ? Yathā ayaṃ, nimi iva rājā, kikī iva, su upadhāritaṃ.

Why `kvaci` (sometimes)? For cases like: Aciraṃ vata’yaṃ kāyo, kimpimāya, tīṇimāni, pañcasupādānakkhandhesu, tassattho, pañcaṅgiko, munindo, satindriyaṃ, lahuṭṭhānaṃ, gacchāmahaṃ, tatridaṃ, pañcahupāli, natthaññaṃ. Why `lutte` (when elided)? For cases like: Yathā ayaṃ, nimi iva rājā, kikī iva, su upadhāritaṃ.

Lokassa [M 0.0012] iti, deva iti, vi ati patanti, vi ati nāmenti, saṅghāṭi api, jīvitahetu api, vijju iva, kiṃsu idha vittaṃ, sādhu iti itīdha parassarānaṃ lope kate –

Of the world thus, a deva thus, they transgress, they spend time, the outer robe also, for the sake of life also, like lightning, what wealth is here, good thus. Here, when the following vowels have been elided—

“Lutte, dīgha”nti ca vattate.

The terms `lutte` (when elided) and `dīghaṃ` (long) are carried forward.

18. Pubbo ca.

18. And the preceding vowel.

Pubbo saro parassare lutte kvacidīghaṃ pappoti. Caggahaṇaṃ luttadīghaggahaṇānukaḍḍhanatthaṃ, taṃ “cānukaḍḍhitamuttaratra nānuvattate”ti ñāpanatthaṃ.

A preceding vowel is sometimes lengthened when a following vowel is elided. The inclusion of `ca` (and) is for the purpose of carrying forward the terms 'elided' and 'long'. This is to make known the principle that 'what is carried forward by `ca` is not carried forward to subsequent rules'.

Lokassāti, devāti, vītipatanti, vītināmenti, saṅghāṭīpi, jīvitahetūpi, vijjūva, kiṃsūdha vittaṃ, sādhūti.

Of the world thus, a deva thus, they transgress, they spend their time, the robe also, for the sake of life also, like lightning, what wealth is here, good thus.

Kvacīti kiṃ? Yassadāni, itissa, idānipi, tesupi, cakkhundriyaṃ, kinnumāva.

Why `kvaci` (sometimes)? For cases like: yassadāni, itissa, idānipi, tesupi, cakkhundriyaṃ, kinnumāva.

Adhigato kho me ayaṃ dhammo, putto te ahaṃ, te assa pahīnā, pabbate ahaṃ, ye assa itīdha pubbalope sampatte –

'Indeed, this Dhamma has been realized by me,' 'I am your son,' 'those would be abandoned by him,' 'I on the mountain,' 'whoever would be.' Here, when elision of the preceding vowel would apply—

19. Yamedantassādeso.

19. `Y` is the substitute for a final `e`.

Ekārassa padantabhūtassa ṭhāne sare pare kvaci yakārādeso hoti. Akāremeteyesaddādissevāyaṃ vidhi, yanti yaṃ rūpaṃ, e eva anto edanto, ādesiṭṭhāne ādissatīti ādeso. “Byañjane”ti adhikicca “dīgha”nti dīgho.

In place of an `e` that is at the end of a word, the substitute `y` sometimes occurs when a vowel follows. This rule applies only to words such as `me`, `te`, and `ye`, not to the particle `e`. `Yaṃ` means the form `y`. `Edanta` is that which has `e` as its end. An `ādesa` is that which is substituted in place of an original sound. Governing 'consonant', 'long' means long.

Adhigato [M 0.0013] kho myāyaṃ dhammo, putto tyāhaṃ, tyāssa pahīnā, pabbatyāhaṃ, yyāssa.

'Indeed, this Dhamma has been realized by me,' 'I am your son,' 'those would be abandoned by him,' 'I am on the mountain,' 'whoever would be.'

Kvacīti kiṃ? Te nāgatā, puttā matthi. Antaggahaṇaṃ kiṃ? Dhammacakkaṃ pavattento, damento cittaṃ.

Why `kvaci` (sometimes)? For cases like: Te nāgatā (They have not come), puttā matthi (I have sons). Why the word `anta` (final)? For cases like: Dhammacakkaṃ pavattento (turning the Wheel of Dhamma), damento cittaṃ (taming the mind).

Yāvatako assa kāyo, tāvatako assa byāmo, ko attho, atha kho assa, ahaṃ kho ajja, yo ayaṃ, so assa, so eva, yato adhikaraṇaṃ, anu addhamāsaṃ, anu eti, su āgataṃ, su ākāro, du ākāro, cakkhu āpāthaṃ, bahu ābādho, pātu akāsi, na tu evātīdha –

As far as his body, so far his fathom, what is the meaning? Then indeed his, I indeed today, who this, he would be, that very one, from which the case, every half-month, follows after, welcome, well-formed, ill-formed, eye's range, much illness, made manifest, but not at all here –

20. Vamodudantānaṃ.

20. Vamodudantānaṃ.

Okārukārānaṃ antabhūtānaṃ sare pare kvaci vakārādeso hoti. Ka kha ya tasaddādiokārassedaṃ gahaṇaṃ.

For those ending in 'o' and 'u', when a vowel follows, sometimes the substitution of 'v' occurs. This refers to the 'o' of words like 'ka', 'kha', 'ya', 'ta', and so forth.

Yāvatakvassa kāyo, tāvatakvassa byāmo, kvattho, atha khvassa, ahaṃ khvajja, yvāyaṃ, svassa, sveva, yatvādhikaraṇaṃ, anvaddhamāsaṃ, anvebhi, svāgataṃ, svākāro, dvākāro, cakkhvāpāthaṃ, bahvābādho, pātvākāsi, na tveva.

As far as his body, so far his fathom, what is the meaning? Then indeed his, I indeed today, who this, he would be, that very one, from which the case, every half-month, follows after, welcome, well-formed, ill-formed, eye's range, much illness, made manifest, but not at all.

Kvacīti kiṃ? Ko attho, atha kho aññatarā, yohaṃ, sohaṃ, cattārome, sāgataṃ, sādhāvuso, hotūti. Antaggahaṇaṃ kiṃ? Savanīyaṃ, viravanti.

Why `kvaci` (sometimes)? For cases like: what is the meaning?, then indeed another, who I am, that I am, these four, welcome, well done, friend, let it be thus. Why the word `anta` (final)? For cases like: conducive to hearing, they cry out.

Paṭisanthāravutti [M 0.0014] assa, sabbā vitti anubhuyyate, vi añjanaṃ, vi ākato, nadī āsanno itīdha maṇḍūkagatiyā “asarūpe”ti vattate.

His welcoming conduct, all experience is undergone, vi-añjanaṃ, vi-ākato, near the river – thus here, by the frog-leap method, the term `asarūpe` (dissimilar) is carried forward.

21. Ivaṇṇo yaṃ navā.

21. Ivaṇṇo yaṃ navā.

Pubbo ivaṇṇo asarūpe sare pare yakāraṃ pappoti navā. I eva vaṇṇo ivaṇṇo, navāsaddo kvacisaddapariyāyo.

The preceding i-vowel, when a dissimilar vowel follows, optionally becomes `y`. The term `ivaṇṇa` means the vowel `i` itself; the word `navā` is a synonym for `kvaci` (sometimes).

Paṭisanthāravutyassa, sabbā vityānubhuyyate, byañjanaṃ, byākato, nadyāsanno.

Paṭisanthāravutyassa, sabbā vityānubhuyyate, byañjanaṃ, byākato, nadyāsanno.

Navāti kiṃ? Pañcahaṅgehi, tāni attani, gacchāmahaṃ, muttacāgī anuddhato. Asarūpeti kiṃ? Itihidaṃ, aggīva, atthīti.

Why `navā` (optionally)? For cases like: with five factors, those in oneself, I go, free from attachment, not arrogant. Why `asarūpe` (dissimilar)? For cases like: thus indeed this, like fire, it is thus.

Ati antaṃ, ati odātā, pati ayo, pati āharati, pati eti, iti assa, iti etaṃ, itiādi itīdha “ivaṇṇo yaṃ navā”ti yakārādese sampatte –

ati-antaṃ, ati-odātā, pati-ayo, pati-āharati, pati-eti, iti-assa, iti-etaṃ, iti-ādi – thus here, when the `y` substitution, according to the rule `ivaṇṇo yaṃ navā`, is obtained –

22. Sabbo canti.

22. Sabbo canti.

Atipatiitīnaṃ tisaddassedaṃ gahaṇaṃ.

This refers to the taking of the 'ti' sound in 'ati', 'pati', and 'iti'.

Sabbo tiicceso saddo sare pare kvaci cakāraṃ pappoti. Tīti niddesato akatayakārassevāyaṃ vidhi, itarathā kvaciggahaṇassa ca “atissa cantassā”tisuttassa ca niratthakatā siyā. “Paradvebhāvo ṭhāne”ti dvittaṃ.

The entire sound `ti`, when a vowel follows, sometimes becomes `c`. This rule, by the indication `tīti`, applies where the `y` substitution has not been made; otherwise, the inclusion of `kvaci` and the rule `atissa cantassā` would be meaningless. By the rule `Paradvebhāvo ṭhāne` (doubling in place of the subsequent), there is doubling.

Accantaṃ[M 0.0015], accodātā, paccayo, paccāharati, pacceti, iccassa, iccetaṃ, iccādi.

Accantaṃ, accodātā, paccayo, paccāharati, pacceti, iccassa, iccetaṃ, iccādi.

Kvacīti kiṃ? Itissa, iti ākaṅkhamānena.

Why `kvaci` (sometimes)? For cases like: Itissa, iti ākaṅkhamānena (by one wishing thus).

“Te na vāivaṇṇe”ti ito “na ivaṇṇe”ti ca vattate.

From the rule 'Te na vāivaṇṇe', the words 'na ivaṇṇe' are also carried over.

23. Atissa cantassa.

23. Of 'ati', and of its final part.

Atiiccetassa antabhūtassa tisaddassa ivaṇṇe pare “sabbo caṃ tī”ti vuttarūpaṃ na hoti. Atissāti atiupasaggānukaraṇametaṃ. Tenevettha vibhattilopābhāvo. Ettha ca antasaddo saddavidhinisedhappakaraṇato atisaddantabhūtaṃ tisaddameva vadati, na ivaṇṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, itarathā idaṃ suttameva niratthakaṃ siyā.

Of the word 'ati', when the 'ti' sound, which is at its end, is followed by an i-vowel, the form stated in the rule 'sabbo caṃ tī' does not occur. 'Atissa' is an imitation of the prefix 'ati'. Therefore, here there is no elision of the inflection. And here, the word 'anta', from the context of the section on prohibiting word-rules, refers only to the 'ti' sound that is at the end of the word 'ati', not to the i-vowel; this should be understood, otherwise this very rule would be meaningless.

“Ivaṇṇo yaṃ navā”tīdha, asarūpādhikārato;

Ivaṇṇassa sarūpasmiṃ, yādeso ca na sambhave.

Here, by the rule 'Ivaṇṇo yaṃ navā', due to the governing principle of dissimilarity (asarūpa), when a similar vowel follows an i-vowel, the substitution to 'y' is not possible.

Cakāro anuttasamuccayattho, tena itipatīnamantassa ca na hoti. Ati isigaṇo atīsigaṇo, evaṃ atīto, atīritaṃ, itīti, itīdaṃ, patīto.

The particle 'ca' has the meaning of including what is not explicitly stated; therefore, this rule also does not apply to the final vowel of 'iti' and 'pati'. For example: Ati isigaṇo becomes atīsigaṇo; similarly, atīto, atīritaṃ, itīti, itīdaṃ, patīto.

Abhi akkhānaṃ, abhi uggato, abhi okāso itīdha yakāre sampatte –

In the cases of Abhi akkhānaṃ, abhi uggato, abhi okāso, when the substitution of 'y' would be obtained–

“Sare”ti vattate.

The word 'sare' (when a vowel follows) is carried over.

24. Abbho abhi.

24. 'Abbha' is substituted for 'abhi'.

Abhiiccetassa sabbassa sare pare abbhādeso hoti.

For the entire prefix 'abhi', when a vowel follows, the substitution 'abbha' occurs.

“Abhī”ti paṭhamantassa, vuttiyaṃ chaṭṭhiyojanaṃ;

Ādesāpekkhato vuttaṃ, “aṃmo”tiādike viya.

'Abhi' is in the first case ending; in the commentary, it is construed as the sixth case. This is stated with reference to the substitution, just as in 'aṃmo' and so forth.

Pubbassaralopo[M 0.0016], abbhakkhānaṃ, abbhuggato, abbhokāso.

There is elision of the preceding vowel, resulting in: abbhakkhānaṃ, abbhuggato, abbhokāso.

Adhi agamā, adhi upagato, adhi ogāhetvā itīdha

In the cases of adhi agamā, adhi upagato, adhi ogāhetvā, thus here–

25. Ajjho adhi.

25. 'Ajjha' is substituted for 'adhi'.

Adhiiccetassa sabbassa sare pare ajjhādeso hoti. Ajjhagamā, ajjhupagato, ajjhogāhetvā.

For the entire prefix 'adhi', when a vowel follows, the substitution 'ajjha' occurs. For example: Ajjhagamā, ajjhupagato, ajjhogāhetvā.

Abhi icchitaṃ, adhi īritaṃ itīdha

In the cases of abhi icchitaṃ, adhi īritaṃ, thus here–

“Abbho abhi, ajjho adhī”ti ca vattate.

The rules 'Abbho abhi' and 'Ajjho adhi' are also carried over.

26. Te na vā ivaṇṇe.

26. Those two do not apply, optionally, when an i-vowel follows.

Te ca kho abhiadhiiccete upasaggā ivaṇṇe pare abbho ajjhoiti vuttarūpā na honti vā. Saralopaparanayanāni. Abhicchitaṃ, adhīritaṃ. Vāti kiṃ? Abbhīritaṃ, ajjhiṇamutto, ajjhiṭṭho.

And these prefixes 'abhi' and 'adhi', when an i-vowel follows, optionally do not become the forms stated as 'abbha' and 'ajjha'. The alternative forms are made by elision of the preceding vowel and carrying forward of the following consonant, as in: Abhicchitaṃ, adhīritaṃ. Why is 'vā' (optionally) stated? To allow for the forms: Abbhīritaṃ, ajjhiṇamutto, ajjhiṭṭho.

Ekamidha ahantīdha

In the expression 'ekaṃ idha ahaṃ', thus here–

27. Do dhassa ca.

27. 'd' for 'dh', and...

Dhaiccetassa sare pare kvaci dakāro hoti. Ekasaddato parassa idhassa dhakārassevāyaṃ, saralopadīghā. Ekamidāhaṃ. Kvacīti kiṃ? Idheva.

For 'dh', when a vowel follows, 'd' sometimes occurs. This is for the 'dh' of 'idha' when it follows the word 'eka', with elision of the preceding vowel and lengthening of the following. For example: Ekamidāhaṃ. Why 'kvaci' (sometimes)? To allow for: Idheva.

Casaddena kvaci sādhussa dhassa hakāro, yathā – sāhu dassanaṃ.

By the word 'ca', sometimes the 'dh' of 'sādhu' becomes 'h', as in: sāhu dassanaṃ.

Yathā eva tathā evātīdha

In the cases of yathā eva, tathā eva, thus here–

“Navā”ti vattate, “saramhā”ti ca.

The word 'navā' (optionally) is carried over, and also 'saramhā' (after a vowel).

28. Evādissa [M 0.0017] ri pubbo ca rasso.

28. For 'eva' and so forth, 'ri' is substituted, and the preceding vowel is shortened.

Yathātathādvayaparassedaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Dīghasaramhā parassa evasaddādibhūtassa ekārassa rikāro hoti, pubbo ca saro rasso hoti navā. Yathariva, tathariva. Navāti kiṃ? Yatheva, tatheva.

This rule applies to what follows the pair 'yathā' and 'tathā'. For the initial 'e' of the word 'eva' and so forth, when it follows a long vowel, there is the substitution 'ri', and the preceding vowel optionally becomes short. For example: Yathariva, tathariva. Why is 'navā' (optionally) stated? To allow for: Yatheva, tatheva.

Ti antaṃ,ti addhaṃ, aggi agāre, sattamī atthe, pañcamī antaṃ, du aṅgikaṃ, bhikkhu āsane, puthu āsane, sayambhū āsane itīdha yavādesesu sampattesu –

In the cases of ti antaṃ, ti addhaṃ, aggi agāre, sattamī atthe, pañcamī antaṃ, du aṅgikaṃ, bhikkhu āsane, puthu āsane, sayambhū āsane, when the substitutions 'y' and 'v' would be obtained–

“Saññā”ti vattate.

The word 'saññā' (designation) is carried over.

29. Ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā jhalā.

29. The i-vowel and the u-vowel are termed 'jhala'.

Ivaṇṇauvaṇṇaiccete yathākkamaṃ jhalasaññā honti. Vaṇṇaggahaṇaṃ savaṇṇaggahaṇatthaṃ.

The i-vowel and the u-vowel are respectively designated 'jhala'. The inclusion of 'vaṇṇa' (vowel) is for the purpose of including similar vowels.

Jhalasaññā pasaññāva, na liṅgantaṃva nissitā;

Ākhyāte liṅgamajjhe ca, dviliṅgante ca dassanā.

The designation 'jhala' is like a general designation, not dependent on the end of a gendered word; it is seen in verbs, in the middle of a gendered word, and at the junction of two gendered words.

30. Jhalānamiyuvā sare vā.

30. Of the 'jhala' vowels, `iy` and `uv` are the substitutions, optionally, when a vowel follows.

Jhalaiccetesaṃ iyauvaiccete ādesā honti vā sare pare, saralopo.

Of these 'jhala' vowels, `iya` and `uva` are the substitutions, which occur optionally when a vowel follows. Vowel elision also occurs.

Tiyantaṃ, tiyaddhaṃ, aggiyāgāre, sattamiyatthe, pañcamiyantaṃ, duvaṅgikaṃ, bhikkhuvāsane, puthuvāsane, sayambhuvāsane. Vāti kiṃ? Agyāgāre, sattamīatthe, bhikkhuāsane nisīdati.

Tiyantaṃ, tiyaddhaṃ, aggiyāgāre, sattamiyatthe, pañcamiyantaṃ, duvaṅgikaṃ, bhikkhuvāsane, puthuvāsane, sayambhuvāsane. Why 'vā' (optionally)? Agyāgāre, sattamīatthe, bhikkhuāsane nisīdati.

Go ajinaṃ, go eḷakaṃ itīdha

'Go ajinaṃ', 'go eḷakaṃ'—in this context.

“Go, avo, samāse”ti ca vattate.

'Go', 'avo', and 'samāse' (in a compound) are carried over.

31. O [M 0.0018] sare ca.

31. And for 'o', when a vowel follows.

Goiccetassa okārassa sare pare avādeso hoti samāse. Gavājinaṃ, gaveḷakaṃ. Casaddaggahaṇena uvaṇṇassa uvaavādesā. Yathā – bhuvi, pasavo.

For the 'o'-sound of 'go', the substitution 'ava' occurs when a vowel follows in a compound. For example: Gavājinaṃ, gaveḷakaṃ. By the inclusion of the word 'ca', for the 'u'-sound, the substitutions 'uva' and 'ava' also occur. For example: bhuvi, pasavo.

Putha evātīdha

'Putha eva'—in this context.

32. Go sare puthassāgamo kvaci.

32. The augment 'ga' for 'putha' sometimes occurs when a vowel follows.

Puthaiccetassa nipātassa ante kvaci gakārāgamo hoti sare pare. Āgacchatīti āgamo, asantuppatti āgamo. Ettha ca “sare”ti nimittāsannavasena puthassa anteti labbhati. Puthageva, putha eva.

For this particle 'putha', at its end, the augment 'ga' sometimes occurs when a vowel follows. An augment is 'that which comes'; an augment is the arising of what was not previously present. And here, 'when a vowel follows', being the cause, is understood by proximity to apply at the end of 'putha'. Puthageva, putha eva.

Pā evātīdha

'Pā eva'—in this context.

“Sare, go, āgamo, kvacī”ti ca vattate.

'Sare' (when a vowel follows), 'ga', 'āgamo' (augment), and 'kvaci' (sometimes) are carried over.

33. Pāssa canto rasso.

33. And the end of 'pā' is short.

Pāiccetassa ante sare pare kvaci gakārāgamo hoti, pāssa anto ca saro rasso hoti. Pageva vutyassa, pā eva.

For 'pā', at its end, when a vowel follows, the augment 'ga' sometimes occurs, and the final vowel of 'pā' becomes short. For example: Pageva, pā eva.

“Vā, sare”ti ca vattate.

And 'vā' (optionally) and 'sare' (when a vowel follows) are carried over.

34. Yava ma da na ta ra lā cāgamā.

34. 'Ya', 'va', 'ma', 'da', 'na', 'ta', 'ra', and 'la' are also augments.

Sare pare yakārādayo aṭṭha āgamā honti vā. Casaddena gakārāgamo ca, vavatthitavibhāsatthoyaṃ vāsaddo.

When a vowel follows, the eight augments beginning with 'ya' optionally occur. And by the word 'ca', the augment 'ga' also occurs. This word 'vā' has the meaning of a fixed option.

Tattha [M 0.0019] yakārāgamo yathādibho ikārekārādīsu. Yathā idaṃ yathayidaṃ, byañjaneti adhikicca “rassa”nti rassattaṃ, yathā idaṃ vā, yathā eva, yathāyeva, yatheva, evaṃ māyidaṃ, māyevaṃ, taṃyidaṃ, taṃyeva, nayidaṃ, nayimassa, nayimāni, navayime dhammā, buddhānaṃyeva, santiyeva, bodhiyāyeva, satiyeva, pathavīyeva, dhātuyeva, tesuyeva, soyeva, pāṭiyekkaṃ.

Among these, the augment 'ya' occurs after 'yathā' and so forth, before words beginning with the vowels 'i', 'e', and so forth. For example: 'yathā idaṃ' becomes 'yathayidaṃ'; with reference to the rule 'byañjaneti', the word 'rassa' indicates shortening. Other examples: yathā idaṃ vā, yathā eva, yathāyeva, yatheva; similarly, māyidaṃ, māyevaṃ, taṃyidaṃ, taṃyeva, nayidaṃ, nayimassa, nayimāni, navayime dhammā, buddhānaṃyeva, santiyeva, bodhiyāyeva, satiyeva, pathavīyeva, dhātuyeva, tesuyeva, soyeva, pāṭiyekkaṃ.

Tathā sare vipariyādito ca. Vi añjanā viyañjanā, byañjanā vā, evaṃ viyākāsi, byākāsi. Pariantaṃ pariyantaṃ, evaṃ pariyādānaṃ, pariyuṭṭhānaṃ, pariyesati, pariyosānamiti niccaṃ. Ni āyogo niyāyogo. Idha na bhavati, parikkhato, upaparikkhati.

And similarly, after the prefixes 'vi', 'pari', and so forth, when a vowel follows. 'Vi añjanā' becomes 'viyañjanā', or optionally 'byañjanā'; similarly, 'viyākāsi', 'byākāsi'. 'Pari antaṃ' becomes 'pariyantaṃ'; similarly, 'pariyādānaṃ', 'pariyuṭṭhānaṃ', 'pariyesati', 'pariyosānaṃ'—in these cases, it is constant. 'Ni āyogo' becomes 'niyāyogo'. Here it does not occur: parikkhato, upaparikkhati.

Vakāro tisaddādito avaṇṇukāresu. Ti aṅgulaṃ tivaṅgulaṃ, evaṃ tivaṅgikaṃ, bhūvādayo, migī bhantā vudikkhati, pavuccati, pāguññavujutā.

The 'v'-augment occurs after the word 'ti' and so forth, before 'a'-sounds and 'u'-sounds. 'Ti aṅgulaṃ' becomes 'tivaṅgulaṃ'; similarly, tivaṅgikaṃ, bhūvādayo, migī bhantā vudikkhati, pavuccati, pāguññavujutā.

Makāro lahuppabhutito sare chandānurakkhaṇādimhi. Lahu essati lahumessati, evaṃ garumessati, idhamāhu, kena te idha mijjhati, bhadro kasāmiva, ākāse mabhipūjayi, ekamekassa, yena midhekacce, āsatimeva.

The 'm'-augment occurs after 'lahu' and so forth when a vowel follows, for purposes such as preserving the meter. For example: 'Lahu essati' becomes 'lahumessati'; similarly, garumessati, idhamāhu, kena te idha mijjhati, bhadro kasāmiva, ākāse mabhipūjayi, ekamekassa, yena midhekacce, āsatimeva.

Dakāro [M 0.0020] uupasagga saki kenaci kiñci kismiñci koci sammā yāva tāva puna ya te’tattasādīhi. Uupasaggato niccaṃ, u aggo udaggo, evaṃ udayo, udapādi, udāhaṭaṃ, udito, udīritaṃ, udeti.

The 'd'-augment occurs after the prefix 'u', and after 'saki', 'kenaci', 'kiñci', 'kismiñci', 'koci', 'sammā', 'yāva', 'tāva', 'puna', 'ya', 'te', 'tatta', and so forth. After the prefix 'u', it is constant: 'u aggo' becomes 'udaggo'; similarly, udayo, udapādi, udāhaṭaṃ, udito, udīritaṃ, udeti.

Nipātato ca, saki eva sakideva, evaṃ sakadāgāmi, mahāvuttisuttena ikārassa akāro. Tathā kenacideva, kiñcideva, kismiñcideva, kocideva, sammā attho sammadattho, rassattaṃ. Evaṃ sammadakkhāto, sammadaññā vimuttānaṃ, sammadeva, yāvadatthaṃ, yāvadeva, tāvadeva, punadeva.

And from particles: 'saki eva' becomes 'sakideva'; similarly 'sakadāgāmi', where, according to a sutta in the Mahāvutti, the 'i' becomes 'a'. Likewise: kenacideva, kiñcideva, kismiñcideva, kocideva. 'Sammā attho' becomes 'sammadattho', with shortening; similarly, sammadakkhāto, sammadaññā vimuttānaṃ, sammadeva, yāvadatthaṃ, yāvadeva, tāvadeva, punadeva.

Nāmato, yadatthaṃ, tadatthaṃ, yadantarā, tadantarā, tadaṅgavimutti, etadatthaṃ, attadatthaṃ, sadatthapasuto siyā. Yatetattasehi samāseyeva.

From nouns: yadatthaṃ, tadatthaṃ, yadantarā, tadantarā, tadaṅgavimutti, etadatthaṃ, attadatthaṃ, sadatthapasuto siyā. This occurs only in compounds involving pronouns such as 'ya', 'ta', and 'eta'.

Ādisaddena aññadatthaṃ, manasādaññā vimuttānaṃ, bahudeva rattiṃ, ahudeva bhayaṃ.

By the word 'ādi' (and so forth), other examples are included: aññadatthaṃ, manasādaññā vimuttānaṃ, bahudeva rattiṃ, ahudeva bhayaṃ.

Vāti kiṃ? Kenaci atthakāmena, sammā aññāya, yāvāhaṃ, tāvāhaṃ, punāparaṃ, attatthaṃ.

Why 'vā' (optionally)? To allow for cases like: Kenaci atthakāmena, sammā aññāya, yāvāhaṃ, tāvāhaṃ, punāparaṃ, attatthaṃ.

Nakāro āyatādimhi. Ito āyati ito nāyati, ciraṃ nāyati.

The 'n'-augment occurs before 'āyati' and so forth. For example: 'ito āyati' becomes 'ito nāyati'; ciraṃ nāyati.

Takāro yasmā tasmā ajjādito ihaggādimhi. Yasmātiha, tasmātiha, ajjatagge.

The 't'-augment occurs after 'yasmā', 'tasmā', 'ajja', and so forth, before 'iha', 'agga', and so forth. For example: Yasmātiha, tasmātiha, ajjatagge.

Rakāro [M 0.0021] ni dupātu puna dhī pāta caturādito. Ni antaraṃ nirantaraṃ, evaṃ nirālayo, nirindhano, nirīhakaṃ, niruttaro, nirojaṃ. Du atikkamo duratikkamo, durāgataṃ, duruttaṃ. Pāturahosi, pāturahesuṃ. Punarāgaccheyya, punaruttaṃ, punareva, punareti. Dhiratthu. Pātarāso.

The 'r'-augment occurs after 'ni', 'du', 'pātu', 'puna', 'dhī', 'pāta', 'catu', and so forth. For example: 'Ni antaraṃ' becomes 'nirantaraṃ'; similarly, nirālayo, nirindhano, nirīhakaṃ, niruttaro, nirojaṃ. 'Du atikkamo' becomes 'duratikkamo'; durāgataṃ, duruttaṃ. Pāturahosi, pāturahesuṃ. Punarāgaccheyya, punaruttaṃ, punareva, punareti. Dhiratthu. Pātarāso.

Catusaddādito, caturaṅgikaṃ, caturārakkhā, caturiddhipādapaṭilābho, caturoghanittharaṇatthaṃ. Bhatturatthe, vuttiresā, pathavīdhāturevesā.

From the word 'catu' onwards: 'caturaṅgikaṃ,' 'caturārakkhā,' 'caturiddhipādapaṭilābho,' 'caturoghanittharaṇatthaṃ.' In the sense of 'bhattu,' this is the usage; this is simply the earth element.

Tathā sarato ivevesu chandānurakkhaṇe. Nakkhattarājāriva tārakānaṃ, vijjurivabbhakūṭe, āraggeriva sāsapo, sāsaporiva āragge, usabhoriva, sabbhireva samāsetha.

Likewise, for the preservation of the meter, in the case of 'iva' and 'eva' by sound. Like the king of stars among the stars, like lightning on a cloud-peak, like a mustard seed on a needlepoint, like a mustard seed on a needlepoint, like a bull, one should associate only with the good.

Vāti kiṃ? Dvādhiṭṭhitaṃ, pātvākāsi, punapi.

What is the example for 'vā'? 'Dvādhiṭṭhitaṃ,' 'pātvākāsi,' 'punapi.'

Lakāro chasaṅkhyāhi. Laḷānamaviseso. Cha abhiññā chaḷabhiññā, chaḷaṅgaṃ, chaḷāsīti, chaḷaṃsā, saḷāyatanaṃ.

The letter 'la' is used with the number six. There is no distinction between 'la' and 'ḷa.' 'Cha abhiññā chaḷabhiññā,' 'chaḷaṅgaṃ,' 'chaḷāsīti,' 'chaḷaṃsā,' 'saḷāyatanaṃ.'

Vāti kiṃ? Cha abhiññā.

What is the example for 'vā'? 'Cha abhiññā.'

Iti sarasandhividhānaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Thus, the explanation of vowel sandhi is completed.

Itthiliṅga

Feminine Gender

Atha [M 0.0081] itthiliṅgāni vuccante.

Now, feminine gender terms are stated.

Akāranto itthiliṅgasaddo appasiddho.

A feminine gender word ending in 'a' is uncommon.

Ākāranto itthiliṅgo kaññāsaddo. “Kañña”iti ṭhite –

The feminine gender word ending in 'ā' is 'kaññā.' When the stem 'kañña' stands thus –

176. Itthiyamato āppaccayo.

176. After a stem ending in 'a', the suffix 'ā' is used to denote the feminine.

Itthiyaṃ vattamānā akārantato liṅgamhā paro āppaccayo hoti.

After a stem ending in 'a' that denotes the feminine, the suffix 'ā' occurs.

Pakatyatthajotakā itthi-ppaccayā syādayo viya;

Ṇādayo paccayatthassa, sakatthassāpi vācakā.

Feminine suffixes, like 'si' and others, are illuminators of the inherent meaning; 'ṇā' and other suffixes are expressive of the meaning of the suffix, and also of their own meaning.

“Saralopo”tiādinā pubbassare lutte, paranayane ca kate “dhātuppaccayavibhattivajjitamatthavaṃ liṅga”nti vuttattāva paccayantassāpi aliṅgattā vibhattuppattiyamasampattāyaṃ “taddhitasamāsakitakā nāmaṃ vā’tavetunādīsu cā”ti ettha vaggahaṇena itthippaccayantassāpi nāmabyapadeso. Pure viya syādyuppatti, “sesato lopaṃ gasipī”ti silopo. Sā kaññā.

By the rule 'saralopo...' and so on, when the preceding vowel is elided and the subsequent vowel is brought forward; and because it is stated that 'a stem is a meaningful term devoid of root, suffix, and inflection,' and because even a word ending in a suffix is not a stem, and thus an inflection cannot arise; here, in the rule 'taddhitasamāsakitakā nāmaṃ vā’tavetunādīsu cā,' by the inclusion of 'vā,' the designation 'noun' is also given to a word ending in a feminine suffix. As before, the inflections 'si,' etc., arise, and by the rule 'sesato lopaṃ gasipī,' the elision of 'si' occurs. Thus: sā kaññā.

Bahuvacane “ālapane si gasañño”ti ito “sañño”, “te itthikhyā po”ti ito “itthikhyā”ti ca vattate.

In the plural, from the rule 'ālapane si gasañño,' the term 'sañño' is carried forward, and from 'te itthikhyā po,' the term 'itthikhyā' is carried forward.

177. Ā gho.

177. The vowel 'ā' is designated 'gha'.

Liṅgassanto ākāro yadā itthikhyo, tadā ghasañño hotīti ghasaññāyaṃ “ghapato ca yonaṃ lopo”ti [M 0.0082] vikappena yolopo. Tā kaññā kaññāyo.

When the final 'ā' of a stem is a feminine marker, it is designated 'gha.' When it is so designated, the elision of 'yo' optionally occurs by the rule 'ghapato ca yonaṃ lopo.' Thus: tā kaññā, kaññāyo.

Ālapane “sakhato gasse vā”ti ito “gassā”ti vattate.

In the vocative, from the rule 'sakhato gasse vā,' the term 'gasse' is carried forward.

178. Ghate ca.

178. And when 'gha' is present.

Ghato parassa gassa ekāro hoti, saralopādi. Bhoti kaññe, bhotiyo kaññā kaññāyo.

For the 'ga' ending that comes after a 'gha' stem, 'e' is substituted, with vowel elision and so on. For example: bhoti kaññe, bhotiyo kaññā, kaññāyo.

Aṃmhi saralopapakatibhāvā kaññaṃ, kaññā kaññāyo.

With the 'aṃ' ending, due to vowel elision and the natural state, the form is 'kaññaṃ'; the plural forms are 'kaññā', 'kaññāyo'.

Tatiyādīsu “āya catutthekavacanassa tū”ti ito “āyo, ekavacanāna”nti ca vattate.

In the third case and so on, from the rule 'āya catutthekavacanassa tū,' the terms 'āya' and 'ekavacanānaṃ' are carried forward.

179. Ghato nādīnaṃ.

179. After a 'gha' stem, for 'nā' and the following endings.

Ghasaññato liṅgassākārā paresaṃ nādīnaṃ smiṃpariyantānaṃ ekavacanānaṃ vibhattigaṇānaṃ āyādeso hoti. Saralopaparanayanāni. Kaññāya, kaññāhi kaññābhi, kaññāya, kaññānaṃ, kaññāya, kaññāhi kaññābhi, kaññāya, kaññānaṃ.

After a stem ending in 'ā' and designated 'gha,' the substitute 'āya' occurs for the singular case endings from 'nā' up to 'smiṃ' that follow. Vowel elision and the bringing forward of the subsequent vowel occur. Kaññāya, kaññāhi, kaññābhi; kaññāya, kaññānaṃ; kaññāya, kaññāhi, kaññābhi; kaññāya, kaññānaṃ.

Smiṃmhi –

In the case of the 'smiṃ' ending –

180. Ghapato smiṃ yaṃ vā.

180. After a 'gha' or 'pa' stem, 'yaṃ' is optionally substituted for 'smiṃ'.

Ghapato parassa smiṃvacanassa yaṃ hoti vā, aññatthāyādeso. Kaññāyaṃ kaññāya, kaññāsu.

After a 'gha' or 'pa' stem, 'yaṃ' is optionally substituted for the 'smiṃ' ending that follows; otherwise, the 'āya' substitution occurs. Thus: kaññāyaṃ, kaññāya, kaññāsu.

Evamaññepi –

Similarly, other words also –

Saddhā medhā paññā vijjā, cintā mantā vīṇā taṇhā;

Icchā mucchā ejā māyā, mettā mattā sikkhā bhikkhā.

Faith, intelligence, wisdom, knowledge; thought, incantation, lute, craving; desire, delusion, agitation, deceit; loving-kindness, measure, training, alms.

Jaṅghā [M 0.0083] gīvā jivhā vācā,

Chāyā āsā gaṅgā nāvā;

Gāthā senā lekhā sālā,

Mālā velā pūjā khiḍḍā.

Lower leg, neck, tongue, speech; shadow, hope, the Ganges, boat; verse, army, writing, hall; garland, time, offering, sport.

Pipāsā vedanā saññā, cetanā tasiṇā pajā;

Devatā vaṭṭakā godhā, balākā parisā sabhā.

Thirst, feeling, perception, volition, craving, progeny; deity, quail, iguana, heron, retinue, assembly hall.

Ūkāsephālikā laṅkā, salākā vālikā sikhā;

Visākhā visikhā sākhā, vacā vañjhā jaṭā ghaṭā.

Louse, sephālikā, Lanka, splinter, sand, crest; Visākhā, street, branch, sweet flag, barren woman, matted hair, pot.

Jeṭṭhā soṇḍā vitaṇḍā ca, karuṇā vanitā latā;

Kathā niddā sudhā rādhā, vāsanā siṃsapā papā.

Eldest, trunk, disputation, compassion, woman, creeper; tale, sleep, nectar, Rādhā, perfume, rosewood, drinking place.

Pabhā sīmā khamā jāyā,

Khattiyā sakkharā surā;

Dolā tulā silā līlā,

Lāle’lā mekhalā kalā.

Light, limit, patience, wife; warrior woman, gravel, spirits; palanquin, balance, rock, grace; saliva, cardamom, girdle, art.

Vaḷavā’lambusā mūsā, mañjūsā sulasā disā;

Nāsā juṇhā guhā īhā, lasikā vasudhādayo.

Mare, Alambusā, crucible, casket, Sulasā, direction; nose, moonlit night, cave, desire, lymph, the earth, and so on.

Ammādīnaṃ ālapaneva rūpabhedo. Ammā, ammā ammāyo.

For 'ammā' and the like, there is a difference of form in the vocative only. Ammā, ammā, ammāyo.

Gassa “ghate cā”ti ekāre sampatte –

When 'e' is obtained for 'ga' by 'ghate ca' –

181. Na ammādito.

181. Not from 'ammā' and the like.

Ammā annāiccevamādito parassa gassa ālapanekavacanassa na ekārattaṃ hoti. “Ākāro vā”ti rassattaṃ.

After 'ammā,' 'annā,' and so on, the substitution to 'e' does not occur for the following vocative singular 'ga'. By 'ākāro vā,' shortening occurs.

Bhoti amma bhoti ammā, bhotiyo ammā ammāyo. Evaṃ annā, annā annāyo, bhoti anna bhoti annā, bhotiyo annā annāyo. Ambā[M 0.0084], ambā ambāyo, bhoti amba bhoti ambā, bhotiyo ambā ambāyo iccādi.

Bhoti amma, bhoti ammā; bhotiyo ammā, ammāyo. Similarly, annā; annā, annāyo; bhoti anna, bhoti annā; bhotiyo annā, annāyo. Ambā; ambā, ambāyo; bhoti amba, bhoti ambā; bhotiyo ambā, ambāyo, and so on.

Ākārantaṃ.

Ending in 'ā'.

Ikāranto itthiliṅgo rattisaddo;

Tatheva syādyuppatti, silopo, ratti.

The word 'ratti' is feminine and ends in 'i'. Likewise, the case endings beginning with 'si' are produced; 'si' is elided, yielding 'ratti'.

Bahuvacane “saññā, ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā”ti ca vattate.

In the plural, 'saññā' and 'ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā' are also carried forward.

182. Te itthikhyā po.

182. Those, when denoting the feminine, are termed 'pa'.

Itthiyā ākhyā saññā itthikhyā, liṅgassantā te ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā yadā itthikhyā, tadā pasaññā hontīti pasaññāyaṃ “ghapato cā”tiādinā yolopo, “yosu kata”iccādinā dīgho. Rattī rattiyo ratyo vā, he ratti, he rattī he rattiyo.

A designation of the feminine is 'itthikhyā'. When those stems ending in 'i' and 'u' are feminine designators, then they are termed 'pa-saññā'. When it is 'pa-saññā', the elision of 'yo' occurs by 'ghapato cā' and so on, and lengthening occurs by 'yosu kata' and so on. Rattī, rattiyo, or ratyo; he ratti, he rattī, he rattiyo.

“Aṃmo”tiādinā niggahītaṃ, rattiṃ, rattī rattiyo;

Tatiyādīsu “ekavacanānaṃ, nādīna”nti ca vattate.

By 'aṃ mo' and so on, the niggahīta is applied: rattiṃ; rattī, rattiyo. In the third case and so on, 'ekavacanānaṃ' and 'nādīnaṃ' are also carried forward.

183. Pato yā.

183. After 'pa', 'yā' is the substitute.

Pasaññato ivaṇṇuvaṇṇehi paresaṃ nādīnamekavacanānaṃ vibhattigaṇānaṃ yāādeso hoti. Rattiyā, rattīhi rattībhi rattihi rattibhi, rattiyā, rattīnaṃ rattinaṃ.

After 'pa-saññā' stems ending in 'i' and 'u', the substitute 'yā' occurs for the following singular case endings beginning with 'nā'. Rattiyā; rattīhi, rattībhi, rattihi, rattibhi; rattiyā; rattīnaṃ, rattinaṃ.

Pañcamiyaṃ –

In the fifth case –

184. Amā pato smiṃsmānaṃ vā.

184. After 'pa', for 'smiṃ' and 'smā', the substitutes are 'aṃ' and 'ā', optionally.

Paiccetasmā paresaṃ smiṃ smāiccetesaṃ yathākkamaṃ aṃ āādesā honti vā. Vavatthitavibhāsatthoyaṃ vāsaddo[M 0.0085], tena uvaṇṇantato na honti, ivaṇṇantatopi yathāpayogaṃ.

After this 'pa', for the following 'smiṃ' and 'smā', 'aṃ' and 'ā' are substituted respectively, optionally. This word 'vā' is for a restricted option; therefore, they do not occur after stems ending in 'u', and after stems ending in 'i' they also occur according to usage.

“Sare, yakāro”ti ca vattate, sīhamaṇḍūkagatīhi yovacanekavacanaggahaṇañca.

'Sare' and 'yakāro' are also carried forward; and by the lion's gait and the frog's leap, the terms for the plural ending 'yo' and the singular endings are also taken.

185. Pasaññassa ca.

185. And for 'pa-saññā'.

Pasaññassa ivaṇṇassa yovacanekavacanavibhattīnamādese sare pare yakāro hoti. Ettha ca yakārassevādhikārato pasaññaggahaṇena ivaṇṇova gayhati, caggahaṇaṃ “ratto”tiādīsu nivattanatthaṃ. Ratyā rattiyā, rattīhi rattībhi rattihi rattibhi, rattiyā, rattīnaṃ rattinaṃ. Smiṃvacane amādesayakārādesā, ratyaṃ. “Ghapato smiṃ yaṃ vā”ti yaṃādeso, rattiyaṃ.

For the 'i' of a 'pa-saññā' stem, 'y' is substituted when a vowel of a substitute for the plural ('yo') and singular case endings follows. Here, due to the governing rule of 'yakāra' itself, by the term 'pasaññā' only the 'i'-vowel is understood, and the inclusion of 'ca' is for preventing the rule in cases like 'ratto' and so on. Ratyā, rattiyā; rattīhi, rattībhi, rattihi, rattibhi; rattiyā; rattīnaṃ, rattinaṃ. In the 'smiṃ' case, the substitutions of 'aṃ' and 'ya' result in 'ratyaṃ'. By 'Ghapato smiṃ yaṃ vā', the substitute is 'yaṃ', yielding 'rattiyaṃ'.

Aññattha “aṃ, smiṃ, vā”ti ca vattate.

Elsewhere, 'aṃ', 'smiṃ', and 'vā' are also carried forward.

186. Ādito o ca.

186. After 'ādi', 'o' is also substituted.

Ādiiccetasmā smiṃvacanassa aṃ oādesā honti vā. Casaddena aññasmāpi ā aṃ oādesā. Ratyā rattiṃ ratto rattiyā, rattīsu rattisu.

After this 'ādi', for the 'smiṃ' case ending, 'aṃ' and 'o' are optionally substituted. By the word 'ca', from others too, 'ā', 'aṃ', and 'o' are substituted. Ratyā, rattiṃ, ratto, rattiyā; rattīsu, rattisu.

Evamaññānipi –

Similarly for others –

Patti yutti vutti kitti, mutti titti khanti kanti;

Santi tanti siddhi suddhi, iddhi vuddhi buddhi bodhi.

Attainment, suitability, conduct, fame; release, satisfaction, patience, loveliness; peace, tradition, accomplishment, purity; psychic power, growth, intelligence, enlightenment.

Bhūmi jāti pīti sūti, nandi sandhi sāṇi koṭi;

Diṭṭhi vuḍḍhi tuṭṭhi yaṭṭhi, pāḷi āḷi nāḷi keḷi;

Sati mati gati cuti, dhiti yuvati vikati.

Earth, birth, joy, childbirth, delight, joint, curtain, crore; view, growth, satisfaction, stick, text, line, tube, play; mindfulness, wisdom, path, death, firmness, young woman, change.

Rati ruci rasmi asani vasani osadhi aṅguli dhūli dundubhi doṇi aṭavi chavi ādīni ikārantanāmāni.

Delight, liking, ray, thunderbolt, garment, herb, finger, dust, drum, trough, forest, skin, and so on are nouns ending in 'i'.

Ikārantaṃ.

Ending in 'i'.

Īkāranto [M 0.0086] itthiliṅgo itthīsaddo;

“Ittha”itīdha “itthiyaṃ, paccayo”ti ca vattate.

The word `itthī` is a feminine noun ending in `ī`. Here, `itthiyaṃ` and `paccayo` are carried forward.

187. Nadādito vā ī.

187. After `nadī` and others, optionally `ī`.

Nadādito vā anadādito vā itthiyaṃ vattamānā liṅgamhā īppaccayo hoti. Vāggahaṇamanadādisampiṇḍanatthaṃ, tena puthugavādito ca ī.

After a stem in the feminine, whether from the `nadī` group or not, the suffix `ī` occurs. The inclusion of `vā` is for gathering those not in the `nadī` group; therefore, `ī` is also added after `puthugava` and others.

Saralope “kvacāsavaṇṇaṃ lutte”ti asavaṇṇe sampatte pakatibhāvo nāmabyapadeso, syādyuppatti. Itthī, itthī “agho rassa”ntiādinā rassattaṃ, itthiyo. Sambodhane “jhalapā rassa”nti rassattaṃ. Bhoti itthi, bhotiyo itthī itthiyo.

When a dissimilar vowel is elided somewhere, upon meeting a dissimilar vowel, the natural state is called a nominal designation, and the origin of case endings. The forms are `Itthī` (nom. sg.) and `itthī` (nom. pl.); by `agho rassa`, etc., shortening occurs, resulting in `itthiyo`. In the vocative, shortening occurs by `jhalapā rassa`: `Bhoti itthi`, `bhotiyo itthī`, `itthiyo`.

Dutiyekavacane “ghapato smiṃ yaṃ vā”ti ito “vā”ti vattate.

In the accusative singular, from `ghapato smiṃ yaṃ vā`, `vā` is carried forward.

188. Aṃ yamīto pasaññato.

188. The `aṃ` ending optionally becomes `yaṃ` after a `pasañña` (long) `ī`.

Pasaññato īkārato parassa aṃvacanassa yaṃ hoti vā. Itthiyaṃ itthiṃ, itthī itthiyo, itthiyā, itthīhi itthībhi, itthiyā, itthīnaṃ, itthiyā, itthīhi itthībhi, itthiyā, itthīnaṃ, itthiyaṃ itthiyā, itthīsu.

After a `pasañña` (long) `ī`, the `aṃ` ending optionally becomes `yaṃ`. `Itthiyaṃ` or `itthiṃ`; `itthī`, `itthiyo`; `itthiyā`; `itthīhi` or `itthībhi`; `itthiyā`; `itthīnaṃ`; `itthiyā`; `itthīhi` or `itthībhi`; `itthiyā`; `itthīnaṃ`; `itthiyaṃ` or `itthiyā`; `itthīsu`.

Evaṃ nadī, nadī. Yolopābhāve “tato yonamo tū”ti ettha tusaddena yonamokāro ca, “pasaññassa cā”ti īkārassa yakāro, “yavataṃ talana”iccādinā dyassa jakāro, dvittaṃ. Najjo sandanti, nadiyo.

Thus `nadī`, `nadī`. In the absence of `yo` elision, by `tato yonamo tū`, the word `tu` implies `yo`, `na`, `mo`; and by `pasaññassa cā`, the `ī` becomes `y`; by `yavataṃ talana` and so on, `dy` becomes `j`, with doubling. `Najjo sandanti`, `nadiyo`.

Ettha [M 0.0087] cevaṃ sijjhantānaṃ najjoādīnaṃ vuttiyaṃ ānattaggahaṇādinā nipphādanaṃ atraja sugatādīnaṃ viya nipphādanūpāyantaradassanatthanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, the derivation of forms like `najjo` and so on, which are thus accomplished in the usage, by means of taking `ānatta` and so on, should be understood as showing another means of derivation, just as in the case of `atraja`, `sugata`, and so on.

He nadi, he nadī he najjo he nadiyo, nadiyaṃ nadiṃ, nadī najjo nadiyo.

`He nadi`, `he nadī`; `he najjo`, `he nadiyo`; `nadiyaṃ`, `nadiṃ`; `nadī`, `najjo`, `nadiyo`.

Amādisutte ā patoti yogavibhāgena kvaci nāsānañcāttaṃ, tena na jaccā vasalo hoti, pathabyā ekarajjenāti ādi ca sijjhati, pure viya yakārajakārādesadvittāni.

In the `Amādi` sutta, by the division of the rule, sometimes the `ā` is not nasalized. Therefore, 'one is not an outcast by birth' and 'by sole sovereignty over the earth' and so on are also accomplished, with substitutions to `y` and `j` and doublings, as before.

Najjā kataṃ nadiyā, nadīhi nadībhi, najjā nadiyā, nadīnaṃ, najjā nadiyā, nadīhi nadībhi, najjā nadiyā, nadīnaṃ, najjaṃ nadiyaṃ nadiyā, nadīsu.

`Najjā`, `nadiyā`; `nadīhi`, `nadībhi`; `najjā`, `nadiyā`; `nadīnaṃ`; `najjā`, `nadiyā`; `nadīhi`, `nadībhi`; `najjā`, `nadiyā`; `nadīnaṃ`; `najjaṃ`, `nadiyaṃ`, `nadiyā`; `nadīsu`.

Aññepi –

Others also:

Mahī vetaraṇī vāpī, pāṭalī kadalī ghaṭī;

Nārī kumārī taruṇī, vāruṇī brāhmaṇī sakhī.

Earth, Vetaraṇī, pond, trumpet flower, banana tree, water pot; Woman, girl, young woman, spirits, Brahmin woman, female friend.

Gandhabbī kinnarī nāgī, devī yakkhī ajī migī;

Vānarī sūkarī sīhī, haṃsī kākī ca kukkuṭī –

Female celestial musician, Kinnarī, female Nāga, goddess, female Yakkha, female goat, female deer; Female monkey, female boar, lioness, female goose, female crow, and hen –

Iccādayo itthīsaddasamā.

These and so on are similar to the word `itthī`.

Tatheva mātulasaddato īppaccaye kate –

Similarly, when the suffix `ī` is applied to the word `mātula` –

189. Mātulādīnamānattamīkāre.

189. For `mātula` and similar terms, the `āna` change occurs when `ī` is present.

Mātula ayyakavaruṇaiccevamādīnamanto ānattamāpajjate īkāre paccaye pare, antāpekkhāyaṃ chaṭṭhī, saralopādi. Mātulānī, evaṃ ayyakānī, varuṇānī, sesaṃ itthīsaddasamaṃ.

The end of `mātula`, `ayyaka`, `varuṇa`, and so on undergoes the `āna` change when the suffix `ī` follows. The sixth case (genitive) is used with respect to the ending; there is vowel elision and so on. Thus: `mātulānī`; similarly `ayyakānī`, `varuṇānī`; the rest are like the word `itthī`.

Anadādīsu [M 0.0088] puthusaddato īppaccayo. “O sare cā”ti ettha casaddena ukārassa avādeso. Puthavī, puthaviyo. Sasmā smiṃsu puthabyā puthaviyā, puthabyā puthaviyā, puthabyaṃ puthaviyaṃ puthaviyā iccādi.

In the non-`nadī` group, the suffix `ī` is applied to the word `puthu`. Here, by the word `ca` in `O sare ca`, the `u` vowel undergoes the `ava` substitution. `Puthavī`, `puthaviyo`. In the `smā` and `smiṃ` cases: `puthabyā`, `puthaviyā`; `puthabyā`, `puthaviyā`; `puthabyaṃ`, `puthaviyaṃ`, `puthaviyā`, and so on.

Gosaddato “nadādito vā ī”ti īppaccayo. Mahāvuttinā vā “gāva se”ti ettha gāvaiti yogavibhāgena vā okārassa āvādeso. Gāvī, gāvī gāviyo iccādi itthīsaddasamaṃ.

From the word `go`, the suffix `ī` is applied by `nadādito vā ī`. Alternatively, in the Mahāvutti, by dividing the rule `gāva se`, the `o` vowel optionally undergoes the `āva` substitution. `Gāvī`, `gāvī`, `gāviyo`, and so on, are similar to the word `itthī`.

“Mānava”itīdha “itthiyaṃ, vā, ī”ti ca vattate.

Here, for `mānava`, `itthiyaṃ`, `vā`, and `ī` are carried forward.

190. Ṇava ṇika ṇeyya ṇantuhi.

190. After `ṇava`, `ṇika`, `ṇeyya`, `ṇantu`.

Ṇava ṇika ṇeyya ṇantuppaccayantehi itthiyaṃ vattamānehi liṅgehi īppaccayo hoti. Vādhikāro katthaci nivattanattho, saralopādi. Mānavī, evaṃ nāvikī, venateyyī, gotamī.

The suffix `ī` occurs for stems ending in the suffixes `ṇava`, `ṇika`, `ṇeyya`, and `ṇantu` when they denote the feminine. The optional rule sometimes serves to prevent a change; there is vowel elision and so on. `Mānavī`; similarly `nāvikī`, `venateyyī`, `gotamī`.

“Guṇavantu ī”itīdha “vā”ti vattate.

Here, for `guṇavantu` and `ī`, `vā` is carried forward.

191. Ntussa tamīkāre.

191. The `ntu` suffix becomes `ta` when `ī` is present.

Sabbasseva ntuppaccayassa takāro hoti vā īkārappaccaye pare, aññattha saralopādi. Guṇavatī, guṇavatī guṇavatiyo, guṇavantī, guṇavantī guṇavantiyo iccādi itthīsaddasamaṃ.

The entire `ntu` suffix optionally becomes `ta` when the `ī` suffix follows; elsewhere, there is vowel elision and so on. `Guṇavatī`, `guṇavatī`, `guṇavatiyo`; `guṇavantī`, `guṇavantī`, `guṇavantiyo`; and so on, are similar to the word `itthī`.

Evaṃ kulavatī, sīlavatī, yasavatī, rūpavatī, satimatī, gottamatī.

Similarly: `kulavatī` (woman of good family), `sīlavatī` (virtuous woman), `yasavatī` (famous woman), `rūpavatī` (beautiful woman), `satimatī` (mindful woman), `gottamatī` (woman of good lineage).

Mahantasaddato “nadādito vā ī”ti īppaccayo, ntubyapadeso vikappena takārādeso. Mahatī mahantī.

From the word mahanta, the suffix ī is applied by the rule nadādito vā ī, and the designation ntu is optionally substituted by the letter ta. Hence: mahatī, mahantī.

“Bhavanta ī”itīdha “īkāre”ti vattate.

Here, in the rule Bhavanta ī, the word īkāre is carried forward.

192. Bhavato [M 0.0089] bhoto.

192. Of bhavant, there is bhot.

Sabbasseva bhavantasaddassa bhotādeso hoti īkāre itthigate pare. Sā bhotī, bhotī bhotiyo, he bhoti, he bhotī bhotiyo iccādi.

The entire word bhavanta is substituted by bhot when the letter ī, indicating the feminine gender, follows. For example: Sā bhotī; bhotī, bhotiyo; he bhoti; he bhotī, bhotiyo, and so on.

“Bhikkhu” itīdha “itthiya”nti vattate “vā”ti ca.

Here, in the rule concerning bhikkhu, the words itthiyaṃ and vā are carried forward.

193. Patibhikkhurājīkārantehi inī.

193. After pati, bhikkhu, rāja, and words ending in the letter ī, the suffix inī is applied.

Pati bhikkhu rāja iccetehi īkārantehi ca itthiyaṃ vattamānehi liṅgehi inīppaccayo hoti.

After these stems—pati, bhikkhu, rāja—and after stems ending in the letter ī, when they denote the feminine, the suffix inī is applied.

“Saralopo’mādesa”iccādisutte tuggahaṇena kvaci pubbalopassa nisedhanato “vā paro asarūpā”ti saralopo. Bhikkhunī, bhikkhunī bhikkhuniyo iccādi.

In the rule beginning saralopo’mādesa, the inclusion of tu sometimes prohibits the elision of the preceding vowel; therefore, by the rule vā paro asarūpā, the vowel is elided. Hence: bhikkhunī; bhikkhunī, bhikkhuniyo, and so on.

Gahapatisaddato inī, “atta”miti vattate.

From the word gahapati, the suffix inī is applied, and the word attaṃ is carried forward.

194. Patissinīmhi.

194. Regarding pati when the suffix inī follows.

Patisaddassa anto attamāpajjate inīppaccaye pare. Tatheva parasare lutte “pubbo cā”ti dīgho, gahapatānī.

The end of the word pati becomes ā when the suffix inī follows. Likewise, when the following vowel is elided, there is lengthening by the rule pubbo cā. Hence, gahapatānī.

Tatheva rājasaddato inī, saralopapakatibhāvā, rājinī. Īkārantesu daṇḍīsaddato inī, saralopādi, daṇḍinī, daṇḍinī daṇḍiniyo, evaṃ hatthinī, medhāvinī, tapassinī, piyabhāṇinī iccādi.

Likewise, from the word rāja, the suffix inī is applied; due to vowel elision and the consonant remaining in its natural state, the form is rājinī. Among words ending in ī, from the word daṇḍī, the suffix inī is applied; due to vowel elision and other operations, the form is daṇḍinī. Hence, daṇḍinī, daṇḍiniyo. Similarly: hatthinī, medhāvinī, tapassinī, piyabhāṇinī, and so on.

“Pokkharinī” itīdha “tesu vuddhī”tiādinā ikāranakārānaṃ akāraṇakārādesā, pokkharaṇī, pokkharaṇī. “Tato yonamo tū”ti sutte tuggahaṇena yonamokāro [M 0.0090] ca, īkārassa yakāro, “yavata”miccādisutte kāraggahaṇena ṇyassa ñakāro, dvittaṃ. Pokkharañño pokkharaṇiyo vā iccādi.

Here, in the case of pokkharinī, by the rule beginning tesu vuddhī, the letters i and n are substituted by the letters a and ṇ, resulting in pokkharaṇī. In the rule tato yonamo tū, the inclusion of tu indicates that before the endings yo, na, and mo, the final ī is substituted by y. Then, in the rule beginning yavataṃ, the inclusion of kāra causes ṇy to be substituted by ñ, which is then doubled. Hence, pokkharañño or optionally pokkharaṇiyo, and so on.

Vādhikāro anuttasamuccayattho, tena vidū yakkhāditopi inī, paracittavidunī, saraloparassattāni, paracittavidunī paracittaviduniyo, yakkhinī yakkhiniyo, sīhinī sīhiniyo iccādi.

The governing word vā has the meaning of including that which is not explicitly stated. Therefore, the suffix inī is also applied after words such as vidū, yakkha, and so on. For example, paracittavidunī; here, vowel elision and shortening occur. Hence: paracittavidunī, paracittaviduniyo; yakkhinī, yakkhiniyo; sīhinī, sīhiniyo, and so on.

Īkārantaṃ.

End of the section on words ending in ī.

Ukāranto itthiliṅgo yāgusaddo.

The word yāgu is a feminine stem ending in the letter u.

Tassa rattisaddasseva rūpanayo. Amādesādiabhāvova viseso.

Its declension is like that of the word ratti. The specific difference is the absence of the substitution of am and so on.

Yāgu, yāgū yāguyo, he yāgu, he yāgū yāguyo, yāguṃ, yāgū yāguyo, yāguyā, yāgūhi yāgūbhi yāguhi yāgubhi, yāguyā, yāgūnaṃ yāgunaṃ, yāguyā, yāgūhi yāgūbhi yāguhi yāgubhi, yāguyā, yāgūnaṃ yāgunaṃ, yāguyaṃ yāguyā, yāgūsu yāgusu.

Yāgu; yāgū, yāguyo; he yāgu; he yāgū, he yāguyo; yāguṃ; yāgū, yāguyo; yāguyā; yāgūhi, yāgūbhi, yāguhi, yāgubhi; yāguyā; yāgūnaṃ, yāgunaṃ; yāguyā; yāgūhi, yāgūbhi, yāguhi, yāgubhi; yāguyā; yāgūnaṃ, yāgunaṃ; yāguyaṃ, yāguyā; yāgūsu, yāgusu.

Evaṃ dhātu dhenu kāsu daddu kacchu kaṇḍu rajju kareṇu piyaṅgu sassuādīni.

Similarly: dhātu, dhenu, kāsu, daddu, kacchu, kaṇḍu, rajju, kareṇu, piyaṅgu, sassu, and so on.

Mātusaddassa bhedo. Tassa pitusaddasseva rūpanayo. “Āratta”miti bhāvaniddesena ārādesābhāve “pato yā”ti yādesova viseso.

The specific declension of the word mātu. Its declension is like that of the word pitu. The specific difference is that, due to the abstract designation in the rule concerning ārattaṃ, there is an absence of the ār substitution, and there is the substitution of yā by the rule pato yā.

Mātā, mātaro, bhoti māta, bhoti mātā bhotiyo mātaro, mātaraṃ, mātare mātaro, mātarā mātuyā matyā, “tesu vuddhī”tiādinā ukāralopo[M 0.0091], rassattañca. Mātarehi mātarebhi mātūhi mātūbhi mātuhi mātubhi, mātu mātussa mātuyā, mātarānaṃ mātānaṃ mātūnaṃ mātunaṃ, mātarā mātuyā, mātarehi mātarebhi mātūhi mātūbhi, mātu mātussa mātuyā, mātarānaṃ mātānaṃ mātūnaṃ mātunaṃ, mātari, mātaresu mātūsu mātusu.

Mātā, mātaro; bhoti māta, bhoti mātā, bhotiyo mātaro; mātaraṃ, mātare, mātaro; mātarā, mātuyā, matyā (in this last form, there is elision of the letter u and shortening by the rule beginning tesu vuddhī); mātarehi, mātarebhi, mātūhi, mātūbhi, mātuhi, mātubhi; mātu, mātussa, mātuyā; mātarānaṃ, mātānaṃ, mātūnaṃ, mātunaṃ; mātarā, mātuyā; mātarehi, mātarebhi, mātūhi, mātūbhi; mātu, mātussa, mātuyā; mātarānaṃ, mātānaṃ, mātūnaṃ, mātunaṃ; mātari; mātaresu, mātūsu, mātusu.

Evaṃ dhītā, dhītaro, duhitā, duhitaro iccādi.

Similarly: dhītā, dhītaro; duhitā, duhitaro, and so on.

Ukārantaṃ.

End of the section on words ending in u.

Ūkāranto itthiliṅgo jambūsaddo.

The word jambū is a feminine stem ending in the letter ū.

Jambū, jambū jambuyo, he jambu, he jambū jambuyo, jambuṃ, jambū jambuyo iccādi itthīsaddasamaṃ.

Jambū; jambū, jambuyo; he jambu; he jambū, jambuyo; jambuṃ; jambū, jambuyo, and so on. It is similar to the word itthī.

Evaṃ vadhū ca sarabhū, sarabū sutanū camū;

Vāmūrū nāganāsūrū, samāni khalu jambuyā.

Similarly, vadhū and sarabhū, sarabū, sutanū, camū; vāmūrū, nāganāsūrū—these are indeed similar to jambū.

Ūkārantaṃ.

End of the section on words ending in ū.

Okāranto itthiliṅgo gosaddo.

The word go is a feminine stem ending in the letter o.

Tassa pulliṅgagosaddasseva rūpanayo.

Its declension is like that of the masculine word go.

Kaññā ratti nadī itthī, mātulānī ca bhikkhunī;

Daṇḍinī yāgu mātā ca, jambū gotitthisaṅgaho.

Kaññā, ratti, nadī, itthī, and mātulānī, bhikkhunī; Daṇḍinī, yāgu, and mātā, jambū, go—this is the summary of feminine stems.

Itthiliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The feminine gender is concluded.

Napuṃsakaliṅga

Neuter Gender

Atha [M 0.0092] napuṃsakaliṅgāni vuccante.

Now the neuter nouns are declared.

Akāranto napuṃsakaliṅgo cittasaddo.

The neuter noun citta ends in -a.

Pure viya syādyuppatti, “citta si” itīdha –

As before, the generation of case endings (syādi-uppatti). Here, in the case of citta + si:

“Napuṃsakehi, ato nicca”nti ca vattate.

And the rule “Napuṃsakehi, ato niccaṃ” (From neuter nouns, always) applies.

195. Siṃ.

195. The siṃ (rule).

Si, aṃiti dvipadamidaṃ. Akārantehi napuṃsakaliṅgehi parassa sivacanassa aṃ hoti niccaṃ. Saralopapakatibhāvādi, cittaṃ.

This is a two-word rule: si, aṃ. For neuter nouns ending in -a, the si case ending always becomes aṃ. After elision of the vowel and restoration to the natural state, etc., the result is cittaṃ.

Bahuvacane “yonaṃ ni napuṃsakehī”ti vattate.

In the plural, the rule “Yonaṃ ni napuṃsakehi” (For yo in neuter nouns, ni) applies.

196. Ato niccaṃ.

196. And “Ato niccaṃ” (From -a, always).

Akārantehi napuṃsakaliṅgehi yonaṃ niccaṃ ni hoti. “Sabbayonīnamāe”ti nissa vā ākāro. Aññattha “yosu kata”iccādinā dīgho. Cittā cittāni.

For neuter nouns ending in -a, the yo case ending always becomes ni. By the rule “Sabbayonīnamāe,” the ni may optionally become ā. Elsewhere, by the rule “Yosu kata,” etc., the vowel is lengthened. The results are cittā, cittāni.

Yonaṃ nibhāve cāette, siddhepi avisesato;

“Ato nicca”nti ārambhā, āettaṃ kvacidevidha.

Even when the yo ending becomes ni and ā, and is thus established without distinction, due to the commencement of the rule “Ato niccaṃ,” the ā form occurs only sometimes here.

Ālapane galopo. He citta, he cittā cittāni, dutiyāyaṃ nissa vikappenekāro. Cittaṃ, citte cittāni. Sesaṃ purisasaddena samaṃ.
