Apiiti sambhāvanā’pekkhā samuccaya garaha pañhādīsu. Sambhāvanāyaṃ api dibbesu kāmesu, merumpi vinivijjhitvā gaccheyya, apekkhāyaṃ ayampi dhammo aniyato, samuccaye itipi arahaṃ, antampi antaguṇampi ādāya, garahe api amhākaṃ paṇḍitaka, pañhe api bhante bhikkhaṃ labhittha.

'Api' is used in the senses of possibility, consideration, conjunction, reproach, question, and so on. For example: in possibility—'api dibbesu kāmesu' (even in divine pleasures), 'merumpi vinivijjhitvā gaccheyya' (one might go, having pierced even Mount Meru); in consideration—'ayampi dhammo aniyato' (this dhamma too is uncertain); in conjunction—'itipi arahaṃ' (thus also, he is an Arahant), 'antampi antaguṇampi ādāya' (including the end and the qualities pertaining to the end); in reproach—'api amhākaṃ paṇḍitaka' (even our little wise one); in question—'api bhante bhikkhaṃ labhittha' (Venerable Sir, did you receive alms?).

Apaiti apagata garaha vajjana pūjā padussanādīsu. Apagate apamāno apeto, garahe apagabbho, vajjane apasālāya āyanti vāṇijā, pūjāyaṃ vuddhāpacāyī, padussane aparajjhati.

'Apa' is used in the senses of departure, disparagement, avoidance, veneration, transgression, and so on. For example: in departure—'apamāno' (without pride), 'apeto' (gone away); in disparagement—'apagabbho' (free from arrogance); in avoidance—'apasālāya āyanti vāṇijā' (merchants come, avoiding the hall); in veneration—'vuddhāpacāyī' (one who honors elders); in transgression—'aparajjhati' (transgresses).

Upaiti upagamana samīpū’papatti sādissā’dhikū’paribhāvā’nasana dosakkhāna saññā pubbakamma pūjā gayhākāra bhusatthādīsu. Upagamane nisinnaṃ vā upanisīdeyya, samīpe upanagaraṃ, upapattiyaṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati, atha vā upapatti yutti, yathā [M 0.0131]– upapattito ikkhatīti upekkhā, sādisse upamānaṃ upamā, adhike upa khāriyaṃ doṇo, uparibhāve upasampanno, anasane upavāso, dosakkhāne paraṃ upapadati, saññāyaṃ upadhā upasaggo, pubbakamme upakkamo upakāro, pūjāyaṃ buddhupaṭṭhāko, mātupaṭṭhānaṃ, gayhākāre soceyyapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, bhusatthe upādānaṃ, upāyāso, upanissayoti. Iti anekatthā hi upasaggā.

'Upa' is used in the senses of approaching, proximity, origination, similarity, being less than, being above, fasting, accusation of faults, designation, prior action, honoring, mode of acceptance, intensity, and so on. In approaching: 'nisinnaṃ vā upanisīdeyya' (one should sit near one who is seated). In proximity: 'upanagaraṃ' (a suburb). In origination: 'saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati' (one is reborn in a heavenly world); or alternatively, origination means suitability, as in 'upapattito ikkhatīti upekkhā' (equanimity is 'looking on with suitability'). In similarity: 'upamānaṃ, upamā' (a comparison, a simile). In being less than: 'upa khāriyaṃ doṇo' (a doṇa is somewhat less than a khārī). In being above: 'upasampanno' (fully ordained). In fasting: 'upavāso' (fasting). In accusation of faults: 'paraṃ upavadati' (he criticizes another). In designation: 'upadhā, upasaggo' (penultimate, prefix). In prior action: 'upakkamo, upakāro' (effort, assistance). In honoring: 'buddhupaṭṭhāko' (attending upon the Buddha), 'mātupaṭṭhānaṃ' (attending upon one's mother). In mode of acceptance: 'soceyyapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ' (the presence of purity). In intensity: 'upādānaṃ' (clinging), 'upāyāso' (distress), 'upanissayo' (strong support). Thus, prefixes indeed have many meanings.

Vuttañca –

And it is said:

“Upasagga nipātā ca, paccayā ca ime tayo;

Nekenekatthavisayā, iti neruttikābravu”nti.

“Prefixes, particles, and suffixes—these three each have many and various meanings as their domain; thus the etymologists have said.”

Tattha upasaggānaṃ nāmākhyātavisesakattā liṅgasaññāyaṃ aniyamena syādimhi sampatte tesaṃ saṅkhyākammādibhedābhāvā tehi paṭhamekavacanameva bhavati.

In this context, since prefixes modify nouns and verbs, and since there is no fixed rule for their gender designation, when the case endings beginning with 'si' are to be applied, only the first case singular ending is employed, because for these prefixes there is no distinction of number, case-function, and so on.

“Lopa”nti vattamāne

When 'lopa' (elision) is the current rule,

282. Sabbāsamāvusopasagganipātādīhi ca.

282. And of all (case endings) after 'āvuso', prefixes, particles, and so forth.

Āvusosaddato, upasagganipātehi ca sabbāsaṃ parāsaṃ vibhattīnaṃ lopo hoti. Ādisaddena kvaci suttapadādīhi ca. Ettha ca āvusotimassa visuṃ gahaṇaṃ sasaṅkhyattadīpanatthanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

After the word 'āvuso', and after prefixes and particles, the elision of all subsequent case endings occurs. By the word 'ādi' (and so forth), this also applies in some cases to words from the suttas and so on. Here, it should be understood that the separate mention of 'āvuso' is for the purpose of indicating that it has a specific number.

Upeccatthaṃ sajjantīti, upasaggā hi pādayo;

Cādī padādimajjhante, nipātā nipatantiti.

“Because they approach and attach to the meaning, they are 'upasaggā' (prefixes), which begin with 'pa'; and because they fall at the beginning, middle, or end of a word, they are 'nipātā' (particles), which begin with 'ca'.”

Paharaṇaṃ pahāro, evaṃ parābhavo, nivāso, nīhāro, uhāro, duhāro, saṃhāro, vihāro, avahāro, anuhāro, parihāro, adhihāro, abhihāro, patihāro, suhāro, āhāro, atihāro, apihāro, apahāro[M 0.0132], upahāro. Paharati, parābhavati, nivasati, nīharati, uddharati iccādi yojetabbaṃ.

`Paharaṇaṃ` is `pahāro` (a blow); similarly `parābhavo` (defeat), `nivāso` (dwelling), `nīhāro` (removal), `uddhāro` (lifting up), `dūhāro` (difficult to carry), `saṃhāro` (gathering), `vihāro` (abiding), `avahāro` (taking away), `anuhāro` (imitation), `parihāro` (protection), `adhihāro` (undertaking), `abhihāro` (offering), `patihāro` (warding off), `suhāro` (easy to bear), `āhāro` (food), `atihāro` (carrying too far), `apihāro` (covering), `apahāro` (theft), `upahāro` (gift). The verbs 'paharati' (he strikes), 'parābhavati' (he is defeated), 'nivasati' (he dwells), 'nīharati' (he removes), 'uddharati' (he lifts up), and so forth, should be construed accordingly.

Dhātvatthaṃ bādhate koci, koci tamanuvattate;

Tamevañño viseseti, upasaggagatī tidhā.

One obstructs the meaning of the root, another follows it; yet another specifies that very meaning—the functions of prefixes are threefold.

Opasaggikapadaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on prefixes is concluded.

Nepātikapada

The Section on Particles

Samuccayavikappanapaṭisedhapūraṇādiatthaṃ asatvavācakaṃ nepātikaṃ padaṃ.

A particle is a word that does not denote a substance, and has meanings such as conjunction, option, negation, filling, and so on.

Tatra caiti samuccayā’nvācaye’tarītarayogasamāhārā’vadhāraṇādīsu.

Therein, 'ca' is used in the senses of conjunction, subsequent connection, mutual connection, collection, emphasis, and so on.

Vāiti vikappanū’pamāna samuccaya vavatthitavibhāsāsu.

'Vā' is used in the senses of option, comparison, conjunction, and established alternative.

Na no mā a alaṃ halaṃ iccete paṭisedhanatthe.

The particles 'na', 'no', 'mā', 'a', 'alaṃ', and 'halaṃ' are used in the sense of negation.

Alaṃ pariyatti bhūsanesu ca.

The particle 'alaṃ' is also used in the senses of sufficiency and adornment.

Pūraṇatthaṃ duvidhaṃ atthapūraṇaṃ padapūraṇañca.

The sense of filling is twofold: filling of meaning and filling of words.

Tattha atha khalu vata vatha atho assu yagghe hi carahi naṃ taṃ vā ca tuva vo pana have kīva ha tato yathā sudaṃ kho ve haṃ enaṃ seyyathidaṃ iccevamādīni padapūraṇāni.

Therein, 'atha', 'khalu', 'vata', 'vatha', 'atho', 'assu', 'yagghe', 'hi', 'carahi', 'naṃ', 'taṃ', 'vā', 'ca', 'tuva', 'vo', 'pana', 'have', 'kīva', 'ha', 'tato', 'yathā', 'sudaṃ', 'kho', 've', 'haṃ', 'enaṃ', 'seyyathidaṃ', and so forth—these are word-fillers.

Tattha – athaiti pañhā’nantariyā’dhikārādīsu ca.

Therein, 'atha' is also used in the senses of question, immediate succession, topic, and so on.

Khaluiti paṭisedhā’vadhāraṇa pasiddhīsu ca.

'Khalu' is also used in the senses of prohibition, ascertainment, and well-known fact.

Vataiti ekaṃsa khedā’nukampasaṅkappesu ca.

'Vata' is also used in the senses of certainty, sorrow, compassion, and intention.

Athoiti anvādese ca.

'Atho' is also used in the sense of a subsequent statement.

Hiiti [M 0.0133] hetu avadhāraṇesu ca.

'Hi' is also used in the senses of cause and ascertainment.

Tuiti visesa hetu nivattanādīsu ca.

The particle 'tu' is used in the sense of distinction, cause, turning back, and so forth.

Panaiti visesepi.

The particle 'pana' is also used in the sense of distinction.

Have, veiccete ekaṃsatthepi.

The particles 'have' and 've' are also used in the sense of certainty.

Haṃiti visāda sambhamesupi.

The particle 'haṃ' is also used in the sense of dejection and agitation.

Seyyathidanti taṃ katamanti atthepi.

The particle 'seyyathidaṃ' is also used in the sense of 'what is that?'.

Atthapūraṇaṃ duvidhaṃ vibhattiyuttaṃ, avibhattiyuttañca.

The filling of meaning is twofold: connected with case endings and unconnected with case endings.

Atthi sakkā labbhā iccete paṭhamāyaṃ.

The particles 'atthi', 'sakkā', and 'labbhā' are used in the sense of the first case.

Āvuso ambho hambho re are hare jeiccete āmantane.

The particles 'āvuso', 'ambho', 'hambho', 're', 'are', 'hare', and 'je' are used in addressing (vocative).

Divā bhiyyo namo iccete paṭhamāyaṃ, dutiyāyañca.

The particles 'divā', 'bhiyyo', and 'namo' are used in the sense of the first case and also in the second case.

Sayaṃ sāmaṃ saṃ sammā kinti iccete tatiyatthe, soto dhāpaccayantā ca. Suttaso padaso aniccato dukkhato ekadhā dvidhā iccādi.

The particles 'sayaṃ', 'sāmaṃ', 'saṃ', 'sammā', and 'kinti' are used in the sense of the third case; and those ending in the suffixes '-so', '-to', and '-dhā'. For example: 'suttaso' (by suttas), 'padaso' (by words), 'aniccato' (impermanently), 'dukkhato' (painfully), 'ekadhā' (in one way), 'dvidhā' (in two ways), and so forth.

Tave tuṃpaccayantā catutthiyā, kātave dātave kātuṃ kāretuṃ dātuṃ dāpetuṃ iccādi.

Those ending in the suffixes '-tave' and '-tuṃ' are in the sense of the fourth case (dative). For example: 'kātave' (to do), 'dātave' (to give), 'kātuṃ' (to do), 'kāretuṃ' (to cause to do), 'dātuṃ' (to give), 'dāpetuṃ' (to cause to give), and so forth.

So topaccayantā pañcamiyatthe, dīghaso oraso rājato vā corato vā iccādi.

Those ending in the suffixes '-so' and '-to' are in the sense of the fifth case (ablative). For example: 'dīghaso' (lengthwise), 'oraso' (from one's own breast), 'rājato' (from the king), or 'corato' (from a thief), and so forth.

To sattamyatthepi, trathādipaccayantā ca. Ekato purato pacchato passato piṭṭhito pādato sīsato aggato mūlato yatra yattha yahiṃ tatra tattha tahiṃ tahaṃ iccādi.

The suffix '-to' is also in the sense of the seventh case (locative), and also those ending in 'trathā' and similar suffixes. For example: 'ekato' (in one place), 'purato' (in front), 'pacchato' (behind), 'passato' (on the side), 'piṭṭhito' (at the back), 'pādato' (at the foot), 'sīsato' (at the head), 'aggato' (at the top), 'mūlato' (at the root), 'yatra' (where), 'yattha' (where), 'yahiṃ' (where), 'tatra' (there), 'tattha' (there), 'tahiṃ' (there), 'tahaṃ' (there), and so forth.

Samantā sāmantā parito abhito samantato ekajjhaṃ ekamantaṃ heṭṭhā upari uddhaṃ adho tiriyaṃ sammukhā [M 0.0134] parammukhā āvi raho tiro uccaṃ nīcaṃ anto antarā ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā bāhirā bāhiraṃ bahi oraṃ pāraṃ ārā ārakā pacchā pure huraṃ pecca iccete sattamiyā.

The particles 'samantā', 'sāmantā', 'parito', 'abhito', 'samantato', 'ekajjhaṃ', 'ekamantaṃ', 'heṭṭhā', 'upari', 'uddhaṃ', 'adho', 'tiriyaṃ', 'sammukhā', 'parammukhā', 'āvi', 'raho', 'tiro', 'uccaṃ', 'nīcaṃ', 'anto', 'antarā', 'ajjhattaṃ', 'bahiddhā', 'bāhirā', 'bāhiraṃ', 'bahi', 'oraṃ', 'pāraṃ', 'ārā', 'ārakā', 'pacchā', 'pure', 'huraṃ', and 'pecca' are used in the sense of the seventh case (locative).

Sampati āyati ajja aparajju parajja suve sve parasuve hiyyo pare sajju sāyaṃ pāto kālaṃ kallaṃ divā nattaṃ niccaṃ satataṃ abhiṇhaṃ abhikkhaṇaṃ muhuṃ muhuttaṃ bhūtapubbaṃ purā yadā tadā kadā iccādayo kālasattamiyā. Iti vibhattiyuttāni.

The particles 'sampati' (now), 'āyati' (in the future), 'ajja' (today), 'aparajju' (the day after tomorrow), 'parajja' (on another day), 'suve' (tomorrow), 'sve' (tomorrow), 'parasuve' (the day after tomorrow), 'hiyyo' (yesterday), 'pare' (the day before yesterday), 'sajju' (immediately), 'sāyaṃ' (in the evening), 'pāto' (in the morning), 'kālaṃ' (at the time), 'kallaṃ' (in the morning), 'divā' (by day), 'nattaṃ' (by night), 'niccaṃ' (always), 'satataṃ' (constantly), 'abhiṇhaṃ' (repeatedly), 'abhikkhaṇaṃ' (frequently), 'muhuṃ' (often), 'muhuttaṃ' (for a moment), 'bhūtapubbaṃ' (formerly), 'purā' (long ago), 'yadā' (when), 'tadā' (then), 'kadā' (when?), and so forth—these are in the sense of the locative of time. Thus, these are words connected with case endings.

Avibhattiyuttesu ca appeva appevanāma nu iccete saṃsayatthe.

And among those unconnected with case endings (indeclinables), the particles 'appeva', 'appevanāma', and 'nu' are used in the sense of doubt.

Addhā aññadatthu taggha jātu kāmaṃ sasakkaṃiccete ekaṃsatthe.

The particles 'addhā', 'aññadatthu', 'taggha', 'jātu', 'kāmaṃ', and 'sasakkaṃ' are used in the sense of certainty.

Evaiti avadhāraṇe.

The particle 'eva' is used in the sense of ascertainment.

Kaccinu’kinnunanukathaṃ kiṃsu kiṃiccete pucchanatthe.

The particles 'kaccinu', 'kinnu', 'nanu', 'kathaṃ', 'kiṃsu', and 'kiṃ' are used in the sense of questioning.

Evaṃ iti itthaṃ iccete nidassane.

The particles 'evaṃ', 'iti', and 'itthaṃ' are used in the sense of illustration.

Iti hetu vākyaparisamattīsu ca.

The particle 'iti' is also used in the sense of cause and the conclusion of sentences.

Yāva tāva yāvatā tāvatā kittāvatā ettāvatā kīva iccete paricchedanatthe.

The particles 'yāva', 'tāva', 'yāvatā', 'tāvatā', 'kittāvatā', 'ettāvatā', and 'kīva' are used in the sense of limitation.

Evaṃ sāhu lahu opāyikaṃ patirūpaṃ āma sādhu iti sampaṭicchanatthe.

The particles 'evaṃ', 'sāhu', 'lahu', 'opāyikaṃ', 'patirūpaṃ', 'āma', and 'sādhu' are used in the sense of acceptance.

Yathā tathā yatheva tatheva evaṃ evameva evamevaṃ evampi yathāpi seyyathāpi seyyathāpināma viya iva yathariva tathariva yathānāma tathānāma yathāhi tathāhi yathācatathāca iccete paṭibhāgatthe.

The particles 'yathā', 'tathā', 'yatheva', 'tatheva', 'evaṃ', 'evameva', 'evamevaṃ', 'evampi', 'yathāpi', 'seyyathāpi', 'seyyathāpināma', 'viya', 'iva', 'yathariva', 'tathariva', 'yathānāma', 'tathānāma', 'yathāhi', 'tathāhi', and 'yathā ca tathā ca' are used in the sense of resemblance.

Yathāiti [M 0.0135] yoggatā vicchā padatthānativattanidassanesu ca.

The particle 'yathā' is also used in the sense of fitness, repetition, not transgressing the word's meaning, and illustration.

Evaṃiti upadesa pañhādīsu ca.

The particle 'evaṃ' is also used in instruction, questions, and so forth.

Kiñcāpiiti anuggahatthe.

The particle 'kiñcāpi' is used in the sense of concession.

Ahoiti garaha pasaṃsana patthanesu ca.

The particle 'aho' is also used in blame, praise, and aspirations.

Nāmaiti garaha pasaṃsana saññā pañhesu ca.

The particle 'nāma' is also used in blame, praise, designation, and questions.

Sādhuiti pasaṃsana yācanesu ca.

The particle 'sādhu' is also used in praise and requests.

Iṅgha handa iccete codanatthe.

The particles 'iṅgha' and 'handa' are used in the sense of urging.

Sādhu suṭṭhu evametanti anumodane.

The particles 'sādhu', 'suṭṭhu', and 'evam' are used in the sense of approval.

Kiraiti anussavaṇa assaddheyyesu.

The particle 'kira' is used in the sense of hearsay and for that which is incredible.

Nūnaiti anumānā’nussaraṇa parivitakkanesu.

The particle 'nūna' is used in the sense of inference, recollection, and speculation.

Kasmāiti kāraṇapucchane.

The particle 'kasmā' is used in asking for a cause.

Yasmā tasmā tathāhi tena iccete kāraṇacchedanatthe.

The particles 'yasmā', 'tasmā', 'tathāhi', and 'tena' are used in the sense of concluding a reason.

Saha saddhiṃ samaṃ amāiti samakriyāyaṃ.

The particles 'saha', 'saddhiṃ', 'samaṃ', and 'amā' are used in the sense of simultaneous action.

Vinā riteiti vippayoge.

The particles 'vinā' and 'rite' are used in the sense of separation.

Nānā puthu bahuppakāre.

The particles 'nānā' and 'puthu' are used in the sense of many kinds.

Puthu visuṃ asaṅghāte ca.

The particles 'puthu' and 'visuṃ' are also used in the sense of being uncombined.

Duṭṭhu ku jigucchāyaṃ.

The particles 'duṭṭhu' and 'ku' are used in the sense of disgust.

Puna appaṭhame.

The particle 'puna' is used in the sense of 'not the first' (i.e., again).

Kathañci kicchatthe ca.

The particle 'kathañci' is also used in the sense of difficulty.

Dhā kkhattuṃ sakiñca saṅkhyāvibhāge.

The particles 'dhā', 'kkhattuṃ', and 'sakiṃ' are used in the sense of division by number.

Īsakaṃ [M 0.0136] appatthe.

The particle 'īsakaṃ' is used in the sense of 'a little'.

Saṇikaṃ mandatthe.

The particle 'saṇikaṃ' is used in the sense of 'slowly'.

Khippaṃ araṃ lahu āsuṃ tuṇṇaṃ aciraṃ sīghatthe.

The particles 'khippaṃ', 'araṃ', 'lahu', 'āsuṃ', 'tuṇṇaṃ', and 'aciraṃ' are used in the sense of 'quickly'.

Ciraṃ cirassaṃ dīghakāle.

The particles 'ciraṃ' and 'cirassaṃ' are used in the sense of a long time.

Ce yadi saṅkāvaṭṭhāne.

The particles 'ce' and 'yadi' are used in a state of doubt.

Dhuvaṃ thirāvadhāraṇesu.

The particle 'dhuvaṃ' is used in the sense of firm ascertainment.

Hā visāde.

The particle 'hā' is used in the sense of dejection.

Tuṇhī abhāsane.

The particle 'tuṇhī' is used in the sense of not speaking.

Sacchi paccakkhe.

The particle 'sacchi' is used in the sense of direct perception.

Musā micchā alikaṃ asacce.

The particles 'musā', 'micchā', and 'alikaṃ' are used in the sense of untruth.

Suvatthi āsīsatthe iccādi.

The particle 'suvatthi' is used in the sense of blessing, and so forth.

Tuna tvāna tvāpaccayantā ussukkanatthe bhavanti.

Those ending in the suffixes '-tuna', '-tvāna', and '-tvā' are used in the sense of eagerness.

Yathā – passituna passiya passitvāna passitvā disvā disvānadassetvā dātuna datvāna datvā upādāya dāpetvā viññāpetvā viceyya vineyya nihacca samecca apecca upecca ārabbha āgamma iccādi.

For example: 'passituna', 'passiya', 'passitvāna', 'passitvā', 'disvā', 'disvāna', 'dassetvā', 'dātuna', 'datvāna', 'datvā', 'upādāya', 'dāpetvā', 'viññāpetvā', 'viceyya', 'vineyya', 'nihacca', 'samecca', 'apecca', 'upecca', 'ārabbha', 'āgamma', and so forth.

Evaṃ nāmākhyātopasaggavinimuttaṃ yadabyayalakkhaṇaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ nipātapadanti veditabbaṃ.

Thus, whatever is free from nouns, verbs, and prefixes, and has the characteristic of an indeclinable, all that should be understood as a particle.

Vuttañca –

And it was said:

“Muttaṃ padattayā yasmā, tasmā nipatatyantarā;

Nepātikanti taṃ vuttaṃ, yaṃ abyaya salakkhaṇa”nti.

“Because it is free from the three kinds of words, therefore it falls in between; it is called a particle, which has the characteristic of being indeclinable.”

Nepātikapadaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on particles is concluded.

Pulliṅgaṃ itthiliṅgañca, napuṃsakamathāparaṃ;

Tiliṅgañca aliṅgañca, nāmikaṃ pañcadhā ṭhitaṃ.

Masculine, feminine, and neuter, and then the common gender and the genderless; the nominal stands in five ways.

Iti padarūpasiddhiyaṃ nāmakaṇḍo dutiyo.

Thus ends the second chapter, on nouns, in the treatise on the accomplishment of word-forms.

3. Kārakakaṇḍa

3. The Chapter on Case Relations

Atha [M 0.0137] vibhattīnamatthabhedā vuccante.

Now, the different meanings of the case endings are explained.

Tattha ekampi atthaṃ kammādivasena, ekattādivasena ca vibhajantīti vibhattiyo, syādayo. Tā pana paṭhamādibhedena sattavidhā.

Herein, because they divide even a single meaning according to case relations, such as the object, and according to number, such as the singular, they are called case endings, such as 'si'. These, however, are of seven kinds, beginning with the first.

Tattha kasmiṃ atthe paṭhamā?

Herein, in what meaning is the first case used?

283. Liṅgatthe paṭhamā.

283. The first case is used in the sense of the nominal stem.

Liṅgatthābhidhānamatte paṭhamāvibhatti hoti.

The first case ending occurs merely to denote the sense of the nominal stem.

Liṅgassa attho liṅgattho. Ettha ca līnaṃ aṅganti liṅgaṃ, apākaṭo avayavo, purisotiādīnañhi pakatippaccayādivibhāgakappanāya nipphāditānaṃ saddappatirūpakānaṃ nāmikapadānaṃ paṭhamaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ pakatirūpaṃ apākaṭattā, avayavattā ca liṅganti vuccati. Atha vā visadāvisadobhayarahitākāravohārasaṅkhātena tividhaliṅgena sahitatthassa, tabbinimuttassupasaggādīnamatthassa ca līnassa gamanato, liṅganato vā liṅganti anvatthanāmavasena vā “dhātuppaccayavibhattivajjitamatthavaṃ liṅga”nti vacanato parasamaññāvasena vā liṅganti idha pāṭipadikāparanāmadheyyaṃ syādivibhatyantapadapakatirūpameva vuccatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The meaning of the nominal stem is 'liṅgattho'. Here, 'liṅga' means 'a hidden part' (līnaṃ aṅgaṃ), an unmanifested constituent (apākaṭo avayavo). For in the case of nominal words like 'puriso', which are sound-forms produced by the analysis of base, suffix, etc., the base form to be established first is called 'liṅga' because it is unmanifested and a constituent. Or, because the meaning associated with the threefold gender (liṅga), and the meaning of prefixes and so on which are free from that, is hidden (līna) or is signified (liṅgana), it is called 'liṅga'. Alternatively, by way of a name consistent with its meaning, or by way of a conventional designation from the statement 'a liṅga is that which possesses meaning but is devoid of root, suffix, and case ending,' here it should be understood that 'liṅga' refers only to the base form of a word ending in a case ending like 'si', which is also known by the other name, 'pāṭipadika'.

Liṅgassattho nāma pabandhavisesākārena pavattamāne rūpādayo upādāya paññāpīyamāno tadaññānaññabhāvena anibbacanīyo samūhasantānādibhedo upādāpaññattisaṅkhāto ghaṭapaṭādivohārattho ca pathavīdhātuphassādīnaṃ sabhāvadhammānaṃ [M 0.0138] kāladesādibhedabhinnānaṃ vijātiyavinivatto sajātiyasādhāraṇo yathāsaṅketamāropasiddho tajjāpaññattisaṅkhāto kakkhaḷattaphusanādisāmaññākāro ca.

The meaning of the nominal stem is that which is designated as a conceptual designation based on a continuant form (upādāpaññatti), being inexpressible as either the same or different from its basis, and having distinctions such as aggregates and continua, which is made known by taking up forms and so on, occurring in a particular arrangement; and it is also the meaning of conventional usage, such as 'pot,' 'cloth,' etc.; and it is also the general characteristic, such as hardness and tactile feeling, which is designated as a conceptual designation based on its own kind (tajjāpaññatti), established by being superimposed according to convention, common to its own kind, distinct from other kinds, and belonging to the inherent nature of elements like the earth element and touch, which are differentiated by distinctions of time, place, etc.

So pana kammādisaṃsaṭṭho, suddho cāti duvidho. Tattha kammādīsu dutiyādīnaṃ vidhīyamānattā kammādisaṃsaggarahito liṅgasaṅkhyāparimāṇayutto, tabbinimuttupasaggādipadatthabhūto ca suddho saddattho idha liṅgattho nāma.

But it is of two kinds: associated with the object, etc., and pure. Herein, because the second case, etc., are enjoined in relation to objects, etc., the pure word-meaning—which is devoid of association with objects, etc., but possessed of gender, number, and measure, and which is also the meaning of words such as prefixes that are free from these—is here called the meaning of the nominal stem.

Yo pana ākhyātakitakataddhitasamāsehi vutto kammādisaṃsaṭṭho attho, sopi dutiyādīnaṃ puna attanā vattabbassa atthavisesassābhāvena avisayattā, liṅgatthamattassa sambhavato ca paṭhamāyeva visayo.

Whatever meaning, connected with the object etc., is expressed by verbs, primary derivatives, secondary derivatives, and compounds, that too is the domain of the first case only, because there is no further special meaning for the other cases to express on their own, and because only the meaning of the nominal stem is possible.

Hoti cettha –

And here it is said:

Paṭhamāvupasaggatthe, kesañcatthe nipātasaddānaṃ;

Liṅgādike ca suddhe-bhihite kammādiatthepi.

The first case is used in the sense of prefixes, in the sense of certain particles, in the pure sense of the nominal stem and so on, and also in the sense of the object and so on when expressed.

Saliṅge tāva – eso puriso, ete purisā, esā kaññā, etā kaññāyo, etaṃ cittaṃ, etāni cittāni.

First, in the case of a word with gender: this man, these men, this girl, these girls, this mind, these minds.

Sasaṅkhye – eko dve.

In the case of a word with number: one, two.

Saparimāṇe – doṇo khārī āḷhakaṃ.

In the case of a word with measure: a doṇa, a khārī, an āḷhaka.

Liṅgādivinimutte sattāmatte – ca vā ha ahaṃ atthi sakkālabbhā iccādi.

In the sense of mere being, free from gender etc.: 'and,' 'or,' 'indeed,' 'I,' 'there is,' 'it is possible,' 'it is obtainable,' and so on.

“Liṅgatthe paṭhamā”ti adhikicca “ālapane cā”ti ālapanatthe ca paṭhamā, abhimukhaṃ katvā lapanaṃ ālapanaṃ, āmantanaṃ avhānanti attho.

Having made 'the first case is used in the sense of the nominal stem' the governing rule, the first case is also used in the sense of address by the rule 'and in address.' Addressing is speaking having turned someone to face one; it means calling or summoning.

Ettha ca āmantanaṃ nāma pageva laddhasarūpassa saddena abhimukhīkaraṇaṃ, katābhimukho pana “gacchā”tiādinā nayena kriyāya [M 0.0139] yojīyati, tasmā āmantanasamaye kriyāyogābhāvato idaṃ kārakavohāraṃ na labhati.

Herein, addressing is the act of making a being who has already obtained a form face one by means of sound. One who has been made to face one is then connected to an action by such means as 'Go!'. Therefore, since there is no connection to an action at the time of addressing, this does not obtain the designation of a case relation.

Vuttañca

And it has been said:

“Saddenābhimukhīkāro, vijjamānassa vatthuno;

Āmantanaṃ vidhātabbe, natthi ‘rājā bhave’tida”nti.

Addressing is the making face-to-face by sound of an existing being; it is not to be applied thus: 'May there be a king!'

Bho purisa ehi, bho purisā vā, bhavanto purisā etha.

O man, come; or O men, come; O sirs, come.

Kasmiṃ atthe dutiyā?

In what meaning is the second case used?

284. Kammatthe dutiyā.

284. The second case is used in the sense of the object.

Kammatthe liṅgamhā dutiyāvibhatti hoti.

The second case ending occurs after the nominal stem in the sense of the object.

Anabhihite evāyaṃ, “kammani dutiyāyaṃ tto”ti vacanañcettha ñāpakaṃ.

This applies only when the object is not otherwise expressed; and the statement 'in the object, the second case' is an indicator here.

Kiṃ kammaṃ?

What is the object?

“Yena vā kayirate taṃ karaṇa”nti ito “vā”ti vattate.

From the rule 'That by which something is done is the instrument,' the word 'or' is carried over here.

285. Yaṃ karoti taṃ kammaṃ.

285. That which one does is the object.

Yaṃ vā karoti, yaṃ vā vikaroti, yaṃ vā pāpuṇāti, taṃ kārakaṃ kammasaññaṃ hoti.

Whatever one does, or whatever one modifies, or whatever one attains, that factor is designated as the object.

Idha liṅgakālavacanamatantaṃ. Karīyatīti kammaṃ. Tattha kārakaṃ, sādhakaṃ kriyānipphattiyā kāraṇamuccate, taṃ pana kārakaṃ chabbidhaṃ kammaṃ kattā karaṇaṃ sampadānamapādānamokāso cāti. Tattha sabhāvato, parikappato vā kammādimhi satiyeva kriyābhāvato kammādīnaṃ channampi kārakavohāro siddhova hoti.

Here, gender, tense, and number are not primary. That which is done is called the object (kamma). In that context, the kāraka, the accomplisher, is called the cause for the accomplishment of the action; that kāraka is sixfold: object (kamma), agent (kattā), instrument (karaṇa), recipient (sampadāna), source (apādāna), and location (okāsa). There, whether by nature or by designation, only when the object and so forth exist is the action possible; thus, the conventional usage of the six kārakas—object, agent, etc.—is already established.

Taṃ [M 0.0140] pana kammaṃ tividhaṃ nibbattanīyaṃ vikaraṇīyaṃ pāpaṇīyañcāti. Yathā – mātā puttaṃ vijāyati, āhāro sukhaṃ janayati. Ghaṭaṃ karoti devadatto, kaṭṭhamaṅgāraṃ karoti, suvaṇṇaṃ keyūraṃ, kaṭakaṃ vā karoti, vīhayo lunāti. Devadatto nivesanaṃ pavisati, ādiccaṃ passati, dhammaṃ suṇāti, paṇḍite payirupāsati.

That object (kamma), however, is threefold: productive (nibbattanīya), transformative (vikaraṇīya), and attainable (pāpaṇīya). For example: a mother gives birth to a child; food produces happiness. Devadatta makes a pot; he makes wood into charcoal; he makes gold into a bracelet or an anklet; he harvests rice. Devadatta enters a house; he sees the sun; he hears the Dhamma; he attends upon the wise.

Vuttañca

And it has been said:

“Nibbattivikatippatti-bhedena tividhaṃ mataṃ;

Kattu kriyābhigammaṃ taṃ, sukhaṅgāraṃ nivesana”nti.

It is considered threefold by the distinctions of production, transformation, and attainment; that object is approached by the agent's action: happiness, charcoal, a house.

Ettha ca icchitānicchitakathitākathitādibhedamanapekkhitvā sabbasaṅgāhakavasena “yaṃ karoti taṃ kamma”nti vuttattā, atthantaravikappanavādhikārato ca sabbattha imināva kammasaññā hoti.

Here, without considering distinctions such as desired or undesired, expressed or unexpressed, etc., it is stated 'that which one does is the object' because it encompasses all; and due to the authority of preventing alternative meanings, the designation of object occurs everywhere only by this rule.

Tattha anicchitakammaṃ yathā – kaṇṭakaṃ maddati, visaṃ gilati, gāmaṃ gacchanto rukkhamūlaṃ upagacchati.

There, an undesired object (kamma) is, for example: he crushes a thorn; he swallows poison; while going to a village, he approaches the foot of a tree.

Akathitakammaṃ yathā – yaññadattaṃ kambalaṃ yācate brāhmaṇo. Ettha hi “kambala”miti kathitakammaṃ dvikammikāya yācanakriyāya pattumicchitatarattā. “Yaññadatta”miti appadhānattā akathitakammaṃ. Tathā samiddhaṃ dhanaṃ bhikkhate, ajaṃ gāmaṃ nayati, parābhavantaṃ purisaṃ, mayaṃ pucchāma gotamaṃ, bhagavā bhikkhū etadavoca iccādi.

An unexpressed object (akathitakamma) is, for example: a brahmin asks Yaññadatta for a blanket. Here, indeed, 'blanket' is the expressed object because it is more desired to be obtained by the verb of asking, which takes two objects. 'Yaññadatta' is the unexpressed object due to its being secondary. Similarly: he begs Samiddha for wealth; he leads a goat to the village; he asks a man who is being defeated; we ask Gotama; the Blessed One said this to the monks; and so on.

Abhihitakamme pana na hoti, yathā – kaṭo karīyate devadattena, sugatena desito dhammo, yaññadatto kambalaṃ yācīyate brāhmaṇena iccādi.

However, it does not occur in the case of an expressed object (abhihitakamma), for example: a mat is made by Devadatta; the Dhamma was taught by the Sugata; Yaññadatta is asked for a blanket by the brahmin; and so on.

“Dutiyā”ti adhikāro.

The heading is 'The Second Case'.

286. Gati [M 0.0141] buddhi bhuja paṭha hara kara sayādīnaṃ kārite vā.

286. Optionally, in the causative with verbs of going, knowing, eating, reciting, carrying, doing, lying down, and so on.

Gamu sappa gatimhi, budha bodhane, budha avagamane vā, bhuja pālanabyavaharaṇesu, paṭha byattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ, hara haraṇe, kara karaṇe, si saye iccevamādīnaṃ dhātūnaṃ payoge kārite sati payojjakakattubhūte kammani liṅgamhā dutiyāvibhatti hoti vā. Niccasampatte vikappatthoyaṃ, tena tassa pakkhe tatiyā hoti.

With gam (to go) and sapp (to crawl) in the sense of going; with budh (to know) in the sense of awakening, or budh in the sense of understanding; with bhuj (to eat/enjoy) in the sense of protecting or using; with paṭh (to recite) in the sense of clear articulation or speech; with har (to carry) in the sense of carrying; with kar (to do) in the sense of doing; with si (to lie down) in the sense of lying down; when these kinds of roots are used in the causative, the second case ending optionally occurs after the nominal stem for the object, which is the instigated agent. This is an option where the third case is otherwise invariably used; therefore, in the alternative, the third case occurs.

Yo koci puriso gāmaṃ gacchati, tamañño payojayati. Puriso purisaṃ gāmaṃ gamayati, purisena vā gāmaṃ gamayati. Evaṃ sissaṃ dhammaṃ bodheti ācariyo, mātā puttaṃ bhojanaṃ bhojayati, sissaṃ dhammaṃ pāṭheti ācariyo, puriso purisaṃ bhāraṃ hāreti, tathā puriso purisaṃ kammaṃ kārayati, purisena vā kammaṃ kārāpayati, puriso purisaṃ sayāpayati. Evaṃ sabbattha kārite kattukammani dutiyā.

If any man goes to the village, another causes him to go. A man causes a man to go to the village, or he causes him to go to the village by a man. Thus, the teacher makes the pupil understand the Dhamma; the mother feeds food to the child; the teacher makes the pupil recite the Dhamma; a man makes a man carry a load; similarly, a man makes a man do work, or he causes work to be done by a man; a man makes a man lie down. Thus, everywhere in the causative, the agent-object is in the second case.

Kāriteti kiṃ? Puriso gāmaṃ gacchati.

What is the purpose of saying 'in the causative'? Example: A man goes to the village.

Abhihite na bhavati, purisena puriso gāmaṃ gamīyate, sisso dhammaṃ bodhīyate iccādi.

It does not occur when the object is expressed, for example: a man is made to go to the village by a man; a pupil is made to understand the Dhamma; and so on.

287. Kāladdhānamaccantasaṃyoge.

287. In continuous connection with time and distance.

Accantaṃ nirantaraṃ saṃyogoaccantasaṃyogo. Kāladdhānaṃ dabbaguṇakriyāhi accantasaṃyoge tehi kāladdhānavācīhi liṅgehi dutiyāvibhatti hoti.

Continuous, uninterrupted connection is 'continuous connection' (accantasaṃyoga). When there is a continuous connection of time and distance with substance, quality, or action, the second case ending occurs after the nominal stems denoting time and distance.

Kāle tāva – sattāhaṃ gavapānaṃ, māsaṃ maṃsodanaṃ, saradaṃ ramaṇīyā nadī, sabbakālaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ nandanaṃ, māsaṃ sajjhāyati, tayo māse abhidhammaṃ desesi.

First, with respect to time: for a week, the cow's drink lasts; for a month, the meat-rice lasts; throughout autumn, the river is delightful; the Nandana grove is delightful at all times; he recites for a month; he taught the Abhidhamma for three months.

Addhāne [M 0.0142] – yojanaṃ vanarāji, yojanaṃ dīgho pabbato, kosaṃ sajjhāyati.

With respect to distance: a forest range extends for a league; the mountain is a league long; he recites over a distance of a kosa.

Accantasaṃyogeti kiṃ? Māse māse bhuñjati, yojane yojane vihāraṃ patiṭṭhāpesi.

What is the purpose of saying 'in continuous connection'? Example: He eats month by month; he established a monastery league by league.

288. Kammappavacanīyayutte.

288. When connected with kammappavacanīyas.

Kammappavacanīyehi nipātopasaggehi yutte yoge sati liṅgamhā dutiyāvibhatti hoti.

When there is connection with kammappavacanīyas, which are particles and prefixes, the second case ending occurs after the nominal stem.

Kammaṃ pavacanīyaṃ yesaṃ te kammappavacanīyā, parasamaññāvasena vā anvādayo kammappavacanīyā.

Those which specify an action are called kammappavacanīyas; or, by way of another's designation, anu and so on are kammappavacanīyas.

Tattha anusaddassa lakkhaṇe, sahatthe, hīne ca kammappavacanīyasaññā vuttā. Yathā – pabbajitamanu pabbajiṃsu, nadimanvavasitā bārāṇasī, nadiyā saha avabaddhāti attho, anu sāriputtaṃ paññavā.

There, the designation of kammappavacanīya is stated for the word anu in the sense of following, co-existence, and inferiority. For example: They went forth following the one who had gone forth; Benares is situated along the river, meaning 'bound together with the river'; he is wise, but inferior to Sāriputta.

Lakkhaṇādīsu “lakkhaṇi’tthambhūtakkhānabhāga vicchāsu pati pari anavo”ti pati pari anūnaṃ kammappavacanīyasaññā vuttā.

In the senses of characteristic, statement of being of such a nature, share, and pervasion, the designation of kammappavacanīya has been stated for pati, pari, and anu.

Lakkhaṇe sūriyuggamanaṃ pati dibbā bhakkhā pātubhaveyyuṃ, rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate cando, rukkhaṃ pari, rukkhaṃ anu.

In the sense of characteristic: Divine food would appear at the rising of the sun; the moon shines upon the tree; around the tree; along the tree.

Itthambhūtakkhāne sādhu devadatto mātaraṃ pati, mātaraṃ pari, mātaraṃ anu.

In the sense of a statement of being of such a nature: Devadatta is good towards his mother, with respect to his mother, and in relation to his mother.

Bhāge yadettha maṃ pati siyā, maṃ pari, maṃ anu, taṃ dīyatu.

In the sense of share: Whatever share here belongs to me, or is connected with me, or is for me, let that be given.

Vicchāyoge [M 0.0143] atthamatthaṃ pati saddo nivisati, rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate cando, rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ pari, rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ anu.

In connection with pervasion: The word applies to each and every meaning; the moon shines upon tree after tree, around tree after tree, and along tree after tree.

“Abhirabhāge”ti abhissa bhāgavajjitesu lakkhaṇādīsu kammappavacanīyasaññā vuttā. Taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato, sādhu devadatto mātaraṃ abhi.

Regarding "Abhirabhāge": The designation 'kammappavacanīya' is stated for 'abhi' in the senses of characteristic and so on, excluding the sense of share. "Indeed, such a fine report about the esteemed Gotama has gone forth." "Devadatta is good towards his mother."

Nipāte dhi brāhmaṇassa hantāra miccevamādi.

Regarding particles: "Fie upon the killer of a brahmin!" and so forth.

289. Kvaci dutiyā chaṭṭhīnamatthe.

289. Sometimes the accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive.

Chaṭṭhīnaṃ atthe kvaci dutiyāvibhatti hoti. Antarāabhito parito pati paṭibhātiyoge ayaṃ. Antarā ca rājagahaṃ antarā ca nāḷandaṃ addhānamaggappaṭipanno, rājagahassa ca nāḷandāya ca majjheti attho. Abhito gāmaṃ vasati, parito gāmaṃ vasati, nadiṃ nerañjaraṃ pati, nerañjarāya nadiyā samīpeti attho. Paṭibhantu taṃ cunda bojjhaṅgā, upamā maṃ paṭibhāti, upamā mayhaṃ upaṭṭhahatīti attho.

Sometimes the accusative case ending occurs in the sense of the genitive. This occurs in conjunction with 'antarā', 'abhito', 'parito', 'pati', and 'paṭibhāti'. For example: "He was traveling the road between Rājagaha and Nāḷanda," which means "in the middle of Rājagaha and Nāḷanda." "He dwells near the village." "He dwells around the village." "Towards the Nerañjarā River," which means "near the Nerañjarā River." "May the factors of enlightenment become clear to you, Cunda." "A simile occurs to me," which means "A simile arises for me."

“Kvaci dutiyā, atthe”ti ca vattate.

And "sometimes the accusative, in the sense" is carried forward.

290. Tatiyāsattamīnañca.

290. And of the instrumental and locative cases.

Tatiyāsattamīnamatthe ca kvaci liṅgamhā dutiyāvibhatti hoti.

Sometimes, in the sense of the instrumental and locative cases, the accusative case ending occurs from the nominal stem.

Tatiyatthe sace maṃ nālapissati, tvañca maṃ nābhibhāsasi, vinā saddhammaṃ kuto sukhaṃ, upāyamantarena na atthasiddhi.

In the sense of the instrumental: If he does not speak to me, and you do not address me. Where is happiness without the true Dhamma? Without a means, there is no attainment of the goal.

Sattamiyatthe [M 0.0144]– kāle, upānvajjhāvasassa payoge, adhisiṭṭhāvasānaṃ payoge, tappānacāre ca dutiyā.

In the sense of the locative, the accusative occurs: in the sense of time; in the use of the root 'vas' with the prefixes 'upa', 'anu', 'adhi', and 'ā'; in the use of the roots 'si' (to lie), 'ṭhā' (to stand), and 'ās' (to sit) with the prefix 'adhi'; and in the sense of drinking and wandering.

Kāle tāva – pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā, ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā. Imaṃ rattiṃ cattāro mahārājāno.

First, in the sense of time: having dressed in the morning; at one time the Blessed One; this night the four great kings.

Upādipubbassa vasadhātussa payoge – gāmaṃ upavasati, gāmaṃ anuvasati, vihāraṃ adhivasati, gāmaṃ āvasati, agāraṃ ajjhāvasati. Tathā pathaviṃ adhisessati, gāmaṃ adhitiṭṭhati, gāmaṃ ajjhāvasati.

In the use of the root 'vas' preceded by 'upa' and so on: he dwells near the village; he dwells near the village; he dwells in the monastery; he dwells in the village; he dwells in the house. Similarly: he will lie down on the ground; he stands over the village; he dwells in the village.

Tappānacāresu – nadiṃ pivati, gāmaṃ carati iccādi.

In the sense of drinking and wandering: "he drinks the river," "he wanders through the village," and so forth.

Kasmiṃ atthe tatiyā?

In what sense is the instrumental case used?

291. Karaṇe tatiyā.

291. The instrumental case is used in the sense of the instrument.

Karaṇakārake tatiyāvibhatti hoti.

The instrumental case ending occurs in the sense of the instrument.

Kiṃ karaṇaṃ?

What is an instrument?

292. Yena vā kayirate taṃ karaṇaṃ.

292. That by which something is done is an instrument.

Yena vā kattā upakaraṇabhūtena vatthunā kriyaṃ abyavadhānena karoti, yena vā vikaroti, yena vā pāpuṇāti, taṃ kārakaṃ karaṇasaññaṃ hoti.

That by which the agent performs an action directly by means of an auxiliary object, or by which he alters something, or by which he obtains something—that case is designated as the instrument.

Karīyate anenāti karaṇaṃ, ettha ca satipi sabbakārakānaṃ kriyāsādhakatte “yena vā kayirate”ti visesetvā vacanaṃ kattūpakaraṇabhūtesu kārakesu sādhakatamasseva gahaṇatthaṃ.

It is done by this, therefore it is an instrument. Here, even though all cases are accomplishers of action, the statement "by which it is done" is made specifically to include only the most effective instrument among the cases that are auxiliary to the agent.

Vuttañca [M 0.0145]

And it has been said:

“Yassa sabbavisesena, kriyāsaṃsiddhihetutā;

Sambhāvīyati taṃ vuttaṃ, karaṇaṃ nāma kāraka”nti.

“That which, in all respects, is considered to be the cause of the complete accomplishment of an action, that is called the case of the instrument.”

Taṃ pana duvidhaṃ ajjhattika bāhiravasena.

That, however, is twofold, by way of internal and external.

Yathā – hatthena kammaṃ karoti, cakkhunā rūpaṃ passati, manasā dhammaṃ viññāya. Dattena vīhayo lunāti, agginā kuṭiṃ jhāpeti.

For example: one does work with the hand; one sees forms with the eye; having cognized a phenomenon with the mind. One harvests rice with a sickle; one burns a hut with fire.

“Tatiyā”ti adhikāro.

“The instrumental case” is the governing rule.

293. Kattari ca.

293. And in the agent.

Kattari ca kārake liṅgamhā tatiyāvibhatti hoti. Caggahaṇena itthambhūtalakkhaṇe, kriyāpavagge, pubbasadisasamūnattha kalaha nipuṇa missaka sakhilatthādiyoge, kāladdhānesu, paccattakammatthapañcamiyatthādīsu ca tatiyā.

And the instrumental case ending occurs from the nominal stem in the agent case. And by the particle 'ca', the instrumental case also occurs in the sense of a mark of being such, in the completion of an action, in conjunction with words meaning prior, similar, deficient, quarrel, skilled, mixed, friendly, and so forth, in expressions of time and distance, and in the sense of the reflexive, the object, the ablative, and so forth.

Ko ca kattā?

And who is the agent?

294. Yo karoti sa kattā.

294. He who performs is the agent.

Yo kriyaṃ attappadhāno hutvā karoti, so kattusañño hoti.

He who performs an action, being primary himself, is designated as the agent.

So tividho suddhakattā hetukattā kammakattāti. Tattha yo sayameva kriyaṃ karoti, so suddhakattā. Yo aññaṃ kātuṃ samatthaṃ akarontaṃ kammaṃ niyojeti, so hetukattā, yathā – gantuṃ samattho devadatto, tamañño payojeti “gamayati devadatta”nti.

That is threefold: the primary agent, the causal agent, and the action-agent. Here, one who performs an action by himself is the primary agent. One who assigns an action to another who is capable of doing it but is not yet doing it, is the causal agent, for example: Devadatta is capable of going, and another employs him, saying, "He makes Devadatta go."

Yaṃ pana tattha tattha gacchati devadatto, tamañño payojayati “gamayati devadatta”nti hetvatthanidassanaṃ, tampi sāmatthiyadassanavasena [M 0.0146] vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. Aññathā yadi sayameva gacchati, kiṃ tattha payojakabyāpārena akarontaṃ balena kārayati, pāsāṇaṃ uṭṭhāpayatītiādikañca na sijjheyya.

But wherever Devadatta goes, another instigates him, as in ‘He makes Devadatta go’—this is an example showing the meaning of a cause, and it should be understood that this too is stated from the perspective of demonstrating capacity. Otherwise, if he goes by himself, what is the use of the instigator's effort? And the meaning of making one who is not acting act by force, and examples such as making a stone rise, would not be established.

Ettha pana

Here, however,

“Kattā”ti vattate.

‘The agent’ is understood.

293. Yo kāreti sa hetu.

293. He who causes another to act is the causal agent.

Yo kattāraṃ kāreti, so hetusañño hoti, kattā cāti hetukattusaññā.

He who causes an agent to act is designated as the causal agent, and he is also an agent; hence the designation ‘causal agent’.

Yo pana parassa kriyaṃ paṭicca kammabhūtopi sukarattā sayameva sijjhanto viya hoti, so kammakattā nāma, yathā – sayaṃ karīyate kaṭo, sayameva paccate odanoti.

But one who, dependent on another's action, even though being an object, appears to accomplish the action by himself due to its ease, is called the action-agent, for example: ‘The mat is made by itself; the rice cooks by itself.’

Vuttañca

And it has been said:

“Attappadhāno kiriyaṃ, yo nibbatteti kārako;

Appayutto payutto vā, sa kattāti pavuccati.

‘That agent who, being primary himself, produces an action, whether unengaged or engaged, is called the agent.

Hetukattāti kathito,

Kattuno yo payojako;

Kammakattāti sukaro,

Kammabhūto kathīyate”ti.

He who is the instigator of the agent is called the causal agent; that which is easily done, being an object, is called the action-agent.’

Nanu ca “saṃyogo jāyate”tiādīsu kathaṃ pure asato jananakriyāya kattubhāvosiyāti? Vuccate – lokasaṅketasiddho hi saddappayogo, avijjamānampi hi loko saddābhidheyyatāya vijjamānaṃ viya gahetvā voharati[M 0.0147], vikappabuddhigahitākāroyeva hi saddenābhidhīyate, na tu vatthusabhāvo, aññathā sutamayañāṇenapi paccakkhena viya vatthusabhāvasacchikaraṇappasaṅgo ca musāvāda kudiṭṭhivādādīnamabhāvappasaṅgo ca siyā, tasmā buddhiparikappitapaññattivasenapi saddappavatti hotīti asato saṃyogādissapi hoteva jananakriyāya kattukārakatāti.

But surely, in cases like ‘a conjunction arises,’ how can something that did not exist before have the state of being an agent for the action of arising? It is said: The use of words is indeed established by worldly convention. For the world speaks of even that which is non-existent as if it were existent, taking it as such due to its being expressible by words. Indeed, what is expressed by a word is merely a form grasped by conceptual thought, not the intrinsic nature of the thing. Otherwise, there would be the unwanted consequence that even knowledge derived from hearing could realize the intrinsic nature of things as if by direct perception, and there would also be the unwanted consequence that false speech, wrong views, and the like would not exist. Therefore, the functioning of words occurs even by the power of a designation conceived by the intellect. Thus, even for a non-existent conjunction and so on, there is indeed the state of being the agent-case for the action of arising.

Yathāha

As it has been said:

“Vohāravisayo saddo, nekantaparamatthiko;

Buddhisaṅkappito attho, tassatthoti pavuccati.

‘The word is the domain of conventional usage, not exclusively of ultimate truth; the meaning conceived by the intellect is called its meaning.

Buddhiyā gahitattā hi, saṃyogo jāyate iti;

Saṃyogo vijjamānova, kattā bhavati jātiyā”ti.

Indeed, because it is grasped by the intellect, it is said, ‘a conjunction arises’; the conjunction, as if existing, becomes the agent of arising.’

Tatra tatiyā jinena desito dhammo, buddhena jito māro, ahinā daṭṭho naro, buddhena bodhito loko, saddhehi kārito vihāro.

Therein, the third case ending is used for the agent: the Dhamma was taught by the Conqueror; Māra was conquered by the Buddha; the man was bitten by the snake; the world was awakened by the Buddha; the monastery was caused to be built by the faithful.

Abhihite na bhavati. Kaṭaṃ karoti devadatto, kāreti vā.

It does not occur when the agent is expressed by the verb. For example: Devadatta makes a mat, or causes it to be made.

Itthambhūtassa lakkhaṇe – sā bhinnena sīsena paggharantena lohitena paṭivissakānaṃ ujjhāpesi, ūnapañcabandhanena pattena aññaṃ navaṃ pattaṃ cetāpeyya, tidaṇḍakena paribbājakamaddakkhi.

In the sense of a mark of being such: She, with her broken head and oozing blood, caused the neighbors to complain; with a bowl lacking five bindings, one should have another new bowl acquired; he saw the wandering ascetic by his triple staff.

Apavagge – ekāheneva bārāṇasiṃ pāyāsi, navahi māsehi vihāraṃ niṭṭhāpesi, yojanena adhītaṃ byākaraṇaṃ, kriyāpavaggoti kriyāya āsuṃ pariniṭṭhāpanaṃ.

In the sense of completion: He went to Bārāṇasī in a single day; he had the monastery completed in nine months; the grammar was mastered over the distance of a yojana. ‘Completion of action’ means the swift finishing of an action.

Pubbādiyoge [M 0.0148]– māsena pubbo, pitarā sadiso, mātarā samo, kahāpaṇena ūno, dhanena vikalo, asinā kalaho, ācārena nipuṇo, vācāya nipuṇo, guḷena missakaṃ, tilena missakaṃ, vācāya sakhilo, maṇinā attho, dhanena attho, pitarā tulyo.

In conjunction with words like ‘pubba’: prior by a month; similar to his father; equal to his mother; less by a kahāpaṇa; deficient in wealth; a quarrel by means of a sword; skilled in conduct; skilled in speech; mixed with molasses; mixed with sesame; friendly in speech; a need for a gem; a need for wealth; equal to his father.

Kāladdhānesu – māsena bhuñjati, yojanena gacchati.

In expressions of time and distance: he eats over a month; he goes for a yojana.

Paccatte – attanāva attānaṃ sammannati.

In the sense of the reflexive: he appoints himself by himself.

Kammatthe – tilehi khette vapati.

In the sense of the object: he sows sesame seeds in the field.

Pañcamiyatthe – sumuttā mayaṃ tena mahāsamaṇena.

In the sense of the ablative: We are well freed from that great ascetic.

296. Sahādiyoge ca.

296. And in conjunction with ‘saha’ and so forth.

Saha saddhiṃ samaṃ nānā vinā alaṃ kimiccevamādīhi yoge liṅgamhā tatiyāvibhatti hoti, casaddena sahatthepi.

In conjunction with ‘saha,’ ‘saddhiṃ,’ ‘samaṃ,’ ‘nānā,’ ‘vinā,’ ‘alaṃ,’ ‘kiṃ,’ and so forth, the third case ending occurs after the nominal stem; and by the particle ‘ca,’ also when it has the meaning of ‘saha’.

Tattha sahasaddena yogo kriyā guṇa dabba samavāye sambhavati. Yathā – vitakkena saha vattati, puttena saha thūlo, antevāsikasaddhivihārikehi saha ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ lābho, nisīdi bhagavā saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena, sahassena samaṃ mitā, sabbehi me piyehi manāpehi nānābhāvo vinābhāvo, saṅgho vināpi gaggena uposathaṃ kareyya, alaṃ te idha vāsena, kiṃ me ekena tiṇṇena, purisena thāmadassinā, kiṃ te jaṭāhi dummedha, kiṃ te ajinasāṭiyā.

Therein, conjunction with the word ‘saha’ occurs in the case of action, quality, substance, or concomitance. For example: he proceeds with thought; he is stout together with his son; the gain of teachers and preceptors is together with their pupils and co-residents; the Blessed One sat down together with the community of monks; measured equally with a thousand; separation and parting from all my dear and beloved ones; the Saṅgha could perform the Uposatha even without Gaggā; enough of your living here; what use to me is one who has crossed over, a man showing strength? What use are matted locks to you, foolish one? What use is an antelope skin robe to you?

Sahatthe [M 0.0149]– devadatto rājagahaṃ pāvisi kokālikena pacchāsamaṇena, dukkho bālehi saṃvāso.

In the sense of ‘with’: Devadatta entered Rājagaha with Kokālika as his junior monk; painful is association with fools.

297. Hetvatthe ca.

297. And in the sense of cause.

Yogaggahaṇamihānuvattate, hetvatthe, hetvatthappayoge ca liṅgamhā tatiyāvibhatti hoti.

The taking up of ‘conjunction’ continues here. In the sense of cause, and in the application of words with the sense of cause, the third case ending occurs after the nominal stem.

Kismiñci phale diṭṭhasāmatthiyaṃ kāraṇaṃ hetu, soyeva attho, tasmiṃ hetvatthe, annena vasati, dhammena vasati, vijjāya vasati.

A cause (hetu) is a reason whose capacity is seen in some result; that is the very meaning. In that sense of cause: he lives by food; he lives by the Dhamma; he lives by knowledge.

Na jaccāvasalo hoti,

Na jaccā hoti brāhmaṇo;

Kammunā vasalo hoti,

Kammunā hoti brāhmaṇo.

Not by birth is one an outcast, not by birth is one a brahmin; by action one is an outcast, by action one is a brahmin.

Dānena bhogavā, ācārena kulī.

By giving, one becomes wealthy; by conduct, one is of good family.

Kena pāṇi kāmadado, kena pāṇi madhussavo;

Kena te brahmacariyena, puññaṃ pāṇimhi ijjhati.

By what is the hand a giver of desires? By what is the hand a source of sweetness? By what holy life of yours does merit prosper in the hand?

Hetvatthappayoge – kena nimittena, kena payojanena, kenaṭṭhena, kena hetunā vasati.

In the application of the sense of cause: by what sign, by what purpose, for what reason, by what cause does one dwell?

298. Sattamyatthe ca.

298. And in the sense of the locative.

Sattamyatthe ca liṅgamhā tatiyāvibhatti hoti.

And in the locative sense, the third case ending is used after the nominal stem.

Kāladdhānadisādesādīsu cāyaṃ. Tena samayena, tena kālena, kālena dhammassavaṇaṃ, so vo mamaccayena satthā, māsena bhuñjati, yojanena dhāvati. Puratthimena dhataraṭṭho, dakkhiṇena virūḷhako, pacchimena virūpakkho, uttarena [M 0.0150] kasivanto janoghamaparena ca, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami iccādi.

And this is used in expressions of time, distance, direction, place, and so forth. For example: at that time, at that period, hearing the Dhamma at the proper time, he is your teacher after my passing away. He eats for a month, he runs for a yojana. In the east is Dhataraṭṭha, in the south is Virūḷhaka, in the west is Virūpakkha, in the north is Kuvera, and beyond is Janogha. He approached where the Blessed One was, and so on.

299. Yenaṅgavikāro.

299. By which limb there is a defect.

Yena byādhimatā aṅgena aṅgino vikāro lakkhīyate, tattha tatiyāvibhatti hoti. Ettha ca aṅgamassa atthīti aṅgaṃ, sarīraṃ. Akkhinā kāṇo, hatthena kuṇī, pādena khañjo, piṭṭhiyā khujjo.

The third case ending is used for that diseased limb of a person by which a defect is observed. Here, aṅga refers to a part of the body. For example: blind in one eye, crippled in the hand, lame in the foot, hunchbacked.

300. Visesane ca.

300. And in specification.

Visesīyati visesitabbaṃ anenāti visesanaṃ, gottādi. Tasmiṃ gottanāmajātisippavayoguṇasaṅkhāte visesanatthe tatiyāvibhatti hoti, casaddena pakatiādīhi ca. Gottena gotamo nātho.

That by which a thing to be distinguished is distinguished is called a 'distinguishing attribute' (visesana), such as clan and so forth. In that sense of a distinguishing attribute, enumerated as clan, name, birth, craft, age, or quality, the third case ending is used; and by the word 'ca', also with natural disposition and so forth. For example: By clan, the Lord is Gotama.

Sāriputtoti nāmena, vissuto paññavā ca so;

Jātiyā khattiyo buddho, loke appaṭipuggalo.

By name he was Sāriputta, renowned and wise; by birth a Khattiya, the Buddha, a person without peer in the world.

Tadahu pabbajito santo, jātiyā sattavassiko;

Sopi maṃ anusāseyya, sampaṭicchāmi matthake.

Being one who went forth on that very day, and seven years old by birth, should even he instruct me, I would receive it upon my head.

Sippena naḷakāro so, ekūnatiṃso vayasā, vijjāya sādhu, paññāya sādhu, tapasā uttamo, suvaṇṇena abhirūpo.

By craft, he is a reed-worker; by age, twenty-nine; good by means of knowledge, good by means of wisdom; supreme in ascetic practice; handsome as gold.

Pakatiādīsu – pakatiyā abhirūpo, yebhuyyena mattikā, samena dhāvati, visamena dhāvati, dvidoṇena dhaññaṃ kiṇāti, sahassena assake kiṇāti iccādi.

In the case of natural disposition and so forth: handsome by nature; mostly clay; he runs evenly; he runs unevenly; he buys grain for two doṇas; he buys horses for a thousand, and so on.

Kasmiṃ atthe catutthī?

In what sense is the fourth case ending used?

301. Sampadāne [M 0.0151] catutthī.

301. The fourth case ending is used for the recipient (sampadāna).

Sampadānakārake liṅgamhā catutthīvibhatti hoti.

In the case-relation of the recipient, the fourth case ending is used after the nominal stem.

Kiñca sampadānaṃ?

And what is the recipient (sampadāna)?

302. Yassa dātukāmo rocate dhārayate vā taṃ sampadānaṃ.

302. The one to whom another wishes to give, to whom something is pleasing, or to whom something is owed, that is the recipient (sampadāna).

Yassa vā dātukāmo, yassa vā rocate, yassa vā dhārayate, taṃ kārakaṃ sampadānasaññaṃ hoti. Sammā padīyate assāti sampadānaṃ, paṭiggāhako.

The case-relation concerning one to whom another wishes to give, or to whom something is pleasing, or to whom something is owed, is termed the recipient (sampadāna). It is called 'sampadāna' because something is properly given to this one; it is the receiver.

Taṃ pana tividhaṃ diyyamānassānivāraṇajjhesanānumativasena. Yathā – buddhassa pupphaṃ yajati, bodhirukkhassa jalaṃ dadāti. Ajjhesane – yācakānaṃ dhanaṃ dadāti. Anumatiyaṃ – bhikkhūnaṃ dānaṃ deti.

That recipient is threefold: by way of non-rejection of what is being given, by way of solicitation, and by way of consent. For example: he offers flowers to the Buddha; he gives water to the Bodhi tree. In the case of solicitation: he gives wealth to beggars. In the case of consent: he gives a gift to the monks.

Yathāha

As it is said:

“Anirākaraṇārādha-nābbhanuññavasena hi;

Sampadānaṃ tidhā vuttaṃ, rukkha yācaka bhikkhavo”ti.

Indeed, the recipient is said to be threefold: by way of non-rejection, solicitation, and permission, exemplified by the tree, the beggar, and the monks.

Dātukāmoti kiṃ? Rañño daṇḍaṃ dadāti.

Why the specification 'wishing to give'? He gives a fine to the king.

Rocanādīsu pana – samaṇassa rocate saccaṃ, māyasmantānampi saṅghabhedo ruccittha, yassāyasmato khamati, devadattassa suvaṇṇacchattaṃ dhārayate yaññadatto.

But in the case of 'pleasing' and so forth: truth is pleasing to the ascetic; a schism in the Sangha was pleasing even to the venerable ones; whatever is acceptable to the venerable one; Yaññadatta owes Devadatta a golden parasol.

“Sampadānaṃ, vā”ti ca vattate.

And the phrase 'or for the recipient' carries forward.

303. Silāgha hanu ṭhā sapa dhāra piha kudha duhi ssāsūya rādhikkha paccāsuṇa anupatigiṇapubbakattārocanatthatadattha tumatthālamattha maññānādarappāṇini gatyatthakammani āsisattha sammuti bhiyyasattamyatthesu ca.

303. Also with verbs meaning: to praise, to conceal, to stand still, to curse, to owe, to desire, to be angry, to harm, to be envious, to disparage, to succeed or to harm, to see or to mark; with promising, with approving; for the agent of a prior action in the sense of informing; in the sense of 'for the purpose of that'; in the sense of the infinitive; in the sense of 'enough for'; with the verb 'to think' in the sense of disregard for an inanimate object; for the object of verbs of motion; in the sense of a blessing; in the sense of agreement; in the sense of 'more than'; and in the sense of the locative.

Catuppadamidaṃ[M 0.0152]. Silāgha katthane, hanu apanayane, ṭhā gatinivattimhi, sapa akkose, dhara dhāraṇe, piha icchāyaṃ iccetesaṃ dhātūnaṃ payoge, kudha kope, duha jighaṃsāyaṃ, issa issāyaṃ, usūya dosāvikaraṇe iccetesaṃ tadatthavācīnañca dhātūnaṃ payoge ca rādha hiṃsāsaṃrādhesu, ikkha dassanaṅkesūti imesaṃ payoge ca pati āpubbassa su savaṇeti imassa ca anupatipubbassa gesaddeti imassa ca pubbakattā ca ārocanatthappayoge, tadatthe, tumatthe, alamatthappayoge ca maññatippayoge anādare appāṇini ca gatyatthānaṃ kammani ca āsisatthappayoge ca sammuti bhiyyappayogesu ca sattamyatthe cāti taṃ kammādikārakaṃ sampadānasaññaṃ hoti, casaddaggahaṇena pahiṇatikappati pahoti upamāñjalikaraṇa phāsu atthaseyyappabhutiyoge ca pure viya catutthī.

This is a four-part rule. In the use of these roots: `silāgha` in the sense of praising, `hanu` in the sense of concealing, `ṭhā` in the sense of ceasing motion, `sapa` in the sense of cursing, `dhara` in the sense of holding or owing, `piha` in the sense of desiring; and in the use of these roots and others with the same meaning: `kudha` in the sense of anger, `duha` in the sense of wishing to harm, `issa` in the sense of envy, `usūya` in the sense of exposing faults; and in the use of these: `rādha` in the senses of harming and succeeding, `ikkha` in the senses of seeing and marking; and in the use of the root `su` (to hear) preceded by `paṭi` and `ā`, and the root `ge` (to sing or recite) preceded by `anu` and `paṭi`; and for the agent of a prior action in the application of the sense of informing; in the sense of 'for that purpose'; in the sense of the infinitive; in the application of the sense of 'enough'; and in the use of `maññati` with disregard towards an inanimate object; and for the object of verbs of motion; and in the application of the sense of a blessing; and in the applications of agreement and excess; and in the sense of the locative—that case-relation, which is the object and so forth, is termed the recipient (sampadāna). And by the inclusion of the word 'ca', the fourth case ending is also used as before in conjunction with `pahiṇati` (to send), `kappati` (to be suitable), `pahoti` (to be able), `upamā` (comparison), `añjalikaraṇa` (making a gesture of reverence), `phāsu` (comfort), `attha` (purpose), `seyya` (lying down), and so forth.

Silāghādippayoge tāva – buddhassa silāghate. Upajjhāyassa silāghate, thometīti attho.

First, in the use of `silāgha` and so forth: one praises the Buddha. One praises the preceptor; the meaning is 'one extols'.

Hanute mayhameva, hanute tuyhameva, apalapatīti attho.

He conceals from me alone; he conceals from you alone; the meaning is 'he conceals'.

Upatiṭṭheyya sakyaputtānaṃ vaḍḍhakī, ettha ca upaṭṭhānaṃ nāma upagamanaṃ. Bhikkhussa bhuñjamānassa pānīyena vā vidhūpanena vā upatiṭṭheyya.

A carpenter should attend to the sons of the Sakyans. And here, 'attending' means approaching. One should attend to a monk while he is eating, with water or with a fan.

Tuyhaṃ sapate, mayhaṃ sapate, ettha ca sapanaṃ nāma saccakaraṇaṃ.

He swears to you, he swears to me. And here, swearing means making an asseveration.

Dhārayatippayoge dhanikoyeva sampadānaṃ, suvaṇṇaṃ te dhārayate, iṇaṃ dhārayatīti attho. Tassa rañño mayaṃ nāgaṃ dhārayāma.

In the use of `dhārayati` (to hold/owe), the creditor is indeed the recipient. 'He owes you gold,' 'he owes a debt'—such is the meaning. We hold the nāga for that king.

Pihappayoge [M 0.0153] icchitoyeva, devāpi tassa pihayanti tādino, devāpi tesaṃ pihayanti, sambuddhānaṃ satīmataṃ, patthentīti attho.

In the use of `piha` (to desire), it is indeed the desired one (who is the dative). Even the gods desire such a one. Even the gods desire them, the perfectly enlightened and mindful ones, meaning they long for them.

Kodhādiatthānaṃ payoge yaṃ pati kopo, tassa kujjha mahāvīra, yadihaṃ tassa kuppeyyaṃ.

In the use of verbs with the meaning of anger, etc., for the one towards whom there is anger: 'Be angry at him, O great hero,' 'If I were to be angry at him.'

Duhayati disānaṃ megho, yo mittānaṃ na dubbhati.

The cloud harms the directions. He who does not harm friends.

Titthiyā issanti samaṇānaṃ.

Heretics are envious of the ascetics.

Dujjanā guṇavantānaṃ usūyanti, kā usūyā vijānataṃ.

The wicked are envious of the virtuous; what envy is there for the discerning?

Rādhikkhappayoge yassa vipucchanaṃ kammavikhyāpanatthaṃ, vādhikārato dutiyā ca. Ārādho me rañño, rañño aparajjhati, rājānaṃ vā aparajjhati, kyāhaṃ ayyānaṃ aparajjhāmi, kyāhaṃ ayye aparajjhāmi vā.

In the use of (verbs from the roots) `rādh` and `ikkh`, when questioning is for the purpose of revealing an action; and optionally, by extension, the second case (accusative) is also used. For example: 'He succeeds for me with the king,' 'He offends the king,' or 'He offends the king.' 'In what do I offend the venerable ones?' or 'In what do I offend the venerable ones?'

Āyasmato upālittherassa upasampadāpekkho upatisso, āyasmantaṃ vā.

Upatissa is a candidate for higher ordination from the venerable elder Upāli, or from the venerable one.

Paccāsuṇa anupatigiṇānaṃ pubbakattā ca suṇotissa dhātussa paccāyoge, giṇassa ca anupatiyoge pubbassa kammuno yo kattā, so sampadānasañño hoti. Yathā – bhagavā bhikkhū etadavoca, ettha “bhikkhū”ti akathitakammaṃ, “eta”nti kathitakammaṃ, pubbassa vacanakammassa kattā bhagavā. Bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ, āsuṇanti buddhassa bhikkhū, tathā bhikkhu janaṃ dhammaṃ sāveti, tassa bhikkhuno jano anugiṇāti, tassa bhikkhuno jano patigiṇāti, sādhukāradānādinā taṃ ussāhayatīti attho.

And the agent of a prior action in the case of `paccāsuṇa` (to listen back) and `anupatigiṇa` (to approve/accept): in the use of the root `suṇa` (to hear) with `paccā`, and `giṇa` with `anupati`, the agent of the prior action is termed the recipient. For example: The Blessed One said this to the monks. Here, 'monks' is the secondary object, 'this' is the primary object, and the Blessed One is the agent of the prior action of speaking. The monks listened back to the Blessed One. The monks listen to the Buddha. Likewise, a monk makes people hear the Dhamma. The people approve of that monk. The people accept that monk, meaning they encourage him with expressions of approval, gifts, and so forth.

Yo vadeti sa kattāti, vuttaṃ kammanti vuccati;

Yo paṭiggāhako tassa, sampadānaṃ vijāniyāti.

He who speaks is the agent, what is spoken is called the object; he who is the receiver thereof should be understood as the recipient.

Ārocanatthappayoge [M 0.0154] yassa āroceti, taṃ sampadānaṃ. Ārocayāmi vo bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo bhikkhave, āmantayāmi te mahārāja, āmanta kho taṃ gacchāmāti vā. Ettha ca ārocanasaddassa kathanappakāratthattā desanatthādippayogepi catutthī. Dhammaṃ vo desessāmi, desetu bhante bhagavā dhammaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ, yathā no bhagavā byākareyya, niruttiṃ te pavakkhāmi iccādi.

In the application of the sense of informing, the one to whom one informs is the recipient. For example: 'I inform you, monks,' 'I declare to you, monks,' 'I address you, great king,' or 'I bid you farewell, I go.' And here, since the word 'informing' has the meaning of various ways of speaking, the fourth case is also used in applications of teaching, etc. For example: 'I will teach you the Dhamma,' 'May the Blessed One, venerable sir, teach the Dhamma to the monks,' 'So that the Blessed One might explain to us,' 'I will declare the etymology to you,' and so on.

Tadatthe sampadānasaññā, catutthī ca.

In that sense (for that purpose), the recipient designation and the fourth case (occur).

“Ato, vā”ti ca vattate.

And the rules 'from this' and 'optionally' are carried forward.

304. Āya catutthekavacanassa tu.

304. Indeed, `āya` is substituted for the singular of the fourth case.

Akārantato liṅgamhā parassa catutthekavacanassa āyādeso hoti vā, saralopādi.

After a nominal stem ending in 'a', the singular of the fourth case ending that follows is optionally substituted by 'āya', involving vowel elision and so forth.

Buddhassatthāya dhammassatthāya saṅghassatthāya jīvitaṃ pariccajāmi, piṇḍapātaṃ paṭisevāmi neva davāya na madāya na maṇḍanāya na vibhūsanāya, ūnassa pāripūriyā, atthāya hitāya sukhāya saṃvattati.

For the sake of the Buddha, for the sake of the Dhamma, for the sake of the Sangha, I relinquish my life. I partake of almsfood not for sport, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification, but for the replenishment of what is lacking. It conduces to benefit, to welfare, to happiness.

Tumatthe – lokānukampāya, lokamanukampitunti attho. Tathā phāsuvihārāya.

In the sense of the infinitive (purpose): 'for compassion for the world,' meaning 'to have compassion for the world.' Likewise, 'for comfortable dwelling.'

Alaṃsaddassa atthā arahapaṭikkhepā. Arahatthe – alaṃ me rajjaṃ, alaṃ bhikkhu pattassa, akkhadhutto purisapuggalo nālaṃ dārabharaṇāya, alaṃ mallo mallassa, arahati mallo mallassa.

The meanings of the word `alaṃ` are fitness and prohibition. In the sense of fitness or sufficiency: 'I have had enough of kingship,' 'A bowl is sufficient for a bhikkhu,' 'A man who is a gambler is not fit to support a wife,' 'A wrestler is a match for a wrestler,' which means 'a wrestler is a match for a wrestler.'

Paṭikkhepe [M 0.0155]– alaṃ te idha vāsena, alaṃ me hiraññasuvaṇṇena, kiṃ me ekena tiṇṇena, kiṃ te jaṭāhi dummedha, kiṃ tettha catumaṭṭhassa.

In the sense of prohibition: 'Enough of your dwelling here,' 'Enough of my gold and silver,' 'What use is one or three to me?' 'What use are your matted locks, O fool?' 'What use is your fourfold staff there?'

Maññatippayoge anādare appāṇini kammaniyeva – kaṭṭhassa tuvaṃ maññe, kaḷiṅgarassa tuvaṃ maññe, jīvitaṃ tiṇāyapi na maññamāno.

In the use of `maññati` (to think) in the sense of disregard towards an inanimate object, (the dative is used). For example: 'I consider you as a piece of wood,' 'I consider you as a log,' 'not regarding life as even worth a blade of grass.'

Anādareti kiṃ? Suvaṇṇaṃ taṃ maññe. Appāṇinīti kiṃ? Gadrabhaṃ tuvaṃ maññe.

Why the specification 'in disregard'? 'I think it is gold.' Why the specification 'inanimate'? 'I think you are a donkey.'

Gatyatthakammani vādhikārato dutiyā ca. Appo saggāya gacchati, appo saggaṃ gacchati, nibbānāya vajantiyā, mūlāya paṭikasseyya, mūlaṃ paṭikasseyya.

For the object of verbs of motion, optionally by extension, the second case (accusative) is also used. For example: 'Few go to heaven,' 'Few go to heaven.' 'For one proceeding to Nibbāna,' 'He might turn back to the root,' 'He might turn back to the root.'

Āsīsanatthe āyubhaddakusalādiyogeyeva, āyasmato dīghāyu hotu, “totitā sasmiṃnāsū”ti ntussa savibhattissa to ādeso. Bhaddaṃ bhavato hotu, kusalaṃ bhavato hotu, anāmayaṃ bhavato hotu, sukhaṃ bhavato hotu, atthaṃ bhavato hotu, hitaṃ bhavato hotu, svāgataṃ bhavato hotu, sotthi hotu sabbasattānaṃ.

In the sense of blessing, only in connection with longevity, auspiciousness, welfare, and so forth: 'May the venerable one be long-lived!' 'May it be auspicious for you,' 'May it be wholesome for you,' 'May you be free from illness,' 'May it be pleasant for you,' 'May it be for your benefit,' 'May it be for your welfare,' 'May you be welcome,' 'May there be well-being for all beings.'

Sammutippayoge – sādhu sammuti me tassa bhagavato dassanāya.

In the usage of agreement: 'Good, I agree to see that Blessed One.'

Bhiyyappayoge bhiyyoso mattāya.

In the usage of 'more,' it is to a still greater degree.

Sattamiyatthe āvikaraṇa pātubhavanādiyoge – tuyhañcassa āvikaromi, tassa me sakko pāturahosi.

In the sense of the locative, in connection with revealing, manifesting, and so on: 'I reveal it to you,' 'Sakka appeared to me.'

Casaddaggahaṇena [M 0.0156] pahiṇādikriyāyoge, phāsuādināmapayoge ca – tassa pahiṇeyya, bhikkhūnaṃ dūtaṃ pāhesi, kappati samaṇānaṃ āyogo, ekassa dinnaṃ dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ pahoti, upamaṃ te karissāmi, añjaliṃ te paggaṇhāmi. Tathā tassa phāsu hoti, lokassattho, maṇinā me attho, seyyo me attho iccādi.

By the inclusion of the word `ca`, (the dative is used) in connection with actions of sending and so on, and with the use of nouns such as 'ease' and so on: 'One should send it to him,' 'He sent a messenger to the bhikkhus,' 'Striving is suitable for ascetics,' 'What is given to one suffices for two or three,' 'I will make a comparison for you,' 'I raise my hands in reverence to you.' Likewise, 'It is comfortable for him,' 'For the benefit of the world,' 'I have need of a jewel,' 'I have need of what is better,' and so on.

“Catutthī”ti vattate.

'The fourth case' is carried forward.

305. Namoyogādīsvapi ca.

305. And also in usages such as 'namo' and so on.

Namosaddayoge, sotthisvāgatādīhi ca yoge liṅgamhā catutthīvibhatti hoti. Namo te buddha vīratthu, namo karohi nāgassa, namatthu buddhānaṃ, namatthu bodhiyā, sotthi pajānaṃ, svāgataṃ te mahārāja, atho te adurāgataṃ.

In the usage of the word 'namo,' and in connection with 'sotthi,' 'svāgata,' and so on, the fourth case ending is used with the noun. 'Homage to you, O Buddha, O hero!', 'Pay homage to the Nāga,' 'Homage to the Buddhas,' 'Homage to the Bodhi Tree,' 'Well-being to the people,' 'Welcome to you, O great king,' and also 'You are most welcome.'

“Kāle, bhavissatī”ti ca vattate.

“In time” and “will be” are also understood.

306. Bhāvavācimhi catutthī.

306. The fourth case occurs in the sense of a state of being.

Bhāvavācimhi catutthīvibhatti hoti bhavissatikāle. Bhavanaṃ bhāvo. Paccissate, pacanaṃ vā pāko, pākāya vajati, pacituṃ gacchatīti attho. Evaṃ bhogāya vajati iccādi.

The fourth case ending occurs in the sense of a state of being in the future tense. Becoming is 'bhāva'. 'He will cook,' or cooking is 'pāka' (ripening); 'He goes for cooking' ('pākāya vajati'), meaning 'he goes to cook' ('pacituṃ gacchati'). Similarly, 'He goes for enjoyment,' and so on.

Kasmiṃ atthe pañcamī?

In what sense is the fifth case used?

307. Apādāne pañcamī.

307. The fifth case is used in the ablative.

Kimapādānaṃ?

What is the ablative?

308. Yasmādapeti [M 0.0157] bhayamādatte vā tadapādānaṃ.

308. That from which one departs, or from which fear arises, that is the ablative.

Yasmā vā avadhito apeti, yasmā vā bhayahetuto bhayaṃ bhavati, yasmā vā akkhātārā vijjaṃ ādadāti, taṃ kārakaṃ apādānasaññaṃ hoti. Apanetvā ito ādadātīti apādānaṃ.

That fixed point from which one departs, or that cause of fear from which fear arises, or that teacher from whom one receives knowledge—that factor is designated as 'apādāna' (ablative). It is called 'apādāna' because it means taking (ādāna) away (apa) from it.

Taṃ pana tividhaṃ visayabhedena niddiṭṭhavisayaṃ, upāttavisayaṃ, anumeyyavisayañcāti.

Moreover, it is threefold according to the distinction of its sphere: the directly indicated sphere, the implied sphere, and the inferable sphere.

Apādānasaññāvisayassa kriyāvisesassa niddiṭṭhattā niddiṭṭhavisayaṃ. Yathā – gāmā apenti munayo, nagarā niggato rājā.

It is the 'directly indicated sphere' because the specific action, which is the sphere for the ablative designation, is explicitly stated. For example: 'Sages depart from the village,' 'The king has gone out from the city.'

Ettha ca “pāpā cittaṃ nivāraye, pāpā nivārentī”tiādīsu yadipi kāyasaṃyogapubbakāpagamanaṃ natthi, tathāpi cittasaṃyogapubbakassa apagamanassa sambhavato iminā ca apādānasaññā.

Here, in instances such as 'One should restrain the mind from evil,' 'They restrain from evil,' and so on, although there is no departure preceded by physical connection, departure preceded by mental connection is possible, and thus it is also designated as ablative.

Yattha pana apagamanakriyaṃ upāttaṃ ajjhāhaṭaṃ visayaṃ katvā pavattati, taṃ upāttavisayaṃ. Yathā – valāhakā vijjotate vijju, kusūlato pacatīti. Ettha ca “valāhakā nikkhamma, kusūlato apanetvā”ti ca pubbakriyā ajjhāharīyati.

That is the 'implied sphere' where the rule operates concerning an implied or supplied action of departure. For example: 'Lightning flashes from the clouds,' 'He cooks from the granary.' Here, a prior action is supplied, such as 'having emerged from the clouds' and 'having taken from the granary.'

Anumeyyavisayaṃ yathā – māthurā pāṭaliputtakehi abhirūpā. Ettha hi kenaci guṇena ukkaṃsīyantīti anumeyyova kriyāviseso. Idha pana dūrantikādisutte vibhattaggahaṇena apādānasaññā.

The inferable sphere is, for example: 'The people of Mathurā are more beautiful than those of Pāṭaliputta.' Here, the specific action is to be inferred, namely that they are exalted by some quality. In this case, however, the ablative designation is due to the inclusion of the case ending in the rule concerning words meaning 'far,' 'near,' and so on.

Vuttañca

And it has been said:

“Niddiṭṭhavisayaṃ kiñci, upāttavisayaṃ tathā;

Anumeyyavisayañcāti, apādānaṃ tidhā mata”nti.

“Some is the directly indicated sphere, likewise the implied sphere, and the inferable sphere—thus, the ablative is considered threefold.”

Tadeva [M 0.0158] calācalavasena duvidhampi hoti.

That same ablative is also twofold, according to whether it is moving or unmoving.

Calaṃ yathā – dhāvatā hatthimhā patito aṅkusadhārī.

Moving, for example: 'The goad-holder fell from a running elephant.'

Acalaṃ yathā – pabbatā otaranti vanacarā.

Unmoving, for example: 'Forest-dwellers descend from the mountain.'

Bhayahetumhi – corā bhayaṃ jāyati, taṇhāya jāyatī bhayaṃ, pāpato uttasati, akkhātari – upajjhāyā sikkhaṃ gaṇhāti, ācariyamhā adhīte, ācariyato suṇāti.

In the sense of a cause of fear: 'Fear arises from a thief,' 'Fear arises from craving,' 'One is terrified of evil.' In the sense of a teacher: 'He receives training from the preceptor,' 'He learns from the teacher,' 'He hears from the teacher.'

“Apādāna”nti adhikāro.

'Ablative' is the governing rule.

309. Dhātunāmānamupasaggayogādīsvapi ca.

309. And also in connection with verbal roots, nouns, prefixes, and so on.

Dhātavo ca nāmāni ca dhātunāmāni, tesaṃ avihitalakkhaṇānaṃ dhātunāmānaṃ payoge, upasaggayoge ca ādisaddena nipātayoge ca taṃyuttaṃ kārakaṃ apādānasaññaṃ hoti.

Verbal roots and nouns are 'dhātunāmāni'. In the usage of these verbal roots and nouns, whose characteristics are not otherwise prescribed, and in connection with prefixes, and—by the word 'ādi'—in connection with particles, the factor associated with them is designated as ablative.

Dhātuppayoge tāva – parājiyoge yo asayho, pabhūyoge pabhavo, janiyoge jāyamānassa pakati ca. Yathā – buddhasmā parājenti aññatitthiyā. Himavatā pabhavanti pañca mahānadiyo, anavatattamhā mahāsarā pabhavanti, aciravatiyā pabhavanti kunnadiyo. Kāmato jāyatī soko, yasmā so jāyate gini, urasmā jāto putto, kammato jātaṃ indriyaṃ.

First, in the usage of verbal roots: in connection with 'parāji' (to be defeated), it is that which is unconquerable; in connection with 'pabhū' (to originate), it is the source; and in connection with 'jani' (to be born), it is the origin of what is being born. For example: 'Other sectarians are defeated by the Buddha.' 'The five great rivers originate from the Himālaya.' 'Great lakes originate from Lake Anotatta.' 'Small rivers originate from the Aciravatī.' 'Sorrow is born from desire.' 'From which that fire is born.' 'A son is born from the chest.' 'The faculty is born from kamma.'

Nāmappayoge aññatthitarādīhi yutte – nāññatra dukkhā sambhoti, nāññaṃ dukkhā nirujjhati, tato aññena kammena, tato itaraṃ, ubhato sujāto putto iccādi.

In the usage of nouns, when connected with 'añña,' 'aññatra,' 'itara,' and so on: 'It arises from nowhere else but suffering,' 'Nothing other than suffering ceases,' 'by another action than that,' 'other than that,' 'a son well-born from both,' and so on.

Upasaggayuttesu [M 0.0159] apaparīhi vajjanatthehi yoge, mariyādābhividhiatthe āyoge patinā patinidhipatidānatthena yoge ca. Yathā – apasālāya āyanti vāṇijā, sālaṃ vajjetvāti attho. Tathā paripabbatā devo vassati, pabbataṃ vajjetvāti attho. Mariyādāyaṃ – āpabbatā khettaṃ. Abhividhimhi – ābrahmalokā saddo abbhuggacchati, brahmalokaṃ abhibyāpetvāti attho.
