Patinidhimhi – buddhasmā pati sāriputto dhammadesanāya ālapati temāsaṃ. Patidāne – ghatamassa telasmā pati dadāti, kanakamassa hiraññasmā pati dadāti.

In connection with prefixes: when used with 'apa' and 'pari' in the sense of exclusion; in connection with 'ā' in the sense of boundary or pervasion; and in connection with 'pati' in the sense of substitution or exchange. For example: 'Merchants come from outside the hall,' meaning 'avoiding the hall.' Similarly, 'Rain falls outside the mountain,' meaning 'avoiding the mountain.' In the sense of a boundary: 'The field extends up to the mountain.' In the sense of pervasion: 'The sound rises up to the Brahma-world,' meaning 'pervading the Brahma-world.' In substitution: 'Sāriputta, in place of the Buddha, teaches the Dhamma for three months.' In exchange: 'He gives him ghee in return for oil,' 'He gives him gold in return for bullion.'

Nipātayuttesu rite nānā vinādīhi yoge – rite saddhammā kuto sukhaṃ labhati. Te bhikkhū nānākulā pabbajitā. Vinā saddhammā natthañño koci nātho loke vijjati. Ariyehi puthagevāyaṃ jano, yāva brahmalokā saddo abbhuggacchati.

In connection with particles, when used with 'rite,' 'nānā,' 'vinā,' and so on: 'Without the true Dhamma, from where can one obtain happiness?' 'Those bhikkhus have gone forth from various families.' 'Without the true Dhamma, no other protector is found in the world.' 'This person is separate from the noble ones.' 'The sound rises as far as the Brahma-world.'

Apiggahaṇena kammāpādānakārakamajjhepi pañcamī kāladdhānehi, pakkhasmā vijjhati migaṃ luddako, ito pakkhasmā migaṃ vijjhatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ māsasmā bhuñjati bhojanaṃ, kosā vijjhati kuñjaraṃ.

By the inclusion of 'api', the fifth case is also used for time and distance between the object and the agent. 'The hunter shoots the deer from a side's distance,' which means 'he shoots the deer from this side.' Similarly, 'He eats a meal over a month,' 'He shoots the elephant from a kosa's distance.'

Casaddaggahaṇena pabhutyādiatthe, tadatthappayoge ca – yatohaṃ bhagini ariyāya jātiyā jāto, yato sarāmi attānaṃ, yato pattosmi viññutaṃ, yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ, yato pabhuti, yato paṭṭhāya, tato paṭṭhāya iccādi.

By the inclusion of the word 'ca', also in the sense of 'pabhuti' (beginning) and so on, and in the usage of words with that meaning: 'Sister, since I was born with the noble birth,' 'since I remember myself,' 'since I have attained understanding,' 'since this was the cause,' 'from when onwards,' 'beginning from when,' 'beginning from then,' and so on.

310. Rakkhaṇatthānamicchitaṃ[M 0.0160].

310. The desired object of [verbs] meaning protection.

Rakkhaṇatthānaṃ dhātūnaṃ payoge yaṃ icchitaṃ, taṃ kārakaṃ apādānasaññaṃ hoti, cakārādhikārato anicchitañca. Rakkhaṇañcettha nivāraṇaṃ, tāyanañca. Kāke rakkhanti taṇḍulā, yavā paṭisedhenti gāvo.

In the application of verbal roots with the meaning of protection, that which is desired, that kāraka is designated as ablative; and due to the governing influence of 'ca', also that which is undesired. Herein, protection means warding off and guarding. 'They protect the rice from crows'; 'They keep the cows from the barley'.

Anicchitaṃ yathā – pāpā cittaṃ nivāraye, pāpānivārenti, rājato vā corato vā aggito vā udakato vā nānābhayato vā nānārogato vā nānāupaddavato vā ārakkhaṃ gaṇhantu.

The undesired, for example: 'One should restrain the mind from evil'; 'They restrain from evil.' 'May they take protection from the king, or from thieves, or from fire, or from water, or from various fears, or from various diseases, or from various calamities.'

“Icchita”miti vattate.

'Desired' is carried forward.

311. Yena vā’dassanaṃ.

311. Or by which disappearance [is desired].

Yena adassanamicchitaṃ antaradhāyantena, taṃ kārakaṃ apādānasaññaṃ hoti vā, antaradhānevāyaṃ. Upajjhāyā antaradhāyati sisso, nilīyatīti attho. Mātāpitūhi antaradhāyati putto.

That by means of which one who is hiding desires disappearance, that kāraka is optionally designated as ablative. This [rule applies] in the sense of disappearance. 'The pupil disappears from the preceptor,' meaning he hides. 'The son disappears from his parents.'

Vāti kiṃ? Jetavane antarahito. Yenāti kiṃ? Yakkho tattheva antaradhāyati.

What is the purpose of 'or'? 'He vanished in Jetavana.' What is the purpose of 'by which'? 'The yakkha disappears right there.'

312. Dūrantikaddhakālanimmānatvālopadisāyogavibhattārappayoga suddhappamocana hetu vivittappamāṇa pubbayoga bandhana guṇavacana pañha kathanathokākattūsu ca.

312. And in [the senses of] distance, nearness, measurement of distance and time, elision of 'tvā', connection with direction, distinction, usage of [words meaning] abstention, purity, release, cause, seclusion, measure, prior connection, binding, expression of quality, question, narration, small amount, and the non-agent.

Dūratthe, antikatthe, addhanimmāne, kālanimmāne, tvālope, disāyoge, vibhatte, āratippayoge, suddhatthappayoge, pamocanatthappayoge, hetvatthe, vivittatthappayoge, pamāṇatthe, pubbayoge, bandhanatthappayoge, guṇavacane[M 0.0161], pañhe, kathane, thokatthe, akattari ca yadavadhibhūtaṃ, hetukammādibhūtañca, taṃ kārakaṃ apādānasaññaṃ hoti, casaddena yathāyogaṃ dutiyā, tatiyā, chaṭṭhī ca.

In the sense of distance, nearness, measurement of distance, measurement of time, elision of the gerund, connection with direction, distinction, usage of [words meaning] abstention, usage of [words meaning] purity, usage of [words meaning] release, in the sense of cause, usage of [words meaning] seclusion, in the sense of measure, prior connection, usage of [words meaning] binding, in the expression of quality, in question, in narration, in the sense of a small amount, and in the non-agent, that kāraka which is the limit, and that which is the cause, object, etc., is designated as apādāna. By the word 'ca', the second, third, and sixth cases also apply as appropriate.

Ettha ca dūrantikañca dūrantikatthañcāti dūrantikanti sarūpekasesaṃ katvā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, tena dūrantikatthappayoge, tadatthe ca apādānasañño hoti.

Herein, it should be understood that 'dūrantika' (distance and nearness) and 'dūrantikattha' (the sense of distance and nearness) are stated as 'dūrantika' by making a `sarūpekasesa` (retention of one of similar forms). Therefore, in the application of words with the sense of distance and nearness, and in that sense itself, it is designated as apādāna.

Dūratthappayoge tāva – kīvadūro ito naḷakāragāmo, tato have dūrataraṃ vadanti, gāmato nātidūre. Ārakā te moghapurisā imasmā dhammavinayā, ārakā tehi bhagavā. Dūratthe – dūratova namassanti, addasa dūratova āgacchantaṃ.

First, in the application of [words with] the sense of distance: 'How far is Naḷakāra village from here?' 'Indeed, they say it is farther than that.' 'Not too far from the village.' 'Those foolish men are far from this Dhamma and Discipline.' 'The Blessed One is far from them.' In the sense of distance: 'They pay homage from afar.' 'He saw him coming from afar.'

Antikatthappayoge – antikaṃ gāmā, āsannaṃ gāmā, samīpaṃ gāmā, gāmassa samīpanti attho.

In the application of [words with] the sense of nearness: 'Near the village,' 'close to the village,' 'adjacent to the village,' meaning 'near the village.'

Dutiyā, tatiyā ca, dūraṃ gāmaṃ āgato, dūrena gāmena āgato, dūrato gāmā āgatoti attho. Dūraṃ gāmena vā. Antikaṃ gāmaṃ āgato, antikaṃ gāmena vā, āsannaṃ gāmaṃ, āsannaṃ gāmena vā iccādi.

And the second and third cases: 'He came to a distant village,' 'he came by a distant village,' meaning 'he came from a distant village.' Or, 'far by way of the village.' 'He came to a nearby village,' 'or near by way of the village,' 'close to the village,' 'or close by way of the village,' and so on.

Addhakālanimmāne nimmānaṃ nāma parimāṇaṃ, tasmiṃ gamyamāne – ito mathurāya catūsu yojanesu saṅkassaṃ, rājagahato pañcacattālīsayojanamatthake sāvatthi.

In the measurement of distance and time, 'nimmāna' means measurement. When that is understood: 'From here, Saṅkassa is four yojanas from Mathurā.' 'Sāvatthī is forty-five yojanas from Rājagaha.'

Kālanimmāne – ito ekanavutikappamatthake vipassī bhagavā loke udapādi, ito vassasahassaccayena buddho loke uppajjissati.

In the measurement of time: 'Ninety-one eons ago from now, the Blessed One Vipassī arose in the world.' 'After the passing of a thousand years from now, a Buddha will arise in the world.'

Tvāpaccayantassa lopo nāma tadatthasambhavepi avijjamānatā, tasmiṃ tvālope kammādhikaraṇesu – pāsādā saṅkameyya, pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvā saṅkameyyāti attho[M 0.0162]. Tathā hatthikkhandhā saṅkameyya, abhidhammā pucchanti, abhidhammaṃ sutvā vā, abhidhammā kathayanti, abhidhammaṃ paṭhitvā vā, āsanā vuṭṭhaheyya, āsane nisīditvā vā.

The elision of the 'tvā' suffix is its absence even when its meaning is present. In that elision, in relation to the object and the location: 'He should descend from the palace,' meaning 'having ascended the palace, he should descend.' Similarly, 'he should descend from the elephant’s shoulder'; 'they ask from the Abhidhamma,' meaning 'having heard the Abhidhamma'; 'they speak from the Abhidhamma,' meaning 'having studied the Abhidhamma'; 'he should rise from the seat,' meaning 'having sat on the seat.'

Disatthavācīhi yoge, disatthe ca – ito sā purimā disā, ito sā dakkhiṇā disā, ito sā pacchimā disā, ito sā uttarā disā, avīcito uparibhavaggā, uddhaṃ pādatalā, adho kesamatthakā iccādi. Disatthe – puratthimato dakkhiṇatotiādi. Ettha pana sattamiyatthe topaccayopi bhavissati.

In connection with words expressing direction, and in the sense of direction: 'From here is the eastern direction, from here is the southern direction, from here is the western direction, from here is the northern direction'; 'from Avīci up to the highest level of existence'; 'upward from the soles of the feet'; 'downward from the crown of the head'; and so on. In the sense of direction: 'from the east, from the south,' and so on. Here, however, the suffix '-to' also occurs in the locative sense.

Vibhattaṃ nāma sayaṃ vibhattasseva tadaññato guṇena vibhajanaṃ, tasmiṃ vibhatte – yato paṇītataro vā visiṭṭhataro vā natthi, attadanto tato varaṃ. Kiñcāpi dānato sīlameva varaṃ, tato mayā sutā assutameva bahutaraṃ, sīlameva sutā seyyo. Chaṭṭhī ca, channavutīnaṃ pāsaṇḍānaṃ pavaraṃ yadidaṃ sugatavinayo.

`Vibhatta` means distinguishing one thing from another by means of a quality. In that [sense of] distinction: 'Than which there is nothing more excellent or more distinguished, one who is self-restrained is better than that.' 'Although morality is indeed better than generosity.' 'Morality is indeed better than learning.' And the sixth case: 'Among the ninety-six sects, the best is this, the discipline of the Sugata.'

Āratippayogo nāma viramaṇatthasaddappayogo. Tattha – asaddhammā ārati, virati pāpā, pāṇātipātā veramaṇī, adinnādānā paṭivirato, appaṭivirato musāvādā.

`Āratippayoga` means the application of words with the meaning of abstaining. Therein: 'Abstinence from the bad Dhamma,' 'refraining from evil,' 'abstaining from killing living beings,' 'abstaining from taking what is not given,' 'not abstaining from false speech.'

Suddhatthappayoge – lobhanīyehi dhammehi suddho asaṃsaṭṭho, mātito ca pitito ca suddho anupakkuṭṭho agarahito.

In the application of [words with] the sense of purity: 'Pure, unmingled with enticing states'; 'pure with respect to mother and father, unblemished, irreproachable.'

Pamocanatthappayoge [M 0.0163]– parimutto dukkhasmāti vadāmi, mutto mārabandhanā, na te muccanti maccunā, muttohaṃ sabbapāsehi.

In the application of [words with] the sense of release: 'I declare, "Completely freed from suffering"'; 'freed from the bonds of Māra'; 'they are not freed from death'; 'I am freed from all snares.'

Hetvatthe, sarūpekasesassa gahitattā hetvatthappayoge ca sabbanāmato – kasmā nu tumhaṃ daharā na mīyare, kasmā idheva maraṇaṃ bhavissati, kasmā hetunā, yasmā ca kammāni karonti, yasmā tiha bhikkhave, tasmā tiha bhikkhave evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ, tasmā buddhosmi brāhmaṇa, yasmā kāraṇā, tasmā kāraṇā, kiṃ kāraṇā. Dutiyā, chaṭṭhī ca, kiṃ kāraṇaṃ, taṃ kissa hetu, kissa tumhe kilamatha.

In the sense of cause, and—because `sarūpekasesa` is employed—in the application of [words with] the sense of cause derived from all pronouns: 'Why indeed do your young ones not die?' 'Why will death occur right here?' 'For what reason?' 'And because they perform actions.' 'Because of this, O monks, therefore, O monks, thus should you train.' 'Therefore, O brahmin, I am the Buddha.' 'For which reason,' 'for that reason,' 'for what reason?' And the second and sixth cases: 'What is the reason?' 'For what reason is that?' 'Why do you toil?'

Kena hetunā, kena kāraṇena, yena midhekacce sattā, tena nimittena, tena vuttamiccādīsu “hetvatthe cā”ti tatiyā.

'By what reason,' 'by what cause,' 'whereby some beings here,' 'by that sign,' 'by that which is said,' and so on—in these instances, the instrumental case is used by the rule 'and in the sense of cause'.

Vivittaṃ nāma vivecanaṃ, tadatthappayoge – vivitto pāpakā dhammā, vivicceva kāmehi, vivicca akusalehi dhammehi.

'Vivitta' means seclusion. In the application of that meaning: 'Secluded from evil states'; 'indeed secluded from sensual pleasures'; 'secluded from unwholesome states.'

Pamāṇatthe tatiyā ca, āyāmato ca vitthārato ca yojanaṃ, gambhīrato ca puthulato ca yojanaṃ candabhāgāya parimāṇaṃ, parikkhepato navayojanasataparimāṇo majjhimapadeso.

And in the sense of measure, the instrumental case: 'A yojana in length and in breadth'; 'a yojana in depth and in thickness, the measure of a half-moon'; 'in circumference, the middle region is measured as nine hundred yojanas.'

Dīghaso nava vidatthiyo sugatavidatthiyā pamāṇikā kāretabbā.

Lengthwise, nine spans, standardized by the Sugata's span, should be made.

Ettha ca “smāhismiṃna”miccādito “smā”ti ca “so, vā”ti ca vattamāne

Here, while from [the rule] 'smāhismiṃna', etc., 'smā' is carried forward, and 'so' and 'vā' are also carried forward:

313. Dīghorehi[M 0.0164].

313. After `dīgha` and `ora`.

Dīgha oraicceteti smāvacanassa soādeso hoti vā.

After 'dīgha' and 'ora', the substitute 'so' occurs for the ending 'smā', optionally.

Dīghaso, dīghamhā vā, [oraso, oramhā vā] tatiyā ca, yojanaṃ āyāmena, yojanaṃ vitthārena, yojanaṃ ubbedhena sāsaparāsi.

Lengthwise, or from length; [near, or from nearness]; and the instrumental case: 'A yojana in length,' 'a yojana in width,' 'a yojana in height,' 'a heap of mustard seeds.'

Paṭhamatthavācakena pubbasaddena yogo pubbayogo, ettha ca pubbaggahaṇaṃ adisatthavuttino pubbādiggahaṇassupalakkhaṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, tena parādiyogepi. Yathā – pubbeva me bhikkhave sambodhā, ito pubbenāhosi, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, dhātuliṅgehi parā paccayā, tato aparena samayena, tato uttarimpi iccādi.

The connection with the word 'pubba', which expresses the meaning of 'prior', is 'pubbayoga'. And here, the inclusion of 'pubba' should be understood as indicative of the inclusion of 'pubba' and so on, which do not express direction; therefore, this also applies to connection with 'para' and so on. For example: 'Before my enlightenment, O monks'; 'before this, there was'; 'beyond that, the border countries'; 'after the roots and stems, the suffixes'; 'then, after some time'; 'then, further still'; and so on.

Bandhanatthappayoge bandhanahetumhi iṇe pañcamī, tatiyā ca hoti, satasmā baddho naro raññā, satena vā baddho naro.

In the application of the sense of binding, the fifth and third cases occur for the cause of binding, in the sense of debt: 'A man bound by the king on account of a hundred (in debt)'; 'or a man bound by a hundred (in debt).'

Phalasādhanahetubhūtassa guṇassa vacanaṃ guṇavacanaṃ, tasmiṃ guṇavacane pañcamī, tatiyā ca, issariyā janaṃ rakkhati rājā, issariyena vā, sīlato naṃ pasaṃsanti, sīlena vā, paññāya vimuttimano iccādi.

The expression of a quality that is the cause for achieving a result is 'guṇavacana'. In that 'guṇavacana', the fifth and third cases occur: 'The king protects the people on account of sovereignty, or by sovereignty'; 'they praise him on account of virtue, or by virtue'; 'the mind is liberated through wisdom'; and so on.

Pañhakathanesu – kutosi tvaṃ, kuto bhavaṃ, pāṭaliputtato. Ettha ca kathanaṃ nāma vissajjanaṃ.

In questions and statements: 'Where are you from?' 'Where is the venerable one from?' 'From Pāṭaliputta.' And here, 'kathana' (statement) means a reply.

Thokatthe asatvavacane karaṇe tatiyā ca, thokā muccati, thokena muccati vā, appamattakā muccati, appamattakena vā, kicchā muccati, kicchena vā.

In the instrumental sense, for a word meaning 'a small amount' that does not denote a being, the fifth and third cases are used: 'He is freed by a little,' or 'he is freed by a little'; 'he is freed by a trifle,' or 'he is freed by a trifle'; 'he is freed with difficulty,' or 'he is freed with difficulty.'

Akattari [M 0.0165] akārake ñāpakahetumhi – kammassa katattā upacitattā ussannattā vipulattā uppannaṃ hoti cakkhuviññāṇa, na tāvidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ ahetukaṃ sabbattha sabbadā sabbesañca ekasadisabhāvāpattito.

In the case of an indicative cause that is not an agent and not a kāraka: 'Eye-consciousness arises on account of kamma having been done, accumulated, amassed, and developed'; 'and this name-and-form is not without a cause, for that would lead to the consequence of a uniform nature for all, everywhere, and always.'

Hutvā abhāvato niccā, udayabbayapīḷanā;

Dukkhā avasavattittā, anattāti tilakkhaṇaṃ.

Because of ceasing to be after having been, it is impermanent; because of oppression by arising and passing away, it is suffering; because of its state of being uncontrollable, it is non-self—these are the three characteristics.

“Pañcamī”ti vattate.

'Pañcamī' (the fifth case) continues.

314. Kāraṇatthe ca.

314. And in the sense of cause.

Karoti attano phalanti kāraṇaṃ, kārakahetu [janakahetu], tasmiṃ kāraṇatthe ca pañcamīvibhatti hoti, vikappenāyaṃ, hetvatthe tatiyāya ca vihitattā, ananubodhā appaṭivedhā catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ adassanā evamidaṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritaṃ, avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho, saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho, viññāṇanirodhā iccādi.

That which produces its own fruit is a cause, an active cause [or generative cause]. And in that sense of cause, the fifth case ending occurs; this is optional, since the third case is also prescribed for the sense of cause. 'Because of not understanding, not penetrating, and not seeing the four noble truths as they really are, for a long time this wandering and transmigration has continued. With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; but with the complete fading away and cessation of that very ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, there is the cessation of consciousness'; and so on.

Kasmiṃ atthe chaṭṭhī?

In what sense is the sixth case used?

315. Sāmismiṃ chaṭṭhī.

315. The sixth case is used in the sense of an owner.

Ko ca sāmī?

And what is an owner?

316. Yassa vā pariggaho taṃ sāmī.

316. He whose possession it is, he is the owner.

Pariggayhatīti pariggaho, yo yassa pariggaho āyatto sambandhī, taṃ pati so attho sāmisañño hoti. Vāggahaṇena sāmitabba rujādiyogepi.

'Possession' (pariggaho) is so called because it is possessed. He to whom something is a possession, on whom it is dependent, or to whom it is related—with respect to that thing, he is designated as the 'owner' (sāmī). By the inclusion of the word 'vā', this also applies in connection with diseases and the like that can be possessed.

Ettha [M 0.0166] ca kriyābhisambandhābhāvā na kārakatā sambhavati. Sāmibhāvo hi kriyākārakabhāvassa phalabhāvena gahito, tathā hi “rañño puriso”ti vutte yasmā rājā dadāti, puriso ca patiggaṇhāti, tasmā “rājapuriso”ti viññāyati. Evaṃ yo yassa āyatto sevakādibhāvena vā bhaṇḍabhāvena vā samīpa samūhāvayavavikāra kāriyaavatthā jāti guṇa kriyādivasena vā, tassa sabbassāpi so sambandhādhārabhūto visesanaṭṭhānī āgamīvasena tividhopi attho sāmī nāmāti gahetabbo.

Here, since there is no direct connection with an action, the status of a 'kāraka' is not possible. For the state of ownership is understood as the result of the action-kāraka relationship. For instance, when 'the king's man' is said, it is understood as such because the king gives and the man receives. Similarly, with regard to whatever is dependent on someone—whether as a servant and so on, or as goods, or by way of proximity, aggregation, part, modification, effect, state, genus, quality, action, and so on—that person, who is the basis of the relationship for all of that and stands in the position of a qualifier, should be known as the 'owner', a term whose meaning is of three kinds by way of derivation.

Vuttañca

And it is said:

“Kriyākārakasañjāto,

Assedaṃ bhāvahetuko;

Sambandho nāma so attho,

Tattha chaṭṭhī vidhīyate.

"Arisen from action and kāraka, whose cause is this state of 'this is his'; that meaning is called connection, and there the sixth case is prescribed."

Pāratantyañhi sambandho,

Tattha chaṭṭhī bhavetito;

Upādhiṭṭhānā gamito,

Na visesyādito tito”ti.

"For dependence is the connection; therefore the sixth case should occur. It is understood from the basis of the qualifier, not from the thing qualified."

Visesanato tāva – rañño purisoti, ettha ca rājā purisaṃ aññasāmito viseseti nivattetīti visesanaṃ, puriso tena visesīyatīti visesitabbo, evaṃ sabbattha visesitabbayoge visesanatova chaṭṭhī.

First, by way of qualification: 'the king's man.' Here, because the king qualifies the man, distinguishing him from other owners, 'king' is the qualifier. Because the man is qualified by that, he is the one to be qualified. Thus, everywhere, in connection with something to be qualified, the sixth case arises from the qualifier.

Bhaṇḍena sambandhe – pahūtaṃ me dhanaṃ sakka, etassa paṭivīso, bhikkhussa pattacīvaraṃ.

In connection with goods: 'I have abundant wealth, Sakka,' 'This is its equivalent,' 'the monk's bowl and robe.'

Samīpasambandhe – ambavanassa avidūre, nibbānasseva santike.

In connection with proximity: 'not far from the mango grove,' 'in the very presence of Nibbāna.'

Samūhasambandhe [M 0.0167]– suvaṇṇassa rāsi, bhikkhūnaṃ samūho.

In connection with a collection: 'a heap of gold,' 'a group of monks.'

Avayavasambandhe – manussasseva te sīsaṃ, rukkhassa sākhā.

In connection with a part: 'your head is just like a human's,' 'the branch of a tree.'

Vikārasambandhe – suvaṇṇassa vikati, bhaṭṭhadhaññānaṃ sattu.

In connection with a modification: 'a product of gold,' 'flour of roasted grains.'

Kāriyasambandhe – yavassa aṅkuro, meghassa saddo, puttāpi tassa bahavo, kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko.

In connection with an effect: 'a sprout of barley,' 'the sound of a cloud,' 'his sons are also many,' 'the fruit of actions is the result.'

Avatthāsambandhe – khandhānaṃ pātubhāvo, khandhānaṃ jarā, khandhānaṃ bhedo.

In connection with a state: 'the arising of the aggregates,' 'the aging of the aggregates,' 'the breaking up of the aggregates.'

Jātisambandhe – manussassa bhāvo, manussānaṃ jāti.

In connection with genus: 'the state of being human,' 'the birth of humans.'

Guṇasambandhe – suvaṇṇassa vaṇṇo, vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassa, buddhassa guṇaghoso, pupphānaṃ gandho, phalānaṃ raso, cittassa phusanā, sippikānaṃ sataṃ natthi, tilānaṃ muṭṭhi, tesaṃ samāyogo, sandhino vimokkho, tathāgatassa paññāpāramiṃ ārabbha, pubbacariyaṃ vā, sukhaṃ te, dukkhaṃ te, cetaso parivitakko udapādi, paññāya paṭubhāvo, rūpassa lahutā, rūpassa mudutā, rūpassa upacayo.

In connection with a quality: 'the color of gold,' 'the Tathāgata's color would not fade,' 'the proclamation of the Buddha's virtues,' 'the fragrance of flowers,' 'the taste of fruits,' 'the contact of the mind,' 'there is not a hundred (like him) among artisans,' 'a handful of sesame seeds,' 'their combination,' 'liberation from a bond,' 'concerning the perfection of wisdom of the Tathāgata,' 'or past conduct,' 'happiness to you,' 'suffering to you,' 'a thought arose in the mind,' 'the manifestation of wisdom,' 'the lightness of form,' 'the softness of form,' 'the accumulation of form.'

Kriyāsambandhe – pādassa ukkhipanaṃ, pādassa avakkhepanaṃ vā, hatthassa samiñjanaṃ, pādānaṃ pasāraṇaṃ, dhātūnaṃ gamanaṃ, dhātūnaṃyeva ṭhānaṃ, nisajjā, sayanaṃ vā. Tathā tassa nāmagottādi, tassa kāraṇaṃ, tassa mātāpitaro, tassa purato pāturahosi, tassa pacchato, nagarassa dakkhiṇato, vassānaṃ tatiye māse, na tassa upamā, kuverassa bali iccādi.

In connection with an action: 'the raising of the foot,' 'or the lowering of the foot,' 'the bending of the hand,' 'the stretching of the feet,' 'the movement of the elements,' 'the very standing, sitting, or lying down of the elements.' Likewise: 'his name and lineage, etc.,' 'his reason,' 'his parents,' 'he appeared before him,' 'behind him,' 'to the south of the city,' 'in the third month of the rains,' 'there is no comparison for him,' 'an offering to Kuvera,' and so on.

Ṭhānito [M 0.0168]– yamedantassādeso, o avassa.

From position: 'where there is the substitution of the dental, 'o' is compulsory.'

Āgamito – puthassāgamo iccādi.

From āgama: 'the augment of putha,' and so on.

Sāmiyoge – devānamindo, migānaṃ rājā.

In connection with ownership: 'the lord of the gods,' 'the king of beasts.'

Tabba rujādiyoge – mahāsenāpatīnaṃ ujjhāpetabbaṃ vikanditabbaṃ viravitabbaṃ, devadattassa rujati, tassa rogo uppajjati, rajakassa vatthaṃ dadāti, musāvādassa ottappaṃ iccādi.

In connection with what should be done using verbs like 'ruj': 'the great generals should be complained about, lamented, and denounced'; 'Devadatta is in pain,' 'his disease arises,' 'he gives cloth to the washerman,' 'moral dread regarding false speech,' and so on.

“Kvaci, tatiyāsattamīna”nti ca vattate.

And it is also said: 'Sometimes, in the sense of the third and seventh cases.'

317. Chaṭṭhī ca.

317. And the sixth case.

Tatiyāsattamīnamatthe kvaci chaṭṭhīvibhatti hoti.

Sometimes, the sixth case-ending occurs in the sense of the third and seventh cases.

Yajassa karaṇe – pupphassa buddhaṃ yajati, pupphena vā, ghatassa aggiṃ juhoti.

In the instrumental sense of 'yaj': 'he worships the Buddha with a flower' (pupphassa), or 'with a flower' (pupphena); 'he offers ghee to the fire' (ghatassa).

Suhitatthayoge – pattaṃ odanassa pūretvā, odanenāti attho. Imameva kāyaṃ pūraṃ nānappakārassa asucino paccavekkhati, pūraṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇassa, pūrati bālo pāpassa.

In connection with the meaning of 'full' or 'satisfied': 'having filled the bowl with rice,' meaning 'with rice' (odanena). 'He reflects on this very body as full of various kinds of impurities,' 'as full of gold and silver.' 'The fool is full of evil.'

Tulyatthakimalamādiyoge – pitussa tulyo, pitarā vā tulyo, mātu sadiso, mātarā sadiso vā, kiṃ tassa ca tuṭṭhassa, kiṃ tena tuṭṭhenāti attho. Alaṃ tassa ca tuṭṭhassa.

In connection with words meaning 'equal,' 'what,' 'enough,' etc.: 'equal to the father' (pitussa), or 'equal to the father' (pitarā); 'similar to the mother' (mātu), or 'similar to the mother' (mātarā); 'what need is there for him who is content' (tassa), meaning 'what need is there with that contented one' (tena). 'Enough for him who is content' (tassa).

Kattari kitappaccayayoge – sobhanā kaccāyanassa kati, kaccāyanena vā, rañño sammato, raññā vā, evaṃ rañño [M 0.0169] pūjito, rañño sakkato, rañño apacito, rañño mānito, amataṃ tesaṃ bhikkhave aparibhuttaṃ, yesaṃ kāyagatāsati aparibhuttā iccādi.

In connection with the agent and 'kita' suffixes: 'beautiful is Kaccāyana's composition' (kaccāyanassa), or 'by Kaccāyana' (kaccāyanena); 'approved by the king' (rañño), or 'by the king' (raññā); thus, 'honored by the king,' 'respected by the king,' 'venerated by the king,' 'esteemed by the king'; 'the Deathless is not partaken of by them, O monks, by whom mindfulness directed to the body is not partaken of,' and so on.

Sattamiyatthe kusalādiyoge – kusalā naccagītassa sikkhitā cāturitthiyo, kusalo tvaṃ rathassa aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ, kusalo maggassa, kusalo amaggassa, santi hi bhante uḷārā yakkhā bhagavato pasannā, divasassa tikkhattuṃ, divase tikkhattuṃ vā, māsassa dvikkhattuṃ iccādi.

In the sense of the seventh case, in connection with 'skilled,' etc.: 'skilled in dancing and singing are the women trained in the four arts'; 'skilled are you in the parts and accessories of the chariot'; 'skilled in the path'; 'skilled in the wrong path'; 'for there are, O Lord, mighty spirits devoted to the Blessed One'; 'thrice a day' (divasassa), or 'thrice in the day' (divase); 'twice a month'; and so on.

“Kvaci, chaṭṭhī”ti ca vattate.

And it is also said: 'Sometimes, the sixth case.'

318. Dutiyāpañcamīnañca.

318. And of the second and fifth cases.

Dutiyāpañcamīnamatthe ca kvaci chaṭṭhīvibhatti hoti.

And sometimes, the sixth case-ending occurs in the sense of the second and fifth cases.

Dutiyatthe kammani kitakayoge – tassa bhavanti vattāro, sahasā kammassa kattāro, amatassa dātā, bhinnānaṃ sandhātā, sahitānaṃ anuppadātā, bodhetā pajāya, kammassa kārako natthi, vipākassa ca vedako, avisaṃvādako lokassa, pāpānaṃ akaraṇaṃ sukhaṃ, catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādo, acchariyo arajakena vatthānaṃ rāgo, acchariyo agopālakena gāvīnaṃ doho.

In the sense of the second case, in connection with the object and 'kita' suffixes: 'there are speakers about it,' 'doers of the deed by force,' 'givers of the Deathless,' 'menders of the broken,' 'providers for the united,' 'awakeners of the people,' 'no doer of the deed exists, nor an experiencer of the result,' 'one who does not deceive the world,' 'non-doing of evil is happiness,' 'clarity arises dependent on the four great elements,' 'strange is the dyeing of garments by one who is not a dyer,' 'strange is the milking of cows without a herdsman.'

Tathā saricchādīnaṃ kammani – mātu sarati, mātaraṃ sarati, na tesaṃ koci sarati, sattānaṃ kammappaccayā, puttassa icchati, puttamicchati.

Likewise, in the object sense of verbs like 'sari' and 'icch,' etc.: 'one remembers the mother' (mātu), 'one remembers the mother' (mātaraṃ); 'no one remembers them'; 'beings are conditioned by kamma'; 'one desires a son' (puttassa), 'one desires a son' (puttaṃ).

Karotissa [M 0.0170] patiyatane ca – patiyatanaṃ abhisaṅkhāro, udakassa patikurute, udakaṃ patikurute, kaṇḍassa patikurute, kaṇḍaṃ patikurute.

And in the sense of 'patiyatana' for 'karoti': 'preparation is volitional formation.' 'One counteracts water' (udakassa), 'one counteracts water' (udakaṃ); 'one counteracts a stick' (kaṇḍassa), 'one counteracts a stick' (kaṇḍaṃ).

Pañcamiyatthe parihānibhayatthayoge – assavanatā dhammassa parihāyanti, kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ tassa sukhassa bhāyāmi, sabbe tasanti daṇḍassa, sabbe bhāyanti maccuno, bhīto catunnaṃ āsivisānaṃ iccādi.

In the sense of the fifth case, in connection with the meaning of 'decline' and 'fear': 'they decline from the Dhamma through not hearing it'; 'why should I fear that happiness?'; 'All tremble at the rod,' 'all fear death,' 'afraid of the four poisonous snakes,' and so on.

Kvacīti kiṃ? Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattā, kālena dhammiṃ kathaṃ bhāsitā hoti, paresaṃ puññāni anumoditā, bujjhitā saccāni, kaṭaṃ kārako, pasavo ghātako.

Why 'sometimes'? 'And a doer of profound speech,' 'one who has spoken Dhamma at the right time,' 'one who has rejoiced in the merits of others,' 'one who has understood the truths,' 'a maker of mats,' 'a slayer of cattle.'

Tathā na niṭṭhādīsu ca – sukhakāmī vihāraṃ kato, rathaṃ katavanto, rathaṃ katāvī, kaṭaṃ katvā, kaṭaṃ karonto, kaṭaṃ karāno, kaṭaṃ kurumāno iccādi.

Likewise, and not in words ending in 'niṭṭha,' etc.: 'one who has made a pleasant dwelling,' 'one who has made a chariot,' 'a chariot-maker,' 'having made a mat,' 'making a mat,' 'making a mat,' 'making a mat,' and so on.

Kasmiṃ atthe sattamī?

In what sense is the seventh case used?

319. Okāse sattamī.

319. The seventh case is used in the sense of location.

Okāsakārake sattamīvibhatti hoti.

The seventh case-ending occurs in the sense of the location-factor.

Ko ca okāso?

And what is location?

320. Yodhāro tamokāsaṃ.

320. That which is the support, that is the location.

Ādhārīyati asminti ādhāro, adhikaraṇaṃ. Kattukammasamavetānaṃ nisajjapacanādikriyānaṃ patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena yo ādhāro, taṃ kārakaṃ okāsasaññaṃ hoti.

That in which something is supported is the support, the locative case. That which is the support in the sense of a foundation for actions involving agent and object, such as sitting or cooking, that factor is called 'location'.

Kaṭe [M 0.0171] nisīdati devadatto, thāliyaṃ odanaṃ pacati. Ettha hi devadattataṇḍulānaṃ kattukammānaṃ dhāraṇato taṃsamavetaṃ āsanapacanasaṅkhātaṃ kriyaṃ dhāreti nāma.

Devadatta sits on a mat; he cooks rice in a pot. Here, because it supports Devadatta and the rice, which are the agent and object, it is called 'supporting' the actions connected with them, namely sitting and cooking.

So panāyamokāso catubbidho byāpiko opasilesiko sāmīpiko vesayikoti.

And this location is fourfold: pervasive, contiguous, proximate, and topical.

Tattha byāpiko nāma yattha sakalopi ādhārabhūto attho ādheyyena patthaṭo hoti, yasmiñca ādheyyabhūtaṃ kiñci byāpetvā tiṭṭhati, taṃ yathā – tilesu telaṃ atthi, khīlesu jalaṃ, dadhimhi sappīti.

Among these, the pervasive location is where the entire supporting object is pervaded by the supported object, and in which the supported object remains, having pervaded it, as in: 'oil exists in sesame seeds,' 'water in sprouts,' 'butter in curds.'

Opasilesiko nāma paccekasiddhānaṃ bhāvānaṃ yattha upasilesena upagamo hoti, yasmiñca ādheyyo upasilissati allīyitvā tiṭṭhati, taṃ yathā – āsane nisinno saṅgho, thāliyaṃ odanaṃ pacati, ghaṭesu udakaṃ atthi, dūre ṭhito, samīpe ṭhitoti.

The contiguous location is that wherein there is a coming together of independently existing things by way of contact, and in which the supported object adheres, remaining attached; as for example: 'the Saṅgha sits on a seat,' 'one cooks rice in a pot,' 'there is water in pots,' 'one stands far away,' 'one stands nearby.'

Sāmīpiko nāma yattha samīpe samīpivohāraṃ katvā tadāyattavuttitādīpanatthaṃ ādhārabhāvo vikappīyati, taṃ yathā – gaṅgāyaṃ ghoso vasati, gaṅgāya samīpe vajo vasatīti attho. Bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane, sāvatthiyā samīpeti attho.

The proximate location is that wherein the state of being a support is conceived by employing a designation of proximity with respect to what is nearby, in order to indicate dependence and so forth; as for example: 'the herdsmen's station resides in the Gaṅgā,' the meaning of which is 'the herdsmen's station resides near the Gaṅgā.' 'The Blessed One dwells in Sāvatthī, at Jetavana,' the meaning of which is 'near Sāvatthī.'

Vesayiko nāma yattha aññatthābhāvavasena, desantarāvacchedavasena vā ādhārabhāvo parikappo, taṃ yathā – ākāse sakuṇā pakkhanti, bhūmīsu manussā caranti, jalesu macchā, pādesu patito, pāpasmiṃ ramatī mano, pasanno buddhasāsane, paññāya sādhu, vinaye nipuṇo, mātari sādhu, pitari nipuṇo iccādi.

The topical location is that wherein the state of being a support is conceived by way of absence elsewhere, or by way of the delimitation of a different region; as for example: 'birds fly in the sky,' 'humans walk on the ground,' 'fish are in the waters,' 'fallen at the feet,' 'the mind delights in evil,' 'pleased with the Buddha’s teaching,' 'good in wisdom,' 'proficient in the discipline,' 'good to his mother,' 'dutiful to his father,' and so on.

Sabbopi [M 0.0172] cāyamādhāro padhānavasena vā parikappitavasena vā kriyāya patiṭṭhā bhavatīti okāsotveva vuttoti veditabbo.

And all this support, whether by way of the principal or by way of the conceived, becomes a foundation for action; thus it is called 'location' only, so it should be understood.

Vuttañcetaṃ

And this has been said:

“Kiriyā kattukammānaṃ,

Yattha hoti patiṭṭhitā;

‘Okāso’ti pavutto so,

Catudhā byāpikādito.

That wherein the action of the agent and the object is established, is called 'location'; it is fourfold, beginning with the pervasive.

Byāpiko tilakhīrādi,

Kaṭo opasilesiko;

Sāmīpiko tu gaṅgādi,

Ākāso visayo mato”ti.

The pervasive is like sesame, milk, and so forth; the contiguous is like a mat; the proximate, however, is like the Gaṅgā and so forth; the sky is considered the topical.

“Chaṭṭhī, sattamī”ti ca adhikāro.

And the heading is 'Sixth case, seventh case.'

321. Sāmissarādhipatidāyādasakkhīpatibhūpasūtakusalehi ca.

321. And with owner, lord, master, heir, witness, guarantor, offspring, and the skilled.

Sāmī issara adhipati dāyāda sakkhipatibhū pasūta kusalaiccetehi yoge chaṭṭhīvibhatti hoti, sattamī ca. Ubhayatthaṃ vacanaṃ.

In connection with these—owner, lord, master, heir, witness, guarantor, offspring, and the skilled—the sixth case-ending occurs, and also the seventh. This statement applies in both instances.

Gavaṃ sāmi, gosu sāmi, gavaṃ issaro, gosu issaro, gavaṃ adhipati, gosu adhipati, gavaṃ dāyādo, gosu dāyādo, gavaṃ sakkhi, gosu sakkhi, gavaṃ patibhū, gosu patibhū, gavaṃ pasūto, gosu pasūto, gavaṃ kusalo, gosu kusalo.

Owner of cattle, owner among cattle; lord of cattle, lord among cattle; master of cattle, master among cattle; heir of cattle, heir among cattle; witness to cattle, witness among cattle; guarantor for cattle, guarantor among cattle; born of cattle, born among cattle; skilled with cattle, skilled among cattle.

322. Niddhāraṇe ca.

322. And in determination.

Nīharitvā dhāraṇaṃ niddhāraṇaṃ, jāti guṇa kriyā nāmehi samudāyato ekadesassa puthakkaraṇaṃ, tasmiṃ niddhāraṇatthe gamyamāne [M 0.0173] tato samudāyavāciliṅgamhā chaṭṭhīvibhatti hoti, sattamī ca.

Determination is the act of determining after having singled out; it is the separation of a part from a whole by means of class, quality, action, or name. When that meaning of determination is understood, the sixth case-ending, and also the seventh, occurs after the nominal stem that denotes the whole.

Manussānaṃ khattiyo sūratamo, manussesu khattiyo sūratamo, kaṇhā gāvīnaṃ sampannakhīratamā, kaṇhā gāvīsu sampannakhīratamā, addhikānaṃ dhāvanto sīghatamo, addhikesu dhāvanto sīghatamo, āyasmā ānando arahataṃ aññataro ahosi, arahantesu vā iccādi.

Of men, the warrior is the bravest; among men, the warrior is the bravest. Of cows, the black cow is the most abundant in milk; among cows, the black cow is the most abundant in milk. Of travelers, the one who is running is the swiftest; among travelers, the one who is running is the swiftest. The Venerable Ānanda was one of the Arahants, or among the Arahants, and so on.

323. Anādare ca.

323. And in disregard.

Anādare gamyamāne bhāvavatā liṅgamhā chaṭṭhīvibhatti hoti, sattamī ca. Akāmakānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ rudantānaṃ pabbaji, mātāpitūsu rudantesu pabbaji.

When disregard is understood, the sixth case-ending, and also the seventh, occurs after the nominal stem of one who possesses a certain state. He went forth, his unwilling parents weeping; he went forth while his parents were weeping.

Ākoṭayanto so neti,

Sivirājassa pekkhato;

Maccu gacchati ādāya,

Pekkhamāne mahājane.

He is led away, being struck, while King Sivi looks on; Death goes, having taken him, while the great multitude looks on.

324. Kammakaraṇanimittatthesu sattamī.

324. The seventh case occurs in the senses of object, instrument, and cause.

Kammakaraṇanimittaiccetesvatthesu liṅgamhā sattamīvibhatti hoti.

In these meanings—object, instrument, and cause—the seventh case-ending occurs after the nominal stem.

Kammatthe – bhikkhūsu abhivādenti, muddhani cumbitvā, purisassa bāhāsu gahetvā.

In the sense of object: they pay respect to the monks; having kissed him on the head; having taken hold of the man’s arms.

Karaṇatthe – hatthesu piṇḍāya caranti, pattesu piṇḍāya caranti, pathesu gacchanti, sopi maṃ anusāseyya, sampaṭicchāmi matthake.

In the sense of instrument: they wander for alms with their hands; they wander for alms with their bowls; they go by way of the paths; 'Even should he instruct me, I will receive it on my head.'

Nimittatthe [M 0.0174]– dīpi cammesu haññate, kuñjaro dantesu haññate, aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī, sampajānamusāvāde pācittiyaṃ, musāvādanimittaṃ musāvādappaccayāti attho.

In the sense of cause: a leopard is killed for its skin; an elephant is killed for its tusks; one who sees danger in the slightest faults; for a deliberate lie, there is an offense requiring expiation. The meaning is: on account of the lie, conditioned by the lie.

“Sattamī”ti adhikāro.

The heading is 'The Seventh Case.'

325. Sampadāne ca.

325. And in the dative.

Sampadānatthe ca liṅgamhā sattamīvibhatti hoti. Saṅghe dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ, saṅghe gotami dehi, saṅghe te dinne ahañceva pūjito bhavissāmi.

And in the sense of the dative, the seventh case-ending occurs after the nominal stem. What is given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit; O Gotamī, give to the Saṅgha; when it is given by you to the Saṅgha, I myself will be honored.

Yā palālamayaṃ mālaṃ, nārī datvāna cetiye;

Alattha kañcanamayaṃ, mālaṃ bojjhaṅgikañca sā.

That woman who, having given a garland made of straw to the shrine, obtained a golden garland and one pertaining to the factors of enlightenment.

326. Pañcamyatthe ca.

326. And in the sense of the fifth case.

Pañcamyatthe ca liṅgamhā sattamīvibhatti hoti. Kadalīsu gaje rakkhanti.

And in the sense of the fifth case, the seventh case-ending occurs after the nominal stem. They protect the elephants from the plantain trees.

327. Kālabhāvesu ca.

327. And in time and state.

Kālo nāma nimesa khaṇa laya muhutta pubbaṇhādiko, bhāvo nāma kriyā, sā cettha kriyantarūpalakkhaṇāva adhippetā, tasmiṃ kālatthe ca bhāvalakkhaṇe bhāvatthe ca liṅgamhā sattamīvibhatti hoti.

Time, by name, is a blink of an eye, an instant, a beat, a moment, the forenoon, and so forth. State, by name, is action, and here it is intended specifically as that which indicates another action. In that temporal sense, and in the sense of a state that indicates another state, the seventh case-ending occurs after the nominal stem.

Kāle – pubbaṇhasamaye gato, sāyanhasamaye āgato, akāle vassati tassa, kāle tassa na vassati, phussamāsamhā tīsu māsesu vesākhamāso, ito satasahassamhi, kappe uppajji cakkhumā.

In time: He went in the morning, he returned in the evening; it rains for him out of season, it does not rain for him in season; the month of Vesākha is three months from the month of Phussa; a hundred thousand aeons from now, the One with Vision arose.

Bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇe [M 0.0175]– bhikkhusaṅghesu bhojīyamānesu gato, bhuttesu āgato, gosu duyhamānāsu gato, duddhāsu āgato, jāyamāne kho sāriputta bodhisatte ayaṃ dasasahassilokadhātu saṃkampi sampakampi sampavedhi.

In the sense of state as a characteristic: He went when the monastic community was being fed; he returned when they had finished eating; he went when the cows were being milked; he returned when they had been milked. Indeed, Sāriputta, when the Bodhisatta was being born, this ten-thousand-world system shook, greatly shook, and trembled.

Pāsāṇā sakkharā ceva, kaṭhalā khāṇukaṇṭakā;

Sabbe maggā vivajjenti, gacchante lokanāyake.

Stones, gravel, and pebbles, stumps and thorns—all avoid the paths as the Leader of the World walks.

Imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti iccādi.

When this is, that is; and so on.

328. Upājhādhikissaravacane.

328. In expressions of superiority and sovereignty.

Dvipadamidaṃ. Adhikatthe, issaratthe ca vattamānehi upaadhiiccetehi yoge adhikissaravacane gamyamāne liṅgamhā sattamīvibhatti hoti.

This is twofold. When superiority and sovereignty are implied, the seventh case ending occurs from the stem in connection with 'upa' and 'adhi', indicating superiority and sovereignty.

Adhikavacane – upa khāriyaṃ doṇo, khāriyā doṇo adhikoti attho. Tathā upa nikkhe kahāpaṇaṃ, adhi devesu buddho, sammutiupapattivisuddhidevasaṅkhātehi tividhehipi devehi sabbaññū buddhova adhikoti attho.

In the expression of superiority: 'upa khāriyaṃ doṇo' means a doṇa is superior to a khārī. Similarly, 'upa nikkhe kahāpaṇaṃ' means a kahāpaṇa is superior to a nikkha. 'adhi devesu buddho' means among the gods, the Buddha is supreme; that is, the Omniscient Buddha is superior to all three kinds of gods, namely, conventional gods, gods by rebirth, and gods by purification.

Issaravacane – adhi brahmadatte pañcālā, brahmadattissarā pañcālāti attho.

In the expression of sovereignty: 'adhi brahmadatte pañcālā' means the Pañcālas are under Brahmadatta's sovereignty; that is, the Pañcālas have Brahmadatta as their lord.

329. Maṇḍitussukkesu tatiyā ca.

329. And the third case occurs in the sense of 'adorned' and 'eager'.

Maṇḍitaussukkaiccetesvatthesu gamyamānesu liṅgamhā tatiyāvibhatti hoti, sattamī ca. Maṇḍitasaddo panettha pasannatthavācako, ussukkasaddo saīhattho. Ñāṇena pasanno, ñāṇasmiṃ pasanno, ñāṇena ussukko, ñāṇasmiṃ ussukko sappuriso.

When these meanings of 'adorned' and 'eager' are implied, the third case ending occurs from the stem, and also the seventh. Here, the word 'adorned' (maṇḍita) conveys the meaning of 'pleased' (pasanna), and the word 'eager' (ussukka) conveys the meaning of 'zealous' (saīha). A virtuous person is pleased by means of knowledge, pleased in knowledge; zealous by means of knowledge, zealous in knowledge.

Kārakaṃ [M 0.0176] chabbidhaṃ saññā-vasā chabbīsatīvidhaṃ;

Pabhedā sattadhā kammaṃ, kattā pañcavidho bhave.

The kāraka is sixfold, and according to designation, twenty-sixfold; the object is sevenfold by division, and the agent is fivefold.

Karaṇaṃ duvidhaṃ hoti, sampadānaṃ tidhā mataṃ;

Apādānaṃ pañcavidhaṃ, ādhāro tu catubbidho.

The instrument is twofold, the dative is considered threefold; the ablative is fivefold, and the locative is fourfold.

Vibhattiyo pana paccattavacanādivasena aṭṭhavidhā bhavanti. Yathāha

The case endings, however, are eightfold, by way of the nominative and so on. As it is said:

“Paccattamupayogañca, karaṇaṃ sampadāniyaṃ;

Nissakkaṃ sāmivacanaṃ, bhummālapanamaṭṭhama”nti.

Nominative, and Accusative, Instrumental, Dative; Ablative, Genitive, Locative, and the eighth is Vocative.

Iti padarūpasiddhiyaṃ kārakakaṇḍo

Thus ends the section on kārakas in the Padarūpasiddhi.

Tatiyo.

The Third Section.

4. Samāsakaṇḍa

4. The Section on Compounds

Atha nāmameva aññamaññasambandhīnaṃ samāsoti nāmanissitattā, sayañca nāmikattā nāmānantaraṃ samāso vuccate.

Now, because a compound is dependent on names that are mutually connected, and because it is itself nominal, the topic of compounds is discussed immediately after that of names.

So ca saññāvasena chabbidho abyayībhāvo kammadhārayo digu tappuriso bahubbīhi dvando cāti.

And that, by way of designation, is sixfold: the abyayībhāva, kammadhāraya, digu, tappurisa, bahubbīhi, and dvanda.

Abyayībhāvasamāsa

The Abyayībhāva Compound

Tatra paṭhamaṃ abyayībhāvasamāso vuccate;

So ca niccasamāsoti assapadaviggaho.

Therein, first, the Abyayībhāva compound is explained. And it is a permanent compound, meaning its analysis is formed with words not present in the compound itself (asvapadaviggaha).

“Upanagaraṃ”itīdha – upasaddato paṭhamekavacanaṃ si, tassa upasaggaparattā “sabbāsamāvusopasagganipātādīhi cā”ti lopo, nagarasaddato chaṭṭhekavacanaṃ sa, nagarassa samīpanti aññapadena viggahe –

Here, in 'upanagaraṃ'—the case ending 'si' after the word 'upa' is elided by the rule 'sabbāsamāvusopasagganipātādīhi cā'. The word 'nagara' takes the sixth case singular ending 'sa', as in the analysis with another word: 'nagarassa samīpaṃ' (near the city).

“Nāmānaṃ samāso yuttattho”ti samāsavidhāne sabbattha vattate.

The statement 'A compound of names has a connected meaning' applies everywhere in the rules for compounding.

330. Upasagganipātapubbako abyayībhāvo.

330. An abyayībhāva compound is one preceded by a prefix (upasagga) or a particle (nipāta).

Upasaggapubbako, nipātapubbako ca nāmiko yuttattho teheva attapubbakehi upasagganipātehi saha niccaṃ samasīyate, so ca samāso abyayībhāvasañño hoti. Idha abyayībhāvādisaññāvidhāyakasuttāneva vā saññāvidhānamukhena samāsavidhāyakānīti daṭṭhabbāni.

A nominal form with a connected meaning, preceded by a prefix or a particle, is always compounded with those very prefixes and particles that precede it; and such a compound is designated an abyayībhāva. Here, the very rules that prescribe designations such as 'abyayībhāva' should be understood as also being the rules that form the compounds, by means of prescribing the designation.

Tattha abyayamiti upasagganipātānaṃ saññā, liṅgavacanabhedepi byayarahitattā, abyayānaṃ atthaṃ vibhāvayatīti abyayībhāvo abyayatthapubbaṅgamattā, anabyayaṃ abyayaṃ bhavatīti vā [M 0.0178] abyayībhāvo. Pubbapadatthappadhāno hi abyayībhāvo, ettha ca “upasagganipātapubbako”ti vuttattā upasagganipātānameva pubbanipāto.

Here, 'abyaya' (indeclinable) is a designation for prefixes and particles, because they are devoid of change even amid differences in gender and number. 'Abyayībhāva' means it clarifies the meaning of indeclinables, because it has the meaning of an indeclinable as its primary element; or alternatively, 'abyayībhāva' means that which is not indeclinable becomes indeclinable. Indeed, the abyayībhāva compound has the meaning of the first member as primary; and here, since it is stated 'preceded by a prefix or particle', only prefixes and particles are placed first.

331. Nāmānaṃ samāso yuttattho.

331. A compound of names has a connected meaning.

Tesaṃ nāmānaṃ payujjamānapadatthānaṃ yo yuttattho, so samāsasañño hoti, tadaññaṃ vākyamiti ruḷhaṃ.

That connected meaning of those names—of the words being used—is designated a compound; what is other than that is conventionally known as a sentence.

Nāmāni syādivibhatyantāni, samassateti samāso, saṅkhipiyatīti attho.

Names ending in case inflections (syādi-vibhatti) are compounded (samassate), hence 'samāsa'; the meaning is that they are contracted (saṅkhipiyate).

Vuttañhi

For it has been said:

“Samāso padasaṅkhepo, padappaccayasaṃhitaṃ;

Taddhitaṃ nāma hotevaṃ, viññeyyaṃ tesamantara”nti.

A compound is a contraction of words. That which is combined with word-suffixes is indeed a taddhita. The distinction between them should be understood.

Duvidhañcassa samasanaṃ saddasamasanamatthasamasanañca, tadubhayampi luttasamāse paripuṇṇameva labbhati. Aluttasamāse pana atthasamasanameva vibhattilopābhāvato, tatthāpi vā ekapadattūpagamanato duvidhampi labbhateva. Dve hi samāsassa payojanāni ekapadattamekavibhattittañcāti.

And its compounding is of two kinds: combination of words (sound) and combination of meanings. Both are fully obtained in a compound where case endings have been elided (luttasamāsa). However, in a compound where case endings have not been elided (aluttasamāsa), only the combination of meanings is obtained due to the absence of case ending elision; but even there, both kinds are indeed obtained due to its becoming a single word. For a compound has two purposes: to become a single word and to have a single case ending.

Yutto attho yuttatto, atha vā yutto saṅgato, sambandho vā attho yassa soyaṃ yuttattho, etena saṅgatatthena yuttatthavacanena bhinnatthānaṃ ekatthībhāvo samāsalakkhaṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettha ca “nāmāna”nti vacanena “devadatto pacatī”tiādīsu ākhyātena samāso na hotīti dasseti. Sambandhatthena pana yuttatthaggahaṇena “bhaṭo rañño putto devadattassā”tiādīsu aññamaññānapekkhesu, “devadattassa kaṇhā dantā”tiādīsu ca aññasāpekkhesu [M 0.0179] ayuttatthatāya samāso na hotīti dīpeti.

The meaning that is joined is 'yuttattho'; or alternatively, 'yuttattho' is that whose meaning is joined, connected, or related. By this term 'yuttattho', which signifies connected meaning, it is said that the unification of distinct meanings into one is the characteristic of a compound. Here, by the word 'nāmānaṃ' (of names), it is shown that in expressions like 'Devadatta cooks', there is no compounding with a verb. Moreover, by the inclusion of 'yuttattha' in the sense of relation, it clarifies that in cases like 'the warrior of the king, the son of Devadatta', where there is mutual non-dependence, or in cases like 'Devadatta's teeth are black', where there is dependence on something else, there is no compounding due to the absence of connected meaning.

“Atthavasā vibhattivipariṇāmo”ti vipariṇāmena “yuttatthāna”nti vattate.

According to the principle 'Alteration of case endings is due to meaning,' the term is carried forward with its case altered to 'yuttatthānaṃ' (of those with connected meaning).

332. Tesaṃ vibhattiyo lopā ca.

332. And their case endings are elided.

Idha padantarena vā taddhitappaccayehi vā āyādippaccayehi vā ekatthībhūtā yuttatthā nāma, tena “tesaṃ yuttatthānaṃ samāsānaṃ, taddhitāyādippaccayantānañca vibhattiyo lopanīyā hontī”ti attho. Samāsaggahaṇādhikāre pana sati tesaṃgahaṇena vā taddhitāyādippaccayanta vibhattilopo. Caggahaṇaṃ “pabhaṅkaro”tiādīsu lopanivattanatthaṃ.

Here, those that have become unified in meaning with another word, or by taddhita suffixes, or by āyādi suffixes, are called 'yuttattha' (connected in meaning). Therefore, the meaning is: 'The case endings of those 'yuttattha'—that is, of compounds and of those ending in taddhita and āyādi suffixes—are to be elided.' However, when the governing rule of 'samāsa' is in effect, the elision of case endings for those ending in taddhita and āyādi suffixes is accomplished by the word 'tesaṃ' (their). The inclusion of 'ca' is for the purpose of preventing elision in examples like 'pabhaṅkaro'.

Vipariṇāmena “luttāsu, vibhattīsū”ti vattate, yuttatthaggahaṇañca.

By alteration of the case ending, 'luttāsu vibhattīsu' (when case endings are elided) is carried forward, and also the term 'yuttattha'.

333. Pakati cassa sarantassa.

333. And for that which ends in a vowel, there is its natural state.

Luttāsu vibhattīsu sarantassa assa yuttatthabhūtassa tividhassapi liṅgassa pakatibhāvo hoti. Casaddena kiṃsamudaya idappaccayatādīsu niggahītantassapi. Nimittābhāve nemittakābhāvassa idha anicchitattā ayamatideso.

When case endings are elided, the natural state occurs for that vowel-ending word which is 'yuttattha' (connected in meaning) and which has all three genders. By the word 'ca', this applies even to those ending in a niggahīta, as in 'kiṃsamudaya', 'idappaccayatā', and so forth. Because the absence of the effect due to the absence of the cause is not desired here, this is an 'atidesa' (extension rule).

Sakatthavirahenidha samāsassa ca liṅgabhāvābhāvā vibhattuppattiyamasampattāyaṃ nāmabyapadesātidesamāha.

Here, due to the absence of its own meaning, and due to the compound's lack of inherent gender and the non-attainment of the arising of case endings, it states the extension of the designation 'name'.

334. Taddhitasamāsakitakā nāmaṃvā’tavetunādīsu ca.

334. Taddhita (derivatives), compounds, and kitaka (kṛt derivatives) are to be considered names, except for those ending in suffixes like 'tave', 'tuna', and so forth.

Taddhitantā[M 0.0180], kitantā, samāsā ca nāmamiva daṭṭhabbā tavetuna tvāna tvādippaccayante vajjetvā. Caggahaṇaṃ kiccappaccayaāīinīitthippaccayantādissapi nāmabyapadesatthaṃ. Idha samāsaggahaṇaṃ atthavataṃ samudāyānaṃ nāmabyapadeso samāsassevāti niyamatthanti apare.

Words ending in taddhita suffixes, words ending in kitaka suffixes, and compounds should be regarded as names, excluding those ending in suffixes like 'tave', 'tuna', 'tvāna', and 'tvā'. The inclusion of 'ca' is for the purpose of designating as names even those ending in kicca suffixes, feminine suffixes like 'ī' and 'inī', and so forth. Here, the mention of 'samāsa' (compound) is for the purpose of restricting that among meaningful aggregates, only compounds are designated as names, according to others.

“Abyayībhāvo”ti vattate.

'Abyayībhāva' is carried forward.

335. So napuṃsakaliṅgo.

335. That (abyayībhāva compound) is of the neuter gender.

So abyayībhāvasamāso napuṃsakaliṅgova daṭṭhabboti napuṃsakaliṅgattaṃ. Ettha hi satipi liṅgātidese “adhipañña”ntiādīsu “adhiñāṇaṃ”ntiādi rūpappasaṅgo na hoti saddantarattā, “tipañña”ntiādīsu viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ, na cāyaṃ atideso, sutte atidesaliṅgassa ivasaddassa adassanato. Pure viya syādyuppatti.

That abyayībhāva compound should be regarded as being only of the neuter gender; thus, its neuter gender is stated. Here, even if there is an extension of gender, in examples like 'adhipañña', the form 'adhiñāṇaṃ' does not arise, because it is a different word, just as in examples like 'tipañña'; this should be understood. And this is not an 'atidesa' (extension rule), because the word 'iva' (like), which indicates extension, is not seen in the sutta. The arising of case endings beginning with 'si' is as before.

“Kvacī”ti vattate.

'Kvacī' (sometimes) is carried forward.

336. Aṃ vibhattīnamakārantā abyayībhāvā.

336. After an abyayībhāva compound ending in 'a', 'aṃ' is substituted for the case endings.

Tasmā akārantā abyayībhāvā parāsaṃ vibhattīnaṃ kvaci aṃ hoti, sesaṃ neyyaṃ.

Therefore, after an abyayībhāva compound ending in 'a', 'aṃ' sometimes occurs as a substitute for the following case endings; the rest is to be inferred.

Taṃ upanagaraṃ, nagarassa samīpaṃ tiṭṭhatīti attho. Tāni upanagaraṃ, ālapanepevaṃ, taṃ upanagaraṃ passa, tāni upanagaraṃ.

'Taṃ upanagaraṃ' (that which is near the city); the meaning is 'it stands near the city'. 'Tāni upanagaraṃ' (those which are near the city); similarly in the vocative. 'Taṃ upanagaraṃ passa' (see that which is near the city); 'Tāni upanagaraṃ' (those which are near the city).

Na pañcamyāyamambhāvo, kvacīti adhikārato;

Tatiyāsattamīchaṭṭhī-nantu hoti vikappato.

This 'aṃ' substitution does not occur for the fifth case ending, due to the governing rule of 'kvaci' (sometimes). But for the third, seventh, and sixth case endings, it occurs optionally.

Tena upanagaraṃ kataṃ, upanagarena vā, tehi upanagaraṃ, upanagarehi vā, tassa upanagaraṃ dehi, tesaṃ upanagaraṃ, upanagarā ānaya, upanagaramhā upanagarasmā, upanagarehi, upanagaraṃ santakaṃ, upanagarassa vā, tesaṃ upanagaraṃ, upanagarānaṃ vā[M 0.0181], upanagaraṃ nidhehi, upanagaramhi upanagarasmiṃ, upanagaraṃ upanagaresu vā. Evaṃ upakumbhaṃ.

Thus: by him `upanagaraṃ` was made, or `upanagarena`; by them `upanagaraṃ`, or `upanagarehi`. Give `upanagaraṃ` to him, `upanagaraṃ` to them. Bring from `upanagarā`, `upanagaramhā`, or `upanagarasmā`; from `upanagarehi`. Belonging to it is `upanagaraṃ`, or `upanagarassa`; belonging to them is `upanagaraṃ`, or `upanagarānaṃ`. Deposit in `upanagaraṃ`, `upanagaramhi`, or `upanagarasmiṃ`; in `upanagaraṃ`, or `upanagaresu`.

Abhāve – darathānaṃ abhāvo niddarathaṃ, nimmasakaṃ.

In the sense of absence: the absence of distress is 'niddarathaṃ'; 'nimmasakaṃ' (without mosquitoes).

Pacchāatthe – rathassa pacchā anurathaṃ, anuvātaṃ.

In the sense of 'behind': `rathassa pacchā` is 'anurathaṃ' (behind the chariot); also 'anuvātaṃ' (with the wind).

Yoggatāyaṃ – yathāsarūpaṃ, anurūpaṃ, rūpayogganti attho.

In the sense of suitability: 'yathāsarūpaṃ', 'anurūpaṃ'; the meaning is 'suitable to the form'.

Vicchāyaṃ – attānamattānaṃ pati paccattaṃ, addhamāsaṃ addhamāsaṃ anu anvaddhamāsaṃ.

In the sense of distribution: `attānaṃ attānaṃ pati` is 'paccattaṃ' (individually); `addhamāsaṃ addhamāsaṃ anu` is 'anvaddhamāsaṃ' (every half-month).

Anupubbiyaṃ – jeṭṭhānaṃ anupubbo anujeṭṭhaṃ.

In the sense of succession: `jeṭṭhānaṃ anupubbena` is 'anujeṭṭhaṃ' (according to seniority).

Paṭilome – sotassa paṭilomaṃ paṭisotaṃ, paṭipathaṃ, pativātaṃ, attānaṃ adhikicca pavattā ajjhattaṃ.

In the sense of opposition: `sotassa paṭilomaṃ` is 'paṭisotaṃ' (against the stream); also 'paṭipathaṃ' (against the path), 'pativātaṃ' (against the wind). `attānaṃ adhikicca pavattā` is 'ajjhattaṃ' (internally).

Pariyādābhividhīsu āpāṇakoṭiyā āpāṇakoṭikaṃ, “kvaci samāsantagatānamakāranto”ti kappaccayo, ākumārehi yaso kaccāyanassa ākumāraṃ.

In the senses of limit and inclusion: `ā pāṇakoṭiyā` is 'āpāṇakoṭikaṃ' (up to the last living being); the suffix 'ka' is applied according to the rule 'kvaci samāsantagatānamakāranto'. `ākumārehi yaso kaccāyanassa` is 'ākumāraṃ' (fame for Kaccāyana from the youths upwards).

Samiddhiyaṃ – bhikkhāya samiddhīti atthe samāseva napuṃsakaliṅgatte ca kate –

In the sense of prosperity: when the compound has been formed and made neuter in gender, in the sense of 'bhikkhāya samiddhi' (prosperity of alms) –

“Samāsassa, anto”ti ca vattate.

And 'samāsassa' (of the compound) and 'anto' (the end) are carried forward.

337. Saro rasso napuṃsake.

337. A vowel becomes short in the neuter gender.

Napuṃsake vattamānassa samāsassa anto saro rasso hoti. Ettha ca abyayībhāvaggahaṇaṃ nānuvattetabbaṃ, tena digudvandabahubbīhīsupi napuṃsake vattamānassa samāsantassarassa rassattaṃ siddhaṃ hoti. “Aṃ vibhattīna”miccādinā amādeso, subhikkhaṃ. Gaṅgāya samīpe vattatīti upagaṅgaṃ, maṇikāya samīpaṃ upamaṇikaṃ.

The final vowel of a compound that is in the neuter gender becomes short. And here, the specification of 'abyayībhāva' should not be carried over; therefore, the shortening of the final vowel of a compound that is in the neuter gender is established even in digu, dvanda, and bahubbīhi compounds. By the rule beginning 'Aṃ vibhattīnaṃ', the substitution of `aṃ` occurs, as in `subhikkhaṃ`. `Upagaṅgaṃ` is from `Gaṅgāya samīpe vattati` (it is near the Ganges); `upamaṇikaṃ` is from `maṇikāya samīpaṃ` (near a jewel).

Itthīsu [M 0.0182] amikiccāti atthe samāsanapuṃsakarassattādīsu katesu –

In the sense of 'concerning women' (`itthīsu adhikicca`), when compounding, assignment to the neuter gender, shortening, and so forth have been applied—

“Abyayībhāvā, vibhattīna”nti ca vattate.

'From an abyayībhāva compound, of case endings' is also carried forward.

338. Aññasmā lopo ca.

338. And elision from another.

Akārantato aññasmā abyayībhāvasamāsā parāsaṃ vibhattīnaṃ lopo ca hoti. Adhitti, itthīsu adhikicca kathā pavattatīti attho. Adhitthi passa, adhitthi kataṃ iccādi, evaṃ adhikumāri, vadhuyā samīpaṃ upavadhu, gunnaṃ samīpaṃ upagu, okārassa rassattaṃ ukāro. Evaṃ upasaggapubbako.

From an abyayībhāva compound other than one ending in `a`, elision of the following case endings also occurs. For example, `Adhitti`; the meaning is 'a discussion proceeds concerning women'. `Adhitthi passa` (see concerning women), `Adhitthi kataṃ` (done concerning women), and so forth. Similarly, `adhikumāri`. `Upavadhu` is from `vadhuyā samīpaṃ` (near a bride). `Upagu` is from `gunnaṃ samīpaṃ` (near cattle); the shortening of `o` is `u`. Thus is the type with a prefix as the first member.

Nipātapubbako yathā – vuḍḍhānaṃ paṭipāṭi, ye ye vuḍḍhā vā yathāvuḍḍhaṃ, padatthānatikkame – yathākkamaṃ, yathāsatti, yathābalaṃ karoti, balamanatikkamitvā karotīti attho. Jīvassa yattako paricchedo yāvajīvaṃ, yāvatāyukaṃ, kappaccayo. Yattakena attho yāvadatthaṃ, pabbatassa parabhāgo tiropabbataṃ, tiropākāraṃ, tirokuṭṭaṃ, pāsādassa anto antopāsādaṃ, antonagaraṃ, antovassaṃ, nagarassa bahi bahinagaraṃ, pāsādassa upari uparipāsādaṃ, uparimañcaṃ, mañcassa heṭṭhā heṭṭhāmañcaṃ, heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ, bhattassa pure purebhattaṃ, evaṃ pacchābhattaṃ.

An example with a particle as the first member is as follows: `yathāvuḍḍhaṃ` from `vuḍḍhānaṃ paṭipāṭi` (in the order of the elders), or `ye ye vuḍḍhā` (whichever elders). In the sense of 'not exceeding the basis': `yathākkamaṃ` (in order); `yathāsatti` (according to ability); one acts `yathābalaṃ` (according to strength), the meaning of which is 'one acts without exceeding one's strength'. `Yāvajīvaṃ` and `yāvatāyukaṃ` are in the sense of `jīvassa yattako paricchedo` (whatever the extent of life is); the suffix is `kappa`. `Yāvadatthaṃ` is from `yattakena attho` (as much as is needed). `Tiropabbataṃ` is from `pabbatassa parabhāgo` (the other side of the mountain); similarly `tiropākāraṃ` (beyond the wall), `tirokuṭṭaṃ` (beyond the rampart). `Antopāsādaṃ` is from `pāsādassa anto` (inside the palace); similarly `antonagaraṃ` (inside the city), `antovassaṃ` (during the rains). `Bahinagaraṃ` is from `nagarassa bahi` (outside the city). `Uparipāsādaṃ` is from `pāsādassa upari` (above the palace); similarly `uparimañcaṃ` (on top of the couch). `Heṭṭhāmañcaṃ` is from `mañcassa heṭṭhā` (below the couch); similarly `heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ` (below the palace). `Purebhattaṃ` is from `bhattassa pure` (before the meal); similarly `pacchābhattaṃ` (after the meal).

Sākallatthe – saha makkhikāya samakkhikaṃ bhuñjati, na kiñci parivajjetīti attho. “Tesu vuddhī”tiādinā sahasaddassa sādeso. Gaṅgāya oraṃ oragaṅgamiccādi.

In the sense of totality: one eats `samakkhikaṃ`, from `saha makkhikāya` (together with the flies); the meaning is 'one avoids nothing'. By the rule beginning 'Tesu vuddhī', the substitution of `sa` for the word `saha` occurs. `Oragaṅgaṃ`, from `Gaṅgāya oraṃ` (this side of the Ganges), and so forth.

Abyayībhāvasamāso niṭṭhito.

The abyayībhāva compound is concluded.

Kammadhārayasamāsa

The Kammadhāraya Compound

Atha [M 0.0183] kammadhārayasamāso vuccate.

Now the kammadhāraya compound is explained.

So ca navavidho visesanapubbapado visesanuttarapado visesanobhayapado upamānuttarapado sambhāvanāpubbapado avadhāraṇapubbapado nanipātapubbapado kupubbapado pādipubbapado cāti.

And it is of nine kinds: the qualifier-first compound, the qualifier-last compound, the qualifier-both compound, the simile-last compound, the conception-first compound, the determination-first compound, the negative particle-first compound, the `ku`-first compound, and the preposition-first compound.

Tattha visesanapubbapado tāva – “mahanta purisa”itīdha ubhayattha paṭhamekavacanaṃ si, tulyādhikaraṇabhāvappasiddhatthaṃ casadda tasaddappayogo, mahanto ca so puriso cāti viggahe –

Therein, first, regarding the qualifier-first compound: here in 'mahanta purisa', in both places the nominative singular ending is `si`. To establish the state of apposition, the words `ca` and `ta` (`so`) are used, as in the analytical phrase: `mahanto ca so puriso ca` (he who is great and is a man)—

Ito paraṃ “vibhāsā rukkhatiṇa”iccādito “vibhāsā”ti samāsavidhāne sabbattha vattate.

From here onward, the term `vibhāsā` (optionally), from the rule beginning 'vibhāsā rukkhatiṇa', is carried forward and applies in all rules concerning the formation of compounds.

339. Dvipade tulyādhikaraṇe kammadhārayo.

339. When two words are in apposition, it is a kammadhāraya compound.

Dve padāni nāmikāni tulyādhikaraṇāni aññamaññena saha vibhāsā samasyante, tasmiṃ dvipade tulyādhikaraṇe sati so samāso kammadhārayasañño ca hoti.

Two nominal terms that are in apposition are optionally compounded with each other. When there is such a two-word phrase in apposition, that compound is also designated a kammadhāraya.

Dve padāni dvipadaṃ, tulyaṃ samānaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ attho yassa padadvayassa taṃ tulyādhikaraṇaṃ, tasmiṃ dvipade tulyādhikaraṇe. Bhinnappavattinimittānaṃ dvinnaṃ padānaṃ visesanavisesitabbabhāvena ekasmiṃ atthe pavatti tulyādhikaraṇatā. Kammamiva dvayaṃ dhārayatīti kammadhārayo. Yathā hi kammaṃ kriyañca payojanañca dvayaṃ dhārayati, kamme sati kriyāya, payojanassa ca sambhavato, tathā ayaṃ samāso ekassa atthassa dve nāmāni dhārayati, tasmiṃ samāse sati ekatthajotakassa nāmadvayassa sambhavato.

`Dvipadam` means 'two words.' `Tulyādhikaraṇaṃ` is a pair of words that has the same (`tulyaṃ`, `samānaṃ`) basis (`adhikaraṇa`), that is, meaning (`attho`); `tasmiṃ dvipade tulyādhikaraṇe` means 'in a two-word phrase in apposition'. Apposition (`tulyādhikaraṇatā`) is the application of two words, which have different grounds for application, to a single meaning through the relationship of qualifier and qualified. A `kammadhāraya` is so called because it 'holds (`dhārayati`) a pair (`dvayaṃ`) like an action (`kamma`).' For just as an action holds a pair—the activity and its purpose, since when there is an action, both activity and purpose are possible—so this compound holds two names for a single meaning, since when this compound exists, the possibility of a pair of names illuminating a single meaning arises.

Pure [M 0.0184] viya samāsasaññāvibhattilopapakatibhāvā, samāseneva tulyādhikaraṇabhāvassa vuttattā “vuttatthānamappayogo”ti casadda tasaddānamappayogo.

As before, there is the designation as a compound, the elision of the case ending, and the retention of the stem's original form. Since the state of apposition is expressed by the compound itself, the words `ca` and `ta` are not used, in accordance with the principle 'what is already expressed is not used' (`vuttatthānamappayogo`).

340. Mahataṃ mahā tulyādhikaraṇe pade.

340. Of `mahant`, `mahā` is the substitute when a word in apposition follows.

Mahanta saddassa mahā hoti tulyādhikaraṇe uttarapade pare. Mahatanti bahuvacanaggahaṇena kvaci mahaādeso ca, ettha ca visesanassa pubbanipāto visesanabhūtassa pubbapadassa mahādesavidhānatova viññāyati.

The word `mahant` becomes `mahā` when a latter member in apposition follows. The use of the plural `mahataṃ` in the rule indicates that sometimes the substitute is also `maha`. And here, the prior placement of the qualifier is understood from the very rule that prescribes the substitution of `mahā` for the prior member, which is the qualifier.

“Kammadhārayo, digū”ti ca vattate.

The terms `kammadhāraya` and `digu` are also carried forward.

341. Ubhe tappurisā.

341. Both are tappurisa compounds.

Ubhe kammadhārayadigusamāsā tappurisasaññā honti.

Both kammadhāraya and digu compounds are designated as tappurisa.

Tassa puriso tappuriso, tappurisasadisattā ayampi samāso anvatthasaññāya tappurisoti vutto. Yathā hi tappurisasaddo guṇamativatto, tathā ayaṃ samāsopi. Uttarapadatthappadhāno hi tappurisoti. Tato nāmabyapadeso syādyuppatti. Ayaṃ pana tappuriso abhidheyyavacano, paraliṅgo ca.

`Tappuriso` means 'his man.' Because this class of compound is similar to that specific `tappurisa`, it is also called `tappurisa` by a name that fits its meaning. For just as the word `tappurisa` has gone beyond its specific meaning, so too has this compound. A `tappurisa` is one in which the meaning of the latter member is predominant. From that comes its nominal designation and the application of case endings. This `tappurisa`, however, expresses the meaning of what is denoted, and its gender is that of the latter member.

Mahāpuriso, mahāpurisā iccādi purisasaddasamaṃ, evaṃ mahāvīro, mahāmuni, mahantañca taṃ balañcāti mahābalaṃ, mahabbhayaṃ, mahaādeso. Santo ca so puriso cāti sappuriso, “santasaddassa so bhe bo cante”ti ettha casaddena santasaddassa samāse abhakārepi sādeso, tathā pubbapuriso, parapuriso, paṭhamapuriso, majjhimapuriso, uttamapuriso, dantapuriso, paramapuriso, vīrapuriso, setahatthī, kaṇhasappo, nīluppalaṃ, lohitacandanaṃ.

`Mahāpuriso`, `mahāpurisā`, etc., are declined like the word `purisa`. Similarly: `mahāvīro` (great hero), `mahāmuni` (great sage). From `mahantañca taṃ balañca`, `mahābalaṃ` (great strength). `Mahabbhayaṃ` (great fear), where `maha` is the substitute. From `santo ca so puriso ca`, `sappuriso` (virtuous man); here, by the word `ca` in the rule 'santasaddassa so bhe bo cante', the substitution of `sa` for `santa` occurs in a compound even when there is no elision of the vowel. Likewise: `pubbapuriso` (former man), `parapuriso` (other man), `paṭhamapuriso` (first man), `majjhimapuriso` (middle man), `uttamapuriso` (highest man), `dantapuriso` (tamed man), `paramapuriso` (supreme man), `vīrapuriso` (heroic man), `setahatthī` (white elephant), `kaṇhasappo` (black snake), `nīluppalaṃ` (blue water lily), `lohitacandanaṃ` (red sandalwood).

Kvaci [M 0.0185] vibhāsādhikārato na bhavati, yathā – puṇṇo mantāniputto, citto gahapati, sakko devarājāti.

Sometimes, due to the governing rule `vibhāsā` (optionally), compounding does not occur, as in: `Puṇṇo Mantāniputto`, `Citto gahapati`, `Sakko devarājā`.

Pumā ca so kokilo cāti atthe samāse kate –

In the sense 'a male and that is a cuckoo,' when the compound has been formed—

“Lopa”nti vattate.

The word `lopa` (elision) is carried forward.

342. Pumassa liṅgādīsu samāsesu.

342. Of `puma`, before `liṅga`, etc., in compounds.

Pumaiccetassa anto akāro lopamāpajjate liṅgādīsu parapadesu samāsesu, “aṃmo niggahītaṃ jhalapehī”ti makārassa niggahītaṃ. Puṅkokilo. Evaṃ punnāgo.

Of this word `puma`, the final `a` is elided in compounds when words such as `liṅga` follow as the latter member. By the rule 'aṃ mo niggahītaṃ jhalapehi', the `m` becomes a `niggahīta` (`ṃ`). Thus, `puṅkokilo`. Similarly, `punnāgo`.

Khattiyā ca sā kaññā cāti viggayha samāse kate –

Having analyzed the phrase 'a Khattiya woman and that maiden,' when the compound is formed—

“Tulyādhikaraṇe, pade, itthiyaṃ bhāsitapumitthī pumāva ce”ti ca vattate.

The rule 'tulyādhikaraṇe pade, itthiyaṃ bhāsitapumitthī pumāva ce' is also carried forward.

343. Kammadhārayasaññe ca.

343. And in a compound designated as Kammadhāraya.

Kammadhārayasaññe ca samāse itthiyaṃ vattamāne tulyādhikaraṇe uttarapade pare pubbabhūto itthivācako saddo pubbe bhāsitapumā ce, so pumā iva daṭṭhabboti pubbapade itthippaccayassa nivatti hoti.

And in a compound designated as Kammadhāraya that refers to a feminine entity, when a latter member in apposition follows, a preceding feminine word that has a corresponding masculine form is to be treated as if it were masculine; that is, the feminine suffix of the prior member is removed.

Khattiyakaññā, khattiyakaññāyo iccādi. Evaṃ rattalatā, dutiyabhikkhā, brāhmaṇī ca sā dārikā cāti brāhmaṇadārikā, nāgamāṇavikā.

Khattiyakaññā (Khattiya maiden), khattiyakaññāyo (Khattiya maidens), etc. Similarly, rattalatā (red creeper), dutiyabhikkhā (second alms-round). From brāhmaṇī ca sā dārikā ca (a brahmin woman and that girl) comes brāhmaṇadārikā (brahmin girl). Nāgamāṇavikā (nāga maiden).

Pubbapadassevāyaṃ pumbhāvātideso, tena “khattiyakumārī kumārasamaṇī taruṇabrāhmaṇī”tiādīsu uttarapadesu itthippaccayassa na nivatti hoti.

This extension of the masculine form applies only to the prior member. Therefore, in the latter members of compounds such as khattiyakumārī (Khattiya princess), kumārasamaṇī (girl novice), and taruṇabrāhmaṇī (young brahmin woman), the feminine suffix is not removed.

Itthiyamicceva [M 0.0186] kiṃ? Kumārīratanaṃ, samaṇīpadumaṃ.

Why the specification 'when it is feminine'? For the sake of kumārīratanaṃ (a maiden-gem) and samaṇīpadumaṃ (a nun-lotus).

Bhāsitapumāti kiṃ? Gaṅgānadī, taṇhānadī, pathavīdhātu. “Nandāpokkharaṇī, nandādevī”tiādīsu pana saññāsaddattā na hoti.

Why the specification 'having a corresponding masculine form'? For the sake of Gaṅgānadī (the river Ganges), taṇhānadī (the river of craving), and pathavīdhātu (the earth element). However, in cases such as Nandāpokkharaṇī (Nandā's Pond) and Nandādevī (Queen Nandā), the change does not occur because these are proper names.

Tathā puratthimo ca so kāyo cāti puratthimakāyo, ettha ca kāyekadeso kāyasaddo. Evaṃ pacchimakāyo, heṭṭhimakāyo, uparimakāyo, sabbakāyo, purāṇavihāro, navāvāso, kataranikāyo, katamanikāyo, hetuppaccayo, abahulaṃ bahulaṃ katanti bahulīkataṃ, jīvitappadhānaṃ navakaṃ jīvitanavakaṃ iccādi.

Thus, from 'eastern and that body' comes puratthimakāyo (the eastern part of the body); here the word kāya refers to a part of the body. Similarly: pacchimakāyo (the western part of the body), heṭṭhimakāyo (the lower part of the body), uparimakāyo (the upper part of the body), sabbakāyo (the whole body), purāṇavihāro (the old monastery), navāvāso (the new residence), kataranikāyo (which group?), katamanikāyo (what group?), hetuppaccayo (root-condition). Bahulīkataṃ is what was not abundant made abundant. Jīvitanavakaṃ is a group of nine of which life is the chief; and so on.

Visesanuttarapade jinavacanānuparodhato therācariyapaṇḍitādi visesanaṃ parañca bhavati. Yathā – sāriputto ca so thero cāti sāriputtatthero. Evaṃ mahāmoggallānatthero, mahākassapatthero, buddhaghosācariyo, dhammapālācariyo, ācariyaguttiloti vā, mahosadho ca so paṇḍito cāti mahosadhapaṇḍito. Evaṃ vidhurapaṇḍito, vatthuviseso.

In the qualifier-last compound, out of respect for the usage of the Conqueror, qualifiers such as thera (elder), ācariya (teacher), and paṇḍita (scholar) are also placed second. For example: from sāriputto ca so thero ca (Sāriputta and that elder) comes sāriputtatthero (the Elder Sāriputta). Similarly, mahāmoggallānatthero (the Elder Mahāmoggallāna), mahākassapatthero (the Elder Mahākassapa), buddhaghosācariyo (the Teacher Buddhaghosa), dhammapālācariyo (the Teacher Dhammapāla), or ācariyaguttilo (the Teacher Guttila). From mahosadho ca so paṇḍito ca (Mahosadha and that scholar) comes mahosadhapaṇḍito (the scholar Mahosadha). Likewise, vidhurapaṇḍito (the scholar Vidhura). This is a special case.

Visesanobhayapado yathā – sītañca taṃ uṇhañcāti sītuṇhaṃ, siniddho ca so uṇho cāti siniddhuṇho, māso. Khañjo ca so khujjo cāti khañjakhujjo. Evaṃ andhabadhiro, katākataṃ, chiddāvachiddaṃ, uccāvacaṃ, chinnabhinnaṃ, sittasammaṭṭhaṃ, gatapaccāgataṃ.

The qualifier-both compound, as in: from sītañca taṃ uṇhañca (cold and that which is hot) comes sītuṇhaṃ (cold-and-hot). From siniddho ca so uṇho ca (greasy and that which is hot) comes siniddhuṇho (greasy-and-hot), for example, a month. From khañjo ca so khujjo ca (lame and that which is hunchbacked) comes khañjakhujjo (lame-and-hunchbacked). Similarly: andhabadhiro (blind-and-deaf), katākataṃ (done-and-undone), chiddāvachiddaṃ (with-and-without-holes), uccāvacaṃ (high-and-low), chinnabhinnaṃ (cut-and-broken), sittasammaṭṭhaṃ (sprinkled-and-swept), gatapaccāgataṃ (gone-and-returned).

Upamānuttarapade abhidhānānurodhato upamānabhūtaṃ visesanaṃ paraṃ bhavati. Yathā – sīho viya sīho, muni ca so sīho cāti munisīho. Evaṃ munivasabho, munipuṅgavo, buddhanāgo, buddhādicco, raṃsi viya raṃsi, saddhammo ca [M 0.0187] so raṃsi cāti saddhammaraṃsi. Evaṃ vinayasāgaro, puṇḍarīkamiva puṇḍarīko, samaṇo ca so puṇḍarīko cāti samaṇapuṇḍarīko, samaṇapadumo. Cando viya cando, mukhañca taṃ cando cāti mukhacando. Evaṃ mukhapadumaṃ iccādi.

In the simile-last compound, according to usage, the qualifier that is the standard of comparison is placed second. For example: a lion is like a lion; from muni ca so sīho ca (a sage and he is a lion) comes munisīho (a sage-lion). Similarly, munivasabho (a sage-bull), munipuṅgavo (a sage-chief), buddhanāgo (a Buddha-elephant), buddhādicco (a Buddha-sun). A ray is like a ray; from saddhammo ca so raṃsi ca (the good Dhamma and it is a ray) comes saddhammaraṃsi (the ray of the good Dhamma). Similarly, vinayasāgaro (the ocean of the Vinaya). A white lotus is like a white lotus; from samaṇo ca so puṇḍarīko ca (a recluse and he is a white lotus) comes samaṇapuṇḍarīko (a recluse-white lotus), samaṇapadumo (a recluse-lotus). The moon is like the moon; from mukhañca taṃ cando ca (the face and it is the moon) comes mukhacando (a moon-face). Similarly, mukhapadumaṃ (a lotus-face), and so on.

Sambhāvanāpubbapado yathā – dhammo iti buddhi dhammabuddhi. Evaṃ dhammasaññā, dhammasaṅkhāto, dhammasammato, pāṇasaññitā, asubhasaññā, aniccasaññā, anattasaññā, dhātusaññā, dhītusaññā, attasaññā, atthisaññā, attadiṭṭhi iccādi.

The conception-first compound, as in: the thought 'it is Dhamma' is dhammabuddhi (thought of Dhamma). Similarly, dhammasaññā (perception of Dhamma), dhammasaṅkhāto (called Dhamma), dhammasammato (considered Dhamma), pāṇasaññitā (perception of a living being), asubhasaññā (perception of foulness), aniccasaññā (perception of impermanence), anattasaññā (perception of not-self), dhātusaññā (perception of elements), dhītusaññā (perception of decay), attasaññā (perception of self), atthisaññā (perception of existence), attadiṭṭhi (view of self), and so on.
