Avadhāraṇapubbapado yathā – guṇo eva dhanaṃ guṇadhanaṃ. Evaṃ saddhādhanaṃ, sīladhanaṃ, paññādhanaṃ, cakkhu eva indriyaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ. Evaṃ cakkhāyatanaṃ, cakkhudhātu, cakkhudvāraṃ, rūpārammaṇamiccādi.

The determination-first compound, as in: guṇo eva dhanaṃ (virtue itself is wealth) is guṇadhanaṃ (the wealth of good qualities). Similarly, saddhādhanaṃ (the wealth of faith), sīladhanaṃ (the wealth of moral virtue), paññādhanaṃ (the wealth of wisdom). Cakkhu eva indriyaṃ (the eye itself is a faculty) is cakkhundriyaṃ (the eye-faculty). Similarly, cakkhāyatanaṃ (the eye-base), cakkhudhātu (the eye-element), cakkhudvāraṃ (the eye-door), rūpārammaṇaṃ (form-object), and so on.

Nanipātapubbapado yathā – na brāhmaṇoti atthe kammadhārayasamāse, vibhattilopādimhi ca kate –

The na-particle-first compound, as in: in the sense 'not a brahmin,' when a Kammadhāraya compound is formed, and after the elision of the case ending and so on has been performed—

“Ubhe tappurisā”ti tappurisasaññā.

The designation ‘Tappurisa’ is applied by the rule ‘Ubhe tappurisā’.

344. Attaṃ nassa tappurise.

344. Na becomes a in a Tappurisa compound.

Nassa nipātapadassa tappurise uttarapade pare sabbasseva attaṃ hoti. Tappurisekadesattā tappuriso, abrāhmaṇo.

The negative particle na becomes a when a subsequent word follows in a Tappurisa compound. A Tappurisa is so-called because it is a part of that compound; for example, abrāhmaṇo (a non-Brahmin).

Na nisedho sato yutto,

Desādiniyamaṃ vinā;

Asato cāphalo tasmā,

Kathamabrāhmaṇoti ce?

Negation is not appropriate for what exists, without a rule of place and so on; and for what does not exist, it is fruitless. Therefore, how can one say ‘non-Brahmin’?

Nisedhatthānuvādena, paṭisedhavidhi kvaci;

Parassa micchāñāṇattā-khyāpanāyopapajjate.

A rule of prohibition, by way of restating the meaning of negation, is sometimes employed to expose another's false knowledge.

Duvidho cassattho pasajjappaṭisedhapariyudāsavasena.

Its meaning is twofold: by way of explicit negation (pasajjappaṭisedha) and by way of exclusion (pariyudāsa).

Tattha [M 0.0188] yo “asūriyapassā rājadārā”tiādīsu viya uttarapadatthassa sabbathā abhāvaṃ dīpeti, so pasajjappaṭisedhavācī nāma. Yo pana “abrāhmaṇa amanussā”tiādīsu viya uttarapadatthaṃ pariyudāsitvā taṃsadise vatthumhi kāriyaṃ paṭipādayati, so pariyudāsavācī nāma.

Here, that which, as in phrases like ‘royal wives who do not see the sun,’ indicates the complete absence of the meaning of the subsequent word, is called an expression of explicit negation. But that which, as in phrases like ‘non-Brahmins, non-humans,’ excludes the meaning of the subsequent word and accomplishes the action in a similar object, is called an expression of exclusion.

Vuttañca

And it has been said:

“Pasajjappaṭisedhassa, lakkhaṇaṃ vatthunatthitā;

Vatthuto aññatra vutti, pariyudāsalakkhaṇa”nti.

“The characteristic of explicit negation is the non-existence of the object; speaking about something other than the object is the characteristic of exclusion.”

Nanvevaṃ santepi “abrāhmaṇo”tiādīsu kathamuttarapadatthappadhānatā siyāti?

But even if it is so, how can there be prominence of the meaning of the subsequent word in cases such as ‘non-Brahmin’ and so on?

Vuccate – brāhmaṇādisaddānaṃ brāhmaṇādiatthasseva taṃsadisādiatthassāpi vācakattā, brāhmaṇādisaddā hi kevalābrāhmaṇādiatthesveva pākaṭā, bhūsaddo viyasattāyaṃ, yadā te pana aññena sadisādivācakena naiti nipātena yujjanti, tadā taṃsadisatadaññatabbiruddhatadabhāvesupi vattanti, bhūsaddo viya anvabhiyādiyoge anubhavanaabhibhavanādīsu, tasmā uttarapadatthajotakoyevettha naiti nipātoti na doso, tena abrāhmaṇoti brāhmaṇasadisoti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ amanusso, assamaṇo.

It is said: because terms like ‘brahmin’ are expressive of the meaning of ‘brahmin’ and so on, as well as of a meaning similar to that; for terms like ‘brahmin’ are well-known only in the meanings of ‘brahmin’ and the like, just as the term ‘bhū’ is in the sense of ‘existence.’ But when they are connected with the particle ‘na,’ which expresses otherness, similarity, and so on, then they also function in the senses of similarity, otherness, opposition, and absence of that; just as the term ‘bhū’ functions in connection with anu, abhi, ādi (etc.) in the senses of experiencing, overcoming, and so on. Therefore, here the particle ‘na’ only illuminates the meaning of the subsequent word, and there is no fault; thus, ‘non-Brahmin’ means ‘similar to a Brahmin.’ Similarly, ‘non-human,’ ‘non-ascetic.’

Aññatthe – na byākatā abyākatā, asaṃkiliṭṭhā, apariyāpannā.

In the sense of otherness: na byākatā (not declared) becomes abyākatā (undeclared); asaṃkiliṭṭhā (undefiled), apariyāpannā (uninvolved).

Viruddhatthe – na kusalā akusalā, kusalapaṭipakkhāti attho. Evaṃ alobho, amitto.

In the sense of opposition: na kusalā (not wholesome) becomes akusalā (unwholesome), meaning the opposite of wholesome. Thus, alobho (non-greed), amitto (non-friend).

Pasajjappaṭisedhe – na katvā akatvā, akātuna puññaṃ akaronto.

In explicit negation: na katvā (not having done) becomes akatvā (having not done); akātuna (not having done), puññaṃ akaronto (not doing merit).

“Nassa, tappurise”ti ca vattate.

And the rule ‘Nassa, tappurise’ is carried forward.

345. Sare [M 0.0189] ana.

345. When a vowel follows, `ana`.

Naiccetassa padassa tappurise uttarapade ana hoti sare pare.

This word `na` becomes `ana` in a Tappurisa compound when a subsequent word beginning with a vowel follows.

Na asso anasso, na ariyo anariyo. Evaṃ anissaro, aniṭṭho, anupavādo, na ādāya anādāya, anoloketvā iccādi.

Not a horse, `anasso`; not noble, `anariyo`. Similarly, `anissaro` (lordless), `aniṭṭho` (undesirable), `anupavādo` (blameless), `na ādāya` (not having taken) becomes `anādāya`, `anoloketvā` (not having looked), and so on.

Kupubbapado yathā – kucchitamannanti niccasamāsattā aññapadena viggaho, kammadhārayasamāse kate –

Regarding a word with `ku` as its first member, for example, `kucchitam annaṃ` (contemptible food)—since it is a permanent compound, the analysis is with another word. When a Kammadhāraya compound is formed—

“Tappurise, sare”ti ca vattate.

And ‘in a Tappurisa’ and ‘when a vowel follows’ are carried over.

346. Kadada kussa.

346. `Kada` is the substitute for `ku`.

Kuiccetassa nipātassa tappurise uttarapade kada hoti sare pare. Kadannaṃ. Evaṃ kadasanaṃ.

This particle `ku` becomes `kada` in a Tappurisa compound when a subsequent word beginning with a vowel follows. For example, `kadannaṃ`. Similarly, `kadasanaṃ`.

Sareti kiṃ? Kudārā, kuputtā, kudāsā, kudiṭṭhi.

Why the stipulation ‘when a vowel follows’? `Kudārā` (a bad wife), `kuputtā` (a bad son), `kudāsā` (a bad slave), `kudiṭṭhi` (a wrong view).

“Kussā”ti vattate.

‘Of `ku`’ is carried over.

347. Kāppatthesu ca.

347. And `kā` is the substitute in the sense of smallness or contempt.

Kuiccetassa appatthe vattamānassa kā hoti tappurise uttarapade pare. Bahuvacanuccāraṇato kucchitatthe ca kvaci tappurise. Appakaṃ lavaṇaṃ kālavaṇaṃ. Evaṃ kāpupphaṃ, kucchito puriso kāpuriso, kupuriso vā.

This particle `ku`, when it has the sense of smallness, becomes `kā` in a Tappurisa compound when a subsequent word follows. From the use of the plural in the rule, it also sometimes occurs in the sense of contempt in a Tappurisa compound. For example, `appakaṃ lavaṇaṃ` (a little salt) becomes `kālavaṇaṃ`. Similarly, `kāpupphaṃ` (a small or bad flower); `kucchito puriso` (a contemptible person) is `kāpuriso` or, alternatively, `kupuriso`.

Pādipubbapado ca niccasamāsova, padhānaṃ vacanaṃ pāvacanaṃ, bhusaṃ vaddhaṃ pavaddhaṃ, sarīraṃ, samaṃ, sammā vā ādhānaṃ samādhānaṃ, vividhā mati vimati, vividho kappo vikappo, visiṭṭho vā kappo [M 0.0190] vikappo, adhiko devo atidevo. Evaṃ adhidevo, adhisīlaṃ, sundaro gandho sugandho, kucchito gandho duggandho, sobhanaṃ kataṃ sukataṃ, asobhanaṃ kataṃ dukkaṭaṃ iccādi.

And a compound with `pa`, etc., as its first member is also a permanent compound. For example: `padhānaṃ vacanaṃ` (principal speech) is `pāvacanaṃ` (scripture); `bhusaṃ vaddhaṃ` (greatly grown) is `pavaddhaṃ` (greatly increased); `sarīraṃ`, `samaṃ`, or `sammā ādhānaṃ` (right placing) is `samādhānaṃ` (concentration); `vividhā mati` (diverse thought) is `vimati` (doubt); `vividho kappo` (various arrangements) or `visiṭṭho vā kappo` (a special arrangement) is `vikappo` (an alternative); `adhiko devo` (a superior deity) is `atidevo` (a surpassing deity). Similarly, `adhidevo` (a supreme deity), `adhisīlaṃ` (higher virtue); `sundaro gandho` (a pleasant scent) is `sugandho` (a good scent); `kucchito gandho` (a foul scent) is `duggandho` (a bad scent); `sobhanaṃ kataṃ` (well done) is `sukataṃ` (a good deed); `asobhanaṃ kataṃ` (ill done) is `dukkaṭaṃ` (a misdeed), and so on.

Ye idha avihitalakkhaṇā nāmanipātopasaggā, tesaṃ “nāmānaṃ samāso”ti yogavibhāgena samāso daṭṭhabbo. Yathā – apunageyyā gāthā, acandamullokikāni mukhāni, assaddhabhojī, alavaṇabhojītiādīsu ayuttatthattā nāññena samāso.

For those nouns, particles, and prefixes for which a rule has not been prescribed here, their compounding should be understood by means of splitting the rule ‘compounding of nouns’. For example: in cases such as `apunageyyā gāthā` (a verse not to be recited again), `acandamullokikāni mukhāni` (faces not looking up at the moon), `assaddhabhojī` (one who eats without faith), `alavaṇabhojī` (one who eats without salt), there is no other type of compounding due to the unsuitability of the meaning.

Tathā diṭṭho pubbanti diṭṭhapubbo tathāgataṃ. Evaṃ sutapubbo dhammaṃ, gatapubbo maggaṃ, kammani diṭṭhā pubbanti diṭṭhapubbā devā tena. Evaṃ sutapubbā dhammā, gatapubbā disā, pahāro, parābhavo, vihāro, āhāro, upahāro iccādi.

Likewise, from the analysis `diṭṭho pubbaṃ` (seen before) comes `diṭṭhapubbo`, as in `diṭṭhapubbo tathāgataṃ` (he has seen the Tathāgata before). Similarly, `sutapubbo dhammaṃ` (he has heard the Dhamma before), `gatapubbo maggaṃ` (he has gone the path before). In the passive sense, from `diṭṭhā pubbaṃ` comes `diṭṭhapubbā`, as in `diṭṭhapubbā devā tena` (the gods were seen by him before). Similarly, `sutapubbā dhammā` (the dhammas were heard before), `gatapubbā disā` (the direction was gone to before). Further examples are `pahāro` (striking), `parābhavo` (defeat), `vihāro` (abiding), `āhāro` (food), `upahāro` (offering), and so on.

Kammadhārayasamāso.

The Kammadhāraya Compound.

Digusamāsa

The Digu Compound

Atha digusamāso vuccate.

Now the Digu compound is explained.

Tayo lokā samāhaṭā cittena sampiṇḍitā, tiṇṇaṃ lokānaṃ samāhāroti vā atthe –

When the meaning is ‘the three worlds are gathered together, compressed by the mind,’ or in the sense of ‘a collection of the three worlds’—

“Nāmānaṃ samāso yuttattho”ti vattamāne “dvipade”tiādinā kammadhārayasamāso, tato samāsasaññāyaṃ, vibhattilope, pakatibhāve ca kate –

While the rule ‘The compounding of nouns has a connected meaning’ is current, a Kammadhāraya compound is formed by the rule beginning ‘dvipade,’ etc.; then, after the designation as a compound, the elision of the case ending, and the restoration of the base form have been effected—

“Kammadhārayo”ti vattate.

The designation ‘Kammadhāraya’ is carried over.

348. Saṅkhyāpubbo [M 0.0191] digu.

348. A Digu has a numeral as its first member.

Saṅkhyāpubbo kammadhārayasamāso digusañño hoti.

A Kammadhāraya compound that has a numeral as its first member receives the designation ‘Digu’.

Dve gāvo digu, digusadisattā ayampi samāso digūti vutto. Atha vā saṅkhyāpubbattanapuṃsakekattasaṅkhātehi dvīhi lakkhaṇehi gato avagatoti digūti vuccati, dvīhi vā lakkhaṇehi gacchati pavattatīti digu. Ettha ca “saṅkhyāpubbo”ti vuttattā saṅkhyāsaddasseva pubbanipāto, “ubhe tappurisā”ti tappurisasaññā.

‘Two cows’ (`dve gāvo`) is the etymology of `digu`; this compound is also called `digu` due to its similarity with this. Or alternatively, it is called `digu` because it is `gato` (understood) by `dvi` (two) characteristics, namely, having a numeral as its first member and being neuter and singular; or it is `digu` because it `gacchati` (proceeds) by two characteristics. And here, since it is stated ‘has a numeral as its first member,’ only a numeral word is placed first; and from the rule ‘both are Tappurisa,’ it receives the Tappurisa designation.

“Napuṃsakaliṅgo”ti vattate.

The rule ‘it is of neuter gender’ is carried over.

349. Digussekattaṃ.

349. A Digu compound is singular.

Digussa samāsassa ekattaṃ hoti, napuṃsakaliṅgattañca.

A Digu compound is singular and of the neuter gender.

Samāhāradigussetaṃ gahaṇaṃ, tattha sabbatthekavacanameva hoti, aññatra pana bahuvacanampi, nāmabyapadesasyādyuppatti amādesādi.

This rule applies to a Samāhāra-Digu (collective) compound; in that case, it is always in the singular. Elsewhere, however, it is also in the plural. The initial derivation of the nominal form, the substitution of `aṃ`, etc., then takes place.

Tilokaṃ, he tiloka, tilokaṃ, tilokena, tilokassa, tilokā tilokasmā tilokamhā, tilokassa, tiloke tilokamhi tilokasmiṃ.

Tilokaṃ (nominative singular), he tiloka (vocative singular), tilokaṃ (accusative singular), tilokena (instrumental singular), tilokassa (dative singular), tilokā, tilokasmā, tilokamhā (ablative singular), tilokassa (genitive singular), tiloke, tilokamhi, tilokasmiṃ (locative singular).

Evaṃ tayo daṇḍā tidaṇḍaṃ, tīṇi malāni samāhaṭāni, tiṇṇaṃ malānaṃ samāhāroti vā timalaṃ, tilakkhaṇaṃ, catussaccaṃ, catasso disā catuddisaṃ, “saro rasso napuṃsake”ti rassattaṃ, pañcasikkhāpadaṃ, saḷāyatanaṃ, sattāhaṃ, aṭṭhasīlaṃ, navalokuttaraṃ, dasasīlaṃ, satayojanaṃ.

Similarly: `tayo daṇḍā` (three staffs) becomes `tidaṇḍaṃ`; `tīṇi malāni samāhaṭāni` (three stains gathered together), or `tiṇṇaṃ malānaṃ samāhāro` (a collection of three stains), becomes `timalaṃ`; `tilakkhaṇaṃ` (the three characteristics); `catussaccaṃ` (the four truths); `catasso disā` (four directions) becomes `catuddisaṃ`, with the vowel shortened by the rule ‘a vowel is short in the neuter’; `pañcasikkhāpadaṃ` (the five training precepts); `saḷāyatanaṃ` (the six sense-spheres); `sattāhaṃ` (a week); `aṭṭhasīlaṃ` (the eight precepts); `navolokuttaraṃ` (the nine supramundane states); `dasasīlaṃ` (the ten precepts); `satayojanaṃ` (a hundred leagues).

Tathā – dve rattiyo dvirattaṃ, tisso rattiyo tirattaṃ, dve aṅguliyo dvaṅgulaṃ, satta godāvariyo, tāsaṃ samāhāroti vā sattagodāvaraṃ.

Likewise: `dve rattiyo` (two nights) becomes `dvirattaṃ`; `tisso rattiyo` (three nights) becomes `tirattaṃ`; `dve aṅguliyo` (two fingers) becomes `dvaṅgulaṃ`; `satta godāvariyo` (seven Godāvarī rivers), or `tāsaṃ samāhāro` (a collection of them), becomes `sattagodāvaraṃ`.

Ettha ca ratti aṅguli godāvarīnamantassa –

And here, for the ending of ‘ratti,’ ‘aṅguli,’ and ‘godāvarī’ –

350. Kvaci samāsantagatānamakāranto.

350. Sometimes, the ending of those that have come to the end of a compound is ‘a’.

Rājādigaṇassetaṃ gahaṇaṃ, tena samāsantagatānaṃ rājādīnaṃ nāmānaṃ anto kvaci akāro hotīti attho. Kāraggahaṇena bahubbīhādimhi samāsante kvaci kappaccayo hoti, surabhi su du pūtīhi gandhantassikāro ca.

This is the inclusion for the group of words beginning with ‘rāja’; by this, the meaning is that sometimes the ending of nouns such as ‘rāja’ that have come to the end of a compound becomes ‘a’. And by the inclusion of ‘kāra’, sometimes the suffix ‘kappa’ occurs at the end of a Bahubbīhi or other compound, and for a word ending in ‘gandha’, the ending becomes ‘i’ when preceded by ‘surabhi,’ ‘su,’ ‘du,’ and ‘pūti’.

Atha vā a ca ko ca akā, rakāro padasandhikaro, tena kvaci samāsantagatānamanto hutvā a ka iccete paccayā hontīti attho. Tena pañca gāvo samāhaṭāti atthe samāsādiṃ katvā samāsante appaccaye, “o sare cā”ti avādese ca kate “pañcagava”ntiādi ca sijjhati. “Dviratta”ntiādīsu pana appaccaye kate pubbasarassa “saralopo”tiādinā lopo.

Or alternatively, ‘a’ and ‘ka’ form ‘akā’; the letter ‘ra’ is for euphonic combination; by this, the meaning is that sometimes the suffixes ‘a’ and ‘ka’ occur as the ending of those that have come to the end of a compound. Thus, in the sense of ‘five cows gathered together,’ having formed a compound and so on, and when the suffix ‘a’ is applied at the end of the compound, and when the substitution of ‘ava’ is made by the rule ‘o sare cā,’ forms such as ‘pañcagava’ are established. However, in cases such as ‘dviratta,’ when the suffix ‘a’ is applied, the preceding vowel is elided by rules such as ‘saralopo’.

Asamāhāradigu yathā – eko ca so puggalo cāti ekapuggalo. Evaṃ ekadhammo, ekaputto, tayo bhavā tibhavā, catasso disā catuddisā, dasasahassacakkavāḷāni iccādi.

An Asamāhāra-Digu compound is, for example: ‘one and that person’ (eko ca so puggalo ca) becomes ekapuggalo. Similarly: ekadhammo (one phenomenon), ekaputto (one son), ‘three states of existence’ (tayo bhavā) becomes tibhavā, ‘four directions’ (catasso disā) becomes catuddisā, dasasahassacakkavāḷāni (ten thousand world-systems), and so on.

Digusamāso.

The Digu Compound.

Tappurisasamāsa

The Tappurisa Compound

Atha tappurisasamāso vuccate.

Now the Tappurisa compound is explained.

So pana dutiyādīsu chasu vibhattīsu bhāvato chabbidho. Tattha dutiyātappuriso gatanissitātītātikkantappattāpannādīhi bhavati.

It is, however, of six kinds, due to its occurrence with the six case endings beginning with the second. Therein, the Second Tappurisa is formed with words such as ‘gone’ (gata), ‘dependent on’ (nissita), ‘past’ (atīta), ‘surpassed’ (atikkanta), ‘attained’ (patta), ‘reached’ (āpanna), and so on.

Saraṇaṃ gatoti viggahe –

In the analytical expression ‘gone to refuge’ (saraṇaṃ gato) –

“Tappuriso”ti vattate.

The rule ‘Tappuriso’ is in effect.

351. Amādayo[M 0.0193] parapadebhi.

351. Words ending in ‘am’ and so on are compounded with subsequent words.

Amādivibhatyantāni yuttatthāni pubbapadāni nāmehi parapadebhi saha vibhāsā samasyante, so samāso tappurisasañño hoti. Ayañca tappuriso abhidheyyavacanaliṅgo.

Prior members ending in case endings beginning with ‘am’ and having a connected meaning are optionally compounded with subsequent nominal members; that compound is designated as a Tappurisa. And this Tappurisa takes the gender and number of the thing denoted.

Gatādisaddā kitantattā tiliṅgā, vibhattilopādi sabbaṃ pubbasamaṃ. So saraṇagato, te saraṇagatā. Sā saraṇagatā, tā saraṇagatāyo. Taṃ kulaṃ saraṇagataṃ, tāni kulāni saraṇagatāni iccādi.

Words such as ‘gata’ are of three genders because they are kṛt-derivatives; the elision of case endings and all else is as before. Thus: so saraṇagato (he has gone for refuge), te saraṇagatā (they [masc.] have gone for refuge); sā saraṇagatā (she has gone for refuge), tā saraṇagatāyo (they [fem.] have gone for refuge); taṃ kulaṃ saraṇagataṃ (that family has gone for refuge), tāni kulāni saraṇagatāni (those families have gone for refuge), and so on.

Evaṃ araññagato, bhūmigato, dhammaṃ nissito dhammanissito, atthanissito, bhavaṃ atīto bhavātīto, kālātīto, pamāṇaṃ atikkantaṃ pamāṇātikkantaṃ. Lokātikkantaṃ, sukhaṃ patto sukhappatto, dukkhappatto, sotaṃ āpanno sotāpanno, nirodhasamāpanno, rathaṃ āruḷho rathāruḷho, sabbarattiṃ sobhano sabbarattisobhano, muhuttasukhaṃ.

Similarly: araññagato (gone to the wilderness), bhūmigato (gone to the ground); ‘relying on the Dhamma’ (dhammaṃ nissito) becomes dhammanissito; atthanissito (dependent on the meaning); ‘past existence’ (bhavaṃ atīto) becomes bhavātīto; kālātīto (beyond time); ‘surpassed the measure’ (pamāṇaṃ atikkantaṃ) becomes pamāṇātikkantaṃ; lokātikkantaṃ (transcending the world); ‘attained happiness’ (sukhaṃ patto) becomes sukhappatto; dukkhappatto (attained suffering); ‘entered the stream’ (sotaṃ āpanno) becomes sotāpanno; nirodhasamāpanno (attained cessation); ‘mounted the chariot’ (rathaṃ āruḷho) becomes rathāruḷho; ‘splendid all night’ (sabbarattiṃ sobhano) becomes sabbarattisobhano; muhuttasukhaṃ (momentary happiness).

Upapadasamāse pana vuttiyeva tassa niccattā. Yathā – kammaṃ karotīti kammakāro, kumbhakāro, atthaṃ kāmetīti atthakāmo, dhammakāmo, dhammaṃ dhāretīti dhammadharo, vinayadharo, saccaṃ vadituṃ sīlamassāti saccavādī iccādi.

However, in an Upapada compound, the formation is obligatory. For example: ‘one who does work’ (kammaṃ karoti) becomes kammakāro (worker); kumbhakāro (potter); ‘one who desires benefit’ (atthaṃ kāmeti) becomes atthakāmo (one who desires benefit); dhammakāmo (one who desires the Dhamma); ‘one who upholds the Dhamma’ (dhammaṃ dhāreti) becomes dhammadharo (upholder of the Dhamma); vinayadharo (upholder of the Vinaya); ‘one whose nature it is to speak truth’ (saccaṃ vadituṃ sīlamassāti) becomes saccavādī (a speaker of truth), and so on.

Tavantumānantādikitantehi vākyameva vavatthitavibhāsādhikārato. Yathā – odanaṃ bhuttavā, dhammaṃ suṇamāno, dhammaṃ suṇanto, kaṭaṃ karāno, anabhidhānato vā, abhidhānalakkhaṇā hi taddhitasamāsakitakāti.

With words ending in kṛt suffixes such as ‘tavantu’ and ‘māna,’ only the phrase is used, because of the governing rule of established optionality. For example: odanaṃ bhuttavā (having eaten rice), dhammaṃ suṇamāno (listening to the Dhamma), dhammaṃ suṇanto (listening to the Dhamma), kaṭaṃ karāno (making a mat); or, it is due to non-expression, for taddhita derivatives, compounds, and kṛt derivatives are indeed characterized by expression.

Dutiyātappuriso.

End of the Second Tappurisa.

Tatiyā [M 0.0194] kitaka pubba sadisa samūnattha kalaha nipuṇa missasakhilādīhi.

The third case ending is compounded with kṛt-derivatives, and with words such as ‘prior’ (pubba), ‘similar’ (sadisa), ‘deficient’ (samūna), ‘purpose’ (attha), ‘quarrel’ (kalaha), ‘skilled’ (nipuṇa), ‘mixed’ (missa), ‘gentle’ (sakhila), and so on.

Buddhena bhāsito buddhabhāsito, dhammo. Evaṃ jinadesito, satthārā vaṇṇito satthuvaṇṇito, viññūhi garahito viññugarahito, viññuppasattho, issarakataṃ, sayaṃkataṃ, sukehi āhaṭaṃ sukāhataṃ, raññā hato rājahato, rogapīḷito, aggidaḍḍho, sappadaṭṭho, sallena viddho sallaviddho, icchāya apakato icchāpakato, sīlena sampanno sīlasampanno. Evaṃ sukhasahagataṃ, ñāṇasampayuttaṃ, mittasaṃsaggo, piyavippayogo, jātitthaddho, guṇahīno, guṇavuḍḍho, catuvaggakaraṇīyaṃ, catuvaggādikattabbaṃ, kākehi peyyā kākapeyyā, nadī.

‘Spoken by the Buddha’ (Buddhena bhāsito) becomes buddhabhāsito, as in dhammo (the Dhamma). Similarly: jinadesito (taught by the Victor); ‘praised by the Teacher’ (satthārā vaṇṇito) becomes satthuvaṇṇito; ‘censured by the wise’ (viññūhi garahito) becomes viññugarahito; viññuppasattho (praised by the wise); issarakataṃ (done by the Lord); sayaṃkataṃ (done by oneself); ‘brought by parrots’ (sukehi āhaṭaṃ) becomes sukāhataṃ; ‘killed by a king’ (raññā hato) becomes rājahato; rogapīḷito (afflicted by disease); aggidaḍḍho (burnt by fire); sappadaṭṭho (bitten by a snake); ‘pierced by an arrow’ (sallena viddho) becomes sallaviddho; ‘removed by desire’ (icchāya apakato) becomes icchāpakato; ‘endowed with virtue’ (sīlena sampanno) becomes sīlasampanno. Similarly: sukhasahagataṃ (accompanied by happiness); ñāṇasampayuttaṃ (associated with knowledge); mittasaṃsaggo (association with friends); piyavippayogo (separation from the beloved); jātitthaddho (stiff with pride of birth); guṇahīno (deficient in virtue); guṇavuḍḍho (grown in virtue); catuvaggakaraṇīyaṃ (to be done by a group of four); catuvaggādikattabbaṃ (to be done starting with a group of four); ‘drinkable by crows’ (kākehi peyyā) becomes kākapeyyā, as in nadī (a river).

Kvaci vuttiyeva, urena gacchatīti urago, pādena pivatīti pādapo. Kvaci vākyameva, parasunā chinnavā, kākehi pātabbā, dassanena pahātabbā.

Sometimes only the compound formation is used, as in: ‘one who goes on its chest’ (urena gacchati) becomes urago (a snake); ‘one that drinks with its foot’ (pādena pivati) becomes pādapo (a tree). Sometimes only the phrase is used, as in: parasunā chinnavā (he cut with an axe), kākehi pātabbā (to be drunk by crows), dassanena pahātabbā (to be abandoned through seeing).

Pubbādiyoge – māsena pubbo māsapubbo. Evaṃ mātusadiso, pitusamo, ekūnavīsati, sīlavikalo, asikalaho, vācānipuṇo, yāvakālikasaṃmissaṃ, vācāsakhilo, satthārā sadiso satthukappo, puññena atthiko puññatthiko, guṇādhiko, guḷena saṃsaṭṭho odano guḷodano, khīrodano, assena yutto ratho assaratho, maggacittaṃ, jambuyā paññāto lakkhito dīpo jambudīpo, ekena adhikā dasa ekādasa, jātiyā andho jaccandho, pakatiyā medhāvī pakatimedhāvī iccādi.

In conjunction with ‘pubba’ and so on: ‘prior by a month’ (māsena pubbo) becomes māsapubbo. Similarly: mātusadiso (like the mother); pitusamo (equal to the father); ekūnavīsati (one less than twenty); sīlavikalo (deficient in virtue); asikalaho (quarrel with a sword); vācānipuṇo (skilled in speech); yāvakālikasaṃmissaṃ (mixed for a limited time); vācāsakhilo (gentle in speech); ‘similar to the Teacher’ (satthārā sadiso) becomes satthukappo (like the Teacher); ‘one who has a purpose for merit’ (puññena atthiko) becomes puññatthiko (one who seeks merit); guṇādhiko (abundant in virtues); ‘rice mixed with molasses’ (guḷena saṃsaṭṭho odano) becomes guḷodano (molasses-rice); khīrodano (milk-rice); ‘a chariot yoked with a horse’ (assena yutto ratho) becomes assaratho (a horse-chariot); maggacittaṃ (path-consciousness); ‘the island known or marked by the rose-apple tree’ (jambuyā paññāto lakkhito dīpo) becomes jambudīpo (the Rose-Apple Island); ‘ten increased by one’ (ekena adhikā dasa) becomes ekādasa (eleven); ‘blind by birth’ (jātiyā andho) becomes jaccandho (born blind); ‘intelligent by nature’ (pakatiyā medhāvī) becomes pakatimedhāvī (naturally intelligent), and so on.

Tatiyātappuriso.

End of the Third Tappurisa.

Catutthī [M 0.0195] tadatthaatthahitadeyyādīhi.

The fourth case ending is compounded with words such as ‘for that purpose’ (tadattha), ‘purpose’ (attha), ‘beneficial’ (hita), ‘to be given’ (deyya), and so on.

Tadatthe – kathinassa dussaṃ kathinadussaṃ, kathinacīvaratthāyāti attho. Evaṃ cīvaradussaṃ, cīvaramūlyaṃ, yāguyā atthāya taṇḍulā yāgutaṇḍulā, bhattataṇḍulā, saṅghassatthāya bhattaṃ saṅghabhattaṃ, āgantukānamatthāya bhattaṃ āgantukabhattaṃ. Evaṃ gamikabhattaṃ, pāsādāya dabbaṃ pāsādadabbaṃ.

In the sense of ‘for that purpose’: ‘cloth for the kathina’ (kathinassa dussaṃ) becomes kathinadussaṃ, the meaning being ‘for the sake of a kathina robe.’ Similarly: cīvaradussaṃ (robe-cloth); cīvaramūlyaṃ (price for a robe); ‘rice for the purpose of gruel’ (yāguyā atthāya taṇḍulā) becomes yāgutaṇḍulā (gruel-rice); bhattataṇḍulā (rice for a meal); ‘food for the purpose of the Saṅgha’ (saṅghassatthāya bhattaṃ) becomes saṅghabhattaṃ (food for the Saṅgha); ‘food for the purpose of newcomers’ (āgantukānamatthāya bhattaṃ) becomes āgantukabhattaṃ (food for newcomers). Similarly: gamikabhattaṃ (food for travelers); ‘material for a palace’ (pāsādāya dabbaṃ) becomes pāsādadabbaṃ (palace-material).

Atthe bhikkhusaṅghassatthāya vihāro bhikkhusaṅghattho vihāro, bhikkhusaṅghatthā yāgu, bhikkhusaṅghatthaṃ cīvaraṃ. Yassatthāya yadattho, yadatthā, yadatthaṃ. Evaṃ tadattho, tadatthā. Tadatthaṃ. Etadattho vāyāmo, etadatthā kathā, etadatthaṃ sotāvadhānaṃ. Kimatthaṃ, attatthaṃ, paratthaṃ, vinayo saṃvaratthāya, sukhaṃ samādhatthāya, nibbidā virāgatthāya, virāgo vimuttatthāya. Tathā lokassa hito lokahito, buddhassa deyyaṃ buddhadeyyaṃ, pupphaṃ. Saṅghadeyyaṃ, cīvaraṃ. Idha na bhavati, saṅghassa dātabbaṃ, saṅghassa dātuṃ iccādi.

In the sense of ‘purpose’: ‘a dwelling for the purpose of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha’ becomes bhikkhusaṅghattho vihāro (a dwelling for the Bhikkhu Saṅgha); bhikkhusaṅghatthā yāgu (gruel for the Bhikkhu Saṅgha); bhikkhusaṅghatthaṃ cīvaraṃ (a robe for the Bhikkhu Saṅgha). Yassatthāya (for whatever purpose), yadattho (for whatever purpose), yadatthā (for whatever purpose), yadatthaṃ (for whatever purpose). Similarly: tadattho (for that purpose), tadatthā (for that purpose), tadatthaṃ (for that purpose). Etadattho vāyāmo (this effort is for this purpose); etadatthā kathā (this talk is for this purpose); etadatthaṃ sotāvadhānaṃ (this attention is for this purpose). Kimatthaṃ (for what purpose?); attatthaṃ (for one’s own benefit); paratthaṃ (for the benefit of others); vinayo saṃvaratthāya (discipline is for the purpose of restraint); sukhaṃ samādhatthāya (happiness is for the purpose of concentration); nibbidā virāgatthāya (disenchantment is for the purpose of dispassion); virāgo vimuttatthāya (dispassion is for the purpose of liberation). Likewise: ‘beneficial to the world’ (lokassa hito) becomes lokahito (beneficial to the world); ‘to be given to the Buddha’ (buddhassa deyyaṃ) becomes buddhadeyyaṃ, as in pupphaṃ (a flower); saṅghadeyyaṃ (to be given to the Saṅgha), as in cīvaraṃ (a robe). Here compounding does not occur, as in saṅghassa dātabbaṃ (what should be given to the Saṅgha), saṅghassa dātuṃ (to give to the Saṅgha), and so on.

Catutthītappuriso.

End of the Fourth Tappurisa.

Pañcamī apagamana bhaya virati mocanatthādīhi.

The fifth case ending is compounded with words having the meaning of ‘going away’ (apagamana), ‘fear’ (bhaya), ‘abstinence’ (virati), ‘release’ (mocana), and so on.

Methunasmā apeto methunāpeto. Evaṃ palāpāpagato, nagaraniggato, piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto. Gāmato nikkhantaṃ gāmanikkhantaṃ, rukkhaggā patito rukkhaggapatito, sāsanacuto, āpattivuṭṭhānaṃ, dharaṇitaluggato, sabbabhavehi nissaṭo sabbabhavanissaṭo.

‘Departed from sexual intercourse’ (methunasmā apeto) becomes methunāpeto. Similarly: palāpāpagato (departed from idle talk); nagaraniggato (gone out from the city); piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto (returned from the alms-round). ‘Gone out from the village’ (gāmato nikkhantaṃ) becomes gāmanikkhantaṃ; ‘fallen from the treetop’ (rukkhaggā patito) becomes rukkhaggapatito; sāsanacuto (fallen from the teaching); āpattivuṭṭhānaṃ (emergence from an offense); dharaṇitaluggato (risen from the surface of the earth); ‘departed from all states of existence’ (sabbabhavehi nissaṭo) becomes sabbabhavanissaṭo.

Bhayatthādiyoge yathā – rājato bhayaṃ rājabhayaṃ, corehi bhayaṃ corabhayaṃ, amanussehi bhayaṃ amanussabhayaṃ, aggito bhayaṃ aggibhayaṃ. Pāpato bhīto pāpabhīto[M 0.0196], pāpabhīruko, akattabbato virati akattabbavirati. Evaṃ kāyaduccaritavirati, vacīduccaritavirati, bandhanā mutto bandhanamutto, vanamutto, bandhanamokkho, kammato samuṭṭhitaṃ kammasamuṭṭhitaṃ, ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭhaṃ, omakomakaṃ.

In conjunction with words meaning fear and so on, for example: ‘fear from the king’ (rājato bhayaṃ) becomes rājabhayaṃ; ‘fear from thieves’ (corehi bhayaṃ) becomes corabhayaṃ; ‘fear from non-humans’ (amanussehi bhayaṃ) becomes amanussabhayaṃ; ‘fear from fire’ (aggito bhayaṃ) becomes aggibhayaṃ. ‘Afraid of evil’ (pāpato bhīto) becomes pāpabhīto; pāpabhīruko (fearful of evil); ‘abstinence from what should not be done’ (akattabbato virati) becomes akattabbavirati. Similarly: kāyaduccaritavirati (abstinence from bodily misconduct); vacīduccaritavirati (abstinence from verbal misconduct); ‘freed from bondage’ (bandhanā mutto) becomes bandhanamutto; vanamutto (freed from the forest); bandhanamokkho (release from bondage); ‘arisen from kamma’ (kammato samuṭṭhitaṃ) becomes kammasamuṭṭhitaṃ; ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭhaṃ (from the highest to the highest); omakomakaṃ (from the lowest to the lowest).

Kvaci vuttiyeva, kammato jātaṃ kammajaṃ. Evaṃ cittajaṃ, utujaṃ, āhārajaṃ. Idha na bhavati, pāsādā patito.

Sometimes it is by usage only: born from kamma is kammajaṃ. Similarly, cittajaṃ (mind-born), utujaṃ (season-born), āhārajaṃ (nutriment-born). Here a compound is not formed, as in pāsādā patito (one fallen from a palace).

Pañcamītappuriso.

The Fifth Tatpuruṣa (Ablative Compound)

Chaṭṭhī rañño putto rājaputto. Evaṃ rājapuriso, ācariyapūjako, buddhasāvako, buddharūpaṃ, jinavacanaṃ, samuddaghoso, dhaññānaṃ rāsi dhaññarāsi, pupphagandho, phalaraso, kāyassa lahutā kāyalahutā, maraṇassati, rukkhamūlaṃ, ayassa patto ayopatto, evaṃ suvaṇṇakaṭāhaṃ, pānīyathālakaṃ, sappikumbho.

The Sixth (Genitive) Tatpuruṣa: The king’s son is rājaputto. Similarly: rājapuriso (a king's man), ācariyapūjako (a worshipper of the teacher), buddhasāvako (a disciple of the Buddha), buddharūpaṃ (an image of the Buddha), jinavacanaṃ (the word of the Victor), samuddaghoso (the sound of the ocean); a heap of grain is dhaññarāsi; pupphagandho (the fragrance of a flower), phalaraso (the taste of fruit); lightness of the body is kāyalahutā; maraṇassati (mindfulness of death), rukkhamūlaṃ (the root of a tree); an iron bowl is ayopatto. Similarly: suvaṇṇakaṭāhaṃ (a golden pan), pānīyathālakaṃ (a drinking bowl), sappikumbho (a pot of ghee).

“Devānaṃ rājā”ti atthe samāsādimhi kate “kvaci samāsantagatānamakāranto”ti akāro, tato “syā cā”ti āttaṃ na bhavati. Devarājo, devarājā, devarājaṃ, devarāje iccādi purisasaddasamaṃ. Attābhāve so devarājā, te devarājāno iccādi rājasaddasamaṃ. Tathā devānaṃ sakhā devasakho, devasakhā, so devasakhā, te devasakhāno iccādi.

When a compound is formed with the meaning 'king of the gods' (devānaṃ rājā), according to the rule 'kvaci samāsantagatānamakāranto', the final member sometimes ends in 'a'; then, the lengthening to 'ā' (by 'syā ca') does not occur. Thus, Devarājo, devarājā, devarājaṃ, devarāje, etc., are like the word purisa. In the absence of this change to an 'a'-ending, the forms are `so devarājā, te devarājāno`, etc., like the word rājan. Similarly, 'the friend of the gods' (devānaṃ sakhā) becomes devasakho, devasakhā; and `so devasakhā, te devasakhāno`, etc.

Pumassa liṅgaṃ pulliṅgaṃ. Evaṃ pumbhāvo, pumantalopādi.

The sign of a male is the masculine gender (pulliṅgaṃ). Similarly, pumbhāvo (maleness), pumantalopādi (the dropping of the final 'm' of pum, etc.).

Hatthipadaṃ, itthirūpaṃ, bhikkhunisaṅgho, jambusākhā, ettha ca “kvacādimajjhuttarāna”ntiādinā majjhe īkārūkārānaṃ rassattaṃ.

Hatthipadaṃ (elephant's footprint), itthirūpaṃ (woman's form), bhikkhunisaṅgho (the community of bhikkhunīs), jambusākhā (the rose-apple branch). Here, according to the rule 'kvacādimajjhuttarāna', etc., the long vowels ī and ū in the middle of a compound are shortened.

Vibhāsādhikārato [M 0.0197] kvaci vākyameva, sahasā kammassa kattāro, bhinnānaṃ sandhātā, kappassa tatiyo bhāgo, yā ca pakkhassa aṭṭhamī, manussānaṃ khattiyo sūratamo.

Due to the governing rule of optionality, sometimes it remains a phrase only: sahasā kammassa kattāro (hasty doers of deeds); bhinnānaṃ sandhātā (the joiner of the divided); kappassa tatiyo bhāgo (a third part of the world-period); yā ca pakkhassa aṭṭhamī (and the eighth day of the fortnight); manussānaṃ khattiyo sūratamo (among humans, the warrior is the bravest).

Yuttattho icceva? “Bhaṭo rañño puriso devadattassā”ti ettha “bhaṭasambandhe chaṭṭhī”ti aññamaññānapekkhatāya ayuttatthabhāvato samāso na bhavati, “kosalassa rañño putto”tiādīsu pana sāpekkhatāya asamatthattā na bhavati, sambandhīsaddānaṃ pana niccaṃ sāpekkhattepi gamakattā samāso, yathā – devadattassa gurukulaṃ, bhagavato sāvakasaṅghotiādi.

Is it only when the meaning is suitable? Here, in the phrase 'the king's soldier, Devadatta's man' (bhaṭo rañño puriso devadattassā), a compound is not formed because of the unsuitability of meaning due to a lack of mutual expectancy—as the genitive is in relation to 'soldier'. However, in cases like 'the son of King Kosala' (kosalassa rañño putto), etc., a compound is not formed due to being incapable of compounding because of dependency. But for relational words, even though there is constant dependency, a compound is formed because it is intelligible, as in—devadattassa gurukulaṃ (Devadatta's teacher's family), bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho (the Blessed One's community of disciples), and so on.

Chaṭṭhītappuriso.

The Sixth Tatpuruṣa (Genitive Compound)

Sattamī rūpe saññā rūpasaññā, evaṃ rūpasañcetanā, saṃsāradukkhaṃ, cakkhumhi sannissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, dhamme rato dhammarato, dhammābhirati, dhammaruci, dhammagāravo, dhammesu nirutti dhammanirutti, dānādhimutti, bhavantarakataṃ, dassane assādo dassanassādo, araññe vāso araññavāso, vikāle bhojanaṃ vikālabhojanaṃ, kāle vassaṃ kālavassaṃ, vane pupphaṃ vanapupphaṃ. Evaṃ vanamahiso, gāmasūkaro, samuddamaccho, āvāṭakacchapo, āvāṭamaṇḍūko, kūpamaṇḍūko, titthanāvā, itthīsu dhutto itthidhutto chāyāya sukkho chāyāsukkho, aṅgārapakkaṃ, cārakabaddho.

The Seventh (Locative) Tatpuruṣa: Perception in form is rūpasaññā; similarly, rūpasañcetanā (intention regarding form), saṃsāradukkhaṃ (suffering in saṃsāra); consciousness dependent on the eye is cakkhuviññāṇaṃ; delighting in the Dhamma is dhammarato; dhammābhirati (rejoicing in the Dhamma), dhammaruci (fondness for the Dhamma), dhammagāravo (reverence for the Dhamma); expression in the Dhamma is dhammanirutti; dānādhimutti (resolve in generosity); bhavantarakataṃ (done in another existence); satisfaction in seeing is dassanassādo; dwelling in the wilderness is araññavāso; eating at the wrong time is vikālabhojanaṃ; raining in season is kālavassaṃ; a flower in the forest is vanapupphaṃ. Similarly: vanamahiso (forest-buffalo), gāmasūkaro (village-pig), samuddamaccho (ocean-fish), āvāṭakacchapo (pit-turtle), āvāṭamaṇḍūko (pit-frog), kūpamaṇḍūko (well-frog), titthanāvā (ford-boat); a debauchee among women is itthidhutto; dry in the shade is chāyāsukkho; aṅgārapakkaṃ (cooked on charcoal); cārakabaddho (bound in prison).

Idha vuttiyeva, yathā – vane caratīti vanacaro, kucchimhi sayatīti kucchisayo, thale tiṭṭhatīti thalaṭṭho. Evaṃ jalaṭṭho, pabbataṭṭho, maggaṭṭho, paṅke jātaṃ paṅkajaṃ, sire ruhatīti siroruhaṃ iccādi.

Here, it is by usage only, as follows: 'one who walks in the forest' (vane carati) is vanacaro (forest-dweller); 'one who lies in the belly' (kucchimhi sayati) is kucchisayo (one who lies in the womb); 'one who stands on dry land' (thale tiṭṭhati) is thalaṭṭho (one who stands on land). Similarly: jalaṭṭho (one who stands in water), pabbataṭṭho (one who stands on a mountain), maggaṭṭho (one who stands on a path); 'that which is born in the mud' (paṅke jātaṃ) is paṅkajaṃ (mud-born); 'that which grows on the head' (sire ruhati) is siroruhaṃ (head-grown), and so on.

Idha [M 0.0198] na bhavati, bhojane mattaññutā, indriyesu guttadvāratā, āsane nisinno, āsane nisīditabbaṃ.

Here a compound is not formed, as in: bhojane mattaññutā (moderation in eating); indriyesu guttadvāratā (guardedness of the sense doors); āsane nisinno (seated on a seat); āsane nisīditabbaṃ (one should sit on a seat).

Sattamītappuriso.

The Seventh Tatpuruṣa (Locative Compound)

“Tadanuparodhenā”ti vuttattā yathābhidhānaṃ tappurise kvaci accantādīsu amādivibhatyantaṃ pubbapadaṃ paraṃ sambhavati.

Because it is said 'without obstructing that' (tadanuparodhena), according to usage, in some Tatpuruṣa compounds, such as accanta, etc., the prior member may be followed by a subsequent member while retaining its case ending beginning with 'aṃ'.

Yathā – antaṃ atikkantaṃ accantaṃ, accantāni, velaṃ atikkanto ativelo, rassattaṃ. Evaṃ mālaṃ atīto atimālo, pattajīviko, āpannajīviko, akkhaṃ patigataṃ nissitanti paccakkhaṃ dassanaṃ, paccakkho attabhāvo, paccakkhā buddhi, atthaṃ anugataṃ anvatthaṃ, kokilāya avakuṭṭhaṃ avakokilaṃ vanaṃ, pariccattanti attho. Avamayūraṃ, ajjhayanāya parigilāno pariyajjhayano, kammassa alaṃ samatthoti alaṃkammo, vacanāya alanti alaṃvacano, vānato nikkhantaṃ nibbānaṃ, kilesehi nikkhanto nikkileso, niraṅgaṇo, kosambiyā nikkhanto nikkosambī, vanato niyyāto nibbano, ācariyato paro pācariyo. Evaṃ payyako, parahiyyo, gaṅgāya upari uparigaṅgaṃ. Evaṃ heṭṭhānadī, antosamāpatti, haṃsānaṃ rājā rājahaṃso, haṃsarājā vā, māsassa addhaṃ addhamāsaṃ, māsaddhaṃ vā, āmalakassa addhaṃ addhāmalakaṃ, āmalakaddhaṃ vā, kahāpaṇassa aḍḍhaṃ aḍḍhakahāpaṇaṃ, aḍḍhamāsakaṃ, rattiyā aḍḍhaṃ aḍḍharattaṃ, rattiyā pubbaṃ pubbarattaṃ, rattiyā pacchā pacchārattaṃ. Ettha ca “kvaci samāsantagatānamakāranto”ti rattisaddantassa attaṃ, ahassa pubbaṃ pubbanhaṃ. Evaṃ sāyanhaṃ, “tesu vuddhī”tiādinā ahassa anhādeso.

For example: 'exceeding the limit' (antaṃ atikkantaṃ) becomes accantaṃ (exceeding), accantāni (exceeding); 'one who has exceeded the boundary' (velaṃ atikkanto) becomes ativelo (excessive), with shortening. Similarly: 'one who has gone beyond the garland' (mālaṃ atīto) becomes atimālo (beyond garlands); pattajīviko (one who has obtained a livelihood), āpannajīviko (one who has attained a livelihood); 'dependent on having gone to the sense organ' (akkhaṃ patigataṃ nissitaṃ) becomes paccakkhaṃ dassanaṃ (direct perception), paccakkho attabhāvo (direct existence), paccakkhā buddhi (direct knowledge); 'that which has followed the meaning' (atthaṃ anugataṃ) becomes anvatthaṃ (etymologically significant); 'a forest decried by cuckoos' (kokilāya avakuṭṭhaṃ vanaṃ) becomes avakokilaṃ vanaṃ, meaning 'abandoned'. Similarly, avamayūraṃ (abandoned by peacocks); 'one who is weary of study' (ajjhayanāya parigilāno) becomes pariyajjhayano (weary of study); 'one who is capable enough for work' (kammassa alaṃ samattho) becomes alaṃkammo (capable of work); 'one who is capable of speech' (vacanāya alaṃ) becomes alaṃvacano (eloquent); 'that which has departed from craving' (vānato nikkhantaṃ) becomes nibbānaṃ (Nibbāna); 'one who has departed from defilements' (kilesehi nikkhanto) becomes nikkileso (undefiled); niraṅgaṇo (without stain); 'one who has departed from Kosambī' (kosambiyā nikkhanto) becomes nikkosambī (departed from Kosambī); 'one who has gone out of the forest' (vanato niyyāto) becomes nibbano (out of the forest); 'one who is beyond the teacher' (ācariyato paro) becomes pācariyo (beyond the teacher). Similarly: payyako (beyond the grandfather), parahiyyo (the day before yesterday); 'above the Ganges' (gaṅgāya upari) becomes uparigaṅgaṃ (above the Ganges). Similarly: heṭṭhānadī (below the river), antosamāpatti (entering within); 'the king of swans' (haṃsānaṃ rājā) becomes rājahaṃso or haṃsarājā; 'half of a month' (māsassa addhaṃ) becomes addhamāsaṃ or māsaddhaṃ; 'half of an āmalaka fruit' (āmalakassa addhaṃ) becomes addhāmalakaṃ or āmalakaddhaṃ; 'half of a kahāpaṇa' (kahāpaṇassa aḍḍhaṃ) becomes aḍḍhakahāpaṇaṃ, aḍḍhamāsakaṃ; 'half of the night' (rattiyā aḍḍhaṃ) becomes aḍḍharattaṃ; 'the first part of the night' (rattiyā pubbaṃ) becomes pubbarattaṃ; 'the latter part of the night' (rattiyā pacchā) becomes pacchārattaṃ. Here, according to 'kvaci samāsantagatānamakāranto', the final 'i' of the word 'ratti' becomes 'a'; 'the first part of the day' (ahassa pubbaṃ) becomes pubbanhaṃ. Similarly, sāyanhaṃ (evening); according to 'tesu vuddhī', etc., 'aha' becomes 'anha'.

Amādiparatappuriso.

Irregular Tatpuruṣa Compounds

Kvaci [M 0.0199] tappurise “pabhaṅkarā”dīsu vibhattilopo na bhavati.

In some Tatpuruṣa compounds, such as pabhaṅkara, etc., the elision of the case ending does not occur.

Yathā – pabhaṃ karotīti atthe “amādayo parapadebhī”ti samāso, “nāmānaṃ samāso yuttattho”ti samāsasaññā, tato “tesaṃ vibhattiyo lopā cā”ti vibhattilope sampatte tattheva caggahaṇena pubbapade vibhattilopābhāvo. Sesaṃ samaṃ. Pabhaṅkaro, amataṃ dadātīti amatandado, raṇaṃ jahātīti raṇañjaho, jutiṃ dhāretīti jutindharo, tathā sahasākataṃ, parassapadaṃ. Attanopadaṃ, bhayato upaṭṭhānaṃ bhayatūpaṭṭhānaṃ, paratoghoso, gavaṃpatitthero, manasikāro, pubbenivāso, pubbenivāsānussati, majjhekalyāṇaṃ, antevāsī, antevāsiko, janesuto, urasilomo, kaṇṭhekāḷo, sarasijamiccādi.

For example: In the sense of 'makes light' (pabhaṃ karotīti), a compound is formed by the rule 'amādayo parapadebhī'; it is designated a compound by 'nāmānaṃ samāso yuttattho'; then, when the elision of the case ending is due to occur according to 'tesaṃ vibhattiyo lopā ca', by the inclusion of 'ca' in that very rule, the elision of the case ending in the prior member does not occur. The rest is similar. Pabhaṅkaro (light-maker); 'one who gives the deathless' (amataṃ dadāti) is amatandado (giver of the deathless); 'one who abandons strife' (raṇaṃ jahāti) is raṇañjaho (abandoner of strife); 'one who holds splendor' (jutiṃ dhāreti) is jutindharo (holder of splendor). Similarly: sahasākataṃ (done hastily); parassapadaṃ (active voice); attanopadaṃ (middle voice); 'arising from fear' (bhayato upaṭṭhānaṃ) is bhayatūpaṭṭhānaṃ (arising from fear); paratoghoso (sound from another); gavaṃpatitthero (the elder Gavampati); manasikāro (attention); pubbenivāso (former dwelling); pubbenivāsānussati (recollection of former dwellings); majjhekalyāṇaṃ (beautiful in the middle); antevāsī (resident disciple); antevāsiko (resident disciple); janesuto (heard among the people); urasilomo (hair on the chest); kaṇṭhekāḷo (black-throated); sarasijaṃ (born in a lake, i.e., a lotus), etc.

Alopatappuriso.

Alopa-Tatpuruṣa (Tatpuruṣa with Non-elision)

Tappurisasamāso niṭṭhito.

The Tatpuruṣa compound is concluded.

Bahubbīhisamāsa

The Bahubbīhi Compound

Atha bahubbīhisamāso vuccate.

Now, the Bahubbīhi compound is explained.

So ca navavidho dvipado tulyādhikaraṇo, dvipado bhinnādhikaraṇo, tipado nanipātapubbapado, sahapubbapado upamānapubbapado saṅkhyobhayapado disantarāḷattho byatihāralakkhaṇo cāti.

And that is ninefold: the two-membered with a common referent, the two-membered with a different referent, the three-membered, the one with a negative particle as its first member, the one with 'saha' as its first member, the one with a standard of comparison as its first member, the one with a numeral in both members, the one with the meaning of direction or interval, and the one characterized by reciprocity.

Tattha dvipado tulyādhikaraṇo bahubbīhi kammādīsu chasu vibhatyatthesu bhavati.

Among these, the two-membered Bahubbīhi compound with a common referent occurs in the meanings of the six cases, beginning with the accusative.

Tattha [M 0.0200] dutiyatthe tāva – “āgatā samaṇā imaṃ saṅghārāma”nti viggahe –

Among these, first, in the accusative meaning: in the analytical phrase “The monks have come to this monastery”—

352. Aññapadatthesu bahubbīhi.

352. The Bahubbīhi is in the meanings of other words.

Samasyamānapadato aññesaṃ paṭhamadutiyādivibhatyantānaṃ padānamatthesu yuttatthāni nāmāni vibhāsā samasyante, so samāso bahubbīhisañño ca hoti.

Nouns with a suitable meaning are optionally compounded when they are in the meaning of other words—that is, words different from those being compounded and which end in the first, second, etc., case endings. That compound is called a Bahubbīhi.

Bahavo vīhayo yassa so bahubbīhi, bahubbīhisadisattā ayampisamāso anvatthasaññāvasena bahubbīhīti vutto, aññapadatthappadhāno hi bahubbīhi.

'He who has much rice' (bahavo vīhayo yassa so) is a `bahubbīhi`. Because this type of compound is similar to the example `bahubbīhi`, it is also called a Bahubbīhi by way of an etymological designation, for the Bahubbīhi is one in which the meaning of another word is primary.

Duvidho cāyaṃ bahubbīhi tagguṇasaṃviññāṇātagguṇasaṃviññāṇavasena, tesu yattha visesanabhūto attho aññapadatthaggahaṇena gayhati, so tagguṇasaṃviññāṇo, yathā – lambakaṇṇamānayāti.

This Bahubbīhi compound is of two kinds: tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa and atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa. Among these, when the meaning of the qualifier is included in the apprehension of the meaning of the other word, it is a tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa, as in “bring the one with long ears” (lambakaṇṇamānaya).

Yattha pana na gayhati, so atagguṇasaṃviññāṇo, yathā – bahudhanamānayāti.

But when it is not included, it is an atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa, as in “bring the one with much wealth” (bahudhanamānaya).

Idha bahubbīhisadde viya visesanassa pubbanipāto, sesaṃ pubbasamaṃ.

Here, as in the word ‘bahubbīhi’ itself, the qualifier is placed first; the rest is as before.

Āgatasamaṇo saṅghārāmo. Ettha ca āgatasaddo, samaṇasaddo ca attano atthe aṭṭhatvā dutiyāvibhatyatthabhūte saṅghārāmasaṅkhāte aññapadatthe vattanti, tadatthajotanatthameva tadanantaraṃ “saṅghārāmo”ti padantaraṃ payujjati, tato samāseneva kammatthassa abhihitattā puna dutiyā na hoti. Idaṃsaddassa ca appayogo, evaṃ sabbattha. Bahubbīhi cāyaṃ abhidheyyaliṅgavacano.

“The monastery to which ascetics have come” (āgatasamaṇo saṅghārāmo). Here, the words ‘āgata’ and ‘samaṇa’, not standing in their own meaning, refer to the meaning of another word, designated as ‘saṅghārāma’, which is the meaning of the second case ending. To clarify that meaning, the other word, ‘saṅghārāma’, is used immediately after. Therefore, since the meaning of the object has been expressed by the compound itself, the second case ending is not used again. And the word ‘idaṃ’ is not used; it is thus in all cases. And this Bahubbīhi compound takes the gender and number of that which is denoted.

Tathā āgatasamaṇā sāvatthi, āgatasamaṇaṃ jetavanaṃ, paṭipannā addhikā yaṃ pathaṃ soyaṃ paṭipannaddhiko patho[M 0.0201], abhiruḷhā vāṇijā yaṃ nāvaṃ sā abhiruḷhavāṇijā nāvā. Evaṃ kammatthe bahubbīhi.

Similarly: “Sāvatthī to which ascetics have come” (āgatasamaṇā sāvatthi), “Jetavana to which ascetics have come” (āgatasamaṇaṃ jetavanaṃ), “the path which travelers have entered” (paṭipannaddhiko patho), “the boat which merchants have boarded” (abhiruḷhavāṇijā nāvā). Thus is the Bahubbīhi in the meaning of the object.

Tatiyatthe bahubbīhi yathā – jitāni indriyāni yena samaṇena soyaṃ jitindriyo samaṇo. Evaṃ diṭṭhadhammo, pattadhammo, katakicco, jitā mārā anenāti jitamāro bhagavā, paṭividdhasabbadhammo.

A Bahubbīhi in the meaning of the third [case is formed] as follows: the ascetic by whom the senses are conquered is ‘one with conquered senses’ (jitindriyo samaṇo). Similarly: ‘one by whom the Dhamma has been seen’ (diṭṭhadhammo), ‘one by whom the Dhamma has been attained’ (pattadhammo), ‘one by whom the task has been done’ (katakicco), the Blessed One by whom Māra has been conquered is ‘jitamāro’, ‘one by whom all things have been penetrated’ (paṭividdhasabbadhammo).

Catutthiyatthe bahubbīhi yathā – dinno suṅko yassa rañño soyaṃ dinnasuṅko rājā, upanītaṃ bhojanaṃ assa samaṇassāti upanītabhojano samaṇo, upahaṭo bali assāti upahaṭabali yakkho.

A Bahubbīhi in the meaning of the fourth [case is formed] as follows: the king to whom tax has been given is a ‘dinnasuṅko’ king; the ascetic to whom food has been brought is an ‘upanītabhojano’ ascetic; the yakkha to whom an offering has been presented is an ‘upahaṭabali’ yakkha.

Pañcamiyatthe bahubbīhi yathā – niggatā janā asmā gāmā soyaṃ niggatajano gāmo, niggato ayo asmāti nirayo, niggatā kilesā etasmāti nikkileso, apetaṃ viññāṇaṃ asmāti apetaviññāṇo matakāyo, apagataṃ bhayabheravaṃ asmāti apagatabhayabheravo arahā.

A Bahubbīhi in the meaning of the fifth [case is formed] as follows: the village from which people have departed is a ‘departed-people’ village (niggatajano gāmo); that from which gain has departed is ‘nirayo’ (hell); one from whom defilements have departed is ‘nikkileso’ (stainless); the dead body from which consciousness has departed is ‘apetaviññāṇo’ (consciousness-departed); the Arahant from whom fear and terror have departed is ‘apagatabhayabheravo’ (fear-and-terror-departed).

Chaṭṭhiyatthe bahubbīhi yathā – chinnā hatthā yassa purisassa soyaṃ chinnahattho puriso. Evaṃ paripuṇṇasaṅkappo, khīṇāsavo, vīto rāgo assāti vītarāgo, dve padāni assāti dvipado, dvihattho paṭo, tevijjo, catuppado, pañca cakkhūni assāti pañcacakkhu bhagavā, chaḷabhiñño, rassattaṃ, navaṅgaṃ satthusāsanaṃ, dasabalo, anantañāṇo, tīṇi dasa parimāṇametesanti tidasā devā, samāsantassa attaṃ, idha parimāṇasaddassa sannidhānato [M 0.0202] dasasaddo saṅkhyāne vattate, ayaṃ paccayo etesanti idappaccayā, ko pabhavo assāti kiṃpabhavo ayaṃ kāyo, vigataṃ malamassāti vimalo, sundaro gandho assāti sugandhaṃ candanaṃ. Evaṃ susīlo, sumukho, kucchito gandho assāti duggandhaṃ kuṇapaṃ, duṭṭhu mano assāti dummano. Evaṃ dussīlo, dummukho, tapo eva dhanaṃ assāti tapodhano, khantisaṅkhātaṃ balaṃ assāti khantibalo, indoti nāmaṃ etassāti indanāmo.

A Bahubbīhi in the meaning of the sixth [case is formed] as follows: the man whose hands are cut off is a ‘cut-handed’ man (chinnahattho puriso). Similarly: ‘one whose aspirations are fulfilled’ (paripuṇṇasaṅkappo); ‘one whose taints are destroyed’ (khīṇāsavo); one from whom lust has departed is ‘vītarāgo’ (free from lust); one who has two feet is ‘dvipado’ (a biped); a cloth of two cubits (dvihattho paṭo); ‘one with the threefold knowledge’ (tevijjo); ‘one with four feet’ (catuppado); the Blessed One who has five eyes is ‘pañcacakkhu’ (five-eyed); ‘one with the six higher knowledges’ (chaḷabhiñño); ‘the Teacher’s dispensation with nine parts’ (navaṅgaṃ satthusāsanaṃ); ‘one with ten powers’ (dasabalo); ‘one with infinite knowledge’ (anantañāṇo); the gods whose measure is three tens are ‘tidasā’ (the thirty), where the final vowel of the compound becomes ‘a’; here, due to the presence of the word ‘parimāṇa’ (measure), the word ‘dasa’ is used in the sense of a number. These for which this is the condition are ‘idappaccayā’ (dependently arisen). This body whose origin is what is ‘kiṃpabhavo’ (of what origin). One whose stain is gone is ‘vimalo’ (stainless); sandalwood whose scent is pleasant is ‘sugandhaṃ’ (fragrant). Similarly: ‘susīlo’ (of good conduct); ‘sumukho’ (of pleasant face). A corpse whose scent is foul is ‘duggandhaṃ’ (foul-smelling); one whose mind is corrupt is ‘dummano’ (sad-minded). Similarly: ‘dussīlo’ (of bad conduct); ‘dummukho’ (of unpleasant face). One whose wealth is austerity itself is ‘tapodhano’ (rich in austerity); one whose strength is that called patience is ‘khantibalo’ (strong in patience); one whose name is ‘Inda’ is ‘indanāmo’ (named Inda).

Chandajātādīsu visesanavisesitabbānaṃ yathicchitattā ubhayaṃ pubbaṃ nipatati, yathā – chando jāto assāti chandajāto, jāto chando assātipi jātachando. Evaṃ sañjātapītisomanasso, pītisomanassasañjāto, māsajāto, jātamāso, chinnahattho, hatthacchinno.

In the case of ‘chandajāta’ and so forth, because the qualifier and the qualified can be arranged as desired, either can be placed first, as in: ‘desire is born in him’, thus ‘chandajāto’; or ‘born is the desire in him’, thus ‘jātachando’. Similarly: sañjātapītisomanasso and pītisomanassasañjāto; māsajāto and jātamāso; chinnahattho and hatthacchinno.

“Dīghā jaṅghāyassā”ti viggayha samāsādimhi kate –

When the analysis, ‘she whose shank is long’ (dīghā jaṅghā yassā), is made at the beginning of a compound—

“Tulyādhikaraṇe, pade”ti ca vattate.

And the rules “in a common referent” and “in a word” also apply.

353. Itthiyaṃ bhāsitapumitthī pumāva ce.

353. A feminine word with a corresponding masculine form, if referring to a feminine, is treated as masculine.

Itthiyaṃ vattamāne tulyādhikaraṇe pade pare pubbe bhāsitapumā itthivācako saddo atthi ce, so pumā iva daṭṭhabboti pubbapade itthippaccayābhāvo, bahubbīhivisayoyaṃ, upari “kammadhārayasaññe cā”ti vakkhamānattā.

When a word with a common referent follows, referring to a feminine entity, if the preceding word is a feminine-denoting word that has a corresponding masculine form, it is to be regarded as if it were masculine. Thus, there is an absence of the feminine suffix in the first word. This is the domain of the Bahubbīhi, because it will be stated later, 'and in the designation of Kammadhāraya' (kammadhārayasaññe ca).

354. Kvacādimajjhuttarānaṃ dīgharassāpaccayesu ca.

354. And sometimes, of initial, middle, and final [vowels], there is lengthening and shortening, with and without suffixes.

Kvaci taddhitasamāsanāmopasaggādīsu padesu ādimajjhuttarabhūtānaṃ sarānaṃ jinavacanānuparodhena dīgharassā honti paccayesu, apaccayesu paresu, aparabhūtesu ca.

Sometimes, in words such as taddhitas, compounds, nouns, prefixes, and so on, the initial, middle, or final vowels become long or short, without contradicting the Buddha’s words, when suffixes follow, when non-suffixes follow, and in other cases.

Tattha [M 0.0203]

Therein:

Dīghattaṃ pākaṭānūpa- ghātādo madhuvādisu;

Rassattaṃ ajjave itthi- rūpādo ca ka, tādisūti.

Lengthening is in ‘pākaṭa’, ‘anūpaghāta’, etc., and in ‘madhuvā’, etc.; shortening is in ‘ajjave’, ‘itthirūpa’, etc., and in ‘ka’, ‘tādisu’, etc.

Bahubbīhisamāse sati pulliṅge uttarapadantassa rassattaṃ. Dīghajaṅgho puriso, tathā pahūtā jivhā assāti pahūtajivho bhagavā. Mahatī paññā assāti mahāpañño. “Mahataṃ mahā tulyādhikaraṇe pade”ti mahādeso.

When there is a Bahubbīhi compound in the masculine gender, the final vowel of the last word is shortened. For example: a man with a long shank (dīghajaṅgho puriso); similarly, the Blessed One who has a large tongue is ‘one with a large tongue’ (pahūtajivho bhagavā). One who has great wisdom is ‘one with great wisdom’ (mahāpañño). The substitution of ‘mahā’ for ‘mahant’ occurs by the rule ‘mahataṃ mahā tulyādhikaraṇe pade’.

Itthiyamiti kiṃ? Khamādhano. Bhāsitapumāti kiṃ? Saddhādhuro, saddhāpakatiko, paññāpakatiko, paññāvisuddhiko, ettha ca “kvaci samāsantagatānamakāranto”ti kappaccayo. Tulyādhikaraṇe icceva? Samaṇibhattiko, kumāribhattiko, kumāribhatti.

Why the word ‘itthiyaṃ’? For ‘khamādhano’. Why the word ‘bhāsitapumā’? For ‘saddhādhuro’, ‘saddhāpakatiko’, ‘paññāpakatiko’, ‘paññāvisuddhiko’; and here the suffix ‘ka’ is applied by the rule “sometimes for those ending in ‘a’ at the end of a compound, there is ‘ka’”. Why ‘tulyādhikaraṇe’? For ‘samaṇibhattiko’, ‘kumāribhattiko’, ‘kumāribhatti’.

Pubbapadassevāyaṃ pumbhāvātideso, tena idha na bhavati. Bahudāsiko puriso. Bahukumārikaṃ kulaṃ.

This extension of the masculine state is only for the first word; therefore, it does not apply here: a man with many female slaves (bahudāsiko puriso); a family with many young women (bahukumārikaṃ kulaṃ).

“Gāṇṭhivo dhanu assā”ti viggayha samāsādimhi kate –

When the analysis, ‘Gāṇḍīva is his bow’ (gāṇṭhivo dhanu assa), is made at the beginning of a compound—

355. Dhanumhā ca.

355. And after ‘dhanu’.

Tipadamidaṃ. Kvacisamāsantagatā dhanusaddā āpaccayo hoti, casaddena dhammādito ca, “vamodudantāna”nti vakāro, gāṇṭhivadhanvā. Evaṃ paccakkhadhammā.

This is a three-word rule. Sometimes, after the word ‘dhanu’ at the end of a compound, the suffix ‘ā’ is added; and by the word ‘ca’, also after ‘dhamma’ and so forth. The letter ‘v’ is inserted by the rule ‘vamodudantānaṃ’, resulting in ‘gāṇṭhivadhanvā’. Similarly, ‘paccakkhadhammā’.

Kvacīti kiṃ? Sahassathāmadhanu, paccakkhadhammo, viditadhammo.

Why the word ‘kvaci’? For ‘sahassathāmadhanu’, ‘paccakkhadhammo’, ‘viditadhammo’.

Nānādumapatitapupphavāsitasānu iccatra – nānappakārā dumā nānādumā, nānādumehi patitāni nānādumapatitāni, nānādumapatitāni ca tāni pupphāni cāti nānādumapatitapupphāni, tehi vāsitā nānādumapatitapupphavāsitā, nānādumapatitapupphavāsitā sānū yassa pabbatassa soyaṃ nānādumapatitapupphavāsitasānu [M 0.0204] pabbato. Ayaṃ pana kammadhārayatappurisagabbho tulyādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

In the case of ‘nānādumapatitapupphavāsitasānu’: ‘various kinds of trees’ are ‘nānādumā’; ‘fallen from various trees’ are ‘nānādumapatitāni’; ‘flowers that are fallen from various trees’ are ‘nānādumapatitapupphāni’; ‘perfumed by them’ are ‘nānādumapatitapupphavāsitā’; the mountain whose slopes are perfumed by flowers fallen from various trees is that ‘nānādumapatitapupphavāsitasānu’ mountain. This, however, is a tulyādhikaraṇa-Bahubbīhi containing Kammadhāraya and Tappurisa compounds.

Tathā byālambo ambudharo byālambambudharo, tassa bindūni byālambambudharabindūni, tehi cumbito byālambambudharabinducumbito, tādiso kūṭo yassa soyaṃ byālambambudharabinducumbitakūṭo iccādi.

Similarly: a hanging cloud is a ‘byālambambudharo’; its drops are ‘byālambambudharabindūni’; kissed by them is ‘byālambambudharabinducumbito’; one whose peak is such is ‘byālambambudharabinducumbitakūṭo’; and so on.

Sattamiyatthe bahubbīhi yathā – sampannāni sassāni yasmiṃ janapade soyaṃ sampannasasso janapado, sulabho piṇḍo imasminti sulabhapiṇḍo deso. Ākiṇṇā manussā yassaṃ rājadhāniyaṃ sā ākiṇṇamanussā rājadhānī, bahavo tāpasā etasminti bahutāpaso assamo, upacitaṃ maṃsalohitaṃ asminti upacitamaṃsalohitaṃ sarīraṃ, bahavo sāmino asminti bahussāmikaṃ nagaraṃ.

A Bahubbīhi in the meaning of the seventh [case is formed] as follows: a country in which crops are abundant is a ‘crop-abundant’ country (sampannasasso janapado); a place in which alms-food is easily obtained is an ‘easy-alms-food’ place (sulabhapiṇḍo deso). A capital city in which people are crowded is a ‘people-crowded’ capital city (ākiṇṇamanussā rājadhānī); a hermitage in which there are many ascetics is a ‘many-ascetic’ hermitage (bahutāpaso assamo); a body in which flesh and blood are accumulated is a ‘flesh-and-blood-accumulated’ body (upacitamaṃsalohitaṃ sarīraṃ); a city in which there are many owners is a ‘many-owner’ city (bahussāmikaṃ nagaraṃ).

“Bahū nadiyo asmi”nti atthe samāsādimhi kate –

When, in the meaning ‘many rivers are in it’ (bahū nadiyo asmiṃ), the beginning of a compound is made—

Samāsantaggahaṇaṃ, kappaccayo ca vattate.

The rule for compound-final suffixes (samāsanta), and the ‘ka’ suffix, apply.

356. Nadimhā ca.

356. And after nadī.

Samāsantagatā nadimhā kappaccayo hoti, casaddena tuantā ca. Niccatthaṃ vacanaṃ. Nadīti cettha itthivācakānaṃ īkārūkārānaṃ parasamaññā, tato “kvacādimajjhuttarāna”ntiādinā nadisaññassa kappaccaye rassattaṃ, bahunadiko janapado. Evaṃ bahujambukaṃ vanaṃ. Bahunārikoti chaṭṭhībahubbīhinā siddhaṃ. Bahavo kattāro asmiṃ, assāti vā bahukattuko deso. Evaṃ bahubhattuko.

After a nadī stem at the end of a compound, the affix kappa occurs; and by the word ca, also after a stem ending in tu. This rule is invariable. Here, nadī is a technical term for feminine stems ending in ī and ū. Then, by the rule beginning 'kvacādimajjhuttarāna', the stem designated as nadī is shortened when the affix kappa is added, as in bahunadiko janapado, 'a country with many rivers'. Similarly, bahujambukaṃ vanaṃ, 'a forest with many jackals'. Bahunāriko is formed by a genitive bahubbīhi compound. From the analysis Bahavo kattāro asmiṃ ('Many doers are in it') or assā ('of it'), is formed bahukattuko deso, 'a country with many doers'. Likewise, bahubhattuko.

Bhinnādhikaraṇo yathā – ekarattiṃ vāso assāti ekarattivāso, samānena janena saddhiṃ vāso assāti samānavāso [M 0.0205] puriso. Ubhato byañjanamassa atthīti ubhabhobyañjanako, chattaṃ pāṇimhi assāti chattapāṇi puriso. Evaṃ daṇḍapāṇi, satthapāṇi, vajirapāṇi, khaggahattho, satthahattho, dāne ajjhāsayo assāti dānajjhāsayo, dānādhimuttiko, buddhabhattiko, saddhammagāravo iccādi.

An example of a bhinnādhikaraṇa (different-case) compound is as follows: from the analysis ekarattiṃ vāso assā'ti, 'one whose dwelling is for one night', comes ekarattivāso. From samānena janena saddhiṃ vāso assā'ti, 'one whose dwelling is with the same people', comes samānavāso puriso. From ubhato byañjanamassa atthī'ti, 'one who has the characteristics of both sexes', comes ubhatobyañjanako. From chattaṃ pāṇimhi assā'ti, 'one who has an umbrella in hand', comes chattapāṇi puriso. Similarly, daṇḍapāṇi ('one with a staff in hand'), satthapāṇi ('one with a knife in hand'), vajirapāṇi ('one with a thunderbolt in hand'), khaggahattho ('one with a sword in hand'), satthahattho ('one with a knife in hand'). From dāne ajjhāsayo assā'ti, 'one whose inclination is towards giving', comes dānajjhāsayo. Also dānādhimuttiko ('one resolved on giving'), buddhabhattiko ('one devoted to the Buddha'), saddhammagāravo ('one who reveres the true Dhamma'), and so forth.

Tipado yathā – parakkamenādhigatā sampadā yehi te bhavanti parakkamādhigatasampadā mahāpurisā. Evaṃ dhammādhigatabhogā, oṇīto pattato pāṇi yena soyaṃ oṇītapattapāṇi, sīhassa pubbaddhaṃ viya kāyo assāti sīhapubbaddhakāyo, mattā bahavo mātaṅgā asminti mattabahumātaṅgaṃ vanaṃ iccādi.

An example of a tipada (three-word) compound is as follows: from the analysis parakkamenādhigatā sampadā yehi te bhavanti, 'they are great beings by whom wealth is attained through effort', comes parakkamādhigatasampadā mahāpurisā. Similarly, dhammādhigatabhogā, 'those whose enjoyments are attained through Dhamma'. From oṇīto pattato pāṇi yena so'yaṃ, 'he is one who has withdrawn his hand from the bowl', comes oṇītapattapāṇi. From sīhassa pubbaddhaṃ viya kāyo assā'ti, 'one whose body is like the forepart of a lion', comes sīhapubbaddhakāyo. From mattā bahavo mātaṅgā asmiṃ'ti, 'a forest in which there are many intoxicated elephants', comes mattabahumātaṅgaṃ vanaṃ, and so forth.

Nanipātapubbapado yathā – natthi etassa samoti asamo bhagavā. Idha “attaṃ nassa tappurise”ti sutte “attaṃ nassā”ti yogavibhāgena nassa attaṃ. Evaṃ appaṭipuggalo, aputtako, ahetuko, “kvaci samāsanta”iccādinā kappaccayo, natthi saṃvāso etesanti asaṃvāsā, na vijjate vuṭṭhi etthāti avuṭṭhiko janapado, abhikkhuko vihāro, natthi etassa uttaroti anuttaro, “sare ana”ti ana, tappurisaggahaṇamupalakkhaṇaṃ, athavā “tesu vuddhī”tiādinā nassa ana. Evaṃ natthi anto assāti anantaṃ, na vijjanti āsavā etesanti anāsavā iccādi.

An example of a compound with the negative particle na as the first member is as follows: from the analysis natthi etassa samo'ti, 'there is no equal to him', comes asamo bhagavā, 'the unequalled Blessed One'. Here, in the rule 'attaṃ nassa tappurise', by splitting the rule (yogavibhāga) into 'attaṃ nassā', the substitution of a for na is obtained. Similarly, appaṭipuggalo ('one without an equal'), aputtako ('one without a son'), ahetuko ('without cause'); by the rule beginning 'kvaci samāsanta', the affix kappa is added. From natthi saṃvāso etesaṃ'ti, 'there is no living together with them', comes asaṃvāsā. From na vijjate vuṭṭhi etthā'ti, 'rain does not exist here', comes avuṭṭhiko janapado, 'a rainless country'. Also, abhikkhuko vihāro, 'a monastery without monks'. From natthi etassa uttaro'ti, 'there is none superior to him', comes anuttaro; by the rule 'sare ana', na becomes ana. The inclusion of tappurisa in that rule is illustrative. Alternatively, by the rule beginning 'tesu vuddhī', na is replaced by ana. Similarly, from natthi anto assā'ti, 'it has no end', comes anantaṃ. From na vijjanti āsavā etesaṃ'ti, 'taints do not exist for them', comes anāsavā, and so forth.

Paṭhamāyatthe sahapubbapado yathā – saha hetunā yo vattateti sahetuko, sahetu vā, “tesu vuddhī”tiādinā [M 0.0206] sahasaddassa sādeso, “kvaci samāsanta”iccādinā kappaccayo ca, saha pītiyā ime vattantīti sappītikā. Evaṃ saha paccayehi vattantīti sappaccayā, sakileso, saupādāno, saparivāro, saha mūlena uddhato samūluddhato rukkho.

An example of a compound with saha as the first member in the sense of the nominative case is as follows: from the analysis saha hetunā yo vattate'ti, 'that which exists with a cause', comes sahetuko, or sahetu. By the rule beginning 'tesu vuddhī', the word saha is replaced by sa, and by the rule beginning 'kvaci samāsanta', the affix kappa is added. From saha pītiyā ime vattantī'ti, 'these exist with joy', comes sappītikā. Similarly, from saha paccayehi vattantī'ti, 'those that exist with conditions', comes sappaccayā. Also sakileso ('with defilements'), saupādāno ('with clinging'), saparivāro ('with a retinue'). From saha mūlena uddhato, 'uprooted together with its root', comes samūluddhato rukkho, 'a tree uprooted with its root'.

Upamānapubbapado paṭhamāyatthe tāva – upamānopameyyabhāvappasiddhatthaṃ ivasaddappayogo, kāyabyāmānaṃ samappamāṇatāya nigrodho iva parimaṇḍalo yo rājakumāro soyaṃnigrodhaparimaṇḍalo rājakumāro. “Vuttatthānamappayogo”ti ivasaddassa appayogo, saṅkho viya paṇḍaro ayanti saṅkhapaṇḍaro, kāko viya sūro ayanti kākasūro, cakkhu iva bhūto ayaṃ paramatthadassanatoti cakkhubhūto bhagavā. Evaṃ atthabhūto. Dhammabhūto, brahmabhūto, andho viya bhūto ayanti andhabhūto bālo. Muñjapabbajamiva bhūtā ayanti muñjapabbajabhūtā kudiṭṭhi. Tantākulakamiva jātā ayanti tantākulakajātā.

First, an example of a compound with a term of comparison as the first member (upamānapubbapado) in the sense of the nominative case: The word iva is used to make clear the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison. For example, from the analysis kāyabyāmānaṃ samappamāṇatāya nigrodho iva parimaṇḍalo yo rājakumāro, 'the prince who is as perfectly proportioned as a banyan tree, his height and reach being of equal measure', comes so'yaṃ nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo rājakumāro. By the maxim 'Vuttatthānamappayogo' ('of things whose meaning is expressed, there is no application'), the word iva is not used in the compound. From saṅkho viya paṇḍaro ayaṃ'ti, 'this is white like a conch', comes saṅkhapaṇḍaro. From kāko viya sūro ayaṃ'ti, 'this is brave like a crow', comes kākasūro. From cakkhu iva bhūto ayaṃ paramatthadassanato'ti, 'he has become like an eye because he sees the ultimate truth', comes cakkhubhūto bhagavā, 'the Blessed One who has become the eye'. Similarly, atthabhūto ('become the truth'), dhammabhūto ('become the Dhamma'), brahmabhūto ('become Brahma'). From andho viya bhūto ayaṃ'ti, 'this one has become like a blind person', comes andhabhūto bālo, 'the fool who has become blind'. From muñjapabbajamiva bhūtā ayaṃ'ti, 'this has become like a thicket of muñja grass', comes muñjapabbajabhūtā kudiṭṭhi, 'wrong view that has become like a thicket of muñja grass'. From tantākulakamiva jātā ayaṃ'ti, 'this one has been born like a tangled skein', comes tantākulakajātā.

Chaṭṭhiyatthe – suvaṇṇavaṇṇo viya vaṇṇo yassa soyaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇo bhagavā. Uttarapadalopo, nāgassa viya assa gatīti nāgagati. Evaṃ sīhagati, nāgavikkamo, sīhavikkamo, sīhahanu, eṇissa viya assa jaṅghāti eṇijaṅgho, sīhassa pubbaddhaṃ viya assa kāyoti sīhapubbaddhakāyo, brahmuno viya aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato saro assāti brahmassaro.

In the sense of the genitive case: from the analysis suvaṇṇavaṇṇo viya vaṇṇo yassa, 'he whose color is like the color of gold', comes so'yaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇo bhagavā, 'that golden-hued Blessed One'. There is elision of the final member (uttarapadalopo). From nāgassa viya assa gatī'ti, 'his gait is like that of an elephant', comes nāgagati. Similarly, sīhagati ('lion-gait'), nāgavikkamo ('elephant-stride'), sīhavikkamo ('lion-stride'), sīhahanu ('lion-jaw'). From eṇissa viya assa jaṅghā'ti, 'his shanks are like those of an antelope', comes eṇijaṅgho. From sīhassa pubbaddhaṃ viya assa kāyo'ti, 'his body is like the forepart of a lion', comes sīhapubbaddhakāyo. From brahmuno viya aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato saro assā'ti, 'his voice is like that of Brahmā, endowed with eight qualities', comes brahmassaro.

Vāsaddatthe [M 0.0207] saṅkhyobhayapado yathā – dve vā tayo vā pattā dvattipattā, “dvekaṭṭhānamākāro vā”ti dvisaddantassa āttaṃ, rassattaṃ, dvīhaṃ vā tīhaṃ vā dvīhatīhaṃ, cha vā pañca vā vācā chappañcavācā. Evaṃ sattaṭṭhamāsā, ekayojanadviyojanāni.

An example of a compound with two numerals (saṅkhyobhayapado) in the sense of the word vā ('or') is as follows: from the analysis dve vā tayo vā pattā, 'two or three bowls', comes dvattipattā. By the rule 'dvekaṭṭhānamākāro vā', the final vowel of the word dvi becomes ā, and then it is shortened. From dvīhaṃ vā tīhaṃ vā, 'for two or three days', comes dvīhatīhaṃ. From cha vā pañca vā vācā, 'six or five words', comes chappañcavācā. Similarly, sattaṭṭhamāsā ('seven or eight months'), ekayojanadviyojanāni ('one or two leagues').

Disantarāḷattho yathā – pubbassā ca dakkhiṇassā ca disāya yadantarāḷaṃ sāyaṃ pubbadakkhiṇā vidisā. Ettha tulyādhikaraṇapadaparattābhāvā na pumbhāvātideso, “kvacādimajjhuttarāna”ntiādinā disantarāḷatthe pubbapadassa rassattaṃ. Evaṃ pubbuttarā, aparadakkhiṇā, pacchimuttarā. Yadā pana dakkhiṇā ca sā pubbā cāti kammadhārayasamāso hoti, tadā pumbhāvātideso uttarapadatthappadhānattā, sabbanāmikavidhānampi niccaṃ bhavatiyeva, yathā – dakkhiṇapubbassā, dakkhiṇapubbassamiti.

An example in the sense of an intermediate direction (disantarāḷattho) is as follows: from the analysis pubbassā ca dakkhiṇassā ca disāya yadantarāḷaṃ, 'the intermediate space between the eastern and southern directions', comes sāyaṃ pubbadakkhiṇā vidisā, 'that is the southeastern intermediate direction'. Here, because there is no subsequent word in apposition, there is no application of the masculine form. By the rule beginning 'kvacādimajjhuttarāna', the first member is shortened in the sense of an intermediate direction. Thus, pubbuttarā (northeast), aparadakkhiṇā (southwest), pacchimuttarā (northwest). However, when there is a kammadhāraya compound, from the analysis dakkhiṇā ca sā pubbā cā'ti, 'that which is southern and eastern', then there is application of the masculine form because the meaning of the final member is predominant, and the rules pertaining to pronouns always apply, as in dakkhiṇapubbassā and dakkhiṇapubbassaṃ.

Byatihāralakkhaṇo yathā – kesesu ca kesesu ca gahetvā idaṃ yuddhaṃ pavattatīti kesākesi, daṇḍehi ca daṇḍehi ca paharitvā idaṃ yuddhaṃ pavattatīti daṇḍādaṇḍi, “kvacādimajjhuttarāna”ntiādinā majjhedīgho, “tesu vuddhī”tiādinā antassikāro.

An example indicating reciprocal action (byatihāralakkhaṇo) is as follows: from the analysis kesesu ca kesesu ca gahetvā idaṃ yuddhaṃ pavattatī'ti, 'this battle proceeds by seizing each other by the hair', comes kesākesi. From daṇḍehi ca daṇḍehi ca paharitvā idaṃ yuddhaṃ pavattatī'ti, 'this battle proceeds by striking each other with sticks', comes daṇḍādaṇḍi. By the rule beginning 'kvacādimajjhuttarāna', the vowel in the middle is lengthened; and by the rule beginning 'tesu vuddhī', the final vowel becomes i.

Paṭhamāvibhatyatthabahubbīhi.

The Bahubbīhi compound in the sense of the nominative case.

Bahubbīhisamāso niṭṭhito.

The section on the Bahubbīhi compound is concluded.

Dvandasamāsa

The Dvanda (Copulative) Compound

Atha dvandasamāso vuccate.

Now the Dvanda compound will be explained.

So ca duvidho itarītarayoga samāhāratthabhedena.

And it is of two kinds, distinguished by meaning as itarītarayoga (mutual connection) and samāhāra (aggregation).

Tattha [M 0.0208] itarītarayoge tāva – “sāriputtamoggallāna”itīdha ubhayatthāpi paṭhamekavacanaṃ, samuccayajotanatthaṃ casaddappayogo ca.

Among these, first, regarding itarītarayoga (mutual connection): here, in the example Sāriputtamoggallāna, each component is in the nominative singular, and the word ca is used to indicate conjunction.

“Sāriputto ca moggallāno cā”ti viggahe –

In the analytical expression, 'Sāriputto ca Moggallāno cā'—

357. Nāmānaṃ samuccayo dvando.

357. The conjunction of nouns is a dvanda.

Nānānāmānameva ekavibhattikānaṃ yuttatthānaṃ yo samuccayo, so vibhāsā samāso bhavati, dvandasañño ca.

A conjunction of different nouns that have the same case ending and a connected meaning optionally becomes a compound, and it is designated a dvanda.

Ettha ca samuccayo nāma sampiṇḍanaṃ, so pana atthavasena kevalasamuccayo anvācayo itarītarayogo samāhāro cāti catubbidho.

Here, conjunction (samuccayo) means 'a grouping together'. By way of meaning, it is fourfold: simple conjunction (kevalasamuccayo), subsequent connection (anvācayo), mutual connection (itarītarayoga), and aggregation (samāhāra).

Tattha kevalasamuccaye, anvācaye ca samāso na bhavati, kriyāsāpekkhatāya nāmānaṃ aññamaññaṃ ayuttatthabhāvato, yathā – cīvaraṃ piṇḍapātañca paccayaṃ sayanāsanaṃ adāsi, dānañca dehi, sīlañca rakkhāhi. Itarītarayoge, samāhāre ca samāso bhavati, tattha nāmānaṃ aññamaññaṃ yuttatthabhāvato.

Among these, in the case of simple conjunction and subsequent connection, a compound is not formed, because the nouns are dependent on a verb and thus lack a mutually connected meaning. For example: cīvaraṃ piṇḍapātañca paccayaṃ sayanāsanaṃ adāsi, 'he gave a robe, almsfood, requisites, and lodging'; and dānañca dehi, sīlañca rakkhāhi, 'give alms and keep the precepts'. In the case of mutual connection and aggregation, however, a compound is formed, because in those cases the nouns do have a mutually connected meaning.

Dve dve padāni dvandā, dvandaṭṭhā vā dvandā, dvandasadisattā ayaṃ samāsopi anvatthasaññāya dvandoti vuccati, ubhayapadatthappadhāno hi dvando.

Words in pairs (dve dve padāni) are dvandā (pairs), or things that stand in a pair are dvandā. Because this type of compound is similar to a pair, it is called dvanda by a meaningful designation. For in a dvanda compound, the meaning of both members is primary.

Nanu ca ubhayapadatthappadhānatte sati dvande kathamekatthībhāvo siyāti? Vuccate – sadisādiatthepi saddappavattisambhavenadvinnaṃ padānaṃ ekakkhaṇeyeva atthadvayadīpakattā na virodho, tañca dvandavisayameva, tesamatthadvayadīpakattā. Yathā hi bhūsaddo anubhavaabhibhavādike atthe anvabhiādiupasaggasahitova dīpeti, na kevalo, evaṃ “gavassaka”ntiādīsu [M 0.0209] gavādīnaṃ assādisaddantarasahitānameva atthadvayadīpanaṃ, na kevalānanti tañca dvandavisayameva, na sabbatthāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā dvinnampi yathāvuttasamuccayadīpakattā atthi dvandepekatthitāti na koci virodho, tato samāsasaññāvibhattilopādi vuttanayameva, samāseneva catthassa vuttattā “vuttatthānamappayogo”ti casaddassa appayogo.

But if, in a dvanda compound, the meaning of both words is primary, how can there be a single meaning? It is said: Because the application of words is possible even in meanings such as 'similar' etc., and because the two words illuminate two meanings in a single moment, there is no contradiction. And that applies only to the domain of dvanda compounds, because they illuminate two meanings. For just as the word 'bhū,' when accompanied by prefixes such as 'anu' and 'abhi,' reveals meanings such as experiencing and overpowering, but not when alone, so too in examples like 'gavassaka,' the meanings of 'go' and the like are revealed only in conjunction with other words like 'assa,' not when alone. And this is to be understood as applying only to the domain of dvanda compounds, not everywhere. Or alternatively, because both words illuminate the collection as stated, there is a single meaning even in a dvanda compound, and thus there is no contradiction. Therefore, the designation as a compound, the elision of case endings, and so on, are as has been stated. Because the meaning is expressed by the compound itself, according to the maxim 'there is no application of words whose meaning has been expressed,' the word 'ca' is not used.

Idha dvande accitataraṃ pubbaṃ nipatati, parasseva liṅgañca. Itarītarayogassa avayavappadhānattā sabbattha bahuvacanameva.

Here, in a dvanda compound, the more honored word is placed first, and the gender is that of the last word. Because in an itarītarayoga dvanda the members are primary, the plural is always used.

Sāriputtamoggallānā, sāriputtamoggallāne, sāriputtamoggallānehi iccādi, samaṇo ca brāhmaṇo ca samaṇabrāhmaṇā. Evaṃ brāhmaṇagahapatikā, khattiyabrāhmaṇā, devamanussā, candimasūriyā, mātā ca pitā ca mātāpitaro, “tesu vuddhī”tiādinā dvande mātuādipubbapadukārassa ākāro. Evaṃ pitāputtā.

Sāriputtamoggallānā (Sāriputta and Moggallāna), sāriputtamoggallāne (to Sāriputta and Moggallāna), sāriputtamoggallānehi (by Sāriputta and Moggallāna), etc.; an ascetic and a brahmin become samaṇabrāhmaṇā (ascetics and brahmins). Similarly, brāhmaṇagahapatikā (brahmins and householders), khattiyabrāhmaṇā (nobles and brahmins), devamanussā (gods and humans), candimasūriyā (the moon and the sun); a mother and a father become mātāpitaro (parents)—in these examples, by the rule 'tesu vuddhī' etc., in a dvanda compound, the 'u' of a first word such as 'mātu' becomes 'ā'. Similarly, pitāputtā (father and son).

“Jāyā ca pati cāti jāyāpati”itīdha –

In 'jāyā ca pati ca' (wife and husband), which becomes 'jāyāpati', here—

“Kvacī”ti vattate.

The word 'kvaci' (sometimes) is carried forward.

358. Jāyāya tudaṃ jāni patimhi.

358. For 'jāyā', 'tudaṃ' and 'jāni' are substituted when 'pati' follows.

Jāyāsaddassa tudaṃ jāniiccete ādesā honti patisadde pare kvaci. Tudaṃpati, jānipati, jayampatikā. Ettha niggahītāgamo, “kvacā”dinā rassattañca.

For the word 'jāyā', the substitutions 'tudaṃ' and 'jāni' occur sometimes when the word 'pati' follows. Examples: tudaṃpati, jānipati, jayampatikā. Here, there is the insertion of a niggahīta, and shortening by the rule beginning 'kvaci' etc.

Kvaci appasaraṃ pubbaṃ nipatati, yathā – cando ca sūriyo ca candasūriyā, nigamā ca janapadā ca nigamajanapadā, surā ca asurā [M 0.0210] ca garuḷā ca manujā ca bhujagā ca gandhabbā ca surāsuragaruḷamanujabhujagagandhabbā.
