Sometimes the word with fewer syllables is placed first, for example: the moon and the sun, thus 'candasūriyā'; towns and districts, thus 'nigamajanapadā'; gods, asuras, garuḍas, humans, serpents, and gandhabbas, thus 'surāsuragaruḷamanujabhujagagandhabbā'.

Kvaci ivaṇṇuvaṇṇantānaṃ pubbanipāto, yathā – aggi ca dhūmo ca aggidhūmā. Evaṃ gatibuddhibhujapaṭhaharakarasayā, dhātavo ca liṅgāni ca dhātuliṅgāni.

Sometimes, words ending in 'i' or 'u' are placed first, for example: fire and smoke, thus 'aggidhūmā'. Similarly, 'gatibuddhibhujapaṭhaharakarasayā'; roots and genders, thus 'dhātuliṅgāni'.

Kvaci sarādiakārantānaṃ pubbanipāto, yathā – attho ca dhammo ca atthadhammā. Evaṃ atthasaddā, saddatthā vā.

Sometimes, words beginning with a vowel and ending in 'a' are placed first, for example: meaning and Dhamma, thus 'atthadhammā'. Similarly, 'atthasaddā' (meaning-words), or 'saddatthā' (word-meanings).

Samāhāre pana – “cakkhu ca sotañcā”ti atthe “nāmānaṃ samuccayo dvando”ti dvandasamāsaṃ katvā vibhattilopādimhi kate –

However, in a samāhāra (collective) dvanda—in the sense of 'eye and ear,' having formed the dvanda compound by the rule 'a collection of nouns is a dvanda,' when the elision of case endings etc. has been made—

“Napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ, ekattañcā”ti vattate.

The words 'napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ, ekattañca' (neuter gender, and singular) are carried forward.

359. Tathā dvande pāṇi tūriya yogga senaṅga khuddajantuka vividha viruddha visabhāgatthādīnañca.

359. Likewise, in a dvanda compound, this also applies to things having the meaning of: parts of living beings, musical ensembles, yokes, and armies; small creatures; various opposites; and things of dissimilar nature, and so on.

Yathā digusamāse, tathā samāhāradvandasamāsepi pāṇi tūriya yogga senaṅgatthānaṃ, khuddajantukavividha viruddhavisabhāgatthaiccevamādīnañca ekattaṃ hoti, napuṃsakaliṅgattañca.

Just as in a digu compound, so too in a samāhāra-dvanda compound, for things having the meaning of parts of living beings, musical ensembles, yokes, and armies; small creatures; various opposites; things of dissimilar nature, and so on, there is singularity and neuter gender.

Pāṇino ca tūriyāni ca yoggāni ca senā cāti pāṇitūriya yoggasenā, tāsamaṅgāni pāṇitūriyayoggasenaṅgāni, dvandato parattā aṅgasaddo paccekamabhisambajjhate. Khuddā ca te jantukā ceti khuddajantukā, vividhenākārena viruddhā vividhaviruddhā, niccavirodhino. Samāno bhāgo yesaṃ te sabhāgā, “tesu vuddhī”tiādinā samānassa saādeso, vividhā ca te lakkhaṇato sabhāgā ca kiccatoti visabhāgā. Pāṇitūriyayoggasenaṅgāni ca khuddajantukā ca vividhaviruddhā ca visabhāgā cāti dvando, idha bahuttā pubbanipātassa aniyamo, te atthā yesaṃ [M 0.0211] te pāṇitūriyayoggasenaṅgakhuddajantukavividhaviruddhavisabhāgatthā, te ādayo yesaṃ te tadādayo.

Living beings, musical instruments, yokes, and armies—thus 'pāṇitūriyayoggasenā'. Their parts are 'pāṇitūriyayoggasenaṅgāni'; because it comes after the dvanda, the word 'aṅga' is connected to each component individually. Small and those living beings—thus 'khuddajantukā'. Opposed in various ways—thus 'vividhaviruddhā', meaning constantly antagonistic. Those whose parts are similar are 'sabhāgā' (homogeneous); by the rule 'tesu vuddhī' etc., 'sa' is substituted for 'samāna'. Those that are diverse in characteristics but similar in function are 'visabhāgā' (dissimilar). 'Pāṇitūriyayoggasenaṅgāni ca khuddajantukā ca vividhaviruddhā ca visabhāgā ca' is a dvanda compound; here, due to the multitude of terms, the precedence is not fixed. Those things which have these meanings are 'pāṇi...atthā'; those which have these as their beginning are 'tadādayo'.

Ādiggahaṇena aññoññaliṅgavisesita saṅkhyāparimāṇattha pacanacaṇḍālattha disatthādīnañca dvande ekattaṃ, napuṃsakaliṅgattañca, iti pāṇyaṅgatthabhāvato cakkhusotasaddānaṃ iminā ekattaṃ, napuṃsakaliṅgattañca katvā samāsattā nāmabyapadese kate syādyuppatti amādesādi.

By the inclusion of 'ādi' (etc.), in a dvanda compound of things specified by different genders, of number and measure, of cooks and outcastes, of directions, and so on, there is also singularity and neuter gender. Thus, because the words 'cakkhu' and 'sota' have the meaning of 'parts of a living being', by this rule singularity and neuter gender are applied. Then, because it is a compound, once it is designated as a nominal stem, case endings such as 'si' are generated, 'aṃ' is substituted, and so on.

Cakkhusotaṃ, he cakkhusota, cakkhusotaṃ, cakkhusotena. Evaṃ sabbatthekavacanameva. Mukhañca nāsikā ca mukhanāsikaṃ, “saro rasso napuṃsake”ti antassa rassattaṃ, hanu ca gīvā ca hanugīvaṃ. Evaṃ kaṇṇanāsaṃ, pāṇipādaṃ, chavimaṃsalohitaṃ. Hatthapādā maṃsalohitānītiādīnaṃ pana itarītarayogena siddhaṃ. Evaṃ pāṇyaṅgatthe.

Cakkhusotaṃ (eye-ear), he cakkhusota (O eye-ear), cakkhusotaṃ (eye-ear), cakkhusotena (by the eye-ear). Thus, in all instances, only the singular form is used. Mouth and nose become mukhanāsikaṃ (mouth-nose); by 'saro rasso napuṃsake' (a short vowel in the neuter), the final vowel becomes short. Jaw and neck become hanugīvaṃ (jaw-neck). Similarly, kaṇṇanāsaṃ (ear-nose), pāṇipādaṃ (hand-foot), chavimaṃsalohitaṃ (skin-flesh-blood). But forms such as 'hatthapādā' (hands and feet) and 'maṃsalohitāni' (flesh and blood) are formed by itarītarayoga (mutual connection). Thus regarding the meaning of parts of a living being.

Tūriyaṅgatthe gītañca vāditañca gītavāditaṃ, sammañca tāḷañca sammatāḷaṃ, sammanti kaṃsatāḷaṃ. Tāḷanti hatthatāḷaṃ. Saṅkhe ca paṇavo ca ḍiṇḍimo ca, saṅkhā ca paṇavā ca ḍaṃṇḍimā cāti vā saṅkhapaṇavaḍiṇḍimaṃ, paṇavādayo dvepi bheriviseso.

In the meaning of musical instruments: singing and playing, thus 'gītavāditaṃ'; 'samma' and 'tāḷa', thus 'sammatāḷaṃ'. 'Samma' means a bronze cymbal. 'Tāḷa' means hand-clapping. Conch and 'paṇava' and 'ḍiṇḍima', or conches and 'paṇavas' and 'ḍiṇḍimas', thus 'saṅkhapaṇavaḍiṇḍimaṃ'. Both 'paṇava' and 'ḍiṇḍima' are types of kettle-drum.

Yoggaṅgatthe yathā – phālo ca pācanañca phālapācanaṃ, yugañca naṅgalañca yuganaṅgalaṃ.

In the meaning of implements, for example: ploughshare and goad, thus 'phālapācanaṃ'; yoke and plough, thus 'yuganaṅgalaṃ'.

Senaṅgatthe hatthino ca assā ca hatthiassaṃ, rathā ca pattikā ca rathapattikaṃ, asi ca cammañca asicammaṃ, cammanti saravāraṇaphalakaṃ. Dhanu ca kalāpo ca dhanukalāpaṃ, kalāpoti tūṇīraṃ.

In the meaning of army divisions: elephants and horses, thus 'hatthiassaṃ'; chariots and infantry, thus 'rathapattikaṃ'; sword and shield, thus 'asicammaṃ'. 'Camma' means a board for warding off arrows. Bow and quiver, thus 'dhanukalāpaṃ'. 'Kalāpa' means a quiver.

Khuddajantukatthe ḍaṃsā ca makasā ca ḍaṃsamakasaṃ. Evaṃ kunthakipillikaṃ, kīṭapaṭaṅgaṃ, kīṭasarīsapaṃ. Tattha kunthā sukhumakipillikā, kīṭā kapālapiṭṭhikapāṇā.

In the meaning of small creatures: gadflies and mosquitoes, thus 'ḍaṃsamakasaṃ'. Similarly, 'kunthakipillikaṃ' (kunthas and ants), 'kīṭapaṭaṅgaṃ' (insects and moths), 'kīṭasarīsapaṃ' (insects and reptiles). There, 'kunthā' are tiny ants, and 'kīṭā' are creatures with shell-like backs.

Vividhaviruddhatthe [M 0.0212] ahi ca nakulo ca, ahī ca nakulā cāti vā ahinakulaṃ. Evaṃ biḷāramūsikaṃ, antassa rassattaṃ, kākolūkaṃ, sappamaṇḍūkaṃ, garuḷasappaṃ.

In the meaning of various opposites: snake and mongoose, or snakes and mongooses, thus 'ahinakulaṃ'. Similarly, 'biḷāramūsikaṃ' (cat and mouse), with shortening of the final vowel; 'kākolūkaṃ' (crow and owl); 'sappamaṇḍūkaṃ' (snake and frog); 'garuḷasappaṃ' (Garuḍa and snake).

Visabhāgatthe sīlañca paññāṇañca sīlapaññāṇaṃ, samatho ca vipassanā ca samathavipassanaṃ. Evaṃ nāmarūpaṃ, hirottappaṃ. Satisampajaññaṃ, lobhamohaṃ, dosamohaṃ, ahirikānottappaṃ, thinamiddhaṃ, uddhaccakukkuccamiccādi. “Aṃmo niggahītaṃ jhalapehī”ti ettha “aṃmo”ti niddesadassanato katthaci napuṃsakaliṅgattaṃ na hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ, tena ādhipaccaparivāro chandapārisuddhi paṭisandhippavattiyantiādi sijjhati.

In the meaning of dissimilar things: virtue and wisdom, thus 'sīlapaññāṇaṃ'; serenity and insight, thus 'samathavipassanaṃ'. Likewise, 'nāmarūpaṃ' (name and form), 'hirottappaṃ' (moral shame and fear), 'satisampajaññaṃ' (mindfulness and clear comprehension), 'lobhamohaṃ' (greed and delusion), 'dosamohaṃ' (hatred and delusion), 'ahirikānottappaṃ' (shamelessness and recklessness), 'thinamiddhaṃ' (sloth and torpor), 'uddhaccakukkuccaṃ' (restlessness and remorse), etc. In the rule 'Aṃmo niggahītaṃ jhalapehī', from the indication 'aṃmo', it should be understood that in some cases the compound does not become neuter in gender. Therefore, examples such as 'ādhipaccaparivāro' (dominance and retinue), 'chandapārisuddhi' (intention and purity), 'paṭisandhippavatti' (rebirth-linking and continuity), etc., are established.

Aññoññaliṅgavisesitānaṃ dvande dāsī ca dāso ca dāsidāsaṃ, “kvacādī”tiādinā majjhe rassattaṃ. Evaṃ itthipumaṃ, pattacīvaraṃ, sākhāpalāsamiccādi.

In a dvanda compound of those specified by different genders: female slave and male slave, thus 'dāsidāsaṃ'; by the rule beginning 'kvaci' etc., the vowel in the middle is shortened. Similarly, 'itthipumaṃ' (woman and man), 'pattacīvaraṃ' (bowl and robe), 'sākhāpalāsaṃ' (branches and leaves), etc.

Saṅkhyāparimāṇatthānaṃ dvande ekakañca dukañca ekakadukaṃ, saṅkhyādvande appasaṅkhyā pubbaṃ nipatati. Evaṃ dukatikaṃ, tikacatukkaṃ, catukkapañcakaṃ, dīgho ca majjhimo ca dīghamajjhimaṃ.

In a dvanda compound of things with the meaning of number and measure: one and two, thus 'ekakadukaṃ'. In a numerical dvanda compound, the smaller number is placed first. Thus, 'dukatikaṃ' (two and three), 'tikacatukkaṃ' (three and four), 'catukkapañcakaṃ' (four and five); long and middle, thus 'dīghamajjhimaṃ'.

Pacanacaṇḍālatthānaṃ dvande orabbhikā ca sūkarikā ca orabbhikasūkarikaṃ. Evaṃ sākuṇikamāgavikaṃ, sapāko ca caṇḍālo ca sapākacaṇḍālaṃ, pukkusachavaḍāhakaṃ, venarathakāraṃ. Tattha venā tacchakā, rathakārā cammakārā.

In a dvanda compound of low castes: the sheep-butcher and the pig-butcher—'orabbhikasūkarikaṃ.' Similarly, 'sākuṇikamāgavikaṃ' (the fowler and the deer-hunter), the dog-cook and the outcaste—'sapākacaṇḍālaṃ,' 'pukkusachavaḍāhakaṃ' (the Pukkusa and the corpse-burner), the bamboo-worker and the chariot-maker—'venarathakāraṃ.' Herein, 'venā' are carpenters, and 'rathakārā' are leather-workers.

Disatthānaṃ dvande pubbā ca aparā cāti atthe dvandasamāsaṃ, vibhattilopañca katvā idhādiggahaṇena ekatte, napuṃsakaliṅgatte ca kate “saro rasso napuṃsake”ti rassattaṃ, pubbāparaṃ[M 0.0213], he pubbāpara, pubbāparaṃ, pubbāparena, pubbāparassa iccādi. Evaṃ puratthimapacchimaṃ, dakkhiṇuttaraṃ, adharuttaraṃ.

In dvanda compounds denoting directions, in the sense of 'pubbā ca aparā ca' (east and west), having formed the dvanda compound and elided the case-endings, and by the initial inclusion rule, when it is made singular and neuter, shortening occurs according to the rule 'a vowel is short in the neuter.' Thus, 'pubbāparaṃ,' vocative 'he pubbāpara,' accusative 'pubbāparaṃ,' instrumental 'pubbāparena,' genitive 'pubbāparassa,' and so on. Similarly, 'puratthimapacchimaṃ' (east and west), 'dakkhiṇuttaraṃ' (south and north), 'adharuttaraṃ' (lower and upper).

“Napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ, ekattaṃ, dvande”ti ca vattate.

The words 'neuter gender,' 'singular number,' and 'in a dvanda compound' are carried forward.

360. Vibhāsā rukkha tiṇa pasu dhana dhañña janapadādīnañca.

360. Optionally for trees, grass, cattle, wealth, grain, countries, and so on.

Rukkha tiṇa pasu dhana dhañña janapadādīnamekattaṃ, napuṃsakaliṅgattañca vibhāsā hoti dvande samāse. Ekattābhāve bahuvacanaṃ, parasseva liṅgañca.

For trees, grass, animals, wealth, grain, countries, and so on, in a dvanda compound, singularity and neuter gender optionally occur. In the absence of singularity, the plural number is used, and the gender is that of the final term.

Tattha rukkhānaṃ dvande assatthā ca kapitthā cāti atthe samāhāre dvandasamāsādimhi kate iminā vikappenekattaṃ, napuṃsakaliṅgattañca. Assatthakapitthaṃ, assatthakapitthā vā. Evaṃ ambapanasaṃ, ambapanasā vā, khadirapalāsaṃ, khadirapalāsā vā, dhavassakaṇṇakaṃ, dhavassakaṇṇakā vā.

Therein, in a dvanda compound of trees, in the sense of 'assatthā ca kapitthā ca,' when a collective dvanda compound is formed, by this option, singularity and neuter gender occur. Thus, 'assatthakapitthaṃ' or 'assatthakapitthā.' Similarly, 'ambapanasaṃ' or 'ambapanasā,' 'khadirapalāsaṃ' or 'khadirapalāsā,' 'dhavassakaṇṇakaṃ' or 'dhavassakaṇṇakā.'

Tiṇānaṃ dvande usīrāni ca bīraṇāni ca usīrabīraṇaṃ, usīrabīraṇāni vā. Evaṃ muñjapabbajaṃ, muñjapabbajā vā, kāsakusaṃ, kāsakusā vā.

In a dvanda compound of grasses: 'usīrāni ca bīraṇāni ca' (usīra grass and bīraṇa grass) becomes 'usīrabīraṇaṃ' or 'usīrabīraṇāni.' Similarly, 'muñjapabbajaṃ' or 'muñjapabbajā,' 'kāsakusaṃ' or 'kāsakusā.'

Pasūnaṃ dvande ajā ca eḷakā ca ajeḷakaṃ, ajeḷakā vā, hatthī ca gāvo ca assā ca vaḷavā ca hatthigavassavaḷavaṃ, hatthigavassavaḷavā vā, “kvacā”tiādinā rassattaṃ, “osare cā”ti avādeso ca, gomahiṃsaṃ, gomahiṃsā vā, eṇeyyavarāhaṃ, eṇeyyavarāhā vā, sīhabyagghataracchaṃ, sīhabyagghataracchā vā.

In a dvanda compound of animals: 'ajā ca eḷakā ca' (a she-goat and a ram) becomes 'ajeḷakaṃ' or 'ajeḷakā.' 'Hatthī ca gāvo ca assā ca vaḷavā ca' (an elephant, cows, horses, and mares) becomes 'hatthigavassavaḷavaṃ' or 'hatthigavassavaḷavā'; shortening occurs by the rule beginning 'kvaci,' and the substitution of 'ava' by the rule 'osare ca.' 'Gomahiṃsaṃ' or 'gomahiṃsā' (a cow and a buffalo). 'Eṇeyyavarāhaṃ' or 'eṇeyyavarāhā' (a deer and a boar). 'Sīhabyagghataracchaṃ' or 'sīhabyagghataracchā' (a lion, a tiger, and a hyena).

Dhanānaṃ dvande hiraññañca suvaṇṇañca hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ, hiraññasuvaṇṇāni vā. Evaṃ jātarūparajataṃ, jātarūparajatāni vā, maṇimuttasaṅkhaveḷuriyaṃ, maṇimuttasaṅkhaveḷuriyā vā.

In a dvanda compound of wealth: 'hiraññañca suvaṇṇañca' (bullion and gold) becomes 'hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ' or 'hiraññasuvaṇṇāni.' Similarly, 'jātarūparajataṃ' or 'jātarūparajatāni' (gold and silver), 'maṇimuttasaṅkhaveḷuriyaṃ' or 'maṇimuttasaṅkhaveḷuriyā' (gems, pearls, conch-shells, and beryl).

Dhaññānaṃ [M 0.0214] dvande sālī ca yavā ca sāliyavaṃ, sāliyavā vā. Evaṃ tilamuggamāsaṃ, tilamuggamāsā vā.

In a dvanda compound of grains: 'sālī ca yavā ca' (rice and barley) becomes 'sāliyavaṃ' or 'sāliyavā.' Similarly, 'tilamuggamāsaṃ' or 'tilamuggamāsā' (sesame, mung beans, and beans).

Janapadānaṃ dvande kāsī ca kosalā ca kāsikosalaṃ, kāsikosalā vā, vajjī ca mallā ca vajjimallaṃ, vajjimallā vā, aṅgā ca magadhā ca aṅgamagadhaṃ, aṅgamagadhā vā.

In a dvanda compound of countries: 'kāsī ca kosalā ca' (Kāsi and Kosala) becomes 'kāsikosalaṃ' or 'kāsikosalā.' 'Vajjī ca mallā ca' (Vajji and Malla) becomes 'vajjimallaṃ' or 'vajjimallā.' 'Aṅgā ca magadhā ca' (Aṅga and Magadha) becomes 'aṅgamagadhaṃ' or 'aṅgamagadhā.'

Ādiggahaṇena aññoññappaṭipakkhadhammānaṃ, sakuṇatthānañca dvande vibhāsā ekattaṃ hoti, napuṃsakaliṅgattañca. Kusalañca akusalañca kusalākusalaṃ, kusalākusalā vā, evaṃ sāvajjānavajjaṃ, sāvajjānavajjā vā, hīnappaṇītaṃ, hīnappaṇītā vā, kaṇhasukkaṃ, kaṇhasukkā vā, sukhadukkhaṃ, sukhadukkhāni vā, paṭighānunayaṃ, paṭighānunayā vā, chāyātapaṃ, chāyātapā vā, ālokandhakāraṃ, ālokandhakārā vā, ratti ca divā ca rattindivaṃ, rattindivā vā, ahañca ratti ca ahorattaṃ, ahorattā vā, “kvaci samāsanta”iccādinā ākārikārānamattaṃ.

By the inclusion of 'ādi' (etc.) in the rule, optional singularity and neuter gender occur in a dvanda compound of mutually opposed things and of birds. 'Kusalañca akusalañca' (the wholesome and the unwholesome) becomes 'kusalākusalaṃ' or 'kusalākusalā.' Similarly, 'sāvajjānavajjaṃ' or 'sāvajjānavajjā' (the blameworthy and the blameless), 'hīnappaṇītaṃ' or 'hīnappaṇītā' (the inferior and the excellent), 'kaṇhasukkaṃ' or 'kaṇhasukkā' (the dark and the bright), 'sukhadukkhaṃ' or 'sukhadukkhāni' (pleasure and pain), 'paṭighānunayaṃ' or 'paṭighānunayā' (resistance and compliance), 'chāyātapaṃ' or 'chāyātapā' (shade and sunlight), 'ālokandhakāraṃ' or 'ālokandhakārā' (light and darkness). 'Ratti ca divā ca' (night and day) becomes 'rattindivaṃ' or 'rattindivā.' 'Ahañca ratti ca' (day and night) becomes 'ahorattaṃ' or 'ahorattā.' By the rule beginning 'kvaci samāsanta,' the final 'ā' and 'i' are shortened to 'a'.

Sakuṇānaṃ dvande haṃsā ca bakā ca haṃsabakaṃ, haṃsabakā vā. Evaṃ kāraṇḍavacakkavākaṃ, kāraṇḍavacakkavākā vā, mayūrakoñcaṃ, mayūrakoñcā vā, sukasālikaṃ, sukasālikā vā.

In a dvanda compound of birds: 'haṃsā ca bakā ca' (swans and herons) becomes 'haṃsabakaṃ' or 'haṃsabakā.' Similarly, 'kāraṇḍavacakkavākaṃ' or 'kāraṇḍavacakkavākā' (ducks and ruddy shelducks), 'mayūrakoñcaṃ' or 'mayūrakoñcā' (peacocks and cranes), 'sukasālikaṃ' or 'sukasālikā' (parrots and mynas).

Samāhāradvando.

The Collective Dvanda Compound.

Yebhuyyena cettha –

And here, for the most part—

Accitappasaraṃ pubbaṃ, ivaṇṇuvaṇṇakaṃ kvaci;

Dvande sarādyakārantaṃ, bahūsvaniyamo bhave.

The more honored term, or one with fewer syllables, is placed first; sometimes one ending in 'i' or 'u' is. In a dvanda, a term beginning with a vowel and ending in 'a' is placed first. Among many terms, there is no fixed rule.

Dvandasamāso niṭṭhito.

The section on dvanda compounds is concluded.

Pubbuttarubhayaññattha-ppadhānattā [M 0.0215] catubbidho;

Samāsoyaṃ digu kamma-dhārayehi ca chabbidho.

This compound is fourfold due to the predominance of the former term, the latter term, both terms, or another meaning; and it is sixfold with the Digu and Kammadhāraya.

Duvidho abyayībhāvo, navadhā kammadhārayo;

Digu dudhā tappuriso, aṭṭhadhā navadhā bhave;

Bahubbīhi dvidhā dvando, samāso caturaṭṭhadhāti.

The Avyayībhāva is twofold, the Kammadhāraya is ninefold; the Digu is twofold, the Tappurisa may be eightfold or ninefold; the Bahubbīhi is twofold, the Dvanda is twofold. Thus, the compound is forty-eight-fold.

Iti padarūpasiddhiyaṃ samāsakaṇḍo

Thus, in the Padarūpasiddhi, the section on compounds.

Catuttho.

The Fourth.

5. Taddhitakaṇḍa

5. The Section on Taddhita Suffixes

Apaccataddhita

Taddhita Suffixes Denoting Offspring

Atha [M 0.0216] nāmato eva vibhatyantā apaccādiatthavisese taddhituppattīti nāmato paraṃ taddhitavidhānamārabhīyate.

Now, since the formation of taddhita suffixes in specific senses such as 'offspring' occurs from a nominal stem ending in a case-inflection, the teaching of the taddhita rules is commenced after the section on nominals.

Tattha tasmā tividhaliṅgato paraṃ hutvā hitā sahitāti taddhitā, ṇādipaccayānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tesaṃ vā nāmikānaṃ hitā upakārā taddhitāti anvatthabhūtaparasamaññāvasenāpi ṇādippaccayāva taddhitā nāma.

Herein, they are called 'taddhita' because they are beneficial ('hitā') to that ('ta(d)') nominal which comes after the section on the three genders; this is a designation for the suffixes beginning with 'ṇa'. Or, they are called 'taddhita' because they are beneficial ('hitā') and helpful to those ('tesaṃ') nominals. Thus, even by way of a conventional designation that accords with the meaning, the suffixes beginning with 'ṇa' are indeed called taddhita.

“Vasiṭṭhassa apacca”nti viggahe –

In the analytical phrase, 'Vasiṭṭhassa apaccaṃ' (the offspring of Vasiṭṭha)—

“Liṅgañca nipaccate”ti ito liṅgaggahaṇamanuvattate.

From the rule 'Liṅgañca nipaccate,' the word 'liṅga' (nominal stem) is carried forward.

361. Vā ṇa’pacce.

361. Optionally, the suffix 'ṇa' in the sense of offspring.

Chaṭṭhiyantato liṅgamhā ṇappaccayo hoti vikappena “tassa apacca”miccetasmiṃ atthe.

From a nominal stem ending in the sixth case, the suffix 'ṇa' is optionally applied in the sense of 'tassa apaccaṃ' (his offspring).

So ca –

And that (suffix)—

362. Dhātuliṅgehi parā paccayā.

362. Suffixes are applied after verbal roots and nominal bases.

Dhātūhi, liṅgehi ca paccayā parāva hontīti paribhāsato apaccatthasambandhiliṅgato chaṭṭhiyantāyeva paro hoti. Paṭicca etasmā attho etīti paccayo, patīyanti anena atthāti vā paccayo, “vuttatthānamappayogo”ti apaccasaddassa appayogo, “tesaṃ vibhattiyo lopā ce”ti vibhattilopo ca.

From the definition that suffixes are applied after verbal roots and nominal bases, the suffix is applied after a nominal base related to the meaning of offspring, which is in the sixth case. A suffix is that from which a meaning comes dependently; or a suffix is that by which meanings are understood. By the rule 'Non-application of words whose meaning is already stated,' there is non-application of the word 'apacca'. And by the rule 'And their case endings are elided,' there is elision of the case ending.

363. Tesaṃ [M 0.0217] ṇo lopaṃ.

363. Of these, the ṇ is elided.

Tesaṃ taddhitappaccayānaṃ ṇānubandhānaṃ ṇakāro lopamāpajjate.

Of those taddhita suffixes that have ṇ as an indicatory letter, the letter ṇ is elided.

364. Vuddhādisarassa vāsaṃyogantassa saṇe ca.

364. And optionally, for the initial vowel of a stem not ending in a conjunct, there is lengthening when a suffix with an indicatory ṇ follows.

Ādisarassa vā ādibyañjanassa vā asaṃyogantassa vuddhi hoti saṇakārappaccaye pare. Saṃyogo anto assāti saṃyoganto, tadañño asaṃyoganto. Atha vā vavatthitavibhāsatthoyaṃ vāsaddo, tadā ca pakatibhūte liṅge sarānamādisarassa asaṃyogantassa vuddhi hoti saṇakāre taddhitappaccaye pareti attho.

For the initial vowel or the initial consonant of a nominal base not ending in a conjunct, there is lengthening when a suffix with the indicatory letter ṇ follows. A word ending in a conjunct is called 'saṃyoganta'; any other is 'asaṃyoganta'. Alternatively, this word 'vā' is for a fixed optionality. In that case, when a taddhita suffix with the indicatory letter ṇ follows, the initial vowel of the nominal base, which is in its natural state and does not end in a conjunct, undergoes lengthening—this is the meaning.

Tena –

By that—

Vāsiṭṭhādīsu niccāyaṃ, aniccoḷumpikādisu;

Na vuddhi nīlapītādo, vavatthitavibhāsato.

In words such as Vāsiṭṭha, this lengthening is constant; in words such as Uḷumpikā, it is optional. There is no lengthening in words such as Nīla and Pīta, due to fixed optionality.

Casaddaggahaṇamavadhāraṇatthaṃ.

The inclusion of the word 'ca' is for the purpose of emphasis.

Tassā vuddhiyā aniyamappasaṅge niyamatthaṃ paribhāsamāha.

When there is the possibility of that lengthening being unregulated, he states a definition for the purpose of regulation.

365. Ayuvaṇṇānañcāyo vuddhī.

365. And the lengthenings of the vowels 'a', 'i', and 'u' are 'ā', 'e', and 'o'.

Tesaṃ akāraivaṇṇuvaṇṇānameva yathākkamaṃ ā eoiccete vuddhiyo honti. Casaddaggahaṇamavuddhisampiṇḍanatthaṃ, avadhāraṇatthaṃ vā. I ca u ca yu, yu eva vaṇṇā yuvaṇṇā, a ca yuvaṇṇā ca ayuvaṇṇā. Ā ca e ca o ca āyo. Puna vuddhiggahaṇaṃ “negamajānapadā”tiādīsu uttarapadavuddhibhāvatthaṃ, ettha ca “ayuvaṇṇāna”nti ṭhānaniyamavacanaṃ āyonaṃ vuddhibhāvappasaṅganivattanatthaṃ.

For those vowels, namely 'a', 'i', and 'u', the lengthenings 'ā', 'e', and 'o' occur respectively. The inclusion of the word 'ca' is for grouping the non-lengthened vowels, or for emphasis. 'I' and 'u' are 'yu'; 'yu' itself is 'vaṇṇa'; 'a' and 'yuvaṇṇa' are 'ayuvaṇṇa'. 'Ā', 'e', and 'o' are 'āyo'. Again, the mention of 'vuddhi' is for the sake of the lengthening of the latter member in phrases like 'negamajānapadā' and others; and here, the statement 'ayuvaṇṇānaṃ' is a rule specifying the locus, to prevent the undesired consequence of the lengthening of 'āyo'.

Yathā [M 0.0218] hi katavuddhīnaṃ, puna vuddhi na hotiha;

Tathā sabhāvavuddhīnaṃ, āyonaṃ puna vuddhi na.

For just as for those vowels that have undergone lengthening, no further lengthening occurs here; so too, for those 'āyo' vowels that are naturally long, no further lengthening occurs.

Tato akārassa ākāro vuddhi, “saralopomādesappaccayādimhi saralope tu pakatī”ti saralopapakatibhāvā, “naye paraṃ yutte”ti paranayanaṃ katvā taddhitattā “taddhitasamāsa”iccādinā nāmabyapadese kate pure viya syādyuppatti.

Then, the vowel 'a' undergoes lengthening to 'ā'. Due to the preceding vowel remaining in its natural state after vowel elision by the rule 'saralopomādesappaccayādimhi saralope tu pakatī', and having brought forward the succeeding consonant by the rule 'naye paraṃ yutte', and because it is a taddhita derivative, after being designated a nominal base by 'taddhitasamāsa...' etc., the derivation of case endings occurs as before.

Vāsiṭṭho, vasiṭṭhassa putto vā, vāsiṭṭhā iccādi purisasaddasamaṃ. Tassa nattupanattādayopi tadupacārato vāsiṭṭhāyeva. Evaṃ sabbattha gottataddhite paṭhamappakatitoyeva paccayo hoti.

'Vāsiṭṭho' means 'the son of Vasiṭṭha'; the forms 'Vāsiṭṭho', 'Vāsiṭṭhā', etc., are declined like the noun 'purisa'. His descendants, such as grandsons and great-grandsons, are also called Vāsiṭṭhā by that conventional usage. Thus, in all 'gotta' taddhita formations, the suffix is applied only to the primary nominal base.

Itthiyaṃ ṇappaccayantattā “ṇava ṇika ṇeyya ṇa ntūhī”ti vāsiṭṭhasaddato īpaccayo. Saralopādiṃ katvā itthippaccayantattā “taddhitasamāsa”iccādisutte caggahaṇena nāmabyapadese kate syādyuppatti, vāsiṭṭhī kaññā, vāsiṭṭhī, vāsiṭṭhiyo iccādi itthisaddasamaṃ.

In the feminine, because it ends with the suffix ṇa, the suffix 'ī' is applied to the word 'vāsiṭṭha' according to the rule 'ṇava, ṇika, ṇeyya, ṇa, ntūhi'. Having performed vowel elision and so on, and because it ends with a feminine suffix, after it is designated a nominal base by the inclusion of 'ca' in the rule 'taddhitasamāsa...' etc., the derivation of case endings occurs; forms like 'vāsiṭṭhī kaññā', 'vāsiṭṭhī', 'vāsiṭṭhiyo', etc., are declined like the noun 'itthi'.

Napuṃsake vāsiṭṭhaṃ apaccaṃ, vāsiṭṭhāni apaccāni iccādi cittasaddasamaṃ. Evaṃ uparipi taddhitantassa tiliṅgatā veditabbā.

In the neuter gender, 'vāsiṭṭhaṃ apaccaṃ', 'vāsiṭṭhāni apaccāni', etc., are declined like the noun 'citta'. Similarly, the three-gender applicability of taddhita derivatives should be understood also in the preceding examples.

Bhāradvājassa putto bhāradvājo, vesāmittassa putto vesāmitto, gotamassa putto gotamo. Ettha ca ayuvaṇṇattābhāvā ākārādīnaṃ na vuddhi hoti. Vasudevassa apaccaṃ vāsudevo, baladevo. “Cittako”tiādīsu pana saṃyogantattā vuddhi na bhavati.

The son of Bhāradvāja is Bhāradvājo; the son of Vesāmitta is Vesāmitto; the son of Gotama is Gotamo. And here, because the initial vowels are not 'a', 'i', or 'u', there is no lengthening of 'ā' etc. The offspring of Vasudeva is Vāsudevo; Baladevo. But in cases like 'Cittako' etc., because the stem ends in a conjunct, there is no lengthening.

“Vacchassa apacca”nti viggahe ṇamhi sampatte “vā ṇa’pacce”ti ito vāti taddhitavidhāne sabbattha vattate, tena sabbattha vākyavuttiyo bhavanti. “Apacce”ti padaṃ yāva saṃsaṭṭhaggahaṇāva vattate.

In the analysis 'Vacchassa apaccaṃ', when the suffix ṇa is to be applied, the word 'vā' from the rule 'Vā ṇa'pacce' applies everywhere in the taddhita section; therefore, analytical phrases are also possible in all cases. The word 'apacce' continues as far as the mention of 'saṃsaṭṭha'.

366. Ṇāyana [M 0.0219] ṇāna vacchādito.

366. The suffixes ṇāyana and ṇāna are applied after Vaccha and others.

Vaccha kaccaiccevamādito chaṭṭhiyantato gottagaṇato ṇāyana ṇānaiccate paccayā honti vā “tassāpacca”miccetasmiṃ atthe. Sabbattha ṇakārānubandho vuddhattho, sesaṃ pubbasamaṃ, saṃyogantattā vuddhiabhāvova viseso.

From words of the 'gotta' group beginning with Vaccha, Kacca, etc., ending in the sixth case, the suffixes ṇāyana and ṇāna are optionally applied in the sense of 'his offspring.' In all cases, the indicatory letter ṇ is for the purpose of lengthening; the rest is the same as before. The special feature is the absence of lengthening because the stem ends in a conjunct.

Vacchāyano vacchāno vacchassa putto vā. Evaṃ kaccassa putto kaccāyano kaccāno, moggallassa putto moggallāyano moggallāno. Evaṃ aggivessāyano aggivessāno, kaṇhāyano kaṇhāno, sākaṭāyano sākaṭāno, muñcāyano muñcāno, kuñjāyano kuñjāno iccādi. Ākatigaṇo’yaṃ.

'Vacchāyano' or 'Vacchāno' means 'the son of Vaccha'. Similarly, the son of Kacca is 'Kaccāyano' or 'Kaccāno'; the son of Moggalla is 'Moggallāyano' or 'Moggallāno'. Likewise, Aggivessāyano, Aggivessāno; Kaṇhāyano, Kaṇhāno; Sākaṭāyano, Sākaṭāno; Muñcāyano, Muñcāno; Kuñjāyano, Kuñjāno, etc. This is an open class of words.

“Kattikāya apacca”nti viggahe –

In the analysis 'Kattikāya apaccaṃ'—

367. Ṇeyyo kattikādīhi.

367. The suffix ṇeyya is applied after Kattikā and others.

Ādisaddoyaṃ pakāre vattate. Kattikā vinatārohiṇīiccevamādīhi itthiyaṃ vattamānehi liṅgehi ṇeyyappaccayo hoti vā “tassāpacca”miccetasmiṃ atthe.

This word 'ādi' functions to denote a type. The suffix ṇeyya is optionally applied after feminine nominal bases like Kattikā, Vinatā, Rohiṇī, etc., in the sense of 'her offspring.'

Vibhattilope “pakati cassa sarantassā”ti pakatibhāvo. Kattikeyyo, kattikāya putto vā. Evaṃ vinatāya apaccaṃ venateyyo, ikārassekāro vuddhi, rohiṇiyā putto rohiṇeyyo, gaṅgāya apaccaṃ gaṅgeyyo, bhaginiyā putto bhāgineyyo, nadiyāputto nādeyyo. Evaṃ anteyyo, āheyyo, kāmeyyo. Suciyā [M 0.0220] apaccaṃ soceyyo, ettha ukārassokāro vuddhi, bālāya apaccaṃ bāleyyo iccādi.

When the case ending is elided, the preceding vowel remains in its natural state by the rule 'pakati cassa sarantassā'. 'Kattikeyyo' means 'the son of Kattikā'. Thus, the offspring of Vinatā is 'Venateyyo', with the vowel 'i' undergoing lengthening to 'e'; the son of Rohiṇī is 'Rohiṇeyyo'; the offspring of Gaṅgā is 'Gaṅgeyyo'; the son of a sister is 'Bhāgineyyo'; the son of a river is 'Nādeyyo'. Thus, Anteyyo, Āheyyo, Kāmeyyo. The offspring of Suci is 'Soceyyo', where the vowel 'u' undergoes lengthening to 'o'; the offspring of Bālā is 'Bāleyyo', and so on.

“Dakkhassāpacca”nti viggahe ṇamhi sampatte –

In the analysis 'Dakkhassa apaccaṃ', when the suffix ṇa is to be applied—

368. Ato ṇi vā.

368. The suffix ṇi is applied optionally after a stem ending in 'a'.

Akārantato liṅgamhā ṇipaccayo hoti vā “tassāpacca”miccetasmiṃ atthe. Dakkhi, dakkhī, dakkhayo, doṇassa apaccaṃ doṇi. Evaṃ vāsavi, sakyaputti, nāṭaputti, dāsaputti, dāsarathi. Vāruṇi, kaṇḍi, bāladevi, pāvaki, jinadattassa apaccaṃ jenadatti, suddhodani, anuruddhi iccādi.

From a nominal base ending in 'a', the suffix ṇi is optionally applied in the sense of 'his offspring.' Examples are: Dakkhi, Dakkhī, Dakkhayo; the offspring of Doṇa is Doṇi. Similarly, Vāsavi, Sakyaputti, Nāṭaputti, Dāsaputti, Dāsarathi, Vāruṇi, Kaṇḍi, Bāladevi, Pāvaki; the offspring of Jinadatta is Jenadatti; Suddhodani, Anuruddhi, and so on.

Puna vāggahaṇena apaccatthe ṇikappaccayo, aditiādito ṇyappaccayo ca. Yathā – sakyaputtassa putto sakyaputtiko, “tesu vuddhī”tiādinā kakārassa yakāro, sakyaputtiyo. Evaṃ nāṭaputtiko, jenadattiko, vimātuyā putto vemātiko.

Again, by the inclusion of the word 'vā', the suffix ṇika is applied in the sense of offspring, and the suffix ṇya is applied after Aditi and others. For example: the son of a Sakyaputta is Sakyaputtiko. By the rule 'tesu vuddhī...' etc., the letter 'ka' becomes 'ya', resulting in Sakyaputtiyo. Similarly, Nāṭaputtiko, Jenadattiko; the son of a stepmother is Vemātiko.

“Aditiyā putto”ti atthe ṇyappaccayo, vuddhi ca.

In the sense 'son of Aditi,' the suffix ṇya is applied, and lengthening also occurs.

369. Avaṇṇo ye lopañca.

369. The 'a' vowel is elided when followed by 'ya'.

Avaṇṇo taddhitabhūte yappaccaye pare lopamāpajjate. Casaddena ivaṇṇopīti ikāralopo, “yavataṃ talanadakārānaṃ byañjanāni ca la ña jakāratta”nti tyakārasaṃyogassa cakāro, “paradvebhāvo ṭhāne”ti dvittaṃ, ādicco. Evaṃ ditiyā putto decco.

The 'a' vowel undergoes elision when the taddhita suffix 'ya' follows. By the word 'ca', the 'i' vowel is also elided, meaning the elision of the letter 'i'. By the rule 'yavataṃ talanadakārānaṃ byañjanāni ca la ña jakārattaṃ,' the conjunct 'ty' becomes 'c'. By the rule 'paradvebhāvo ṭhāne,' doubling occurs, resulting in Ādicco. Similarly, the son of Diti becomes Decco.

“Kuṇḍaniyā putto”ti atthe ṇyappaccaye kate –

In the sense 'son of Kuṇḍanī,' when the suffix ṇya has been applied –

“Kvacādimajjhuttaresū”ti vattate.

The rule 'Sometimes in initial, medial, and final syllables' is carried forward.

370. Tesu [M 0.0221] vuddhilopāgamavikāraviparītādesā ca.

370. Among these, in initial, medial, and final syllables, there are lengthening, elision, augmentation, modification, and contrary substitution.

Tesu ādimajjhuttaresu avihitalakkhaṇesu jinavacanānuparodhena kvaci vuddhi lopa āgama vikāra viparītaādesā hontīti saṃyogantattepi ādivuddhi, ikāralope nyassañādeso, koṇḍañño, kuruno putto korabyo, etthāpi teneva ukārassa avādeso, bhātuno putto bhātabyo.

Among these initial, medial, and final syllables, where specific characteristics are not prescribed, without contradicting the word of the Jina, sometimes lengthening, elision, augmentation, modification, or contrary substitution occurs. Thus, even when ending in a conjunct, initial lengthening occurs; when the 'i' vowel is elided, 'ñā' is substituted for 'nya', resulting in Koṇḍañño. The son of Kuru becomes Korabyo; here too, by the same rule, 'ava' is substituted for the 'u' vowel. A brother's son becomes Bhātabyo.

“Upagussa apacca”nti viggahe –

In the analysis 'Upagussa apaccaṃ' –

371. Ṇavopagvādīhi.

371. The suffix ṇava is applied after words such as Upagu and others.

Upagu manuiccevamādīhi ukārantehi gottagaṇehi ṇavappaccayo hoti vā “tassāpacca”miccetasmiṃ atthe. Ādisaddassa cettha pakāravācakattā ukārantatoyevāyaṃ. Opagavo, opagavī, opagavaṃ, manuno apaccaṃ mānavo, “mānuso”ti ṇappaccaye, sāgame ca kate rūpaṃ, bhagguno apaccaṃ bhaggavo, paṇḍuno apaccaṃ paṇḍavo, upavindussa apaccaṃ opavindavo iccādi.

From words such as Upagu, Manu, and so forth, which end in 'u' and belong to the clan group, the suffix ṇava is optionally applied in the sense of 'his offspring.' Here, because the word 'ādi' functions to denote a type, this rule applies only to those ending in 'u'. Opagavo, Opagavī, Opagavaṃ; the offspring of Manu is Mānavo; the form 'mānuso' is derived with the suffix ṇa and when the augment 'sa' is applied. The offspring of Bhaggu is Bhaggavo; the offspring of Paṇḍu is Paṇḍavo; the offspring of Upavindu is Opavindavo, and so on.

“Vidhavāya apacca”nti atthe –

In the sense 'offspring of a widow' –

372. Ṇera vidhavādito.

372. The suffix ṇera is applied after Vidhavā and others.

Vidhavādito ṇerappaccayo hoti vā apaccatthe. Vigato dhavo pati etissāti vidhavā, vedhavero, bandhukiyā abhisāriṇiyā putto bandhukero, samaṇassa upajjhāyassa putto puttaṭṭhāniyattāti sāmaṇero, nāḷikero iccādi.

After Vidhavā and others, the suffix ṇera optionally occurs in the sense of 'offspring'. 'Vidhavā' means 'one whose husband (dhava, pati) has departed (vigato)'; thus, Vedhavero. The son of an unchaste woman (bandhukī) or a courtesan (abhisāriṇī) is Bandhukero. The son of a recluse's preceptor, being in the position of a son, is Sāmaṇero. Nāḷikero, and so on.

Apaccataddhitaṃ.

Taddhita Suffixes Denoting Offspring.

Saṃsaṭṭhādianekatthataddhita

Taddhita Suffixes with the Meaning 'Mixed With' and Various Others.

“Tilena [M 0.0222] saṃsaṭṭha”nti viggahe –

In the analysis, 'mixed with sesame' –

373. Yena vā saṃsaṭṭhaṃ tarati carati vahati ṇiko.

373. The suffix ṇika is applied in the sense of that with which something is mixed, or by which one crosses, moves, or carries.

Yena vā saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, yena vā tarati, yena vā carati, yena vā vahati, tato tatiyantato liṅgamhā tesu saṃsaṭṭhādīsvatthesu ṇikappaccayo hoti vā. Telikaṃ bhojanaṃ, tilena abhisaṅkhatanti attho. Telikī yāgu. Guḷena saṃsaṭṭhaṃ egāḷikaṃ. Evaṃ ghātikaṃ, dādhikaṃ, māricikaṃ, loṇikaṃ.

After a nominal stem ending in the third case, the suffix ṇika optionally occurs in those senses of 'mixed with,' 'crosses by,' 'moves by,' or 'carries by.' 'Telikaṃ bhojanaṃ' means 'food prepared with sesame.' 'Telikī yāgu' is gruel with sesame. 'Egāḷikaṃ' is that which is mixed with jaggery. Similarly, ghātikaṃ, dādhikaṃ, māricikaṃ, loṇikaṃ.

Nāvāya taratīti nāviko, uḷumpena taratīti oḷumpiko, vuddhiabhāvapakkhe uḷumpiko. Evaṃ kulliko, gopucchiko. Sakaṭena caratīti sākaṭiko. Evaṃ pādiko, daṇḍiko, dhammena carati pavattatīti dhammiko. Sīsena vahatīti sīsiko, vāggahaṇena īkārassa vuddhi na hoti. Evaṃ aṃsiko, khandhiko, hatthiko, aṅguliko.

One who crosses by boat is a nāviko. One who crosses by a raft is an oḷumpiko; in the case where lengthening (vuddhi) does not occur, it is uḷumpiko. Similarly, kulliko, gopucchiko. One who travels by cart is a sākaṭiko. Similarly, pādiko, daṇḍiko. One who proceeds or acts by the Dhamma is dhammiko. One who carries with the head is a sīsiko; due to the inclusion of 'vā' (or), the lengthening of the 'ī' does not occur. Similarly, aṃsiko, khandhiko, hatthiko, aṅguliko.

Puna vāggahaṇena aññatthesupi ṇikappaccayo, paradāraṃ gacchatīti pāradāriko, pathaṃ gacchatīti pathiko.

Again, by the inclusion of 'vā' (or), the suffix ṇika also occurs in other senses. For example, one who goes to another’s wife is a pāradāriko; one who goes on a path is a pathiko.

“Vinayamadhīte, aveccādhīte”ti vā viggahe –

In the analysis, 'he studies the Vinaya,' or 'he studies thoroughly' –

“Ṇiko”ti vattate.

The suffix 'ṇika' is carried forward.

374. Tamadhīte tenakatādisannidhānaniyogasippabhaṇḍajīvikatthesu ca.

374. And in the senses of 'he studies that,' 'made by that,' 'presence,' 'appointment,' 'craft,' 'merchandise,' and 'livelihood.'

Catuppadamidaṃ. Tamadhīteti atthe, tena katādīsvatthesu ca tamhi sannidhāno, tattha niyutto, tamassa sippaṃ, tamassa bhaṇḍaṃ[M 0.0223], tamassa jīvikā iccetesvatthesu ca dutiyādivibhatyantehi liṅgehi ṇikappaccayo hoti vā. Venayiko. Evaṃ suttantiko, ābhidhammiko.

This rule has four parts. In the sense of 'he studies that,' and in the senses of 'made by that,' 'present in that,' 'appointed to that,' 'that is his craft,' 'that is his merchandise,' 'that is his livelihood'—in these senses, the suffix ṇika optionally occurs after stems ending in the second case and others. For example, venayiko. Similarly, suttantiko, ābhidhammiko.

“Byākaraṇamadhīte”ti atthe ṇikappaccayādimhi kate –

In the sense of 'he studies grammar,' when the suffix ṇika, etc., is applied –

“Vuddhādisarassa vāsaṃyogantassa saṇe cā”ti vattamāne –

While the rule ‘There is optionally lengthening of the initial vowel of a stem not ending in a conjunct before the suffixes sa and ṇa’ is current –

375. Māyūnamāgamo ṭhāne.

375. For i and u, there is no (lengthening), but an augment in its place.

I uiccebhesaṃ ādisarānaṃ asaṃyogantānaṃ mā vuddhi hoti saṇe, tatreva vuddhi āgamo hoti ca ṭhāneti ekāravuddhāgamo.

For these initial vowels 'i' and 'u' of stems not ending in a conjunct, lengthening (vuddhi) does not occur before the suffixes sa and ṇa; however, in that very place, a strengthening-augment occurs, namely the augment consisting of the vuddhi vowels e and o.

“Ṭhāne”ti vacanā cettha, yūnamādesabhūtato;

Yavehi pubbeva eo-vuddhiyo honti āgamā.

Here, due to the word 'ṭhāne' (in place), and because it is a substitute for 'i' and 'u' (yūnaṃ), the 'e' and 'o' lengthenings occur as augments before 'y' and 'v'.

Yakārassa dvibhāvo.

There is doubling of the letter 'y'.

Veyyākaraṇiko, nyāyamadhīteti neyyāyiko. Evaṃ takkiko, vediko, nemittiko, kāyena kato payogo kāyiko, kāyena kataṃ kammaṃ kāyikaṃ, vacasā kataṃ kammaṃ vācasikaṃ. Evaṃ mānasikaṃ, ettha ca “sasare vāgamo”ti sutte vavatthitavāsaddena paccaye parepi sāgamo, therehi katā saṅgīti therikā. Evaṃ pañcasatikā, sattasatikā, ettha “ṇavaṇikā”disutte anuvattitavāggahaṇena īpaccayo na hoti.

One who studies grammar is a ‘veyyākaraṇiko.’ One who studies logic is a ‘neyyāyiko.’ Similarly, a ‘takkiko’ (logician), a ‘vediko’ (one versed in the Vedas), a ‘nemittiko’ (interpreter of omens). An application made by the body is ‘kāyiko’; an action done by the body is ‘kāyikaṃ’; an action done by speech is ‘vācasikaṃ.’ Similarly, ‘mānasikaṃ.’ And here, in the rule ‘sasare vāgamo,’ due to the established word ‘vā,’ an augment occurs even when a suffix follows. The compilation made by the elders is ‘therikā.’ Similarly, ‘pañcasatikā’ (the council of five hundred) and ‘sattasatikā’ (the council of seven hundred). Here, in the rule ‘ṇavaṇikā,’ etc., due to the carrying forward of the word ‘vā,’ the suffix ‘ī’ does not occur.

Sannidhānatthe sarīre sannidhānā vedanā sārīrikā, sārīrikaṃ dukkhaṃ. Evaṃ mānasikā, mānasikaṃ.

In the sense of ‘presence’: feelings present in the body are ‘sārīrikā’; bodily suffering is ‘sārīrikaṃ dukkhaṃ.’ Similarly, ‘mānasikā’ (mental feelings), ‘mānasikaṃ’ (mental suffering).

Niyuttatthe [M 0.0224] dvāre niyutto dovāriko, ettha “māyūnamāgamo ṭhāne”ti vakārato pubbeokārāgamo. Evaṃ bhaṇḍāgāriko, nāgariko, navakammiko, vanakammiko, ādikammiko, odariko, rathiko, pathiko, upāye niyutto opāyiko, cetasi niyuttā cetasikā.

In the sense of ‘appointed’: one appointed at the gate is a ‘dovāriko’ (doorkeeper). Here, by the rule concerning augments in place, the augment ‘o’ occurs before the letter ‘v.’ Similarly, ‘bhaṇḍāgāriko’ (storekeeper), ‘nāgariko’ (citizen), ‘navakammiko’ (one in charge of new works), ‘vanakammiko’ (forest worker), ‘ādikammiko’ (beginner), ‘odariko’ (glutton), ‘rathiko’ (charioteer), ‘pathiko’ (traveler). One appointed to a means is ‘opāyiko’ (resourceful). States associated with the mind are ‘cetasikā’ (mental factors).

Sippatthe vīṇāvādanaṃ vīṇā, vīṇā assa sippaṃ veṇiko. Evaṃ pāṇaviko, modiṅgiko, vaṃsiko.

In the sense of ‘craft’: playing the lute is ‘vīṇā’; one whose craft is the lute is a ‘veṇiko’ (lute-player). Similarly, ‘pāṇaviko’ (a player of the pāṇava drum), ‘modiṅgiko’ (a player of the modiṅga drum), ‘vaṃsiko’ (flute-player).

Bhaṇḍatthe gandho assa bhaṇḍanti gandhiko. Evaṃ teliko, goḷiko, pūviko, paṇṇiko, tambūliko, loṇiko.

In the sense of ‘merchandise’: one whose merchandise is perfume is a ‘gandhiko’ (perfumer). Similarly, ‘teliko’ (oil merchant), ‘goḷiko’ (seller of molasses balls), ‘pūviko’ (cake seller), ‘paṇṇiko’ (vegetable seller), ‘tambūliko’ (betel-leaf seller), ‘loṇiko’ (salt seller).

Jīvikatthe urabbhaṃ hantvā jīvati, urabbhamassa jīvikāti vā orabbhiko. Evaṃ māgaviko, ettha vakārāgamo. Sūkariko, sākuṇiko, macchiko iccādi.

In the sense of ‘livelihood’: one who lives by killing sheep, or one whose livelihood is sheep, is an ‘orabbhiko’ (butcher of sheep). Similarly, ‘māgaviko’ (hunter of deer), where there is an augment ‘v.’ ‘Sūkariko’ (butcher of pigs), ‘sākuṇiko’ (bird-catcher), ‘macchiko’ (fisherman), etc.

“Tena katādī”ti ettha ādiggahaṇena tena hataṃ, tena baddhaṃ, tena kītaṃ, tena dibbati, so assa āvudho, so assa ābādho, tattha pasanno, tassa santakaṃ, tamassa parimāṇaṃ, tassa rāsi, taṃ arahati, tamassa sīlaṃ, tattha jāto, tattha vasati, tatra vidito, tadatthāya saṃvattati, tato āgato, tato sambhūto, tadassa payojananti evamādiatthe ca ṇikappaccayo hoti. Yathā – jālena hato, hanatīti vā jāliko. Evaṃ bāḷisiko, vākariko, suttena baddho suttiko, varattāya baddho vārattiko nāgo.

In the phrase ‘tena katādi,’ the inclusion of ‘ādi’ (etc.) indicates that the suffix ‘ṇika’ also occurs in such senses as: killed by that, bound by that, bought with that, he plays with that, that is his weapon, that is his affliction, devoted to that, belonging to that, that is its measure, that is its heap, he deserves that, that is his practice, born there, dwells there, known there, it conduces to that, come from there, originated from there, that is its purpose, and so on. For example: one who is killed by a net, or who kills with a net, is a ‘jāliko.’ Similarly, a ‘bāḷisiko’ (one who fishes with a hook), a ‘vākariko’ (one who hunts with a snare). Bound by a thread is ‘suttiko.’ An elephant bound by a strap is a ‘vārattiko nāgo.’

Vatthena [M 0.0225] kītaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ vatthikaṃ. Evaṃ kumbhikaṃ, phālikaṃ, sovaṇṇikaṃ, sātikaṃ. Akkhena dibbatīti akkhiko. Evaṃ sālākiko, tindukiko, ambaphaliko. Cāpo assa āvudhoti cāpiko. Evaṃ tomariko, muggariko, mosaliko.

Goods bought with cloth are ‘vatthikaṃ.’ Similarly, ‘kumbhikaṃ’ (bought with a pot), ‘phālikaṃ’ (bought with a ploughshare), ‘sovaṇṇikaṃ’ (bought with gold), ‘sātikaṃ’ (bought for a hundred). One who plays with dice is an ‘akkhiko.’ Similarly, ‘sālākiko’ (one who plays with sticks), ‘tindukiko’ (one who plays with tinduka fruits), ‘ambaphaliko’ (one who plays with mango fruits). One whose weapon is a bow is a ‘cāpiko’ (archer). Similarly, ‘tomariko’ (spearman), ‘muggariko’ (club-bearer), ‘mosaliko’ (mace-bearer).

Vāto assa ābādhoti vātiko. Evaṃ semhiko, pittiko.

One whose ailment is wind is ‘vātiko.’ Similarly, ‘semhiko’ (one afflicted by phlegm), ‘pittiko’ (one afflicted by bile).

Buddhe pasanno buddhiko. Evaṃ dhammiko, saṅghiko. Buddhassa santako buddhiko. Evaṃ dhammiko, saṅghiko vihāro, saṅghikā bhūmi, saṅghikaṃ cīvaraṃ, puggalikaṃ.

One devoted to the Buddha is ‘buddhiko.’ Similarly, ‘dhammiko’ (devoted to the Dhamma), ‘saṅghiko’ (devoted to the Saṅgha). What belongs to the Buddha is ‘buddhiko.’ Similarly, ‘dhammiko’ (belonging to the Dhamma), ‘saṅghiko’ (belonging to the Saṅgha), as in ‘saṅghiko vihāro’ (a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha), ‘saṅghikā bhūmi’ (land belonging to the Saṅgha), ‘saṅghikaṃ cīvaraṃ’ (a robe belonging to the Saṅgha), and ‘puggalikaṃ’ (personal).

Kumbho assa parimāṇanti kumbhikaṃ. Evaṃ khārikaṃ, doṇikaṃ. Kumbhassa rāsi kumbhiko. Kumbhaṃ arahatīti kumbhiko. Evaṃ doṇiko, aṭṭhamāsiko, kahāpaṇiko, āsītikā gāthā, nāvutikā, sātikaṃ, sāhassikaṃ. Sandiṭṭhamarahatīti sandiṭṭhiko, “ehi passā”ti imaṃ vidhiṃ arahatīti ehipassiko.

That which has a pot as its measure is ‘kumbhikaṃ.’ Similarly, ‘khārikaṃ’ (measured by a khāri), ‘doṇikaṃ’ (measured by a doṇa). A heap of pots is ‘kumbhiko.’ One who deserves a pot is ‘kumbhiko.’ Similarly, ‘doṇiko’ (deserving a doṇa), ‘aṭṭhamāsiko’ (worth eight māsas), ‘kahāpaṇiko’ (worth a kahāpaṇa). ‘Āsītikā gāthā’ (a collection of eighty stanzas), ‘nāvutikā’ (a collection of ninety), ‘sātikaṃ’ (a collection of a hundred), ‘sāhassikaṃ’ (a collection of a thousand). That which is worthy of being seen for oneself is ‘sandiṭṭhiko.’ That which is worthy of the invitation ‘Come and see’ is ‘ehipassiko.’

Sīlatthe paṃsukūladhāraṇaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ, taṃ sīlamassāti paṃsukūliko. Evaṃ tecīvariko, ekāsane bhojanasīlo ekāsaniko, rukkhamūle vasanasīlo rukkhamūliko, tathā āraññiko, sosāniko.

In the sense of ‘practice’: wearing rag-robes is ‘paṃsukūlaṃ’; one whose practice this is, is a ‘paṃsukūliko’ (rag-robe wearer). Similarly, ‘tecīvariko’ (one who practices wearing only three robes), ‘ekāsaniko’ (one whose practice is eating in one sitting), ‘rukkhamūliko’ (one whose practice is dwelling at the foot of a tree). Likewise, ‘āraññiko’ (forest-dweller), ‘sosāniko’ (charnel-ground-dweller).

Jātatthe apāye jāto āpāyiko. Evaṃ nerayiko, sāmuddiko maccho, vassesu jāto vassiko, vassikā, vassikaṃ pupphaṃ, sāradiko, hemantiko, vāsantiko, cātuddasiko, rājagahe jāto, rājagahe [M 0.0226] vasatīti vā rājagahiko jano, magadhesu jāto, vasatīti vā māgadhiko, māgadhikā, māgadhikaṃ, sāvatthiyaṃ jāto, vasatīti vā sāvatthiko, kāpilavatthiko, vesāliko.

In the sense of ‘born’: one born in a state of woe is ‘āpāyiko.’ Similarly, ‘nerayiko’ (one born in hell). ‘Sāmuddiko maccho’ (a sea fish). Born in the rainy season is ‘vassiko’; ‘vassikā’ (feminine); ‘vassikaṃ pupphaṃ’ (a rainy-season flower). ‘Sāradiko’ (autumnal), ‘hemantiko’ (wintry), ‘vāsantiko’ (of the spring), ‘cātuddasiko’ (related to the fourteenth day). A person born in Rājagaha or dwelling in Rājagaha is a ‘rājagahiko.’ One born in Magadha or dwelling there is a ‘māgadhiko’; ‘māgadhikā’ (feminine); ‘māgadhikaṃ’ (neuter). One born in Sāvatthī or dwelling there is a ‘sāvatthiko.’ Similarly, ‘kāpilavatthiko’ (from Kapilavatthu), ‘vesāliko’ (from Vesālī).

Loke vidito lokiko, lokāya saṃvattatītipi lokiko. Tathā mātito āgataṃ mātikaṃ, pitito āgataṃ pettikaṃ nāmaṃ.

Known in the world is ‘lokiko’ (worldly); that which conduces to the world is also ‘lokiko.’ Similarly, that which comes from the mother is ‘mātikaṃ’; a name that comes from the father is ‘pettikaṃ nāmaṃ.’

Sambhūtatthe mātito sambhūtaṃ mattikaṃ. Evaṃ pettikaṃ. Upadhitassa payojanaṃ opadhikaṃ.

In the sense of ‘originated from’: that which originated from the mother is ‘mattikaṃ.’ Similarly, ‘pettikaṃ.’ That which has acquisitions as its purpose is ‘opadhikaṃ.’

Sakatthepi asaṅkhāroyeva asaṅkhārikaṃ. Evaṃ sasaṅkhārikaṃ, nāmameva nāmikaṃ. Evaṃ ākhyātikaṃ, opasaggikaṃ, nepātikaṃ, catumahārāje bhatti etesanti cātumahārājikā. Evaṃ aññatthepi yojetabbaṃ.

Even in its own sense: ‘asaṅkhārikaṃ’ is simply ‘asaṅkhāro’ (unprompted). Similarly, ‘sasaṅkhārikaṃ’ (prompted). ‘Nāmikaṃ’ (nominal) is simply ‘nāma’ (name). Similarly, ‘ākhyātikaṃ’ (verbal), ‘opasaggikaṃ’ (prefixed), ‘nepātikaṃ’ (indeclinable). Those who have devotion to the Four Great Kings are ‘cātumahārājikā.’ Similarly, this should be applied in other senses as well.

“Kasāvena ratta”nti viggahe –

In the analysis ‘dyed with an astringent dye’:

376. Ṇa rāgā tenarattaṃ tassedamaññatthesu ca.

376. The suffix ‘ṇa’ is applied after a word for a color, in the senses ‘dyed by that,’ ‘this belongs to that,’ and in other senses.

Rāgatthavācakā liṅgamhā “tena ratta”miccetasmiṃ atthe, “tasse”ti chaṭṭhiyantato “ida”miccetasmiṃ atthe ca aññatthesu ca ṇappaccayo hoti vā.

The suffix ‘ṇa’ optionally occurs after a stem denoting a color in the sense of ‘dyed by that,’ and after a stem ending in the sixth case in the sense of ‘this belongs to that,’ and in other senses.

Kāsāvaṃ vatthaṃ. Evaṃ kāsāyaṃ, kusumbhena rattaṃ kosumbhaṃ, haliddiyā rattaṃ hāliddaṃ, pattaṅgaṃ, mañjiṭṭhaṃ, kuṅkumaṃ, nīlena rattaṃ nīlaṃ. Evaṃ pītaṃ.

‘Kāsāvaṃ vatthaṃ’ (a cloth dyed with an astringent dye). Similarly, ‘kāsāyaṃ.’ Dyed with safflower is ‘kosumbhaṃ.’ Dyed with turmeric is ‘hāliddaṃ.’ Similarly, ‘pattaṅgaṃ’ (dyed with sappan wood), ‘mañjiṭṭhaṃ’ (dyed with madder), ‘kuṅkumaṃ’ (dyed with saffron). Dyed with blue is ‘nīlaṃ.’ Similarly, ‘pītaṃ’ (yellow).

Idamatthe [M 0.0227] mahiṃsassa idaṃ māhiṃsaṃ maṃsaṃ, dadhi sappi cammādikaṃ vā, sūkarassa idaṃ sūkaraṃ, kaccāyanassa idaṃ kaccāyanaṃ byākaraṇaṃ. Evaṃ sogataṃ sāsanaṃ.

In the sense of ‘this belongs to that’: ‘this meat of a buffalo’ is ‘māhiṃsaṃ maṃsaṃ,’ or its curds, ghee, hide, etc. ‘This of a pig’ is ‘sūkaraṃ.’ ‘This grammar of Kaccāyana’ is ‘kaccāyanaṃ byākaraṇaṃ.’ Similarly, ‘sogataṃ sāsanaṃ’ (the teaching of the Sugata).

“Isissa ida”nti atthe ṇappaccaye kate vuddhimhi sampatte –

In the sense of ‘this belongs to a seer,’ when the suffix ‘ṇa’ is applied and vuddhi is due:

“Saṇe, yūnamāgamo ṭhāne”ti ca vattate.

And the rule concerning the augment of ‘i’ and ‘u’ in place before ‘sa’ and ‘ṇa’ also applies.

377. Āttañca.

377. And lengthening to ‘ā’.

I uiccetesaṃ ādisarānaṃ āttañca hoti saṇakārappaccaye pare, casaddena rikārāgamo ca ṭhāneti ikārassa āttaṃ.

For the initial vowels ‘i’ and ‘u,’ there is also lengthening to ‘ā’ when a suffix containing ‘sa’ or ‘ṇa’ follows; and by the word ‘ca,’ there is an augment ‘ri’ in place. Thus, for ‘i’ there is lengthening to ‘ā’.

Ṭhānādhikārato āttaṃ, isūsabhaujādinaṃ;

Isissa tu rikārāga-mo cāttānantare bhave.

Due to the authority of ‘in place,’ lengthening to ‘ā’ occurs for ‘isi,’ ‘usabha,’ ‘oja,’ etc. But for ‘isi,’ the augment ‘ri’ occurs after the lengthening to ‘ā’.

Ārisyaṃ, usabhassa idaṃ āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ, āsabhī vācā.

‘Ārisyaṃ’ (belonging to a seer). ‘This place of a bull’ is ‘āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ’; ‘āsabhī vācā’ (bull-like speech).

Aññatthaggahaṇena pana avidūrabhavo, tatra bhavo, tatra jāto, tato āgato, so assa nivāso, tassa issaro, kattikādīhi niyutto māso, sāssa devatā, tamaveccādhīte, tassa visayo deso, tasmiṃ dese atthi, tena nibbattaṃ, taṃ arahati, tassa vikāro, tamassa parimāṇanti iccevamādīsvatthesu ca ṇappaccayo. Yathā – vidisāya avidūre bhavo vediso gāmo, udumbarassa avidūre bhavaṃ odumbaraṃ vimānaṃ.

By the inclusion of ‘other senses,’ however, the suffix ‘ṇa’ is also used in such senses as: existing not far from, existing there, born there, come from there, that is his dwelling, he is its master, the month connected with Kattikā and so on, that is his deity, he studies it having understood it, that country is his domain, it exists in that country, produced by that, worthy of that, its modification, and that is its measure. For example, a village existing not far from Vidisa is ‘vediso’; a celestial mansion existing not far from an Udumbara tree is ‘odumbaraṃ’.

Bhavatthe manasi bhavaṃ mānasaṃ sukhaṃ, sāgamo. Sare bhavo sāraso sakuṇo, sārasā sakuṇī, sārasaṃ pupphaṃ[M 0.0228], urasi bhavo oraso putto, urasi saṃvaḍḍhitattā, mitte bhavā mettā, mettī vā, pure bhavā porī vācā.

In the sense of ‘existing’: existing in the mind is ‘mānasaṃ sukhaṃ’ (mental happiness); with an augment ‘sa.’ Existing in a lake is a ‘sāraso sakuṇo’ (sārasa bird), a ‘sārasā sakuṇī’ (female sārasa bird), a ‘sārasaṃ pupphaṃ’ (sārasa flower). Existing in the breast is an ‘oraso putto’ (legitimate son), because of being raised at the breast. Existing towards a friend is ‘mettā’ or ‘mettī’ (loving-kindness). Existing in a city is ‘porī vācā’ (urban speech).

Jātādīsu pāvuse jāto pāvuso megho, pāvusā ratti, pāvusaṃ abbhaṃ, sarade jāto sārado māso, sāradā ratti, sāradaṃ pupphaṃ. Evaṃ sisiro, hemanto, vasanto, vimho, mathurāyaṃ jāto māthuro jano, māthurā gaṇikā, māthuraṃ vatthaṃ. Mathurāya āgato māthuro, mathurā assa nivāsoti māthuro, mathurāya issaro māthuro rājā. “Sabbato ko”ti ettha puna sabbatoggahaṇena taddhitatopi kvaci sasarakakārāgamo, māthurako vā, rājagahe jāto, rājagahā āgato, rājagaho assa nivāsoti vā, rājagahassa issaroti vā rājagaho, rājagahako vā. Evaṃ sāgalo, sāgalako vā, pāṭaliputto, pāṭaliputtako vā, vesāliyaṃ jātotiādiatthe vesālo, vesālako vā, kusināre jāto kosināro, kosinārako vā. Evaṃ sāketo, sāketako vā, kosambo, kosambako vā, indapatto, indapattako vā, kapillo, kapillako vā, bhārukaccho, bhārukacchako vā, nagare jāto, nagarā āgato, nagare vasatīti vā nāgaro, nāgarako vā. Evaṃ jānapado.

In the sense of birth, etc.: born in the rainy season is a rainy cloud (pāvuso megho), a rainy night (pāvusā ratti), a rainy sky (pāvusaṃ abbhaṃ); born in autumn is an autumnal month (sārado māso), an autumnal night (sāradā ratti), an autumnal flower (sāradaṃ pupphaṃ). Similarly, winter (sisiro), the cold season (hemanto), spring (vasanto), summer (gimho). Born in Mathurā is a person from Mathurā (māthuro jano), a courtesan from Mathurā (māthurā gaṇikā), cloth from Mathurā (māthuraṃ vatthaṃ). One who has come from Mathurā is māthuro; one whose dwelling is Mathurā is māthuro; the ruler of Mathurā is a king from Mathurā (māthuro rājā). In the rule 'Sabbato ko,' by the inclusion of 'sabbato,' the augment of the letter 'ka' with its vowel sometimes occurs even after a taddhita derivative, as in māthurako. Or, born in Rājagaha, come from Rājagaha, whose dwelling is Rājagaha, or the ruler of Rājagaha is Rājagaho, or Rājagahako. Similarly, Sāgalo or Sāgalako; Pāṭaliputto or Pāṭaliputtako. In the sense of 'born in Vesālī,' etc., it is Vesālo or Vesālako; born in Kusinārā is Kosināro or Kosinārako. Likewise, Sāketo or Sāketako; Kosambo or Kosambako; Indapatto or Indapattako; Kapillo or Kapillako; Bhārukaccho or Bhārukacchako. Born in a city, come from a city, or dwelling in a city is Nāgaro or Nāgarako. Similarly, Jānapado.

Janapadanāmesu pana sabbattha bahuvacanameva bhavati. Yathā – aṅgesu jāto, aṅgehi āgato, aṅgā assa nivāso, aṅgānaṃ issaro vā aṅgo, aṅgako vā, māgadho, māgadhako vā, kosalo, kosalako vā[M 0.0229], vedeho, vedehako vā, kambojo, kambojako vā, gandhāro, gandhārako vā, sovīro, sovīrako vā, sindhavo, sindhavako vā, assako, kāliṅgo, pañcālo, sakko, tathā suraṭṭhe jāto, suraṭṭhassa issaro vā soraṭṭho, soraṭṭhako vā. Evaṃ mahāraṭṭho, mahāraṭṭhako vā iccādi.

In the names of countries, however, the base noun is always in the plural form. For example: born in the Aṅgas, come from the Aṅgas, whose dwelling is the Aṅgas, or the lord of the Aṅgas is Aṅgo, or Aṅgako. Similarly, Māgadho or Māgadhako; Kosalo or Kosalako; Vedeho or Vedehako; Kambojo or Kambojako; Gandhāro or Gandhārako; Sovīro or Sovīrako; Sindhavo or Sindhavako; Assako, Kāliṅgo, Pañcālo, Sakko. Likewise, born in Suraṭṭha, or the lord of Suraṭṭha is Soraṭṭho, or Soraṭṭhako. Thus, Mahāraṭṭho, or Mahāraṭṭhako, and so on.

Nakkhattayoge kattikāya puṇṇacandayuttāya yutto māso kattiko, magasirena candayuttena nakkhattena yutto māso māgasiro. Evaṃ phussena yutto māso phusso, maghāya yutto māso māgho, phagguniyā yutto māso phagguno, cittāya yutto māso citto, visākhāya yutto māso vesākho, jeṭṭhāya yutto māso jeṭṭho, uttarāsāḷhāya yutto māso āsāḷho, āsāḷhī vā, savaṇena yutto māso sāvaṇo, sāvaṇī. Bhaddena yutto māso bhaddo, assayujena yutto māso assayujo, buddho assa devatāti buddho. Evaṃ sogato, māhindo, yāmo, somo.

In the conjunction of constellations: the month connected with the full moon joined with Kattikā is Kattiko; the month connected with the constellation Magasira joined with the moon is Māgasiro. Thus, the month connected with Phussa is Phusso; the month connected with Maghā is Māgho; the month connected with Phaggunī is Phagguno; the month connected with Cittā is Citto; the month connected with Visākhā is Vesākho; the month connected with Jeṭṭhā is Jeṭṭho; the month connected with Uttarāsāḷhā is Āsāḷho, or Āsāḷhī; the month connected with Savaṇa is Sāvaṇo, or Sāvaṇī. The month connected with Bhadda is Bhaddo; the month connected with Assayuja is Assayujo. One whose deity is the Buddha is a Buddhist (buddho). Similarly, Sogato, Māhindo, Yāmo, Somo.

Byākaraṇaṃ aveccādhīte veyyākaraṇo. Evaṃ mohutto, nemitto, aṅgavijjo, vatthuvijjo. Vasātīnaṃ visayo deso vāsāto, udumbarā asmiṃ padese santīti odumbaro deso.

One who has thoroughly studied grammar is a grammarian (veyyākaraṇo). Similarly, a mohutto (astrologer), a nemitto (interpreter of omens), an aṅgavijjo (interpreter of bodily marks), a vatthuvijjo (expert in site-planning). The region that is the domain of the Vasātī is Vāsāto; the territory where Udumbara trees exist is the Odumbaro region.

Sahassena nibbattā sāhassī parikhā, payasā nibbattaṃ pāyāsaṃ, sahassaṃ arahatīti sāhassī gāthā, ayaso [M 0.0230] vikāro āyaso. Evaṃ sovaṇṇo, puriso parimāṇamassāti porisaṃ udakaṃ.

A moat constructed for a thousand is a sāhassī parikhā; a dish made from milk is pāyāsaṃ; a verse worthy of a thousand is a sāhassī gāthā; a modification of iron is āyaso. Similarly, sovaṇṇo (golden). Water whose measure is a man's height is porisaṃ udakaṃ.

Caggahaṇena tattha jāto, tattha vasati, tassa hitaṃ, taṃ arahatītiādīsu ṇeyyappaccayo. Bārāṇasiyaṃ jāto, vasatīti vā bārāṇaseyyako, pure viya kakārāgamo. Evaṃ campeyyako, sāgaleyyako, mithileyyako jano, gaṅgeyyo maccho, silāya jātaṃ seleyyakaṃ, kule jāto koleyyako sunakho, vane jātaṃ vāneyyaṃ pupphaṃ. Evaṃ pabbateyyo mānuso, pabbateyyā nadī, pabbateyyaṃ osadhaṃ, pathassa hitaṃ pātheyyaṃ, sapatissa hitaṃ sāpateyyaṃ dhanaṃ, padīpeyyaṃ telaṃ, mātu hitaṃ matteyyaṃ. Evaṃ petteyyaṃ. Dakkhiṇamarahatīti dakkhiṇeyyo iccādi.

By the inclusion of 'ca' in the rule, the suffix 'ṇeyya' is applied in such senses as: born there, dwelling there, beneficial to that, worthy of that, etc. Born in Bārāṇasī, or dwelling there, is bārāṇaseyyako, with the augment of 'ka' as before. Similarly, a person from Campā (campeyyako), from Sāgala (sāgaleyyako), from Mithilā (mithileyyako); a fish from the Ganges is gaṅgeyyo; born from a rock is seleyyakaṃ; a well-bred dog is a koleyyako sunakho; a flower from the forest is a vāneyyaṃ pupphaṃ. Similarly, a person from a mountain (pabbateyyo mānuso), a river from a mountain (pabbateyyā nadī), a herb from a mountain (pabbateyyaṃ osadhaṃ). Beneficial for a journey is pātheyyaṃ; wealth beneficial for a co-wife is sāpateyyaṃ dhanaṃ; oil for a lamp is padīpeyyaṃ; beneficial for one's mother is matteyyaṃ. Similarly, petteyyaṃ (beneficial for one's father). Worthy of an offering is dakkhiṇeyyo, and so on.

378. Jātādīnamimiyā ca.

378. And the suffixes 'ima' and 'iya' are applied to words in the sense of 'born,' etc.

Jātaiccevamādīnaṃ saddānaṃ atthe ima iyaiccete paccayā honti vā.

In the meaning of words such as 'jāta,' these suffixes 'ima' and 'iya' are optionally applied.

Pacchā jāto pacchimo, pacchimā janatā, pacchimaṃ cittaṃ, ante jāto antimo, antimā, antimaṃ. Evaṃ majjhimo, purimo, uparimo, heṭṭhimo, paccantimo, gopphimo, ganthimo.

Born after is pacchimo (the last); the last people (pacchimā janatā), the last mind (pacchimaṃ cittaṃ). Born at the end is antimo (the final), antimā (feminine), antimaṃ (neuter). Similarly, majjhimo (middle), purimo (foremost), uparimo (upper), heṭṭhimo (lower), paccantimo (bordering), gopphimo (relating to the ankle), ganthimo (relating to a knot).

Tathā [M 0.0231] iyappaccaye manussajātiyā jāto manussajātiyo, manussajātiyā, manussajātiyaṃ. Evaṃ assajātiyo, hatthijātiyo, bodhisattajātiyo, dabbajātiyo, samānajātiyo, lokiyo iccādi.

Likewise, with the 'iya' suffix: born of the human race is manussajātiyo (masculine), manussajātiyā (feminine), manussajātiyaṃ (neuter). Similarly, assajātiyo (of the horse race), hatthijātiyo (of the elephant race), bodhisattajātiyo (of the Bodhisatta race), dabbajātiyo (of the grass kind), samānajātiyo (of the same race), lokiyo (worldly), and so on.

Ādiggahaṇena tattha niyutto, tadassa atthi, tattha bhavotiādīsvapi ima iyappaccayā honti, casaddena ikappaccayo ca. Ante niyutto antimo, antiyo, antiko, putto assa atthi, tasmiṃ vā vijjatīti puttimo, puttiyo, vuttiko, kappo assa atthīti kappiyo, jaṭā assa atthīti jaṭiyo, hānabhāgo assa atthīti hānabhāgiyo. Evaṃ ṭhitibhāgiyo, bodhissa pakkhe bhavā bodhipakkhiyā, pañcavagge bhavā pañcavaggiyā. Evaṃ chabbaggiyā, udariyaṃ, attano idanti attaniyaṃ, nakārāgamo.

By the inclusion of 'ādi' in the rule, in senses such as 'appointed there,' 'that exists for him,' or 'existing there,' the suffixes 'ima' and 'iya' are also applied; and by the word 'ca,' the 'ika' suffix is also applied. Appointed at the end is antimo, antiyo, or antiko. One for whom a son exists, or in whom a son is found, is puttimo, puttiyo, or puttiko. One for whom a proper way of life exists is kappiyo. One for whom matted hair exists is jaṭiyo. One for whom a share in loss exists is hānabhāgiyo. Similarly, ṭhitibhāgiyo (one having a share in stability). Those existing on the side of enlightenment are bodhipakkhiyā. Those existing in the group of five are pañcavaggiyā. Likewise, chabbaggiyā (those belonging to the group of six). Udariyaṃ (relating to the belly). 'This is one's own,' thus attaniyaṃ, with the augment of 'n'.

Casaddaggahaṇena kiya yaṇyappaccayā ca. Jātiyā niyutto jātikiyo. Evaṃ andhakiyo, jaccandhe niyutto jaccandhakiyo. Sassa ayanti sakiyo. Evaṃ parakiyo.

By the inclusion of the word 'ca,' the suffixes 'kiya,' 'ya,' and 'ṇya' are also applied. Appointed to a certain birth is jātikiyo. Similarly, andhakiyo; appointed to congenital blindness is jaccandhakiyo. 'This is his own,' thus sakiyo. Likewise, parakiyo (belonging to another).

Yappaccayo sādhuhitabhavajātādiatthesu. Yathā – kammani sādhu kammaññaṃ. Sabhāyaṃ sādhu sabbhaṃ, “yavataṃ talanā”dinā ukārādi. Evaṃ medhāya hitaṃ mejjhaṃ ghaṭaṃ. Pādānaṃ hitaṃ pajjaṃ telaṃ, rathassa hitā racchā, gāme bhavo gammo[M 0.0232], gave bhavaṃ gabyaṃ, “osare cā”ti sutte casaddena yappaccaye parepi avādeso. Kavimhi bhavaṃ kabyaṃ, divi bhavā dibyā, thanato jātaṃ thaññaṃ, dhanāya saṃvattatīti dhaññaṃ.

The 'ya' suffix is applied in senses such as suitability, benefit, existence, birth, and so on. For example: suitable for action is kammaññaṃ. Suitable for an assembly is sabbhaṃ; the initial vowel becomes 'u' according to the rule 'yavataṃ talanā,' etc. Similarly, beneficial for wisdom is mejjhaṃ (ghee). Beneficial for the feet is pajjaṃ (oil). Beneficial for a chariot is racchā (a road). Existing in a village is gammo. Existing in cattle is gabyaṃ; by the word 'ca' in the rule 'osare cā,' the substitution of 'ava' occurs even when the 'ya' suffix follows. Existing in a poet is kabyaṃ (poetry). Existing in heaven is dibyā (divine). Born from the breast is thaññaṃ (milk). Conducive to wealth is dhaññaṃ (grain).

Ṇyappaccayo parisāyaṃ sādhu pārisajjo, dakārāgamo, samaṇānaṃ hitā sāmaññā janā, brāhmaṇānaṃ hitā brāhmaññā, arūpe bhavā āruppā iccādi.

The 'ṇya' suffix is applied. Suitable for an assembly is pārisajjo, with the augment of 'da'. Beneficial to ascetics are sāmaññā people. Beneficial to Brahmins are brāhmaññā. Existing in the formless realm are āruppā, and so on.

“Rājaputtānaṃ samūho”ti viggahe –

In the analysis 'a group of princes'—

379. Samūhatthe kaṇaṇā.

379. The suffixes 'ka' and 'ṇa' are applied in the sense of a group.

Chaṭṭhiyantato “tesaṃ samūho”ti atthe kaṇaṇaiccete paccayā honti. Rājaputtako, rājaputtakaṃ vā, rājaputto. Evaṃ mānussako, mānusso, māthurako, māthuro, porisako, poriso, vuddhānaṃ samūho vuddhako, vuddho. Evaṃ māyūrako, māyūro, kāpoto, kokilo, māhiṃsako, māhiṃso, oṭṭhako, orabbhako, aṭṭhannaṃ samūho aṭṭhako, rājānaṃ samūho rājako, bhikkhānaṃ samūho bhikkho, sikkhānaṃ samūho sikkho, dvinnaṃ samūho dvayaṃ, “tesu vuddhī”tiādinā ikārassa ayādeso. Evaṃ tiṇṇaṃ samūho tayaṃ iccādi.

From a word ending in the sixth case, in the sense of 'a group of them,' these suffixes 'ka' and 'ṇa' are applied. Thus, from 'rājaputtānaṃ samūho' (a group of princes) comes rājaputtako, or rājaputtakaṃ, or rājaputto. Similarly, mānussako or mānusso (a group of humans); māthurako or māthuro (a group from Mathurā); porisako or poriso (a group of men). A group of elders is vuddhako or vuddho. Likewise, māyūrako or māyūro (a group of peacocks); kāpoto (a group of pigeons); kokilo (a group of cuckoos); māhiṃsako or māhiṃso (a group of buffaloes); oṭṭhako (a group of camels); orabbhako (a group of sheep). A group of eight is aṭṭhako. A group of kings is rājako. A group of monks is bhikkho. A group of trainings is sikkho. A group of two is dvayaṃ; by the rule 'tesu vuddhī,' etc., the substitution of 'aya' for 'i' occurs. Similarly, a group of three is tayaṃ, and so on.

“Samūhatthe”ti vattate.

The phrase 'in the sense of a group' continues to apply.

380. Gāmajanabandhusahāyādīhi tā.

380. The suffix 'tā' is applied after words such as 'gāma,' 'jana,' 'bandhu,' 'sahāya,' and so on.

Gāmajanabandhusahāyaiccevamādīhi tāpaccayo hoti samūhatthe. Gāmānaṃ samūho gāmatā. Evaṃ janatā, bandhutā, sahāyatā, nāgaratā. “Tā”ti yogavibhāgena sakatthepi devoyeva devatā, tāpaccayantassa niccamitthiliṅgatā.

From words such as gāma, jana, bandhu, sahāya, and so on, the suffix tā is applied in the sense of a group. The group of villages is gāmatā. Similarly, janatā (a group of people), bandhutā (kinship), sahāyatā (friendship), nāgaratā (a group of citizens). By splitting the rule for tā, even in its own sense, deva itself becomes devatā (divinity). A word ending with the tā suffix is always in the feminine gender.

381. Tadassa ṭhānamiyo ca.

381. And the suffix iya is applied in the sense of 'that is its place'.

“Tadassa ṭhāna”miccetasmiṃ atthe chaṭṭhiyantato iyappaccayo hoti. Madanassa ṭhānaṃ madaniyo, madaniyā, madaniyaṃ, bandhanassa ṭhānaṃ bandhaniyaṃ. Evaṃ mucchaniyaṃ. Rajaniyaṃ, gamaniyaṃ, dassaniyaṃ, upādāniyaṃ, pasādaniyaṃ. Casaddena hitādiatthepi upādānānaṃ hitā upādāniyā iccādi.

In the sense of 'that is its place', the iya suffix is applied to a word ending in the sixth case. The place of intoxication is madaniyo (masculine), madaniyā (feminine), or madaniyaṃ (neuter). The place of bondage is bandhaniyaṃ. Similarly, mucchaniyaṃ (a place of infatuation), rajaniyaṃ (a place of passion), gamaniyaṃ (a place of going), dassaniyaṃ (a place of seeing), upādāniyaṃ (a place of grasping), pasādaniyaṃ (a place inspiring faith). By the word ca, it is also applied in senses such as 'beneficial', etc. For example, beneficial for grasping is upādāniyā, and so on.

382. Upamatthāyitattaṃ.

382. The suffix -āyitatta in the sense of simile.

Upamatthe upamāvāciliṅgato āyitattappaccayo hoti. Dhūmo viya dissatīti dhūmāyitattaṃ. Evaṃ timirāyitattaṃ.

In the sense of resemblance, the affix -āyitatta is used after a word denoting comparison. 'It appears like smoke' is dhūmāyitattaṃ (smoke-like appearance). Similarly, timirāyitattaṃ (darkness-like appearance).

“Tadassa ṭhāna”nti vattate.

The rule 'that is its place' continues to apply.

383. Tannissitatthe lo.

383. The affix -la is used in the sense of 'dependent on that'.

“Tannissita”nti atthe, “tadassaṭhāna”nti atthe ca lappaccayo hoti. Duṭṭhu nissitaṃ, duṭṭhu ṭhānaṃ vā duṭṭhullaṃ, duṭṭhullā vācā, lassa dvibhāvo. Evaṃ vedallaṃ.

In the sense of 'dependent on that' and in the sense of 'that is its place,' the affix -la occurs. Badly dependent, or a bad place, is duṭṭhullaṃ; duṭṭhullā vācā (obscene speech), with duplication of 'l'. Similarly, vedallaṃ.

“Abhijjhā [M 0.0234] assa pakati, abhijjhā assa bahulā”ti vā viggahe –

'Greed is his nature, or greed is abundant for him'—in this analysis:

384. Ālu tabbahule.

384. The affix -ālu is used in the sense of 'abundant in that'.

Paṭhamāvibhatyantato āluppaccayo hoti “tadassa bahula”miccetasmiṃ atthe. Abhijjhālu, abhijjhālū, abhijjhālavo. Evaṃ sītālu, dhajālu, dayālu. “Sabbato ko”ti ettha puna sabbatoggahaṇena kakārāgamo, abhijjhāluko, abhijjhālukā, abhijjhālukaṃ. Evaṃ sītāluko, dayāluko, tathā hīnova hīnako. Evaṃ potako, kumārako, māṇavako, muduko, ujuko, appamattakaṃ, oramattakaṃ, sīlamattakaṃ iccādi.

The affix -ālu is used after a word ending in the nominative case, in the sense of 'that is abundant in him.' Abhijjhālu, abhijjhālū, abhijjhālavo (greedy). Similarly, sītālu (sensitive to cold), dhajālu (bannered), dayālu (compassionate). By taking 'sabbato' again in the rule 'sabbato ko,' the augment -ka is added: abhijjhāluko, abhijjhālukā, abhijjhālukaṃ. Similarly, sītāluko, dayāluko. Likewise, hīna becomes hīnako (inferior). Similarly, potako (a young one), kumārako (a young boy), māṇavako (a young man), muduko (soft), ujuko (straight), appamattakaṃ (a small amount), oramattakaṃ (a trifling amount), sīlamattakaṃ (a small amount of virtue), etc.

“Yadanupapannā nipātanā sijjhantī”ti iminā paṭibhāgakucchitasaññānukampādiatthesu kappaccayo. Paṭibhāgatthe hatthino iva hatthikā. Evaṃ assakā. Kucchitatthe kucchito samaṇo samaṇako. Evaṃ brāhmaṇako, muṇḍako, paṇḍitako, veyyākaraṇako. Saññāyaṃ katako, bhaṭako. Anukampāyaṃ puttako.

By the rule 'What is not regularly formed is accomplished by irregular formation (nipātana),' the affix -ka occurs in the senses of resemblance, contempt, designation, compassion, and so on. In the sense of resemblance, like an elephant (hatthi), there is hatthikā (a small elephant). Similarly, assakā (a small horse). In the sense of contempt, a contemptible ascetic is samaṇako (a petty ascetic). Likewise, brāhmaṇako (a petty brahmin), muṇḍako (a petty shaven one), paṇḍitako (a petty scholar), veyyākaraṇako (a petty grammarian). In the sense of designation, katako (a maker), bhaṭako (a hireling). In the sense of compassion, puttako (a little son).

Tathā kiṃyatetato parimāṇatthe ttakavantuppaccayā. Kiṃ parimāṇamassāti kittakaṃ. Evaṃ yattakaṃ, tattakaṃ, ettakaṃ. Vantumhi āttañca, yaṃ parimāṇamassāti yāvā, yāvanto[M 0.0235], guṇavantusamaṃ. Evaṃ tāvā, tāvanto. Etāvā, etāvanto iccādi.

Similarly, from kiṃ, ya, ta, and eta, in the sense of measure, the affixes -ttaka and -vantu are used. 'What is its measure?' is kittakaṃ (how much?). Similarly, yattakaṃ (as much as), tattakaṃ (so much), ettakaṃ (this much). With -vantu, there is also -āvat: 'What is its measure?' is yāvā, yāvanto (as much as, as many as), like guṇavantu (virtuous). Likewise, tāvā, tāvanto (so much, so many), etāvā, etāvanto (this much, this many), etc.

“Suvaṇṇena pakata”nti viggahe –

'Made of gold'—in this analysis:

385. Tappakativacane mayo.

385. The affix -maya is used in the sense of 'made of that'.

Tappakativacanatthe mayappaccayo hoti, pakarīyatīti pakati, tena pakati tappakati, tappakatiyā vacanaṃ kathanaṃ tappakativacanaṃ. Suvaṇṇamayo ratho, sovaṇṇamayo vā, suvaṇṇamayā bhājanavikati, suvaṇṇamayaṃ bhājanaṃ. Evaṃ rūpiyamayaṃ, rajatamayaṃ, jatumayaṃ, dārumayaṃ, mattikāmayaṃ, iddhiyā nibbattaṃ iddhimayaṃ.

In the sense of 'made of that material,' the affix -maya occurs. 'It is made' (pakarīyati) is 'material' (pakati); therefore 'made of that material' is tappakati, and the expression for that is tappakativacanaṃ. A chariot made of gold is suvaṇṇamayo ratho, or sovaṇṇamayo; a vessel fashioned of gold is suvaṇṇamayā bhājanavikati; a golden vessel is suvaṇṇamayaṃ bhājanaṃ. Similarly, rūpiyamayaṃ (made of silver), rajatamayaṃ (made of silver), jatumayaṃ (made of resin), dārumayaṃ (made of wood), mattikāmayaṃ (made of clay); produced by psychic power is iddhimayaṃ.

Manato nipphannā manomayā, ayasāpakataṃ ayomayaṃ. Ettha ca “manogaṇādīna”nti vattamāne –

Produced from the mind is manomaya (mind-made); made of iron is ayomaya. Here, when the rule concerning the mano-group and others is current:

386. Etesamo lope.

386. For these, the final becomes 'o' upon elision.

Etesaṃ manogaṇādīnaṃ anto ottamāpajjate vibhattilope kateti okāro.

For these words of the mano-group and others, the final vowel becomes 'o' when the case ending is elided; thus, 'o' is formed.

Gavena pakataṃ karīsaṃ, goto nibbattanti vā gomayaṃ. “Mayo”tiyogavibhāgena sakatthepi dānameva dānamayaṃ, sīlamayaṃ iccādi.

Dung made by a cow, or produced from a cow, is gomayaṃ. By splitting the rule for 'maya,' even in its own sense, giving itself is dānamayaṃ, virtue itself is sīlamayaṃ, and so on.

Saṃsaṭṭhādianekatthataddhitaṃ.

Taddhita Affixes in the Senses of Mixture and Other Various Meanings.

Bhāvataddhita

Taddhita in the Sense of State (Bhāvataddhita)

“Alasassa [M 0.0236] bhāvo”ti viggahe –

'The state of being lazy'—in this analysis:

387. Ṇyattatā bhāve tu.

387. The affixes ṇya, tta, and tā occur in the sense of 'bhāva' (state).

Chaṭṭhiyantato ṇyattatāiccete paccayā honti “tassa bhāvo” iccetasmiṃ atthe, tusaddaggahaṇena ttanaṇeyyādippaccayā ca. Bhavanti etasmā buddhisaddā iti bhāvo, saddappavattinimittaṃ vuccati, vuttañca – “yassa guṇassa hi bhāvā dabbe saddaniveso tadabhidhāneṇyattatādayo”ti. Ṇyattattanantānaṃ niccaṃ napuṃsakattaṃ, tāpaccayantassa sabhāvato niccamitthiliṅgatā. Ṇyappaccayoyaṃ guṇavacane brāhmaṇādīhi, tattha “avaṇṇo ye lopañcā”ti avaṇṇalopo, ādivuddhi.

From a word ending in the sixth case, these affixes—ṇya, tta, and tā—occur in the sense of 'the state of that'; and by the inclusion of the word 'tu,' affixes like -ttana, -ṇeyya, etc., also occur. 'Bhāva' is that from which concepts arise; it is said to be the cause for the application of a word. And it has been said: 'Due to the existence of whichever quality a word is applied to a substance, the affixes ṇya, tta, tā, etc., are used to denote that quality.' Words ending in ṇya, tta, and ttana are always neuter; a word ending in the affix tā is by its nature always feminine. The affix ṇya occurs after words denoting qualities, such as brāhmaṇa, and so on; there, by the rule `avaṇṇo ye lopañca`, the elision of the vowel 'a' occurs, and the initial vowel is lengthened.

Ālasyaṃ. Evaṃ ārogyaṃ, udaggassa bhāvo odagyaṃ, sakhino bhāvo sakhyaṃ, aṇaṇassa bhāvo āṇaṇyaṃ, vidhavāya bhāvo vedhabyaṃ, dubbalassa bhāvo dubbalyaṃ, capalassa bhāvo cāpalyaṃ.

Ālasyaṃ (laziness). Similarly, ārogyaṃ (health); the state of being elated is odagyaṃ (elation); the state of a friend is sakhyaṃ (friendship); the state of being debtless is āṇaṇyaṃ (debtlessness); the state of a widow is vedhabyaṃ (widowhood); the state of weakness is dubbalyaṃ (weakness); the state of fickleness is cāpalyaṃ (fickleness).

Viyattassa bhāvo veyyattiyaṃ, maccharassa bhāvo macchariyaṃ. Evaṃ issariyaṃ, ālasiyaṃ, muṇḍiyaṃ, mūḷhiyaṃ. Ettha “veyyattiya”ntiādīsu “tesu vuddhī”tiādinā yamhi ikārāgamo.

The state of being skilled is veyyattiyaṃ (skillfulness); the state of being miserly is macchariyaṃ (miserliness). Similarly, issariyaṃ (lordship), ālasiyaṃ (laziness), muṇḍiyaṃ (baldness), mūḷhiyaṃ (foolishness). Here, in 'veyyattiya' and so on, by the rule `tesu vuddhī`, etc., the augment 'i' is inserted before 'ya'.

“Paṇḍitassa bhāvo paṇḍitya”ntiādīsu “yavataṃ talanadakārānaṃ byañjanāni calañajakāratta”nti tyakārasaṃyogādīnaṃ calañajakārādesā[M 0.0237], dvittaṃ. Paṇḍiccaṃ, bahussutassa bhāvo bāhussaccaṃ, “tesu vuddhī”tiādinā ukārassa akāro, evaṃ porohiccaṃ, adhipatissa bhāvo ādhipaccaṃ, muṭṭhassatissa bhāvo muṭṭhassaccaṃ, ivaṇṇalopo. Kusalassa bhāvo kosallaṃ. Evaṃ vepullaṃ, samānānaṃ bhāvo sāmaññaṃ, gilānassa bhāvo gelaññaṃ, “kvacādimajjhuttarā”disuttena saṃyoge pare rassattaṃ.

In 'the state of being wise is paṇḍitya' and so on, by the rule `yavataṃ talanadakārānaṃ byañjanāni calañajakāratta`, for conjuncts such as `tya`, substitutions like `ca`, `la`, `ña`, and `ja` occur, followed by doubling. Paṇḍiccaṃ (wisdom); the state of being very learned is bāhussaccaṃ; by the rule `tesu vuddhī`, etc., 'u' becomes 'a'; thus, porohiccaṃ (priesthood); the state of being a master is ādhipaccaṃ (mastery); the state of being forgetful is muṭṭhassaccaṃ, with the elision of the vowel 'i'. The state of being skillful is kosallaṃ (skill). Thus, vepullaṃ (abundance); the state of being equal is sāmaññaṃ (commonality); the state of being sick is gelaññaṃ (sickness); by the rule `kvacādimajjhuttarā...`, shortening occurs before a conjunct consonant.

Suhadassa bhāvosohajjaṃ. Evaṃ vesārajjaṃ, kusīdassabhāvokosajjaṃ, “tesu vuddhī”tiādinā īkārassa akāro. Tathā “purisassa bhāvo porisa”ntiādīsu “yavataṃ talanā”disutte kāraggahaṇena yavataṃ sakārakacaṭapavaggānaṃ sakārakacaṭapavaggādesā. Sumanassa bhāvo somanassaṃ. Evaṃ domanassaṃ, sovacassaṃ, dovacassaṃ, ettha sakārāgamo. Tathā nipakassa bhāvo nepakkaṃ, dvittaṃ. Evaṃ ādhikkaṃ, dubhagassa bhāvo dobhaggaṃ, vāṇijassa bhāvo vāṇijjaṃ, rājino bhāvo rajjaṃ, “kvacā”dinā rassattaṃ. Sarūpassa bhāvo sāruppaṃ. Evaṃ opammaṃ, sokhummaṃ.

The state of being good-hearted is sohajjaṃ (friendliness). Thus, vesārajjaṃ (confidence); the state of being lazy is kosajjaṃ (laziness); by the rule `tesu vuddhī`, etc., 'ī' becomes 'a'. Similarly, in 'the state of being a man is porisa' and so on, by the rule `yavataṃ talanā...`, with the inclusion of 'ka', the assimilation of the consonants `sa, ka, ca, ṭa, pa` and their respective classes occurs. The state of being joyful is somanassaṃ (joy). Thus, domanassaṃ (sorrow), sovacassaṃ (obedience), dovacassaṃ (disobedience); here the augment 'sa' occurs. Similarly, the state of being wise is nepakkaṃ (wisdom), with doubling. Thus, ādhikkaṃ (excess); the state of being unlucky is dobhaggaṃ (unluckiness); the state of a merchant is vāṇijjaṃ (commerce); the state of a king is rajjaṃ (kingship); by the rule `kvacā...`, the vowel is shortened. The state of being fitting is sāruppaṃ (fitness). Thus, opammaṃ (comparison), sokhummaṃ (subtlety).

Tathassa bhāvo tacchaṃ, dummedhassa bhāvo dummejjhaṃ, samaṇassa bhāvo sāmaññaṃ. Evaṃ brāhmaññaṃ, nipuṇassa bhāvo nepuññaṃ. “Taccha”ntiādīsupi kāraggahaṇeneva yavataṃ thadhaṇakārānaṃ chajhañakārādesā.

The state of being true is tacchaṃ (truth); the state of being foolish is dummejjhaṃ (folly); the state of being an ascetic is sāmaññaṃ (the ascetic life). Thus, brāhmaññaṃ (the holy life); the state of being skilled is nepuññaṃ (skill). In 'taccha' and so on, also by the inclusion of 'ka' in the previous rule, the replacement of the letters 'tha, dha, ṇa' by 'cha, jha, ña' respectively occurs.

Ttatāpaccayesu [M 0.0238]– paṃsukūlikassa bhāvo paṃsukūlikattaṃ, paṃsukūlikatā. Evaṃ tecīvarikattaṃ, tecīvarikatā, odarikattaṃ, odarikatā, manussattaṃ, manussatā jāti, nīlattaṃ, nīlatā guṇo, yācakattaṃ, yācakatā kriyā, daṇḍittaṃ, daṇḍitā dabbaṃ, saccavāditā, pāramitā, kataññutā, sabbaññutā, “kvacā”dinā tāpaccaye rassattaṃ, appicchatā, asaṃsaggatā, bhassārāmatā, niddārāmatā, lahutā iccādi.

In the case of the affixes -tta and -tā: the state of being a rag-robe wearer is paṃsukūlikattaṃ, paṃsukūlikatā.
