Gotthu vaṃse, gotthulo. Puthu vitthāre, puthulo. Bahu saṅkhyāne, bahulaṃ, paralopo. Yadā pana lā ādāne iti dhātu, tadā gotthuṃ lātīti gotthulo. Evaṃ puthulo, bahulaṃ.

The root `gotthu` is in the sense of 'lineage', forming `gotthulo`. The root `puthu` is in the sense of 'spreading', forming `puthulo`. The root `bahu` is in the sense of 'number', forming `bahulaṃ`, with elision of the preceding vowel. However, when the root is `lā` in the sense of 'taking', then `gotthulo` is 'one who takes lineage'. Similarly, `puthulo` and `bahulaṃ`.

Maṅga maṅgalye, maṅgalaṃ. Baha vuddhimhi, bahalaṃ. Kamba sañcalane, kambalaṃ. Sabi maṇḍale, sambalaṃ, niggahītāgamo, sabalo vā. Agga gatikoṭille, aggalaṃ. Maḍi bhūsāyaṃ, maṇḍalaṃ. Kuḍi dāhe, kuṇḍalaṃ iccādi.

The root `maṅg` is in the sense of 'auspiciousness', forming `maṅgalaṃ`. The root `bah` is in the sense of 'increase', forming `bahalaṃ`. The root `kamb` is in the sense of 'shaking', forming `kambalaṃ`. The root `sab` is in the sense of 'a group', forming `sambalaṃ`, with the insertion of a niggahīta, or `sabalo`. The root `agg` is in the sense of 'crooked movement', forming `aggalaṃ`. The root `maḍi` is in the sense of 'adornment', forming `maṇḍalaṃ`. The root `kuḍi` is in the sense of 'burning', forming `kuṇḍalaṃ`, and so on.

676. Puthassa puthupathāmo vā.

676. For the root `putha`, there are the substitutes `puthu` and `patha`, and the suffix `ama`, optionally.

Puthaiccetassa dhātussa puthu pathaiccete ādesā honti, amappaccayo ca hoti vā, kvacatthoyaṃ vāsaddo. Putha vitthāre, patthaṭāti atthe kvippaccayo, iminā puthassa puthupathādesā, kvilopo. Itthiyaṃ īpaccayo, “o sare cā”ti sutte casaddena avādeso, puthavī, pathavī, padhavī, thassa vattaṃ, amappaccaye pathādeso, pathamo.

For the root `putha`, the substitutes `puthu` and `patha` occur, and the suffix `ama` is optionally applied; this word `vā` here means 'in some cases'. The root `putha` is in the sense of 'spreading'. In the sense of 'that which is spread out' (`patthaṭa`), the suffix `kvi` is applied. By this rule, for `putha` there are the substitutes `puthu` and `patha`, with elision of `kvi`. In the feminine, the suffix `ī` is applied, and by the rule 'o sare cā', on account of the particle `ca`, the substitute `ava` occurs, forming `puthavī`. Also `pathavī`, and `padhavī`, with the change of `th` to `d`. When the suffix `ama` is applied, the substitute is `patha`, resulting in `pathamo`.

677. Sasvādīhi tudavo.

677. From `sasu` and so on, the suffixes `tu` and `du` are applied.

Sasuiccevamādīhi dhātūhi tu duiccete paccayā honti. Sasu hiṃsāgatīsu, tuppaccayo, “kvaci dhātū”tiādinā dhātvantassa takāro, sattu. Jana janane, jattu. Dada dāne, daddu kuṭṭhaviseso. Ada bhakkhaṇe, addu. Madaummāde, maddu iccādi.

From the roots beginning with `sasu` and so on, the suffixes `tu` and `du` are applied. The root `sasu` is in the sense of 'harming' or 'motion'. With the suffix `tu`, by the rule beginning 'kvaci dhātū', the final of the root becomes `t`, forming `sattu`. The root `jan` is in the sense of 'birth', forming `jattu`. The root `dad` is in the sense of 'giving', forming `daddu`, a type of skin disease. The root `ad` is in the sense of 'eating', forming `addu`. The root `mad` is in the sense of 'intoxication', forming `maddu`, and so on.

678. Jhādīhi [M 0.0418] īvaro.

678. From `jhā` and so on, the suffix `īvara` is applied.

Cipādhāiccevamādīhi dhātūhi īvarappaccayo hoti. Ci caye, cīyatīti cīvaraṃ. Pā pāne, pātīti pīvaro pīno. Dhā dhāraṇe, dhīvaro kevaṭṭo.

From the roots beginning with `ci`, `pā`, `dhā`, and so on, the suffix `īvara` is applied. The root `ci` is in the sense of 'collecting'; `cīvaraṃ` is so called because it is collected (`cīyati`). The root `pā` is in the sense of 'drinking'; `pīvaro` (fat) or `pīno` (plump) is so called because one drinks (`pātī`). The root `dhā` is in the sense of 'holding'; `dhīvaro`, a fisherman (`kevaṭṭo`).

679. Munādīhi ci.

679. From `muna` and so on, the suffix `i` is applied.

Munādīhi dhātūhi ippaccayo hoti, casaddena pāṭipadikehi ca. Muna ñāṇe, munātīti muni, vādhikārā na vuddhi. Yata yatane, yatatīti yati. Agga gatikoṭille, aggi. Pata gatimhi, pati. Suca socakammani, suci. Ruca dittimhi, ruci. Isa pariyesane, sīlādiguṇe esatīti isi. Ku sadde, kavi, vuddhi, avādeso ca. Ru sadde, ravi, dadhi, kuṭi. Asu khepane, asi. Rāja dittimhi, rāji. Gapu, sappa gatimhi, sappi. Acca pūjāyaṃ, acci. Juta dittimhi, joti, nandi, dīpi, kimi, akārassa ittaṃ. Tamu kaṅkhāyaṃ, timi. Budha bodhane, bujjhatīti bodhi. Kasa vilekhane, kasi. Kapi calane, kapi, kali, bali, masi, dhani, hari, ari, giri iccādayo.

From the roots beginning with `muna` and so on, the suffix `i` is applied, and by the particle `ca`, also from nominal stems. The root `mun` is in the sense of 'knowledge'; `muni` is so called because he knows (`munāti`); there is no `vuddhi` due to the governing option. The root `yat` is in the sense of 'effort'; `yati` is so called because he strives (`yatati`). The root `agg` is in the sense of 'crooked movement', forming `aggi`. The root `pat` is in the sense of 'motion', forming `pati`. The root `suc` is in the sense of 'purifying action', forming `suci`. The root `ruc` is in the sense of 'shining', forming `ruci`. The root `is` is in the sense of 'seeking'; `isi` is so called because he seeks virtues such as morality (`sīlādigune esati`). The root `ku` is in the sense of 'sound', forming `kavi`, with `vuddhi` and the `ava` substitute. The root `ru` is in the sense of 'sound', forming `ravi`; also `dadhi`, `kuṭi`. The root `as` is in the sense of 'throwing', forming `asi`. The root `rāj` is in the sense of 'shining', forming `rāji`. The roots `gap` and `sapp` are in the sense of 'motion', forming `sappi`. The root `acc` is in the sense of 'worship', forming `acci`. The root `jut` is in the sense of 'shining', forming `joti`; also `nandi`, `dīpi`, `kimi`, where the vowel `a` becomes `i`. The root `tam` is in the sense of 'longing', forming `timi`. The root `budh` is in the sense of 'awakening'; `bodhi` is so called because one awakens (`bujjhati`). The root `kas` is in the sense of 'ploughing', forming `kasi`. The root `kap` is in the sense of 'trembling', forming `kapi`; also `kali`, `bali`, `masi`, `dhani`, `hari`, `ari`, `giri`, and so on.

Pāṭipadikato pana mahāli, bhaddāli, maṇi, araṇi, taraṇi, dharaṇi, saraṇi, dhamaṇi, avani, asani, vasani iccādi.

From nominal stems, however: `mahāli`, `bhaddāli`, `maṇi`, `araṇi`, `taraṇi`, `dharaṇi`, `saraṇi`, `dhamaṇi`, `avani`, `asani`, `vasani`, and so on.

680. Vidādīhyūro.

680. From `vida` and so on, the suffix `ūra` is applied.

Vidaiccevamādīhi dhātūhi ūrappaccayo hoti. Vida lābhe, vandituṃ alaṃ anāsannattāti atthe ūrappaccayo. Vidūro, vijjūro vā, vidūre jāto vedūro maṇi. Vala, valla [M 0.0419] sādhāraṇabandhanesu, vallūro. Masa āmasane, masūro. Sida siṅgāre, sindūro, niggahītāgamo. Du gatimhi, dūro. Ku sadde, kūro. Kapu hiṃsātakkalagandhesu, kappūro, dvittaṃ. Maya gatimhi, mayūro, mahiyaṃ ravatīti vā mayūroti.

From the roots beginning with `vid` and so on, the suffix `ūra` is applied. The root `vid` is in the sense of 'gaining'. The suffix `ūra` is applied in the sense of 'able to praise, due to not being near'. Thus `vidūro` or `vijjūro` are formed. `Vedūro`, a gem, is so called because it is born in a distant place (`vidūre jāto`). The roots `val` or `vall` are in the sense of 'common binding', forming `vallūro`. The root `mas` is in the sense of 'touching', forming `masūro`. The root `sid` is in the sense of 'adornment', forming `sindūro`, with the insertion of a niggahīta. The root `du` is in the sense of 'motion', forming `dūro`. The root `ku` is in the sense of 'sound', forming `kūro`. The root `kap` is in the sense of 'harming', 'reasoning', or 'smelling', forming `kappūro`, with doubling. The root `may` is in the sense of 'motion', forming `mayūro`; or `mayūro` is so called because it cries out on the earth (`mahiyaṃ ravati`).

“Vaṇṇāgamo vaṇṇavipariyayo ca,

Dve cāpare vaṇṇavikāranāsā;

Dhātussa catthātisayena yogo,

Taduccate pañcavidhaṃ nirutta”nti –

The addition of a letter, the transposition of a letter, and two others: modification and elision of a letter; and the connection of a root with a meaning by extension—this is called the fivefold `nirutti` (etymological explanation).

Vuttaniruttilakkhaṇānusārena “tesu vuddhī”tiādinā, “kvaci dhātū”tiādinā ca rūpasiddhi veditabbā.

According to the stated characteristics of `nirutti`, the formation of words should be understood by the rules beginning 'tesu vuddhī' and 'kvaci dhātū'.

Udi pasavanakledanesu, unditumalaṃ samatthoti undūro. Khajja bhakkhaṇe, khādituṃ alanti khajjūro. Kura akkose, akkositumalanti kurūro. Su hiṃsāyaṃ, sūro.

The root `ud` is in the sense of 'flowing' and 'wetting'; `undūro` (rat) is so called because it is capable (`samattho`) of wetting (`undituṃ`). The root `khajj` is in the sense of 'eating'; `khajjūro` (date palm) is so called because it is fit to be eaten (`khādituṃ alaṃ`). The root `kur` is in the sense of 'scolding'; `kurūro` (cruel) is so called because it is capable of scolding (`akkosituṃ alaṃ`). The root `su` is in the sense of 'harming', forming `sūro` (hero).

681. Hanādīhi ṇunutavo.

681. From `han` and so on, the suffixes `ṇu`, `nu`, and `tu` are applied.

Hanaiccevamādīhi dhātūhi ṇu nu tuiccete paccayā honti. Ṇuppaccaye hana hiṃsāgatīsu, hanatīti haṇu. Jana janane, jāyatīti jāṇu, dhātvantalopo, dīgho. Bhā dittimhi, bhātīti bhāṇu. Ri santāne, rayatīti reṇu rajo. Khanu avadāraṇe, khanti, khaññatīti vā khāṇu. Ama gatyādīsu, amatīti aṇu, dhātvantalopo.

From the roots beginning with `han` and so on, the suffixes `ṇu`, `nu`, and `tu` are applied. With the suffix `ṇu`: the root `han` is in the sense of 'harming' or 'motion'; `haṇu` (jaw) is so called because it harms or moves (`hanati`). The root `jan` is in the sense of 'birth'; `jāṇu` (knee) is so called because it is born (`jāyati`), with elision of the root-final and lengthening. The root `bhā` is in the sense of 'shining'; `bhāṇu` (sun) is so called because it shines (`bhāti`). The root `ri` is in the sense of 'continuity'; `reṇu` (dust) or `rajo` is so called because it spreads (`rayati`). The root `khan` is in the sense of 'digging'; `khāṇu` (stump) is so called because one digs (`khanti`) or because it is dug (`khaññati`). The root `am` is in the sense of 'motion' etc.; `aṇu` (atom) is so called because it moves (`amati`), with elision of the root-final.

Nuppaccaye – ve tantasantāne, vāyatīti venu, veṇu vā. Dhe pāne, dhāyati vacchaṃ pāyetīti dhenu, bhātīti bhānu.

With the suffix `nu`: The root `ve` is in the sense of 'weaving' and 'continuity'; `venu` or `veṇu` (bamboo) is so called because it weaves (`vāyati`). The root `dhe` is in the sense of 'suckling'; `dhenu` (a milk-cow) is so called because she suckles or gives suck to the calf (`dhāyati vacchaṃ pāyeti`). `Bhānu` (the sun) is so called because it shines (`bhāti`).

Tuppaccaye [M 0.0420] – dhā dhāraṇe, kriyaṃ, lakkhaṇaṃ vā dhāretīti dhātu. Si bandhane, sīyati bandhīyatīti setu. Kī dhanaviyoge, ki unnatimhi, uddhaṃ gacchatīti ketu. Hi gatimhi, hinotīti hetu. Jana janane, jāyatīti jantu. Tanu vitthāre, tanotīti tantu. Vasa nivāse, vasati ettha phalaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti vatthu, “kvaci dhātū”tiādinā satakārasaṃyogassa tthādeso.

With the suffix `tu`: The root `dhā` is in the sense of 'holding'; `dhātu` (element) is so called because it holds an action or a characteristic. The root `si` is in the sense of 'binding'; `setu` (bridge) is so called because it is bound. The roots `kī` ('separation from wealth') and `ki` ('elevation'); `ketu` (banner) is so called because it goes upwards. The root `hi` is in the sense of 'going'; `hetu` (cause) is so called because it impels (`hinoti`). The root `jan` is in the sense of 'being born'; `jantu` (creature) is so called because it is born. The root `tan` is in the sense of 'stretching'; `tantu` (thread) is so called because it stretches. The root `vas` is in the sense of 'dwelling'; `vatthu` (ground, object) is so called because a result dwells here, its existence being dependent on that; by the rule beginning 'kvaci dhātū', the consonant cluster `st` is substituted by `tth`.

682. Kuṭādīhiṭho.

682. From `kuṭa` and so on, the suffix `ṭha` is applied.

Kuṭādīhi dhātūhi ṭhappaccayo hoti. Kuṭa chedane, kuṭati chindatīti kuṭṭho byādhi. Kusa chedanapūraṇagandhesu, kusatīti koṭṭho udaraṃ, dhātvantalopadvittāni. Kaṭamaddane, kaṭati maddatīti kaṭṭhaṃ. Kaṇa nimīlane, kaṇṭho.

From the roots `kuṭa` and so on, the suffix `ṭha` is applied. The root `kuṭ` is in the sense of 'cutting'; `kuṭṭho`, a disease, is so called because it cuts (`kuṭati chindati`). The root `kus` is in the senses of 'cutting', 'filling', and 'smelling'; `koṭṭho`, the belly (`udaraṃ`), is so called because it cuts (`kusati`), with elision of the root-final and doubling. The root `kaṭ` is in the sense of 'crushing'; `kaṭṭhaṃ` (wood) is so called because it crushes (`kaṭati maddati`). The root `kaṇ` is in the sense of 'closing the eyes', forming `kaṇṭho` (throat).

683. Manupūrasuṇādīhi ussanusisā.

683. From `man`, `pūr`, `suṇ`, and so on, the suffixes `ussa`, `nu`, and `isa` are applied.

Manu pūra suṇaiccevamādīhi dhātūhi, pāṭipadikehi ca ussanusaisaiccete paccayā honti.

From roots such as `man`, `pūr`, and `suṇ`, and also from nominal stems, these suffixes are applied: `ussa`, `nu`, and `isa`.

Manu bodhane, ussa nusā, manate jānātīti manusso, mānuso vā, dhātvantassa āttaṃ.

The root `man` is in the sense of 'understanding'; with the suffixes `ussa` and `nu`. `Manusso`, or `mānuso` (a human being), is so called because one understands, one knows (`manate jānāti`); in the latter case, the final of the root becomes `ā`.

Pūra dānapūraṇesu, pūratīti puriso, rassattaṃ, poso, rakārikārānaṃ lopo, vuddhi ca, pure ucce ṭhāne setīti puriso.

The root `pūr` is in the senses of 'giving' and 'filling'; `puriso` (a person) is so called because one fills (`pūrati`), with shortening. Or `poso`, with elision of `r` and `i`, and with `vuddhi`. Alternatively, `puriso` is so called because one lies (`seti`) in a high place, a city (`pure`).

Suṇa hiṃsākulasandhānesu, suṇati kulaṃ sandahatīti suṇisā. Ku kucchite, kavīyatīti karīsaṃ malaṃ, kussa [M 0.0421] karattaṃ, dīgho ca. Su hiṃsāyaṃ, andhakāravidhamanena sattānaṃ bhayaṃ hiṃsatīti sūriyo, rakārāgamo, sakārassa yattañca. Maha pūjāyaṃ, mahatīti mahiso, mahiyaṃ setītipi mahiso. Si bandhane, sīyati bandhīyatīti sīsaṃ iccādi.

The root `suṇ` is in the senses of 'harming' and 'uniting a family'; `suṇisā` (daughter-in-law) is so called because she unites the family (`suṇati kulaṃ sandahati`). The root `ku` is in the sense of 'being contemptible'; `karīsaṃ` (excrement), filth (`malaṃ`), is so called because it is contemptible (`kavīyati`); `ku` becomes `kar`, and there is lengthening. The root `su` is in the sense of 'harming'; `sūriyo` (the sun) is so called because it harms the fear of beings by dispelling darkness, with the augment `r` and the change of `s` to `y`. The root `mah` is in the sense of 'worshipping'; `mahiso` (buffalo) is so called because he is worshipped (`mahati`); alternatively, `mahiso` is so called because he lies (`seti`) on the earth (`mahiyaṃ`). The root `si` is in the sense of 'binding'; `sīsaṃ` (head) is so called because it is bound (`sīyati bandhīyati`), and so on.

684. Akkharehi kāra.

684. After letters, the suffix `kāra` is applied.

Akkharehi akkharavācakehi vaṇṇehi kārappaccayo hoti. Taddhitādisutte caggahaṇena nāmabyapadese syādyuppatti, akāro, akāraṃ, akārena iccādi, ākāro, okāro, kakāro, yakāro, hakāro, ḷakāro. Evakārādīsu pana karīyati uccārīyatīti kāro saddo, eva ca so kāro cāti evakāro. Evaṃ dhikāro, huṃkāro, sādhukāro.

After letters, that is, after phonemes that denote letters, the suffix kāra occurs. By the inclusion of ca in the sutta on taddhita suffixes, these formations are designated as nouns, and case endings such as si are generated. For example: akāro, akāraṃ, akārena, etc.; ākāro, okāro, kakāro, yakāro, hakāro, ḷakāro. In words like evakāro, however, kāro means 'sound,' because it is made or uttered; thus, 'the sound eva' is evakāro. Similarly, dhikāro, huṃkāro, sādhukāro.

Ikāro dhātuniddese, vikaraṇandhitoti ca;

Bhavantettha gamissādi, hanatyādīti ñāpakā.

The letter i is used in the citation of roots and in the term vikaraṇandhita; here, forms like gamissati and hanati serve as indicators.

Uṇādippaccayantanayo.

The Section on Words Ending in Uṇādi Suffixes.

Tabbādī ṇādayo niṭṭhā, tave tunādayo tathā;

Mānantādi uṇādīti, chaddhā kitakasaṅgaho.

The suffixes beginning with tabba; those beginning with ṇa; the niṭṭhā suffixes; likewise those beginning with tave and tuna; those beginning with māna and nta; and the uṇādi suffixes—thus the collection of primary (kitaka) suffixes is sixfold.

Iti padarūpasiddhiyaṃ kibbidhānakaṇḍo

Thus ends the Chapter on the Procedure of the Kibbidhāna Affix in the Padarūpasiddhi.

Sattamo.

The Seventh.

Nigamana

Conclusion

Sandhi nāmaṃ kārakañca, samāso taddhitaṃ tathā;

Ākhyātaṃ kitakaṃ kaṇḍā, sattime rūpasiddhiyaṃ.

Sandhi, Nouns, and Cases; Compounds and also Secondary Derivatives; Verbs and Primary Derivatives—these seven are the chapters in the Rūpasiddhi.

Tedhā sandhiṃ catuddhā padamapi catudhā pañcadhā nāmikañca,

Byāsā chakkārakaṃ chassamasanamapi chabbhedato taddhitañca;

Ākhyātaṃ aṭṭhadhā chabbidhamapi kitakaṃ paccayānaṃ pabhedā,

Dīpentī rūpasiddhī ciramidha janatābuddhivuḍḍhiṃ karotu.

Sandhi is threefold, the word fourfold, and the nominal fourfold and fivefold; the case system is sixfold, compounding also sixfold, and the secondary derivative has six divisions; the verb is eightfold, and the primary derivative is sixfold. Illuminating these divisions of affixes, may this Rūpasiddhi long bring about an increase of wisdom for the people here.

Vikhyātānandatheravhayavaragurunaṃ tambapaṇṇiddhajānaṃ,

Sisso dīpaṅkarākhyaddamiḷavasumatī dīpaladdhappakāso;

Bālādiccādivāsadvitayamadhivasaṃ sāsanaṃ jotayī yo,

Soyaṃ buddhappiyavho yati imamujukaṃ rūpasiddhiṃ akāsi.

The disciple of the noble teacher called the renowned Elder Ānanda, a banner of Tambapaṇṇi; he who, also named Dīpaṅkara, gained renown on the island of the Tamil land; who, dwelling in the two residences beginning with Bālādicca, illuminated the Dispensation—this very ascetic called Buddhappiya has composed this straightforward Rūpasiddhi.

Iti padarūpasiddhipakaraṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Thus the treatise Padarūpasiddhi is completed.
